item.title: [SCMP] Can Singapore be the ‘natural choice’ to bridge Asean and Central Asia?
item.description:
Singapore is positioning itself as a bridge between Central Asia and Asean, as both regions increasingly look to each other amid growing disruption to global trade and intensifying superpower rivalry.

The political appetite exists, but analysts say trade benefits will still hinge on overcoming obstacles such as geography and a lack of connectivity.

Singapore’s Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong pitched the city state to Central Asian businesses during his visits to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan from August 24 to 31.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore is positioning itself as a bridge between Central Asia and Asean, as both regions increasingly look to each other amid growing disruption to global trade and intensifying superpower rivalry.

The political appetite exists, but analysts say trade benefits will still hinge on overcoming obstacles such as geography and a lack of connectivity.

Singapore’s Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong pitched the city state to Central Asian businesses during his visits to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan from August 24 to 31.

“Singapore has long been a gateway to Southeast Asia, a region of more than 700 million people and one of the fastest-growing parts of the world,” he told the Uzbekistan parliament on Monday.

Lee said the city state, set to assume chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations next year, would explore ways to boost cooperation between both regions in potential sectors such as transport, connectivity and energy.

“We strive for a Southeast Asia which is linked to many countries and regions, where many partners can participate in and benefit from Southeast Asia’s stability and success, and Central Asia fits well into this vision.”

Lee also voiced hopes for an increase in bilateral cooperation with Central Asian states. Singapore and Tashkent have agreed to start negotiating a free-trade agreement to further boost “nascent economic ties”.

“Amidst all the uncertainty and turbulence in the world, smaller countries like us must continue to strengthen our partnership and cooperation – globally, between our regions, and bilaterally,” he said.

Other Asean states have also recently stepped up efforts to advance cooperation with Central Asian countries.

Leaders from Vietnam and Kyrgyzstan agreed to expand cooperation in potential areas such as science, technology, transport and people-to-people exchanges on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Plus Summit on Monday.

They also vowed to promote both parties’ bridging role in enhancing connectivity between Southeast Asia and Central Asia, according to local media.

In June, Thailand and Kazakhstan signed a 2027-2028 road map outlining plans to advance cooperation in multiple sectors such as food security, hospitality and medical tourism. Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow had earlier said Bangkok was ready to serve as a bridge in developing cooperation with Asean states.

Converging interests

Disruptions to trade routes due to global conflicts have reinforced the importance of cooperation between both regions, analysts say.

Central Asia, which acts as a “land bridge” connecting China, Europe and the Middle East, is increasingly important to Asean as the bloc seeks investment opportunities and a stronger supply chain, according to Sabina Insebayeva, assistant professor of political science and international relations at Kazakhstan’s Nazarbayev University.

Interest in the Middle Corridor – which runs through Kazakhstan across the inland Caspian Sea by ship to Azerbaijan, onwards to Georgia and into Turkey – as an alternative trade route has grown due to disruptions to established channels, she noted.

Meanwhile, the landlocked Central Asia was likely to view Southeast Asia’s maritime routes as a link to Eurasia, as it tried to secure resources and capital to strengthen economic resilience, said Hoo Chiew-Ping, senior fellow at the East Asian International Relations Caucus.

“Southeast Asia offers an attractive blueprint as a high-growth, neutral hub that maintains balanced relations with major global powers, including the US, Europe, China and Russia,” she said.

While there is ample goodwill and willingness to enhance bilateral and regional cooperation, analysts warn that geographical differences and a lack of connectivity may hamper the development of a partnership which is still in its early stages.

Regulatory and institutional gaps also risked the effectiveness of advancing partnerships and business relations, as both regions had limited familiarity and knowledge of each other’s markets, they said.

“The main constraint is geography,” said Barbora Valockova, a research fellow at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy’s Centre on Asia and Globalisation. “Central Asia is landlocked and far from Southeast Asia, and overland routes involve multiple borders, transport modes and regulatory systems.”

Lin noted that both regions were in the “early stages” of cooperation, and said the challenge of turning agreements into commercially viable projects remained.

“Governments can open doors and establish frameworks, but private companies will only support initiatives if there is sufficient market demand, scale and profitability,” she said. “Differences in regulatory systems, market conditions and business practices can also slow implementation.”

Central Asia also lacked a centralised and institutionally integrated bloc, such as an Asean equivalent, to ensure the effectiveness of an inter-regional mechanism, Hoo said.

Economic ties between both regions had been experiencing “emerging momentum”, said Insebayeva, who urged greater support and working mechanisms in the form of business forums, investment facilitation and educational exchanges.

Singapore’s role

While Singapore is well positioned to bridge both regions due to its connectivity and business-friendly environment, analysts say direct links between all economies are needed for commercial viability.

The city state was a “natural choice” due to its institutional credibility and technical expertise, and could provide a trusted platform for firms unfamiliar with Southeast Asia, Insebayeva said.

She noted that Kazakhstan had long drawn inspiration from Singapore in areas such as public administration and financial services, a practice that built trust.

Singapore’s existing partnerships with countries in the region could be a model for multi-regional cooperation, Insebayeva said, citing a bilateral services and investment agreement with Astana which came into effect in March last year.

“Singapore should be seen as a facilitator rather than the sole gateway,” said Joanne Lin, senior fellow and Asean Studies Centre coordinator at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

“It can connect businesses, capital and expertise across the two regions, but success will ultimately depend on commercially viable opportunities and stronger transport and business links.”

Singapore’s coming Asean chairmanship was an optimal time to take its existing strong bilateral ties to a multi-regional level, Valockova said, but added that deeper multi-regional ties would require participation from other major Southeast Asian economies such as Indonesia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

“The realistic goal is an open and flexible network of partnerships that strengthens economic resilience and connectivity,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Exclusive: The Boar brings authentic British pub experience to Hong Kong’s Central
item.description:
If a good pint is what you’re after, Matt Richardson may have a solution. As one of the brains behind The Boar, a new British public house (where the shortened form and better-known term, “pub”, comes from) and restaurant in Central, he has been working to bring an authentic watering-hole experience to Hong Kong – even travelling to Ireland to perfect the Guinness pour in time for the establishment’s September 1 opening.

“I’m going to Dublin in two weeks, just to study it,” Richardson tells me about his late-August plans to visit the Guinness Storehouse. We’re sitting inside his office on Elgin Street, just one step from his latest venture. “Between me going right to the source and us [ensuring] that we’ve got the best beer lines, coolers and cleanliness … that’s the best we can do, that’s what makes a great Guinness. Every little bit counts, because the liquid in the barrel is not even the main element.”

Originally from Milton Keynes, northwest of London, Richardson has kept himself busy in the nine years he’s been in Hong Kong. He is the founder and managing director of Big Top Hospitality, the group behind Australian restobar Bourke’s, American-style saloon Honky Tonks Tavern, Mediterranean seaside terrace Terracotta Lamma, fresh pasta bar Twist in Sheung Wan, and bagel joint and delicatessen Mendel’s.
item.content:encoded:
If a good pint is what you’re after, Matt Richardson may have a solution. As one of the brains behind The Boar, a new British public house (where the shortened form and better-known term, “pub”, comes from) and restaurant in Central, he has been working to bring an authentic watering-hole experience to Hong Kong – even travelling to Ireland to perfect the Guinness pour in time for the establishment’s September 1 opening.

“I’m going to Dublin in two weeks, just to study it,” Richardson tells me about his late-August plans to visit the Guinness Storehouse. We’re sitting inside his office on Elgin Street, just one step from his latest venture. “Between me going right to the source and us [ensuring] that we’ve got the best beer lines, coolers and cleanliness … that’s the best we can do, that’s what makes a great Guinness. Every little bit counts, because the liquid in the barrel is not even the main element.”

Originally from Milton Keynes, northwest of London, Richardson has kept himself busy in the nine years he’s been in Hong Kong. He is the founder and managing director of Big Top Hospitality, the group behind Australian restobar Bourke’s, American-style saloon Honky Tonks Tavern, Mediterranean seaside terrace Terracotta Lamma, fresh pasta bar Twist in Sheung Wan, and bagel joint and delicatessen Mendel’s.

With five restaurants already in his portfolio, the British restaurateur is finally opening something that connects him to his roots, but with a name that pays homage to his time in both Hong Kong and Britain. “Boars are the largest land mammals in Hong Kong, but you can also find them all around the UK,” explains Richardson. “Here, they’re kind of loved, aren’t they? You walk up The Peak, and people are super excited to see a little family of boars walking around. I quite enjoy it.”

Behind the pass, he has brought on two British chefs with fine-dining pedigrees: executive chef Graham Long, who has worked in Michelin-rated kitchens across London and launched culinary concepts for luxury hotels in Hong Kong. Day-to-day kitchen operations are run by head chef Jake Bennett, who cut his teeth at several Simon Rogan restaurants, including three-Michelin-star L’Enclume in Britain’s Lake District. Most recently, he was at The Baker and The Bottleman, in Wan Chai.

“I jumped on board as soon as I found out [Richardson was opening a pub],” says Long. He recalls how the pair began brainstorming the making of The Boar over a few pints.

“I’ve always felt that pubs were missing in Hong Kong to a degree. You’d think there would be more, given Hong Kong’s history and the expat community that’s here.”

Despite its name, however, the pub and dining room will not be serving wild boar. In Hong Kong, it’s illegal to kill or capture the animal. In Britain, they were hunted to extinction several hundred years ago, before being reintroduced into the ecosystem in recent decades by farms. “I’ve cooked it professionally before. It’s not that common any more, but we used to get it from our game dealer. I actually prefer normal pork, to be honest, but it’s nice,” Long admits.

So, if boar is not on the menu, what is? Classic pub grub, of course, including Welsh rarebit, sticky toffee pudding and pork cheek and lobster pie, as well as courses that speak to British sensibilities, such as Eton mess and coronation chicken salad.

With both chefs coming from haute-cuisine backgrounds, the dishes reflect their technical discipline. “We want to make the best version of everything. Yes, we’re going to do fish and chips, but we want to make sure it’s the best fish and chips we can possibly do,” Long explains.

As for their Scotch eggs, these will be made with British sausage meat, black pudding and Japanese eggs, then fried to order. “You know, nothing beats a Scotch egg. Hopefully, nothing will beat our Scotch egg,” says Long.

The Boar will offer two menus, with “downstairs” serving casual bites such as prawn cocktail toast, the signature BLT sandwich, Guinness and treacle bread with salted English butter, broccoli and Stichelton tart, and more, while “upstairs” hosts a more formal dining format, with celeriac and mushroom Wellington, roasted turbot chop, baked Chilean sea bass and chargrilled rib-eye steak to look forward to. (Sunday roasts are in the works, too.) “It’s where we get to have a little bit more fun, be a bit more chef-y, have a few more luxury ingredients and a more sit-down experience,” says Long.

One of the highlights of the upstairs menu is the roasted duck, dry-aged for two weeks in-house – no short cuts, all processed by the Boar team – and served with buttered turnips, carrots, a sauce of port and citrus, and toller’s pie, a play on the timeless shepherd’s pie in reference to the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever, a medium-sized gun-dog breed traditionally trained by hunters to find, flush out and retrieve shot game.

Moving into Flaming Frango’s old space on Elgin Street, the two-storey location, with an expansive ground floor and quirky structural nooks, has just the right bones to make it feel like a British pub – but Richardson has a fresher take in mind.

“We want it to feel more like a modern pub, because we feel it would be unjust to try and transport something you’d find from the laneways in London [to Hong Kong] – that would be too theatrical,” says Richardson. Instead, he explains he was inspired by his favourite pub, The Pelican, a Michelin Bib Gourmand spot in London’s Notting Hill neighbourhood.

“It’s a totally different experience from what people might know of the pub world, but the aesthetics, the feel, is that,” he says. “So, downstairs, think brighter colours and nice wood textures, but lots of nods to the things you might recognise from a pub back home, like the way we do the edgings on the tables and footrests and textures. And then when you move upstairs, this will have a different feel – more green, a bit more opulent.”

For Long and Richardson, The Boar is more than just another restaurant opening. “I spent most of my adult life in London and, generally, when I wasn’t working in a kitchen, I was in a pub,” recalls Long, whose time in the city included a stint at two-Michelin-star Pied à Terre, then helmed by Shane Osborn.

“Wherever you grow up, everyone has their local pub,” Long says. “[A pub is] shaped by the community that it’s in.”

Richardson agrees: “When I’m back home [in Britain, the go-to pub is] just wherever my friends are.”

Creating that sense of community here in Hong Kong – where both restaurateur and chef have settled, and for not an insignificant amount of time – is top of their minds when it comes to shaping the destination. “We let the food, the drinks and the genuine hospitality speak for themselves,” says Richardson, adding that every visit to The Boar “feels like coming home”.

item.title: [SCMP] Word on the StrEAT: 6 Hong Kong chefs share pre-service rituals that fuel their kitchens
item.description:
Before the first ticket lands, every restaurant team prepares for a night of service in its own way. In kitchens where the pace can shift from quiet to chaotic in minutes, those final moments are crucial for getting mentally and physically ready.

From espresso shots and sparkling water to staff karaoke, rotating playlists and meticulous station checks, rituals – both practical and personal – help chefs set the tone for the hours ahead. Here, chefs from across Hong Kong’s dining scene share the routines, superstitions and small acts of self-care that help them find focus before their doors open.

Chef Tony Mok, Path
item.content:encoded:
Before the first ticket lands, every restaurant team prepares for a night of service in its own way. In kitchens where the pace can shift from quiet to chaotic in minutes, those final moments are crucial for getting mentally and physically ready.

From espresso shots and sparkling water to staff karaoke, rotating playlists and meticulous station checks, rituals – both practical and personal – help chefs set the tone for the hours ahead. Here, chefs from across Hong Kong’s dining scene share the routines, superstitions and small acts of self-care that help them find focus before their doors open.

Chef Tony Mok, Path

“We have a fairly small team of four – including [a] dishwasher! We [start the night] by greeting everyone and checking on each other. Show a bit of love to everyone.

“The playlist changes from Cantopop to more casual lofi pop songs like Keshi. Andy Hui is one of Sean’s (our Texan GM’s) favourites. Our team ritual is to sing together. It opens up our voice more before the night starts. ⁠After service begins, we are definitely more locked in to serve our guests.

“We also always stash gummies inside our kitchen to sweeten our service – a bit of a sugar rush also helps!”

Chef Sean Yuen, Jija by Vicky Lau

“Five minutes before service is the ‘calm before the storm’. Everyone is running their final checks, and the air is noticeably tense. I review tonight’s cover count, find out when the peak hour hits, and check for any VIPs or special dietary requirements. Once I have those numbers in mind, the rhythm of the night becomes completely clear.

“Downing a shot of espresso right before service not only wakes me up, but also acts as a mental trigger to switch into battle mode. [We] turn on all the heat lamps at the pass and the moment those lights go on, it means all the prep work is done.

“One hour into service, everyone is fully in the zone – hyper-focused, with the entire kitchen running at a fast yet meticulously organised pace. During peak rush hours, taking a two-second break to grab a sip of water gives me a quick moment to pause, clear my mind, and jump straight back into position.”

Chef Tara Margarita, Bourke’s

“Music is essential for us. Kitchens get hot and high-stress, so the right tunes keep the energy light during prep before the inevitable service rush. Anyone in hospitality knows the absolute pain of listening to the exact same pre-service loop for years on end. We’re lucky to have a diverse team with different cultural backgrounds, so we like to rotate the prep-DJ duties.

“If I’m on the aux, my recent go-to tracks are ‘Summer Romance’ by Incubus, ‘Given Up’ by Linkin Park and ‘Killing in the Name’ by Rage Against the Machine.

“Work is intense, but work isn’t life – it’s important not to lose sight of that. So personally, I always make time to stretch and check in with my team on a human level.

“On fully staffed days, those last five minutes are pure ‘calm before the storm’ and your final chance to double-check line set-ups or fire off last-minute backups. I change into my shift shoes and jacket and pull my hair back in a way that’s guaranteed to hold up for the next 14 hours.

“During service, front of house has made a habit of buying me Kinder Buenos – especially if I’m looking a bit stressed on the pass. I keep a dedicated 1/9 pan in my lowboy [refrigerator] stocked with bite-sized Kinder Buenos to get through the push.”

Chef Ryo Matsui, Torikaze Hong Kong

“Before anything else, I want to see, touch and taste what has arrived that day. It tells me how we need to cook.

“We make sure every station is clean, organised and complete. It may sound simple, but this is important – the state of your station reflects the state of your mind. I need to see the charcoal glowing properly and have my fan beside the grill. The fire is alive, and it changes constantly, so the fan is not only a tool to control the heat; it is how I communicate with it. When the binchotan is ready, the whole station feels ready.

“There is a quiet tension. Everyone is focused on their own station, checking small details one more time. [Then] the kitchen becomes more fluid – less thinking, more instinct. Communication is shorter, movements become more precise, and the team finds its rhythm together.

“When it becomes busy, I return to the next plate. Not the whole service, not the tickets waiting behind it, just the dish in front of me. You cannot control everything at once, but you can always control the quality of the next action.”

Chef Uwe Opocensky, Petrus

“As a junior cook, I was on a station, and being ‘ready’ meant my mise en place was perfect and I was set for whatever came at me during service. These days I run the pass, so readiness looks different. It’s less about my own station and more about checking that everyone else is ready and everything is exactly where it should be.

“The first thing I always do is greet everyone; that sets the tone for the whole day. Then I do a walk-through to see what’s going on: checking the bookings, events and anything that may have changed since the night before. After that, I sit down with my senior chefs and go through notes I’ve written the night before – ideas, things we could do better, things I think we can improve on. It’s important to me that the day starts with the team, not just with the food.

“Consistency is the ritual. I go over the booking sheet one more time. I check that everything is set up and ready – down to the tasting spoons and seat numbers. Then I get a large glass of sparkling water for myself before service starts. By the time I step through the doors of Petrus, I’m focused.

“The one constant through all of it has been a small espresso. It’s less about the caffeine and more about the signal; it’s my way of telling myself I’m ready to go.”

Chef Alex Fargas, La Paloma

“I believe every dish matters, and every person we work with and serve matters. Every day at 5pm we hold a team meeting. We dedicate the first 20 minutes to discussing the previous day’s situations and focusing on customer satisfaction. The next 20 minutes are dedicated to staff training, motivation and development. Finally, the last 10 minutes are spent discussing personal healthy habits, life goals or any important matters anyone has on their mind.

“We take that time to connect, share how we’re feeling, and discuss what we are aiming to achieve on that particular day.

“We set clear objectives for every day and week, assigning both individual and team goals. This keeps everyone connected, aligned with our targets, and fully engaged during our daily meetings.

“We take it one dish and one person at a time, ensuring we give everything the attention it needs to achieve excellence. One step at a time – that’s how we operate at La Paloma.”

item.title: [SCMP] US universities curb international student internships following federal warning
item.description:
International students in the United States are facing new hurdles when it comes to internships and off-campus work after several major universities paused or restricted certain forms of Curricular Practical Training (CPT).

CPT is a form of work authorisation that allows foreign students to take part in internships and other practical training related to their studies.

The changes follow two directives in August from the Student and Exchange Visitor Programme (SEVP), a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which take a stricter view of when CPT can be authorised.
item.content:encoded:
International students in the United States are facing new hurdles when it comes to internships and off-campus work after several major universities paused or restricted certain forms of Curricular Practical Training (CPT).

CPT is a form of work authorisation that allows foreign students to take part in internships and other practical training related to their studies.

The changes follow two directives in August from the Student and Exchange Visitor Programme (SEVP), a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which take a stricter view of when CPT can be authorised.

Universities including the University of Pennsylvania, New York University, the University of Southern California, the University of Washington, the University of Rochester and the University of California, Berkeley have paused pending applications or limited CPT to internships that are mandatory parts of a degree programme.

What changed?

CPT itself has not been banned.

On August 12, the SEVP issued a message reminding school officials of their responsibility when approving CPT.

The guidance said CPT must be an integral part of an established curriculum and directly related to a student’s major. It also stressed that the training should generally be necessary to complete the degree and required for all students in that programme.

The SEVP also warned the school officials that approving CPT carried personal responsibility. By signing off on a student’s work authorisation paperwork, officials certify that the position meets federal requirements. Improper approvals could have consequences for both the university and the individual official, including possible loss of the school’s SEVP certification.

The agency also warned schools against using CPT to provide employment opportunities rather than as part of an academic programme.

On August 24, the SEVP issued another message reinforcing that CPT was allowed only as an integral part of an established curriculum. It again warned that violations could put a university’s certification at risk.

Universities begin tightening CPT rules

UC Berkeley was among the first major universities to respond.

In an August 13 letter to students, the university’s international office said the new federal criteria were “narrow in nature” and raised questions about existing CPT practices.

The university then suspended applications for “course credit CPT” that were considered integral to a programme but were not formal degree requirements. The university said it would continue processing CPT that was required for the degree.

The university described the move as a precaution, saying it was acting to minimise risk to its international office advisers and the university. It said it was temporarily suspending course credit CPT applications until further notice.

UC Berkeley’s current CPT guidance continues to reflect the suspension. The university now considers “integral” practical training to mean either a degree requirement for all students in the programme or a necessary component of a master’s thesis or doctoral dissertation.

The university later warned students that the suspension could continue for the foreseeable future.

The University of Pennsylvania announced a universitywide pause on August 29, putting new and pending CPT requests on hold while it reviewed its academic programmes and procedures in response to the federal guidance.

The university stressed that CPT had not been eliminated and that pending applications had not been denied.

It also highlighted a key change in how academic credit was treated, telling students: “Under the guidance, receiving academic credit is not enough by itself.”

NYU updated its guidance on August 31, saying the federal guidance established a stricter interpretation of CPT rules.

Under the university’s reading, CPT may be authorised only when it is an explicit, mandatory degree requirement of a programme.

NYU said CPT authorisations already approved for the autumn term would remain valid, but pending requests had been frozen.

USC has taken a similar position. It said CPT based on an elective course did not meet the federal requirements. As of August 24, the university said CPT would generally be limited to practical training required for graduation.

The University of Washington has also paused new CPT requests that are not required work experience for all students in a degree programme.

At the University of Rochester, optional internships, clinical experience and other practical training, including those tied to elective internship courses, are no longer considered eligible under the university’s interpretation of the guidance.

Other campuses within the University of California system, including UCLA and UC Davis, have also issued guidance.

What Chinese students need to know

The changes apply to international students from all countries on F-1 visas, not just Chinese students.

However, the restrictions could have a major impact on Chinese students, who make up one of the largest international student groups in the US and often rely on internships during undergraduate and master’s degree programmes.

For students who already have internship offers for the autumn semester, the key question is whether the CPT has already been authorised.

At universities that have issued guidance, CPT already authorised on official paperwork generally remains valid.

Students should also remember that they cannot begin off-campus work until they have received the required CPT authorisation.

On the Chinese social media platform RedNote, a user identifying as a Columbia University PhD graduate said the policy was “truly driving international students into a corner”.

“Doesn’t this completely cut off any path for international students to intern in the US?” the user wrote.

A user who said they were a UC Berkeley journalism student noted that a “short-term policy reversal” appeared unlikely. The person cited an email from the university’s international office stating that the suspension of CPT approvals had been “extended indefinitely”.

Another RedNote user, who listed the University of Southern California as his school, posted a scathing reflection, saying that he had “really believed it” when people had promised him the STEM fields – science, technology, engineering and mathematics – were stable and technical skills were in demand in the US.

“I was completely misled. When policies shift like this, all of it falls apart in an instant,” he wrote.

Frustration over US President Donald Trump’s second term has been a dominant theme of discussions on the Chinese platform.

One user, whose post showed an Illinois IP address, said: “This is only one year and eight months into Trump’s term; the ‘good days’ are still ahead of us.”

A Los Angeles-based user replied: “It’s only been a year and a half? It feels like half a lifetime has passed.”

Additional reporting by Cao Jiaxuan

item.title: [SCMP] How Japan aims to convert ageing warships into leverage to counter China
item.description:
Japan’s plans to transfer ageing warships to the Philippines and Indonesia could turn older military hardware into geopolitical leverage, deepening regional security ties while helping Tokyo counterbalance Beijing’s growing influence, observers say.

Such transfers, they said, fit into Tokyo’s broader security assistance toolkit to strengthen partners’ capabilities and forge longer-term defence relationships through equipment, training, maintenance and interoperability – expanding Japan’s regional influence without demanding alignment against Beijing.

The broader effort is aimed at cultivating what Tokyo calls a “desirable security environment” by taking a more active role in shaping the region’s security architecture.
item.content:encoded:
Japan’s plans to transfer ageing warships to the Philippines and Indonesia could turn older military hardware into geopolitical leverage, deepening regional security ties while helping Tokyo counterbalance Beijing’s growing influence, observers say.

Such transfers, they said, fit into Tokyo’s broader security assistance toolkit to strengthen partners’ capabilities and forge longer-term defence relationships through equipment, training, maintenance and interoperability – expanding Japan’s regional influence without demanding alignment against Beijing.

The broader effort is aimed at cultivating what Tokyo calls a “desirable security environment” by taking a more active role in shaping the region’s security architecture.

Providing retiring warships is an important element of that push. The Philippines expects to receive five Abukuma-class destroyer escorts within two to three years, while Tokyo and Jakarta are discussing the transfer of Asagiri-class destroyers, the first of which was retired in March after 38 years of service.

An analysis published on August 25 by Japan’s National Institute for Defence Studies (NIDS), the defence ministry’s main research institute, suggests Tokyo could eventually broaden the pool of equipment for such transfers.

NIDS researcher Akinori Ishihara pointed to Japan’s transfer of ageing but still operational warships to Russia during World War I after newer vessels reduced their relative importance in Japan’s future fleet.

Ishihara argued that the key consideration was not whether equipment was new or old, or active or retired, but whether Japan could transfer it and still maintain the defence capabilities it needed.

That could open the door to retiring equipment early to make it available for transfer, the NIDS analysis suggests. As Japan introduces more advanced, automated and uncrewed systems, some older platforms could become less critical to the Japan Self-Defence Forces structure before reaching the end of their planned service lives, expanding the pool of equipment available for transfer to regional partners.

Hirohito Ogi, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Tokyo, said such an approach made sense for vessels with relatively limited air-defence capabilities designed mainly for peacetime and grey-zone operations. As China’s precision-strike capabilities became increasingly sophisticated, such ships were unlikely to survive high-intensity combat, he said, arguing that Japan should retire them as early as possible and renew its capabilities.

Retiring equipment, however, is only one part of Tokyo’s expanding security aid toolkit.

A key mechanism is the Official Security Assistance framework, a grant-based military aid programme Japan launched in 2023 to provide equipment and infrastructure to partner countries. Tokyo has increased its budget from 2 billion yen (US$12.5 million) in the 2023 financial year to a record 18.1 billion yen this financial year and plans to continue expanding the number of countries covered by the programme.

Tokyo has used the programme to supply equipment ranging from patrol boats and coastal radars, to surveillance systems and drones, with maritime security being a major focus. Both the Philippines and Indonesia are recipients, reflecting Japan’s efforts to strengthen partners along strategically important waterways.

Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo’s Institute of Social Science, said Japan had increasingly embraced arms transfers as a foreign policy tool since overhauling its export restrictions in 2014, a process that culminated in a further major easing of the rules earlier this year.

He said Japan’s main strategic objective was to strengthen defence cooperation with Indo-Pacific partners to deter China’s growing influence.

Japan’s evolving strategy was “designed to counterbalance China’s rise by preserving the status quo in the region” with arms transfers, helping Tokyo arrive at the centre of emerging bilateral and minilateral defence networks, according to Maslow.

The Philippines provides a concrete example of that strategic logic. Maslow pointed to increasingly active mainland Chinese naval operations southeast of Taiwan, particularly around the Bashi Channel and Philippine Sea, with vessels subsequently deploying deeper into the Pacific and around Japan’s islands.

Ogi said that strengthening the Philippine Navy’s ability to monitor and track those movements would “directly contribute to Japan’s security” and could also help deter a Taiwan contingency.

The warships would add to a growing range of Japanese maritime security equipment provided or offered to Manila, including coastguard vessels and TC-90 aircraft, while the two sides have also explored the potential transfer of Japan’s ageing Type 88 surface-to-ship missiles.

The value of second-hand platforms could also extend beyond the hardware itself. Tokyo is discussing training, maintenance and sustainment with Manila, potentially keeping Japan involved throughout much of the equipment’s remaining service life.

Indonesia presents a different case as Jakarta seeks to preserve its strategic autonomy, even as defence cooperation with Tokyo expands.

Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, said Indonesia’s value to Japan did not depend on Jakarta siding with Tokyo against Beijing. She described Tokyo’s approach as “influence without demanding alignment”.

Cooperation with Jakarta could show that Japan’s expanding security role did not necessarily amount to bloc-building, she said, a particularly significant point given Indonesia’s influence within Asean and the region’s broader preference for strategic autonomy.

Building on this perspective, an analysis for Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies by Chaula Rininta Anindya and Adhi Priamarizki described Jakarta’s ties with Japan as one of “strategic convenience” rather than alignment, while cautioning that Beijing might still view closer defence cooperation as an attempt to constrain China.

Maslow said Indonesia’s position as both a Japanese security partner and a close partner of China would test “how China will respond to new defence cooperation in the region”.

For Matsuoka, Japan’s longer-term influence could lie less in locking Indonesia into Japanese hardware than in making itself more relevant within the country’s security institutions through training, maintenance and other cooperation.

Japan’s influence, she said, could be greatest when it did not require Indonesia to become “Japan-aligned”.

According to Maslow, that reflects a broader transformation in Japan’s regional role. He said Tokyo was expanding its traditional economic role into the security sphere, moving “from building production networks to establishing defence networks”.

item.title: [SCMP] EU trade enforcers descend on Beijing demanding China fix ‘untenable’ imbalances
item.description:
A delegation from the European Commission has been locked in talks with Chinese officials in Beijing, as the sides look to find a diplomatic off-ramp from a looming trade war before an October deadline set by Brussels.

The EU team was spearheaded by Denis Redonnet, the bloc’s top trade enforcement officer, who was recently made point person on China trade policy – a recognition that in EU circles, talk of partnership has largely been usurped by rivalry and competition.

Later this month, the European Union’s top trade official, Ditte Juul Jorgensen, will follow Redonnet to the Chinese capital, she confirmed on Wednesday, as Brussels assesses whether Beijing is willing to make the sort of concessions that could see them avoid sliding into a damaging tit-for-tat exchange in the autumn.
item.content:encoded:
A delegation from the European Commission has been locked in talks with Chinese officials in Beijing, as the sides look to find a diplomatic off-ramp from a looming trade war before an October deadline set by Brussels.

The EU team was spearheaded by Denis Redonnet, the bloc’s top trade enforcement officer, who was recently made point person on China trade policy – a recognition that in EU circles, talk of partnership has largely been usurped by rivalry and competition.

Later this month, the European Union’s top trade official, Ditte Juul Jorgensen, will follow Redonnet to the Chinese capital, she confirmed on Wednesday, as Brussels assesses whether Beijing is willing to make the sort of concessions that could see them avoid sliding into a damaging tit-for-tat exchange in the autumn.

“We see an engaged China in these talks, but of course the challenges are very, very significant,” Jorgensen told a hearing at the European Parliament on Wednesday.

The commission wants Beijing to commit to reducing its surging exports to the bloc, which have expanded at breakneck speed in recent months. In July alone, China extended its trade surplus over all but three EU members compared with a year earlier.

“What we see in relation to China is … increasing concentration dependencies, including in strategic sectors – that is a risk to the EU,” Jorgensen said.

“We see that as a result of a number of Chinese domestic policies, but of course also of China’s competitiveness in a number of these sectors, we have an increasing trade deficit,” she added, describing it as an “untenable situation”.

Brussels suspects that the exports are turbo-boosted by undeclared subsidies, an undervalued currency, and rampant industrial overcapacity caused by weak domestic demand, years of investment-led growth and state support that has kept production expanding even as consumption has lagged.

It fears that these factors propel products to European shores at prices that are undercutting local producers and that could, if left unchecked, deindustrialise swathes of the European economy.

“We are working with very concrete proposals. Let’s see how our Chinese counterparts would react to them … But if simply there will be no action, then of course it will be much more difficult for us just to talk about these issues,” EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic told Politico on Monday.

But in the Belgian capital, expectations are well managed as to what can be achieved before October, when it must decide what to do. The face-to-face meetings followed a stream of online contacts through August, but these sessions produced no breakthroughs.

While Beijing has made conciliatory noises around reducing its gaping trade surplus with the EU, it is thought to prefer to do this by buying more European goods. Such a dynamic would resemble, in part, what US President Donald Trump agreed with China during his first term – the “phase one” trade deal that analysts say did little to address structural problems in the relationship.

“These ongoing talks are not just talks – they have to give a proof of concept by October. We have been very clear that these global imbalances that exist cannot continue and there has to be a rebalancing,” Jorgensen said.

The Beijing meetings are expected to inform how tough European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen talks on China during her State of the Union speech on September 16, which will in turn help set the agenda for a meeting between Sefcovic and Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao, planned for the second week of October.

In the past, von der Leyen has used her annual address to announce investigations into subsidies in China’s electric vehicle sector, a ban on products made using forced labour, and a rival to Beijing’s core infrastructure drive, the Belt and Road Initiative.

There is speculation that if negotiations do not make progress, she could announce new instruments or investigations. Jorgensen confirmed on Wednesday that the bloc was developing a “diversification instrument”, which could compel companies in critical sectors to increase their number of suppliers, but added that it was still “early days” in the tool’s development.

“That is a consideration relevant for climate, relevant for the energy transition, relevant for our economic security, and the need to rebalance. To be clear, it is that degree of concentration, that degree of dependence on any one supplier – whoever that supplier is – that is in and of itself a risk,” Jorgensen said.

During a speech last week von der Leyen warned that “being a partner [with China] does not mean accepting permanent imbalances”, noting that while Chinese imports into the EU had risen 45 per cent in five years, “our exports to China are falling”.

“We have seen that this dependence can be used as leverage against us. We must therefore ensure that fair conditions are respected. Dialogue with China remains necessary, but it must produce results. And when dialogue is not enough, we must be ready to make full use of our instruments,” von der Leyen said at the annual conference of France’s main employers’ federation, MEDEF.

Her State of the Union remarks later this month will help set the tone for a debate between the bloc’s national leaders in Brussels in mid-October, when they are expected to bless defensive measures against Chinese goods. Already, influential member states have been laying the groundwork for this scenario.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has flip-flopped dramatically on China policy since coming to office, appears to have come closer to Brussels’ thinking in recent weeks. Asked last week whether he backed car industry calls for EU tariffs on Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, Merz said he had instructed his cabinet to come up with proposals.

“I have asked the Federal Cabinet to now quickly gather and document all proposals that we could consider in terms of appropriate responses. We note that German industry has also apparently changed its opinion regarding these global imbalances. We will not only address this issue, but we will make decisions,” Merz said after a cabinet retreat.

At the same press conference, Vice-Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said that “when we see that others are not playing by the rules, we cannot be naive”.

“The issue now is protecting the steel industry, the automotive industry, the chemical industry and the pharmaceutical industry, both in Germany and in Europe,” Klingbeil said.

“We had a very serious debate about where we need to improve in order to reposition ourselves economically, but also about how we face competition, especially the increasingly unfair competition we are experiencing. Therefore, we agreed – the chancellor confirmed this – that we will discuss appropriate measures in the cabinet soon.”

Also last week, an advisory board to the Dutch government urged The Hague to back tougher measures on China, or see industry hollowed out.

“Doing nothing in this situation therefore also comes at a high price. Our dependencies will increase and we will be hit hard economically. A strong response also comes at a price,” read the report from Wetenschappelijke Raad voor het Regeringsbeleid, an independent advisory council.

“The longer we wait, the greater the pain will be in the future.”

item.title: [SCMP] US military carries out new strikes on Iranian targets as hostilities flare
item.description:
US President Donald Trump launched new air strikes on Iran on Tuesday, the latest chapter as the president has swung in recent weeks between economic and military pressure tactics, all the while claiming that Tehran was on its heels.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on social media that the attacks were in response to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) recent attempted attacks on commercial ships in the strategic Strait of ‌Hormuz and against American service ‌members deployed ‌to the ‌region.

“The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait, which currently has no mines,” Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump launched new air strikes on Iran on Tuesday, the latest chapter as the president has swung in recent weeks between economic and military pressure tactics, all the while claiming that Tehran was on its heels.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on social media that the attacks were in response to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) recent attempted attacks on commercial ships in the strategic Strait of ‌Hormuz and against American service ‌members deployed ‌to the ‌region.

“The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait, which currently has no mines,” Trump said on his Truth Social platform.

“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level.”

CENTCOM said it attacked Iranian air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, minelaying capabilities and communications sites.

Oil prices rose sharply as tensions escalated. Brent crude climbed above US$96 a barrel, its highest level in about two and a half months, coming just weeks ahead of the US midterm election, where affordability has been a central theme.

Iranian media reported explosions on Qeshm Island, Bandar Abbas, Konarak and Chabahar. Near Sirik, a strike on a wedding killed five people and wounded 50, according to the Iranian Red Crescent.

Tehran responded by launching a wave of retaliatory strikes, with the IRGC saying it targeted US interests in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan.

Jordan’s military said it intercepted and destroyed 10 ballistic missiles, while three others crashed in unpopulated remote areas, according to state news agency Petra. The Kuwaiti Army said on X that its air defences intercepted drone attacks “following the criminal Iranian aggression”. There was no immediate word from Bahrain.

In recent weeks, as US military pounding showed few signs of forcing Iran into submission, the Trump administration turned to economic pressure, which saw oil shipments through the strait return to around half their pre-war levels as attacks abated.

Tehran continues to show fight despite US pressure

In late August, Washington doubled down with an aggressive campaign of sanctions and financial isolation, a so-called “Economic D-Day” under the US Treasury Department’s Operation Economic Outcast.

But Tehran has displayed surprising resilience after enduring decades of US and global sanctions, and the US announcements gave few specifics on what was new.

Evidently concluding that financial pressure was not having the desired effect – in part, analysts say, because Washington has appeared unwilling to impose secondary sanctions on China, which bought some 80 per cent of Iran’s oil in 2025 – the US attacked Iran’s Larak ‌Island on Sunday, marking the first known strikes in several weeks. This prompted Iran to respond with missiles at two US airbases in Jordan, leading to Tuesday’s US attack.

Tuesday’s US strikes came a day after two oil supertankers were hit in quick succession as they tried to exit the strait, according to maritime security consultant Marisks.

Trump said on Monday the recent US response did not signal a return to full-scale war. But a day later, he turned up the rhetoric should Iran hit back.

“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level,” Trump wrote on social media.

“But it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!”

Analysts said US pressure on China to end its financial support for Iran, a nation it has maintained diplomatic relations with for 55 years, has clear limits. Beijing’s grip on the global supply of strategic rare earth minerals means that Washington is reluctant to push too hard. And Trump wants a successful summit in Washington with Chinese President Xi Jinping later this month.

Trump has become increasingly frustrated with his inability to prevail over Tehran in a war he started after criticising his predecessors for becoming entrenched in “forever wars”.

But that has not stopped him from declaring victory.

“We’ve already won in many ways, but we haven’t won enough,” he said at one point in recent months. “We won everything. We have all the cards,” he said at another.

US pressure may result in modest concessions from Beijing

With enough US pressure, Beijing might be willing to make some modest concessions, said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund of the United States, citing Chinese contacts.

“The Chinese aren’t going to abandon Iran, but could there be a reduced amount of oil imported for a while? That could be a possibility,” she said. “But it’s not something China is going to want to announce.”

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said early on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a 60-day June Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) aimed at halting the conflict.

“I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the MOU, the Islamic Republic of ⁠Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek at a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), which includes Russia and China.

But Iranian officials have shown little outward sign of bowing to pressure.

“If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will ‌be able to export oil,” Iranian parliament speaker ‌Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf was quoted as saying by Iranian media.

Washington is “addicted to making excessive demands”, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran, “and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”.

Analysts added that Iran used the just-concluded SCO summit, where Pezeshkian spoke, to reach out internationally.

“The summit was important for Iran, especially given close ties with Beijing, as it followed the US ‘Economic D-Day’ threats,” said Farwa Aamer, South Asia initiatives director with the Asia Society Policy Institute.

“Iran is looking to mobilise support from fellow members and would likely make the same ask when the Brics summit convenes in a few weeks,” she added, referring to a key grouping of emerging market economies. “The anti-West signalling, while avoided by some, will find its way into these summits.”

item.title: [SCMP] North Korea’s next ruler? Kim Jong-un’s daughter, Seoul’s spies say
item.description:
North Korea has never named her, confirmed her age or acknowledged her as Kim Jong-un’s heir. Yet South Korea’s spy agency says the evidence is now unmistakable: his daughter Kim Ju-ae has “effectively” become the successor-in-waiting.

The assessment, delivered in a closed-door briefing to the National Assembly’s intelligence committee, was shared with journalists by Youn Kun-young of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea on Monday.

“The NIS sees Kim Ju-ae as having effectively entered the stage of being designated as successor,” he said, referring to South Korea’s National Intelligence Service.
item.content:encoded:
North Korea has never named her, confirmed her age or acknowledged her as Kim Jong-un’s heir. Yet South Korea’s spy agency says the evidence is now unmistakable: his daughter Kim Ju-ae has “effectively” become the successor-in-waiting.

The assessment, delivered in a closed-door briefing to the National Assembly’s intelligence committee, was shared with journalists by Youn Kun-young of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea on Monday.

“The NIS sees Kim Ju-ae as having effectively entered the stage of being designated as successor,” he said, referring to South Korea’s National Intelligence Service.

Youn added that the agency believed Ju-ae’s increasingly frequent appearances in state media formed part of a deliberate effort to imprint “her image as a leader on the North Korean people’s minds”.

The assessment adds weight to Seoul’s view that Kim Jong-un is preparing his daughter to extend the Kim dynasty’s hereditary rule into a fourth generation.

Kim Ju-ae made her public debut in November 2022, when North Korean state media released photographs of her accompanying her father to the test launch of a Hwasong-17 intercontinental ballistic missile.

She has since appeared at a growing number of military, political and diplomatic events, fuelling speculation that she is being prepared as heir apparent.

Her public profile has broadened beyond military events. She joined her father on a trip to Beijing in September, her first known appearance abroad, and in January this year made her first public visit to the Kumsusan Palace of the Sun, the mausoleum housing the remains of her grandfather and great-grandfather, Kim Jong-il and Kim Il-sung.

That appearance was widely seen as symbolically significant given the regime’s dynastic succession.

State media has also been keen to promote a more martial image, photographing her inspecting and firing a new type of sniper rifle before senior military officials in February, test-firing a pistol and operating a new main battle tank alongside her father in March and attending a performance in July marking the 73rd anniversary of the Korean war armistice.

Most recently, she joined her parents at Pyongyang’s Liberation Tower, which honours former Soviet troops, and at the Daesongsan Revolutionary Martyrs Cemetery for the 81st anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japanese rule.

‘Princess training’

Though many details about Ju-ae remain shrouded in secrecy, analysts broadly agree she is being groomed as a potential successor – but add that she is still young for a formal declaration.

Believed to be 13, Ju-ae would need another five years to reach adulthood and become eligible to join the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea, seen as a prerequisite for any formal path towards leadership.

“She is still receiving princess training for possible succession. There is no sign that the party has made any decision to make her successor, even internally,” said Oh Gyeong-seob of the Korea Institute for National Unification.

Oh and others argue that the real marker to watch for is bureaucratic, not photographic: an appointment to a senior party or military post, such as a seat on the Central Military Commission or the Party Central Committee.

Ri Il-gyu, a former North Korean diplomat who defected after serving as a political counsellor at the embassy in Cuba, described a shift in terminology in the Chosun Daily last month.

Ju-ae was first called “beloved offspring”, he wrote, then “respected offspring”, before being elevated to “the great one who guides the way”.

Internal party lecture materials now describe her as “the new star of Joseon” and “General of the New Star”, he added.

“Her central role in public appearances carries clear political meaning,” Ri wrote. “Kim Jong-un’s early efforts to imprint his young daughter on the public reflect long-term calculations for succession.”

State protocol reinforces the message in subtler ways too: Ju-ae is invariably positioned beside or near the centre of the action alongside her father, dressed at times in a leather coat that echoes his own – visual shorthand tying her to the “sacred” Paektu bloodline from which the Kim family claims its legitimacy.

A three-rung ladder

Succession in North Korea is a three-rung ladder, according to Professor Yang Moo-jin of the University of North Korean Studies: education, internal designation and finally, an official announcement.

By his reckoning, Ju-ae has barely stepped onto the first rung.

“She has no party post and there is no sign that Ju-ae is at the centre of a personality cult,” he said.

Ju-ae featured in no discussion at the Workers’ Party’s ninth congress in February, he said, and was conspicuously absent when a senior Chinese delegation led by No 4 official Wang Huning met Kim Jong-un in Pyongyang in July.

The real test of her status would come at the next party congress, Yang said. “We have to wait and see until the 10th party congress due in 2031, when she will be 18, to see what kind of official title she dons.”

Even reaching adulthood clears only the first hurdle. North Korea’s deeply patriarchal political culture could complicate any attempt to install a daughter rather than a son as supreme leader.

North Korea has never had a female leader and defectors describe a society where Confucian-inflected male chauvinism endures beneath the state’s official socialist ideology.

Oh said Kim Jong-un could help clear the way for his daughter by removing potential rivals within the ruling elite.

“Her father would pave the way for her succession through purges and executions as he himself did after seizing power following his father Kim Jong-il’s death in 2011,” Oh said.

“But at the end of the day, it would depend on her own ability to overcome those challenges in the future by removing uncooperative political elites.”

Summit signals

The succession assessment was not the only headline to emerge from Monday’s briefing. The NIS also reportedly told lawmakers that it had obtained blueprints for North Korean missiles and was analysing them.

It further said that a summit between Kim Jong-un and US President Donald Trump “could be possible at any time”, according to Youn – though it stressed there was no confirmed evidence of direct contact between the two governments, only “signs” pointing towards dialogue.

It would be their fourth meeting. Trump and Kim met three times in 2018 and 2019, but talks collapsed after their ill-fated Hanoi summit failed to produce a deal on denuclearisation.

Speculation over a repeat encounter has been building for weeks, driven largely from the American side. Pyongyang has offered no direct response to Trump’s overtures and continues to denounce what it calls Washington’s hostile policy towards the North.

As Oh put it: “These differences are very hard to be narrowed down.”

item.title: [SCMP] China, global trading partners watch closely as Trump takes on Canada
item.description:
The latest trade war between the United States and Canada marks a turning point with key lessons for China and other major US trading partners as well as risks, say analysts and former trade officials, as US President Donald Trump continues to put his blunt stamp on global institutions.

The breakdown in ties between Washington and Ottawa, one of the largest trade relationships in the world, opens one more front in the president’s disruptive path that could fuel a backlash and further distrust to Beijing’s benefit.

“Should Canada succeed in weathering the storm of US retaliation while standing up for its national interests, others may follow a similar ‘get tough’ approach,” said Wendy Cutler, senior vice-president with the Asia Society Policy Institute.
item.content:encoded:
The latest trade war between the United States and Canada marks a turning point with key lessons for China and other major US trading partners as well as risks, say analysts and former trade officials, as US President Donald Trump continues to put his blunt stamp on global institutions.

The breakdown in ties between Washington and Ottawa, one of the largest trade relationships in the world, opens one more front in the president’s disruptive path that could fuel a backlash and further distrust to Beijing’s benefit.

“Should Canada succeed in weathering the storm of US retaliation while standing up for its national interests, others may follow a similar ‘get tough’ approach,” said Wendy Cutler, senior vice-president with the Asia Society Policy Institute.

“There is no doubt that a growing number of partners are relating to Canada’s growing frustration with Washington, overall, and the heavy-handedness it brings to the negotiating table.”

“Beijing must be enjoying watching the volley of words and actions between Washington and Ottawa,” added Cutler, a former senior negotiator at the Office of the US Trade Representative.

“It would not be surprising if Beijing steps up its efforts to woo Ottawa into its court.”

Talks collapsed late last month after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney broke off negotiations, accusing the US of acting in bad faith with “unfair and uneconomic” late-stage changes.

The US countered that Ottawa was abandoning prior commitments, as Trump weighed in, calling Canadian negotiators “clowns” and “nasty people”.

Never one to back down from a fight, the mercurial president then set his sights on Ontario Premier Doug Ford, calling him “Flunky Ford” after Ford said that Trump could “kiss my a**”.

Trump followed this up with an executive order to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, known as such for almost 400 years, as “Lake America”.

Ford countered that Trump’s name game resembled a skit from the television comedy show Saturday Night Live.

“I have a lot of real estate on my a**, so he has a lot of room to kiss,” he said. “I just do. I’m a big dude. What can I say?”

Amid the mudslinging are huge stakes involving a US$900 billion annual trade relationship, the world’s second-largest after the US and Mexico, and huge risks for Canada, whose economy is 8 per cent of its southern neighbour’s size.

Trump has a long history of issuing oversized threats to show dominance and gain leverage. Wall Street traders hope he will back down, a pattern dubbed “taco”, short for “Trump always chickens out”.

As it stands, however, Washington has imposed 50 per cent tariffs effective August 22 on some US$20 billion of Canadian imports; raised concerns over Canadian imports of Chinese EVs; demanded veto power over Canada’s independent trade policy; and tried to undermine Canada’s French labelling and media content requirements, a huge red line for the bilingual nation.

Ottawa has countered with a pledge to match the punitive US measures “dollar for dollar” effective September 8.

Trump further threatened to raise tariffs to 50 per cent effective January 1 on the hugely consequential steel and auto trades. And he has declined to automatically renew the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement, leading to a July 1, 2027, review deadline.

One lesson voiced by Carney and increasingly internalised by the 200 nations that trade with the US is the lack of certainty in any agreement negotiated with Washington.

“There’s no such thing as a deal any more when it comes to the US, at least with the current administration,” said Abishur Prakash, geopolitical strategist at The Geopolitical Business, a Toronto-based advisory firm.

“This is a Wild West-type scenario.”

The European Union and United Kingdom crafted deals with the US, Japan pledged US$500 billion and South Korea pledged US$350 billion, only to see the US administration come back for more, examples not lost on Carney, he said.

“That’s proven to him that it’s never-ending, that every six months the trade demands return,” Prakash said.

“He’s trying to say, ‘hey, you want a deal, let’s make a deal. But if you don’t want to make a deal, this is the consequence’.”

Or, in Carney’s words, Washington’s signature is increasingly “written in pencil”.

What had distinguished Carney, previewed in his World Economic Forum speech last January, was the need for middle powers led by Canada to push back, he said, even as other world leaders had rushed to Washington to appease the transactional president.

By some indications, China led the way by forcing Washington to blink after Liberation Day, using its grip on strategic rare earth minerals. But Canada is far smaller and more interdependent.

That said, Canada is the single-largest export market for almost all major rust belt and battleground states, including Michigan, Pennsylvania and North Carolina, coming into the midterm elections, according to the Ottawa-based Macdonald-Laurier Institute.

“While some might be predisposed to think that China holds more aces in hand than Canada, that’s not necessarily true because Canada still holds the energy and fertiliser [cards],” said Nicole Bivens Collinson, managing principal with law firm Sandler, Travis and Rosenberg, formerly with the USTR and the Commerce Department.

“We have to be careful we’re not overplaying our hand.”

But Carney is walking a delicate line. While he has a few “nuclear” options, such as cutting off Canadian electricity that some 20 US states draw on, he wants to avoid alienating Americans, most of whom have soured on Trump.

And while Carney’s domestic popularity has soared – over 70 per cent of respondents supported his decision to end trade negotiations with the US leader, according to an Abacus Data survey – that will almost certainly decline if the crisis drags on and Canadian employment and economic growth sink.

“It will last and increase if Canada turns out to be right,” Prakash said. “However, if Washington doesn’t fold … the US has so many cards to play. And if Trump were to play just two of them, we would all be bleeding to bits in Canada.”

Another lesson reinforced by this crisis is that global trade negotiations increasingly move at a blistering pace. And while China has used its rare earths leverage effectively, the US, Japan and others are racing to blunt this massive vulnerability by rapidly expanding mining and processing.

“If I were China, I would probably know that I have a limited amount of time,” Bivens Collinson said.

“If the United States is willing to do that to their trading partners to the north of the border, they’re going to be willing to do that to China.”

“I would be taking this as a lesson to be heeded, and to recognise that I’ve got a shelf life on these cards that I’m holding.”

While the immediate US-Canada mud fight dominates headlines, the crisis also has more fundamental implications as long-standing US-led structures are increasingly unwound and economies race to bolster bilateral ties that exclude Washington as the US hub frays and its many spokes start to break away.

Canada’s 10-year diversification target aims to expand non-US exports by US$300 billion, an effort being replicated worldwide.

“You have to adapt to survive and sometimes when you’re forced to adapt, diversification is the only way,” said Ashley Kalyn, international trade specialist with Peacock Tariff Consulting.

“This is a case study for China and other countries right now because it shows both the possibilities and the limits of responding to US pressure.”

“China will be watching Canada very closely,” she added. “Canada demonstrates that this isn’t only about China or the other state’s practices. Washington right now is fundamentally changing how things are.”

Analysts questioned whether, given how economically and politically counterproductive the Canada trade war was, Trump offered terms knowing they would be rejected and had other geopolitical reasons for challenging Canadian sovereignty.

Instability could serve his repeated call for Canada to become the “51st state”, which has amplified pro-independence movements in Western Canada.

Others see this test of wills as a precursor to the dissolution of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) covering 520 million people and a combined GDP of over US$33 trillion, which was negotiated during Trump’s first term.

His decision to delay imposing 50 per cent car tariffs until after the election, unpopular in both countries, has fuelled this theory.

“US-Canada relations are more fraught than the market is pricing in,” said Henrietta Treyz, economic policy director with consultancy Veda Partners.

“US businesses have been able to stave off the ‘nuclear option’ of triggering a withdrawal from the USMCA within six months, but they haven’t been able to do more than that, despite months of opportunity and years of forewarning.”

Increasingly erratic US policy has seen China’s soft power grow almost by default as Washington has launched wars, undercut allies, embraced unilateralism, taken on the United Nations and Nato and alienated many US voters.

But Trump’s willingness to threaten other countries’ sovereignty – whether through one-sided trade deals, language politics or force – could also concern Beijing, analysts said, given sensitivities over Xinjiang, Hong Kong and Tibet.

“Chinese are playing a fabulous game of staying quiet and observing, just watching, keeping its doors open, quite confident if this trade fight snowballs,” Prakash said, adding that anti-Washington anger is palpable in Canadian pubs and coffee shops.

“If the USMCA is scrapped, it may also push Mexico to say no, then you have both sides of the US open to China.

“The biggest question mark is what is going to be achieved by a trade fight with Canada?”

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Aloof’ but engaged: what India’s SCO comeback reveals
item.description:
Two years ago, Narendra Modi skipped the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s (SCO) summit in Astana entirely, sending his foreign minister instead.

That absence was redressed first at last year’s summit in Tianjin and again this week in Kyrgyzstan, where India’s prime minister stood shoulder to shoulder with China’s Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and the leaders of other SCO member states.

Analysts say New Delhi’s revived engagement with the 10-member bloc reflects both its hedging against an evermore unpredictable United States and its desire to counterbalance China’s influence at the SCO – even if they expect it to remain a “somewhat aloof member”.
item.content:encoded:
Two years ago, Narendra Modi skipped the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s (SCO) summit in Astana entirely, sending his foreign minister instead.

That absence was redressed first at last year’s summit in Tianjin and again this week in Kyrgyzstan, where India’s prime minister stood shoulder to shoulder with China’s Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and the leaders of other SCO member states.

Analysts say New Delhi’s revived engagement with the 10-member bloc reflects both its hedging against an evermore unpredictable United States and its desire to counterbalance China’s influence at the SCO – even if they expect it to remain a “somewhat aloof member”.

Founded in 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, the SCO was originally envisaged as a vehicle for Eurasian security cooperation, expanding over the years to include Pakistan, Iran and Belarus as full members, with a wider circle of Asian and Middle Eastern countries as observers and partners.

India joined in 2017, but it has never been an entirely comfortable fit. China is widely seen as the bloc’s dominant force, bankrolling regional trade and infrastructure projects at a scale no other member can match, while the presence of Pakistan, Delhi’s arch-rival, serves as a perpetual irritant.

Still, Modi arrived in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek on Sunday to attend the 26th SCO summit, a two-day gathering concluding on Tuesday, where he was expected to address fellow heads of state on regional stability, counterterrorism and economic cooperation.

‘Anti-Western’ aversion

Before last year’s summit in Tianjin, there were signs that Delhi was downgrading its engagement with the bloc, said Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia at British think tank Chatham House – citing not only Modi’s 2024 absence but India’s last-minute decision to make the meeting it hosted in 2023 virtual.

“This reflects India’s aversion to being part of any organisation that is regarded as overtly anti-Western,” Bajpaee said.

That aversion had not simply disappeared, he said, but improved ties with China and strained relations with a US that had imposed steep trade tariffs and pressured India not to buy Russian oil helped motivate Modi’s move.

It also came with a price tag, of sorts. “Delhi’s renewed support for the SCO likely came in exchange for Beijing’s support for India’s Brics chairmanship this year,” Bajpaee said, pointing to the next Brics summit, scheduled to be held in Delhi from September 12-13.

The two Asian giants, both members of Brics and the SCO, have been gradually normalising ties – opening new military hotlines, resuming direct flights and easing visa restrictions – after the deadly border clashes in 2020 that froze relations for years.

Still, “Delhi prefers to project an image as a non-Western rather than an anti-Western power”, Bajpaee said, noting India’s parallel push for deeper ties with the West.

The result would likely be India remaining “a somewhat aloof member of the SCO”, he said – engaged, but not fully at home.

Yet Delhi’s presence is also what keeps the SCO from becoming dominated by Beijing, according to Ivan Lidarev, a political scientist and research fellow at the National University of Singapore’s Institute of South Asian Studies.

An SCO without India might solidify into a Chinese sphere of influence

Ivan Lidarev, political scientist

“An SCO without India might solidify into a Chinese sphere of influence in Eurasia to India’s detriment and turn the organisation into an anti-US bloc,” he said, adding that this concern was part of why Russia pushed for India’s admission in the first place.

For both Beijing and Moscow, the SCO served as a way of keeping Delhi close and limiting how far it drifted towards Washington, Lidarev said, while enabling the slow accumulation of trust.

“The SCO has acted as a giant confidence-building measure between Delhi and Beijing,” he said. “It has committed the two to the same vision of multipolarity, with an emphasis on the Global South.”

Modi’s appearance in Bishkek serves another, more immediate purpose: paving the way for Xi’s possible attendance at this month’s Brics summit in Delhi.

“A no-show by Xi will be a blow to the summit, particularly in light of Modi’s participation in last year’s Tianjin SCO summit and to the thaw in China-India relations,” Lidarev said, adding it could also complicate next year’s Brics summit that China is set to host.

There is a message for Washington embedded in all of this, too.

India’s push to strengthen the “non-Western side” of its multi-alignment foreign policy strategy amounted to “a careful and increasingly difficult international balancing act”, Lidarev said – one intended to subtly remind the US that India had other options, at a time when trade talks between the two countries appeared to have hit a wall.

Diminishing returns?

Other observers cast doubt on the continued utility of SCO membership for India, with Shanthie Mariet D’Souza, founder and president of the Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies in Goa, seeing an organisation that offers the country less and less.

“China’s growing dominance and the organisation’s consensus-based structure limit New Delhi’s ability to shape its political and security agenda, particularly on issues such as terrorism and regional conflicts,” she said.

But she stopped short of calling for India’s withdrawal, noting that the SCO was one of the few forums where India can sit across the negotiating table from China, Russia and the Central Asian states all at once.

“Its value is therefore increasingly tactical,” D’Souza said – giving Delhi a venue to raise concerns about terrorism as its presence prevented the bloc becoming an “exclusively China-Russia sphere”.

“India may no longer expect major geopolitical outcomes from the SCO, but it cannot afford to abandon it,” she added.

Modi’s regional diplomacy did not begin in Bishkek. He spent two days in Uzbekistan first, on a state visit from Saturday to Sunday, meeting President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and formally elevating ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership.

The visit yielded increased Indian access to Uzbek uranium and critical minerals, and a bilateral pledge to push two-way trade past US$5 billion by 2030.

That stop was no accident of scheduling, according to Balaji Chandramohan, a foreign-policy analyst and research scholar at the University of Madras.
