He said the SCO allowed India to reaffirm its commitment to Central Asia and the Middle East at a time of considerable global disruption, shoring up both regional connectivity and its own energy security.

“India will expand its strategic outreach in the Central Asian region as a part of its extending Look West and Look North Policy,” he said, referring to Delhi’s parallel diplomatic strategies for deepening ties with West and Central Asia as extensions of its own neighbourhood.

item.title: [SCMP] Starship could create more debris than an anti-satellite test if it explodes in orbit
item.description:
As Starship, the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, gears up for an attempt to finally reach Earth’s orbit, experts say the risk of an in-flight catastrophe – and a cloud of debris – “needs to be of concern”.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX is expected to launch the Starship spacecraft and Super Heavy booster for the launch system’s 14th test flight and first orbital test flight later this month.

According to one aerospace expert, if the Starship’s upper stage explodes in orbit it could produce debris on a scale larger than previous in-orbit incidents, including an anti-satellite missile test.
item.content:encoded:
As Starship, the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, gears up for an attempt to finally reach Earth’s orbit, experts say the risk of an in-flight catastrophe – and a cloud of debris – “needs to be of concern”.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX is expected to launch the Starship spacecraft and Super Heavy booster for the launch system’s 14th test flight and first orbital test flight later this month.

According to one aerospace expert, if the Starship’s upper stage explodes in orbit it could produce debris on a scale larger than previous in-orbit incidents, including an anti-satellite missile test.

During that test, in November 2021, Russia intentionally blew up a defunct Soviet intelligence satellite called Cosmos-1408.

Moriba Jah, a professor of aerospace engineering at The University of Texas at Austin, said the Russian test had detrimental consequences for the operation of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite constellation.

He said if Starship were to explode in orbit, it could create a lot of debris that could become hazards to other objects as well as humans.

“If something like that happened in low-Earth orbit, it would be like the Russian anti-satellite test, but probably a few scales larger in terms of the amount of debris it would generate,” Jah said.

As of the end of August, SpaceX was still awaiting final regulatory approval for the test flight from the US Federal Aviation Administration, which regulates American commercial space launches.

“The FAA is responsible for the safety oversight of licensed commercial space vehicle launch and re-entry operations,” the FAA told the South China Morning Post in August. “Our safety oversight authority does not extend to in-orbit activities.”

The Russian satellite – which had a radius of around 2.5 metres (eight feet) and weighed some two tonnes – produced 1,500 trackable pieces of debris and hundreds of thousands more smaller fragments, according to National Geographic.

The reusable Starship launch system consists of a powerful 72-metre first-stage booster called the Super Heavy, which separates from the upper stage of the rocket after launch and does not reach orbit.

The 52-metre, 100-tonne upper stage of the rocket – known as the Starship – is designed to reach orbit. Both rocket stages are designed to be reusable and to be caught on Earth by a tower with “chopstick” arms.

A variant of the Starship called the human landing system (HLS) was selected to take part in Nasa’s Artemis programme, which aims to bring American astronauts to the lunar surface for the first time since the end of the Apollo missions in 1972.

After astronauts launch from Earth aboard the Orion spacecraft, the Starship HLS, or Blue Origin’s Blue Moon landing system, will ferry astronauts to and from the lunar surface.

To escape Earth’s gravity and reach the moon, the Starship HLS will reportedly need to be fuelled with around 1,500 tonnes of liquid oxygen and liquid methane propellant.

This will involve multiple docking missions in low-Earth orbit using depot and fuel tanker variants of the Starship.

SpaceX has had a string of incidents involving the launch system in recent years, including in April 2023 when two rocket stages failed to separate and exploded, and in June last year when a Starship upper stage blew up on a test stand.

Asked if there was any cause for concern given SpaceX’s track record, Jah said: “The fact that we’re launching it, the fact that the thing can explode, makes it a possibility. So, it needs to be of concern.”

An explosion could potentially send a cloud of bullet-like shrapnel into low-Earth orbit.

Jah said rocket bodies owned by the US had previously exploded in higher, geostationary transfer orbits where there was still a debris risk.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

According to the European Space Agency, the main cause of orbital explosions is residual fuel left in tanks and fuel lines or other energy sources. Over time, the mechanical integrity of spacecraft parts can degrade, leading to leaks or fuel mixing that triggers self-ignition.

Starship’s planned test flight – which was originally slated for August and is now expected in mid-September – will be an attempt to launch the spacecraft into orbit. Previous attempts have only reached suborbital trajectories.

According to the FAA website, protecting public safety during launches is central to its licencing and approval process.

The US, China and Russia are all parties to the Outer Space Treaty, a basic framework for international space law that took effect in 1967.

According to Article 7 of the treaty, any state that launches a space object is internationally liable for compensation for any damage the object causes to another state on Earth or in space.

Ella Atkins, a professor of aerospace engineering at Virginia Tech, said the primary Starship explosion risk lay in the booster, which did not enter orbit.

She said that once Starship or any other payload entered low-Earth orbit, there was a risk of collision when its orbit was not coordinated with other space objects or junk. That made it “critical” for launch authorities and companies to coordinate and collaborate.

“All space missions pose a risk of collision. On-orbit testing and refuelling are unlikely to generate anything close to the space junk problem amassed over all objects that persist in orbit today,” Atkins said.

She noted that the high orbiting speeds required for objects to counter Earth’s gravity were dependent on Earth’s mass rather than on spacecraft mass. Because of this speed, every orbiting object posed a risk to other objects.

“It is therefore critical that no orbiting object hit another orbiting object, regardless of the two objects’ mass or relative masses,” she said.

When a debris-generating event occurs in Earth’s orbit, it poses a threat to nearby satellites and spacecraft. Over time, fragments disperse across orbital lanes, with some of the debris being pulled down by atmospheric drag to burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere.

Across the history of space travel, thousands of launches have resulted in tens of thousands of tracked objects in orbit, including both spacecraft and debris, according to the European Space Agency.

Many more pieces of space debris are too small to track.

According to a paper published in the peer-reviewed Chinese-language Journal of Astronautics in May, space debris is a big factor in the safety of missions.

Researchers from Sun Yat-sen University and Northwestern Polytechnical University pointed to a 2016 incident where the solar panels of the ESA Sentinel-1A satellite were struck by a centimetre-sized piece of debris, creating a 40cm (16-inch) impact crater.

They also noted an incident in November, when a window of the Shenzhou-20 spacecraft docked at China’s Tiangong space station was struck by a tiny piece of debris, delaying the return of astronauts.

The rapid growth of internet megaconstellations in Earth’s orbit, driven by SpaceX’s Starlink, has added to the issue of debris, according to the paper.

Starlink’s more than 11,000 satellites in orbit have to perform hundreds of thousands of collision-avoidance manoeuvres each year to get out of the path of debris and other spacecraft.

Orbital crowding has meanwhile led to concerns about Kessler Syndrome – a theoretical scenario where the density of objects in orbit becomes so high that collisions could create a chain reaction, making certain orbital regions unusable.

According to Jah, no evidence has led him to believe that an uncontrolled event in space would continue ad infinitum. “Even if cascading does happen, at some point an equilibrium state will be achieved because Mother Nature is always seeking some form of equilibrium,” he said.

Jah said more coordination and planning would be needed as the number of satellite constellations rose.

He said it could be comparable to the International Telecommunication Union’s role in distributing spectrum – the frequencies and wavelengths used for wireless communication between space and ground.

“If something similar could be done for orbital carrying capacity or something like that, I think that could be useful,” Jah said, referring to the maximum number of space objects in a specific orbital region.

“The first come, first served sort of thing is very colonial, very extractive, exploitative,” he said. “SpaceX pretty much has a monopoly in low-Earth orbit. That, and rightfully so, upsets other countries and entities.”

Jah said the incentive for better coordination was long-term sustainability. But in the near term, he said the three powers dominating space traffic – the US, China, and Russia – wanted “unlimited freedom of action” and it was unlikely they would sign a treaty to manage such issues.

item.title: [SCMP] In flood-hit Philippines, ‘out of touch’ Marcos slammed for private birthday serenade
item.description:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s birthday serenade for his wife might have been a private gesture, but as floodwaters overwhelmed much of Luzon – the country’s largest and most populous island and home to the capital Manila – a viral clip of him singing became a public-relations crisis.

Observers told This Week in Asia that Marcos’ celebration of his wife, Marie Louise “Liza” Araneta-Marcos, on her 67th birthday struck the wrong chord with a public already angered by deadly floods, the government’s handling of disaster relief and long-running allegations of corruption in flood-control projects.

By August 26, when Marcos quietly staged his wife’s party with a live band attended by family, close friends and political allies, Manila was almost at a standstill after days of heavy rain.
item.content:encoded:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s birthday serenade for his wife might have been a private gesture, but as floodwaters overwhelmed much of Luzon – the country’s largest and most populous island and home to the capital Manila – a viral clip of him singing became a public-relations crisis.

Observers told This Week in Asia that Marcos’ celebration of his wife, Marie Louise “Liza” Araneta-Marcos, on her 67th birthday struck the wrong chord with a public already angered by deadly floods, the government’s handling of disaster relief and long-running allegations of corruption in flood-control projects.

By August 26, when Marcos quietly staged his wife’s party with a live band attended by family, close friends and political allies, Manila was almost at a standstill after days of heavy rain.

Online responses sarcastically thanked the president and government for the scandal-hit flood-control projects under his watch.

Two days later, a video of Marcos crooning “You” and “I Love Her” to his wife, taken by one of the party guests, Vigan City Mayor Bonito Singson, surfaced on social media.

The clip soon went viral and several comments beneath one widely shared repost framed the video as proof of Marcos’ detachment. “No empathy,” one user wrote, while another called the president “out of touch” and a third said: “He really knows his priorities.”

The national weather bureau Pagasa had earlier predicted strong monsoon rains for most of the week, enhanced by the near convergence of at least four cyclones, typhoons, tropical depressions and low-pressure areas.

Rain had been falling almost nonstop since the middle of August, prompting Pagasa to issue multiple flood warnings, including the most severe Red alerts, late into the night.

At least 33 people have died in various parts of the country because of the floods, according to the Office of Civil Defence, including a man who fell into an open street manhole concealed by raging waters in the central Luzon province of Pampanga.

The backlash over the singing clip came despite Marcos staging photo events where he handed out ayuda (government flood aid) in the form of cash and goods and inspected flood-control pumping stations and dykes.

A statement issued over the weekend by presidential communications undersecretary Claire Castro did little to stem the criticism.

“The President is the President wherever he is,” Castro said in Filipino. “His devoting a few hours for his family does not mean his responsibility towards the nation stops and government operations stop. In the midst of severe rains, his monitoring and orders to agencies to ensure the safety and swift aid to our countrymen have continued.”

For Dr Pamela Cajilig, a disaster anthropologist at the University of the Philippines, the criticisms against Marcos “show that citizens do not compartmentalise their expectations of a public servant of the highest order from that of a family man”.

She said repeated disasters had taught Filipinos to expect that politicians and bureaucrats demonstrate kapwa (concern for others) that went beyond just handing out ayuda.

“This means seeing oneself in their constituents – feeling the latter’s pain as they struggle – and sincerely demonstrating that,” Cajilig, who is also an architect and urban designer, told This Week in Asia.

“This expectation of pakikipagkapwa [brotherly concern] is heightened by the deep distrust generated by the perceived lack of accountability and transparency in the flood-control programme.”

Marcos’ staging of festivities amid a national tragedy, therefore, offended “a related collective value that is at stake: malasakit [compassion]”, Cajilig said. “Malasakit requires acting out of an ethics of care for your kapwa who is suffering, often at the cost of personal sacrifice.”

Public anger over the floods was also sharpened by a wider loss of trust in Marcos’ handling of flood-control projects at the centre of corruption allegations. Recent surveys showed broad dissatisfaction regarding corruption, accountability and the president’s own role in the controversy.

Momentum Research founding CEO Cleve Arguelles told This Week in Asia that Marcos’ singing video invited such scathing attacks because “political images are interpreted through the public mood in which they circulate”.

“On its own, a president singing for his wife is ordinary and even potentially endearing. But President Marcos is currently operating in a very unfavourable political environment,” said Arguelles, who also teaches political science at the University of the Philippines.

He pointed to Momentum’s latest survey in August, which found only 36.4 per cent satisfied with Marcos’ performance and 57.4 per cent dissatisfied, as well as its July poll showing “overwhelming dissatisfaction” with the administration’s handling of corruption in flood-control projects.

“So the video encounters a public already predisposed to read presidential behaviour critically,” Arguelles said.

The floods had acquired political meaning because they were now closely associated in the public imagination with “allegations of corruption, failed or nonexistent flood-control projects, and questions about government competence”, he added.

“So the timing of the video’s circulation makes the contrast especially powerful: images of people struggling through floodwaters alongside images of the president singing at a private celebration.”

While the events did not happen simultaneously, “social media collapses that chronology into a single political image”, Arguelles said.

“The larger problem is therefore not really that Marcos sang for his wife. It is that, amid widespread frustration and suffering over floods and corruption, the video provided an unusually vivid image onto which that frustration could be projected.”

Vic Rodriguez, a political ally of Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio, criticised the administration for “[worsening] the sufferings of the lives of ordinary people” by failing to ensure “full accountability” over flood-control funds.

He said critics were justified in demanding “transparency on how the average annual budget of 227 billion pesos for flood control was utilised”, as well as accountability for those who had allegedly misused public funds.

Rodriguez also noted that Marcos had spent 1.333 trillion pesos for flood-control projects from 2023 to 2025 but that “has not in any way mitigated any of the supposed flooding that it was meant to address […] making the misery on the lives of the hundreds of thousands [of] affected citizens unbearable”.

For University of the Philippines political scientist Dr Jean Franco, “the optics of the president having a good time at a time when the country is reeling from floods is not good” given Marcos’ position.

“He is accountable to the public in need of answers and assistance,” Franco said, noting that if the party could not be postponed, Marcos’ staff should have barred people from taking pictures and videos.

Franco said the criticisms were directed at Marcos’ “perceived insensitivity” in light of the corruption scandal.

“They were made not because they want to deprive the president from being a devoted husband but because the public is seeking accountability and empathy from the country’s highest official.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will a new insurance scheme get China’s ageing population the long-term care it needs?
item.description:
Wu Boyao was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease 26 years ago. Now 86, he lives with his wife and one of their two daughters in a suburb straddling the border between the eastern Chinese cities of Shanghai and Suzhou.

Originally from Shanghai, they moved to the area – which is administered by Suzhou – in search of a larger home. The trade-off was that Wu would no longer qualify for home care service sessions that were almost free.

A decade ago, Shanghai was one of the first cities in China to roll out a pilot long-term care insurance (LTCI) scheme. Wu, who by then was largely dependent on others for daily functionality, had his application approved.
item.content:encoded:
Wu Boyao was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease 26 years ago. Now 86, he lives with his wife and one of their two daughters in a suburb straddling the border between the eastern Chinese cities of Shanghai and Suzhou.

Originally from Shanghai, they moved to the area – which is administered by Suzhou – in search of a larger home. The trade-off was that Wu would no longer qualify for home care service sessions that were almost free.

A decade ago, Shanghai was one of the first cities in China to roll out a pilot long-term care insurance (LTCI) scheme. Wu, who by then was largely dependent on others for daily functionality, had his application approved.

The social security fund covered the lion’s share of the cost, leaving him with a token co-payment of just 6 yuan (88 US cents) a session. In exchange, he received daily one-hour visits from a carer who helped with bathing, foot and nail care, massages and other tasks.

“It was a short service, but eased the burden for the family,” said his daughter Jenny Wu, who lives with him.

But because local governments’ financing and payment arrangements are separate, that arrangement ceased after the family crossed the municipal border, even though Suzhou has also been piloting its own LTCI system in recent years.

Wu is one of more than 40 million frail or cognitively impaired older adults in China, and among the first to use social insurance specifically designed for the needs of the country’s rapidly greying population. But coverage remains far from complete.

The LTCI programme is a government-led system to cover the costs of daily living support and basic care for functionally disabled senior citizens. Funded jointly by individuals, employers and fiscal subsidies, similar models have been in place for decades in a handful of other countries, including Germany, Japan and South Korea.

After 10 years of pilot programmes spanning more than 90 cities, the central government announced in March that it would expand the initiative nationwide, establishing a system covering all residents by 2028.

While building a long-term care system could spur new industries, create jobs and boost consumption in a slowing Chinese economy, researchers say the country faces challenges that have yet to be fully confronted: a breakneck pace of ageing, stark regional economic disparities, and per capita GDP levels that remain a fraction of those in more developed economies.

Ensuring the fund’s sustainability and providing sufficient professional carers will also be headaches, they added.

“China is still in a phase of economic transition, with uneven development between regions and between urban and rural areas, and very uneven affordability,” said Wu Bei, a professor of public health and expert in gerontology at NYU Shanghai.

“While Shanghai may have a fair number of nursing homes and care facilities, it may be quite difficult to find one in the central and western regions, or rural areas,” she said, adding that caring for rural “empty-nest” seniors – those whose adult children have left home – presented one of the biggest challenges.

Last week, Chinese lawmakers incorporated language on LTCI into a Healthcare Security Law that will take effect from the beginning of next year, including a line saying the country will “establish and improve” a long-term care insurance system.

According to guidelines issued by the central government in March, payments for the nationwide system will be split between workers and their employers. For those without jobs, the costs will be covered by the individual and government subsidies. Once a contributor is assessed and certified as being in a state of disability for more than six months, they will be able to apply for insurance benefits to receive care services either in a nursing home or at home.

Only a small portion of contributors to the pilot schemes have benefited so far. They covered 308 million people around the country last year, but only 1.93 million received benefits, according to data released by the National Healthcare Security Administration in July.

China had about 36 million senior citizens with disabilities and 17 million with dementia at the end of last year, according to a report issued recently by the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, the country’s top political advisory body.

That number is expected to surge as population ageing deepens. By the end of last year, there were over 223 million people aged 65 or older in China, accounting for around 16 per cent of the population, according to data from the Ministry of Civil Affairs.

It is on track to become a “super-aged” society by the early 2030s, when those 65 or older will account for 20 per cent of the population, according to a United Nations estimate.

Globally, social insurance is not the mainstream model for providing long-term care for the elderly.

They’re not used to buying insurance – if they don’t get a payout, they feel cheated

He Wenjiong, Zhejiang University

Systems in northern Europe primarily rely on public finance supported by high taxation, with local governments responsible for the delivery of services. In the United States, a combination of public aid and commercial insurance is used.

He Wenjiong, a professor at Zhejiang University who specialises in social security, said it could solve some problems but could not be expected to solve them all, due to a lack of mature international experience and the absence of an “insurance gene” in Chinese cultural tradition.

“Our society lacks a culture of mutual aid,” said He, who took part in preliminary research on China’s LTCI system. “Many people prefer to save money and get back their principal with interest. But they’re not used to buying insurance – if they don’t get a payout, they feel cheated.”

At the current, early stage, contribution levels are relatively low. A worker earning 10,000 yuan (US$1,487) a month needs to pay 15 yuan a month, with their employer matching that amount, according to the central government’s guidelines.

For rural residents and unemployed urban residents, if the local per capita disposable income from the previous year was 40,000 yuan – close to the national average last year – the annual contribution is set at 60 yuan, split equally between the individual and government subsidies.

But He said even such seemingly low rates would be unaffordable for many rural residents, and called for full government coverage for those unable to pay.

In countries such as Germany and Japan, LTCI premiums are dynamically adjusted rather than fixed to ensure the insurance fund’s sustainability.

But sustaining these funds over the long term is no easy job. In June, Germany’s Health Ministry published a draft law designed to overhaul the country’s financially strained LTCI system, which is facing a multibillion-euro deficit, with proposed changes including raising the contribution assessment ceiling for higher earners and imposing stricter qualification criteria for lower care levels.

“A few decades ago, we predicted that China would grow old before it grew rich,” said Wu of NYU Shanghai. “Today, we might say it’s at least growing old while growing rich.”

While noting that the system used in the US had its own problems, she said its idea of a multi-tiered, income-based safety net was worth learning from.

Her research shows that in the US, public funding – primarily Medicaid and Medicare – accounts for nearly 70 per cent of long-term care spending, with commercial insurance covering about 10 per cent and out-of-pocket expenses making up the remaining 20 per cent.

Following a similar strategy, she said China should prioritise basic needs and direct more fiscal support to low-income families, while providing affluent households with diversified, personalised private insurance or high-end nursing homes.

She said another step China could take would be offering more support to family carers. That could include the provision of adult day care centres, which would allow a family carer to work half a day instead of having to devote all their time to a disabled relative.

Jenny Wu said that was critical. As her mother – her father’s primary carer – gets older and weaker, she has had to take on more duties.

“I quit my job before retirement age and now take flexible work at home for lower pay to care for my family,” she said.

Her experience since moving to the suburbs made her realise that at-home care services are, for now, still largely an urban privilege.

Though they could not use the LTCI system in Suzhou, the local government offered a separate subsidy programme that was similar in principle and covered both in-home and nursing-home care.

“But in reality, when I placed orders, no carer accepted them,” she said. “The suburbs are too far away – travelling an hour for a one-hour visit just isn’t worth it for them.

“For users, one hour is also too short. You still have to have someone home to open the door – disabled people can’t – and there’s not even enough time for the family carer to make a round trip to the supermarket.”

According to government data, China, with its tens of millions of disabled elderly people, had just 13,000 designated long-term care service institutions last year and 402,800 care workers.

Zhejiang University’s He said the government’s push for LTCI was partly intended to boost employment.

“There will be some kind of positive impact on the job market anyway – at least some people who could not afford a carer before can now hire one,” he said. “But the jobs created are unstable and low-quality.”

Most people employed as carers nowadays were less educated and older than those in other fields, but some vocational schools had expanded elderly care programmes to bring in younger workers in recent years.

“In the long run, things will improve,” He said. “But in the short term, it’s bleak – many graduates leave their positions within a short time of being hired. Retention is relatively low. The work is demanding, but benefits are not proportional.”

That is an almost universal phenomenon.

In more than one-third of Japanese households where care was provided at home, both the carer and the care recipient were aged 75 or older – a phenomenon known as “elderly-to-elderly caregiving” – the country’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare said last month, adding that was a record high.

Despite all the challenges, Wu said ageing should not be seen only as a burden, arguing that for China it was also a strategic opportunity.

“If done right, it could professionalise the care industry, create many jobs, and boost economic development,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] How a tree in Hanoi points to flowering of dissent among Vietnam’s Gen Z
item.description:
A tree in Hanoi has become a symbol of how Vietnam’s Gen Z views its country – but it is not the enviable growth story sold by the government.

Tree 55 on Nguyen Huy Tu Street – now dubbed the “Justice Tree” – was buried under bouquets earlier this month. It was an act of digital-age defiance over the death of a teenager in a road traffic accident in the area that went unpunished.

Response to the accident, which triggered a belated explanation from the state, reveals unease with a system many young Vietnamese no longer believe can deliver on its socialist promises, analysts say.

A tree in Hanoi has become a symbol of how Vietnam’s Gen Z views its country – but it is not the enviable growth story sold by the government.

Tree 55 on Nguyen Huy Tu Street – now dubbed the “Justice Tree” – was buried under bouquets earlier this month. It was an act of digital-age defiance over the death of a teenager in a road traffic accident in the area that went unpunished.

Response to the accident, which triggered a belated explanation from the state, reveals unease with a system many young Vietnamese no longer believe can deliver on its socialist promises, analysts say.

The Communist Party is seen to be cracking down on free expression since the rise of To Lam, a former police chief who is now both president and party general secretary – perhaps the most powerful Vietnamese leader in decades.

The national narrative is one of a Southeast Asian nation on the rise, with region-topping economic growth and an international profile to match. But there is also simmering discontent from its 100 million population – especially from youth, connected to parts of the internet even one of the world’s tightest surveillance regimes is slow to reach.

Tree No 55 is a case in point. Last May, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy and her father were hit by a BMW that swerved into their lane. The seriously wounded teenager died 10 days before her high school graduation exam.

State-controlled media initially identified the driver as a 64-year-old man with the initials NSC. Rumours circulated that they stood for Nguyen Sy Cuong, a former Vietnam National Assembly deputy and husband of a high-ranking party official.

The case went quiet for a year – until social media users revived it with memes about impunity and injustice. Virtual rebellion turned into real-life tributes as masked citizens laid flowers by the tree at the accident spot.

Alarmed by the spontaneous public protest, Vietnamese authorities sent uniformed officers to cordon off the tree. Then, on August 17, they took the rare step of confirming the driver was Cuong – adding that his contrition was enough to avoid punishment.

For many young Vietnamese the admission fell well short of accountability.

“Justice is nonexistent. The rich and powerful can seal themselves off from the consequences of their actions,” claimed Nam*, 27, a Canada-based activist who uses Threads to organise political events.

Social media – particularly Meta Platforms’ Threads – has helped the younger generation express their discontent.

Threads “allows the youth to come together and occupy it easily, creating a culture sphere of their own”, said Susann Pham, a German-based researcher on Vietnam’s social movements, civil society and politics.

“Threads also gives them some sort of anonymous identity compared to Facebook, where your network, your face, your family members might be easily seen.”

The teenager’s death provided “an emotional identity – a hook – that the younger generation can jump on”, she added. “They can easily identify with the victim.”

Gen Z rise

From India’s ‘’cockroach’’ movement to revolutions in Nepal and Bangladesh, angry Gen Z protesters have proved to be powerful challengers to governments that had seemed firmly entrenched.

While experts say opposition in Vietnam is a long way from turning into a similar threat – and a critical culture may stay in the digital world – the gripes of its youth are building.

“Vietnam is also at an inflection point right now,” said Phil Robertson, the director of Asian Human Rights and Labour Advocates. “The economy is growing rapidly, but there is a widening gap between the rich and the poor, the connected and the disconnected, between party members and the ordinary people.”

Even as the government aims for 10 per cent annual growth over coming years, anger is stirring in Gen Z over stagnant wages, rising property prices, pollution, corruption and environmental destruction.

Gia*, a 26-year-old university graduate, earns 10 million dong (US$400) a month teaching English in a northern province. Even double that in Hanoi would not be enough to cover her cost of living, she said, locking her out from home ownership, a key metric of a middle class that is supposed to be surfing the country’s wave of growth.

“There should be a range of affordable choices for people who want to settle,” she said.

In Vietnam, average monthly wages are around 9 million dong. Yet Hanoi homes cost around 123 million dong per square metre – meaning that people, even university graduates, would have to work their whole life to afford a small flat.

“One of the biggest issues facing us right now is the wages of everyday people. They are very low and creating a lot of pressure on the population,’’ said Nam, who is studying business in Canada.

That struggle, juxtaposed against Vietnam’s surging economy, with its luxury malls and supercars, has raised awkward questions of the government’s core narrative.

“I always thought we were living in a communist country, but now I see that it operates pretty much like a capitalist one, and a very ruthless one at that,’’ said Linh*, a 24-year-old now based in the UK.

Vietnam in the past decade has deployed 10,000-strong military cyber-troops, known as Force 47, to fight off “wrongful information and anti-state propaganda”.

Since To Lam became president in April, his government has stepped up its censorship and crackdown on dissent. Vietnamese journalist Le Anh Hung was arrested in March for “propagandising against the state”, while rapper MCK had to pull out over half the tracks on a new album after being approached by authorities “over sensitive content” and vulgar language.

“Gen Z is critical of elites and children of elites … and in the short term: the censoring of the rapper – or the censoring of Gen Z culture – is felt like a personal insult to their identity,” Pham added.

Mounting state repression is butting up against the aspirations of Vietnam’s politically aware youth, according to Robertson.

“Authorities can repress it this time but it is going to keep coming up. You can’t have elite systems that operate in the dark with impunity,” he said.

*Nicknames have been changed to protect identities

item.title: [SCMP] Visa policy brings in more foreigners on short-term jobs and HK$20,000 salaries
item.description:
About 80 per cent of the foreign nationals granted working visas under Hong Kong’s General Employment Policy (GEP) last year were hired on short-term contracts, while nearly half of successful applicants earned less than HK$20,000 (US$2,564) a month.

According to the latest Immigration Department data, 31,278 GEP working visas for foreigners were approved last year. Mainland Chinese residents cannot apply to the scheme.

While the figure marked the second consecutive year the scheme had cleared the 30,000-level, the number was still shy of the more than 40,000 recorded annually in 2018 and 2019.
item.content:encoded:
About 80 per cent of the foreign nationals granted working visas under Hong Kong’s General Employment Policy (GEP) last year were hired on short-term contracts, while nearly half of successful applicants earned less than HK$20,000 (US$2,564) a month.

According to the latest Immigration Department data, 31,278 GEP working visas for foreigners were approved last year. Mainland Chinese residents cannot apply to the scheme.

While the figure marked the second consecutive year the scheme had cleared the 30,000-level, the number was still shy of the more than 40,000 recorded annually in 2018 and 2019.

The latest statistics showed that 79.7 per cent of successful candidates, or 24,929, held short-term positions or jobs lasting less than a year. Among those granted visas, 47.5 per cent, or 14,850, were earning below HK$20,000 a month.

The proportion of approved applicants holding short-term contracts last year also marked an increase from 72.1 per cent in 2024 and 64 per cent in 2023.

The data also showed 13,640 GEP visas were approved in the first half of this year, with 68.6 per cent on short-term contracts and 49.8 per cent earning less than HK$20,000.

Alexa Chow Yee-ping, managing director of human resources consultancy ACTS Consulting, attributed the uptick in GEP visa holders taking on short-term work to the government’s mega-events drive to stimulate fresh economic growth.

“As an international city, Hong Kong needs to create its own character to retain its attractiveness and charm. Not just focus on properties and finance. We need [economic] diversification,” she said.

The department said the GEP also had a new “creative industry and performing arts services” category since April 1, with 2,340 applications approved so far.

Chow said such applicants could be performers and crew for mega-events, which also brought valuable experience to local people in event production.

Despite the temporary nature of the jobs, Chow said that such talent still benefited Hong Kong economically as mega-events drove growth in tourism, catering, retail and hospitality.

Earlier this month, the government revealed that about 1.75 million visitors were drawn to more than 130 major events between January and June this year, generating around HK$5.8 billion in spending and contributing HK$3.3 billion to the economy.

In terms of industry, the sports and recreation sector accounted for the highest number of GEP applicant approvals, at 4,517, followed by arts and culture, academic research and education, financial services, and commerce and trade.

Gordon Yau Yick-chung, a sports public relations leader and chairman of concern group Hong Kong Fitness Guide, which closely monitors sports industrialisation, said the actual number of sports events could be higher than the public knew.

“I am not surprised. The figures reflected the trend of more sports competitions held in Hong Kong, to the extent that sometimes we may not notice [a match was held],” he said.

Yau said that apart from recent high-profile friendly matches featuring European football teams, there had been many small and large international sports events and competitions in the city.

Such events included baseball, wrestling and golf as well as emerging sports such as pickleball, he said, adding that some were organised by shopping centres to draw visitors.

He said many of these international competitions hired overseas judges and organisers, while global sports icons invited for commercial events would bring their managers and entourage, creating short-term visa applications.

In terms of location, South Korea accounted for the largest proportion of approved GEP applicants last year, at 17.6 per cent.

The number of South Koreans approved for the visas surpassed 5,500 annually in 2024 and 2025, representing a surge of nearly 85 per cent from 2019.

This momentum also carried into the first half of 2026, with South Korea accounting for the largest number of approved GEP candidates, at 2,226, followed by Japan with 1,974.

Korean Sky Lee Sang-ju, 25, said he came to Hong Kong in 2024 to teach taekwondo at NRG Taekwondo Korea despite not finishing his final year at university.

The 25-year-old said he chose Hong Kong over the United States and Canada because of its lower taxes and better salaries, in addition to its more systematic and well-organised working environment.

He added that his employer had provided him with professional development, including customer relationship management training, something that was rarely offered at traditional taekwondo schools in South Korea.

The vibrant local Korean community and widespread appreciation of K-pop culture among locals had also helped him adapt to life in Hong Kong, Lee said.

“I like Hong Kong, and I hope to stay here in the long term,” he said.

Lee said that after completing his university degree through distance learning, he encouraged classmate Jerry Kim Seong-hun, 26, to come and teach at the same school last year.

Kim said he enjoyed working in Hong Kong as the work culture back home was more “conservative” and stressed seniority.

Chang Hyo-suk, general manager of the Korean Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, said he had noticed many more Koreans coming to work in the city in recent years due to the geographical proximity, low taxes and minimal regulations.

He said that many Koreans worked in the city’s trading industry, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises or start-ups.

Roy Ying Fai, co-chair of the Hong Kong Institution of Human Resource Management’s advocacy and policy research committee, attributed the growth to the “Dedicated Team for Attracting Businesses and Talent” government initiative.

The policy, which launched in 2022, seeks to attract talent through the city’s overseas Economic and Trade Offices, including its Tokyo branch.

He added that Hong Kong was still attractive to financial talent, pointing to the boom in initial public offerings and the growing presence of family offices.

“Hong Kong is attractive to them. First, it is easy to find a job. Second, the tax is low. Third, if they want to apply for permanent residence, it is relatively easier than in Singapore,” he said.

But the Japanese consulate in Hong Kong said it had not observed an increasing trend in the number of Japanese nationals in the city following the Covid-19 pandemic, citing its own figures.

Meanwhile, the number of approved visas for British and US nationals, the two top demographics before the pandemic, recorded significant drops.

Last year, 2,472 British and 2,121 Americans were granted GEP visas to work in Hong Kong, a fall of 53.2 per cent and 47.9 per cent, respectively, from 2019.

Australians accounted for 883 applicants last year, a drop of 48.7 per cent from 2019.

Chow, the human resources consultant, said the downward trend reflected the geopolitical tensions between China and the West.

“Under this relatively hostile sentiment, the whole situation changed. Governments’ stances changed. Media coverage [on China] changed … How would I move to [China] for development?” she said.

But the British Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong said that the GEP figures alone failed to provide a complete picture, adding that a significant proportion of senior executives and graduates from top UK universities now entered the city under another policy, the Top Talent Pass Scheme.

The business chamber noted that the number of UK GEP approvals had increased steadily each year since 2023 and the number of UK-parented companies in Hong Kong had also grown by 20 per cent between 2023 and 2025, while the country remained the city’s largest corporate presence among European nations.

“British businesses are not just returning; they are adapting and expanding their presence to access the Greater Bay Area and wider Asia-Pacific opportunities from Hong Kong,” it said.

Government figures also showed rents for flats, as well as the number of international school applications, had increased as expatriates returned.

The private residential rental index, maintained by the Rating and Valuation Department, surged by 18.5 per cent as of June to 205.8 from the Covid-19 pandemic trough in January 2023.

Real estate services company JLL said that a primary driver of the increase was the “influx of expatriate professionals attracted by resurgent IPO activity and asset management business growth”.

The firm’s latest report, released earlier this month, showed that the overall grade A office vacancy rate fell to 12.8 per cent at the end of July, its lowest point in 31 months.

Education Bureau statistics also showed the number of places offered at international schools in Hong Kong rose by 4 per cent from 2023-24 to 2025-26, standing at 48,413.

Among those arriving in the city was Korean national Philip Jung, who was sent by his food industry company to lead the Hong Kong office in May.

The 36-year-old said he expected to spend three to five years working in the city, adding that his wife had come with him on a dependent visa.

Jung said the couple were expecting a baby next year and were considering having the child study in Hong Kong to learn English, Chinese and Korean.

“It is not easy to get in our home country,” he said.

Jung also said that while Hong Kong’s catering industry was struggling, he hoped it would gradually improve.

He added that his company expected him to help open up southern China and expand existing markets in Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam.

“Hong Kong is the platform for Asian markets, so there could be opportunities to make more business,” Jung said.

item.title: [SCMP] How the Nepal flash flood unleashed a wave of anti-China misinformation
item.description:
To scientists, the cause of this week’s deadly flash flood on the border between China and Nepal is clear: a glacier high on the Nepal side of the Himalayan range collapsed, sending catastrophic amounts of water and debris downstream.

Initial uncertainty over the cause of the event fuelled a wave of misinformation on social media, some of which pinned the blame for the event on Chinese-built infrastructure in the region.

But a war of information over China’s activities in the region continued to brew online even after Beijing and Kathmandu agreed on the scientific analysis.
item.content:encoded:
To scientists, the cause of this week’s deadly flash flood on the border between China and Nepal is clear: a glacier high on the Nepal side of the Himalayan range collapsed, sending catastrophic amounts of water and debris downstream.

Initial uncertainty over the cause of the event fuelled a wave of misinformation on social media, some of which pinned the blame for the event on Chinese-built infrastructure in the region.

But a war of information over China’s activities in the region continued to brew online even after Beijing and Kathmandu agreed on the scientific analysis.

When news of the flood broke, social media users began to speculate whether the cause of the event was natural or the result of human activity, with suggestions that the disaster had originated from the Chinese side of the border.

Some posts claimed that the flood was caused by the collapse of a Chinese dam in Tibet, while others blamed it on mega infrastructure projects in the region.

The social media account Nepal Correspondence, which claims to be a Nepal-based platform for investigative journalism, said in a post on Wednesday that the flash flood was caused by Chinese construction in the Himalayas.

“This is not only a purposeful ecological disaster but is cruel too,” the post read.

In another post on the same day, Tunku Varadarajan, an Indian-British journalist, said: “China will be the death of everyone and everything downstream of it. Literally, and metaphorically.”

In a preliminary assessment on Wednesday, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said the cause was a sudden release from a Tibetan river that had been blocked by an avalanche, Nepali news portal Republica reported.

Another report by the Kathmandu Post on Thursday, citing a technical report from the Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research, also said a flood had entered Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River from the Tibetan side.

However, satellite analysis later pointed authorities in Nepal and China – and further abroad – to a glacier collapse in Nepal, rather than Chinese infrastructure, as the cause.

The analysis indicated that the glacier collapse occurred on the Nepalese side of the mountains, near the Langtang Lirung peak.

Daniel Shugar, an earth scientist and associate professor at the University of Calgary, told The Guardian on Thursday that initial analysis showed a large chunk of ice at 5,200 metres (17,060 feet) above sea level had collapsed vertically, falling around 1.2km (0.74 miles) into the valley floor.

“This ice and rock then flowed into a river, turning into the devastating debris flow and flash flood that we see in the CCTV footage at the border,” said Bethan Davies, the chair of glaciology at Newcastle University, told the Science Media Centre on Thursday.

That same day, China’s Ministry of Natural Resources confirmed that the deadly mudslide was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal.

Some initially believed that the ice-rock avalanche had been caused by an earthquake, as the impact of the avalanche was so strong that it registered on seismographs as a magnitude 5.2 tremor.

Brahma Chellaney, an Indian geostrategist and columnist, referred to the earthquake claims in a social media post on Wednesday, saying that a moderate seismic event could trigger a cascading disaster.

He also linked the dangers to Chinese construction.

“This will renew global attention on China’s folly in persisting with the construction of the world’s largest dam in the middle of the Himalayan seismic zone,” he said, adding that its plan to build the dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in Tibet was a “water bomb in the making”.

In another post on Thursday, Chellaney wrote: “It is now clear that the Nepal disaster was caused by a natural trigger … but amplified by Chinese hydrological modifications and infrastructure footprint along the Tibetan side of the border.

“In other words, China’s upstream actions did not cause the glacier failure but contributed to the disaster’s severity and cascading impacts downstream.”

Scientists are still not sure exactly what triggered the initial glacier collapse, but catastrophic events like this have happened elsewhere in the region, including a glacier collapse and avalanche in India’s Chamoli district in 2021.

Shugar told Associated Press on Friday that clearer satellite images indicated the bedrock underneath the glacier might have also collapsed, which could explain the glacier collapse.

But that has not prevented a blame game over early warnings.

Republica quoted NDRRMA spokeswoman Shanti Mahat as saying the authority only learned about the disaster after the flood had reportedly already swept through Gyirong Port.

She said that a lack of timely information on the Tibetan side made it impossible to issue an early warning in Nepal.

Parshuram Kaphle, a Nepali journalist, echoed the sentiment in a social media post on Wednesday, saying China had “significantly undermined us”.

“By failing to provide early warning of such a massive disaster, we suffered immense loss of human life,” Kaphle wrote.

Ouyang Chaojun, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told state broadcaster CCTV that the debris flow was moving at about 40-50 metres per second (131-164 feet per second).

“Furthermore, because the debris flow reached the Gyirong border crossing in a very short time – only about 7 minutes – there was no time for evacuation,” he added.

Hydrologist Hannah Cloke, a professor at the University of Reading, told the Science Media Centre that high up in the valley near the source of the flood, early warnings were “exceptionally difficult, no matter how advanced the technology”.

The centre quoted a number of scientists as saying that while it was not known whether climate change was behind Wednesday’s collapse, warming was exacerbating the risk of catastrophic mountain failures and flooding due to melting glaciers, thawing permafrost, and increased meltwater run-off.

“A warming environment can make these kinds of events more common or likely,” Davies said.

Ouyang said that following the mudslide, some of the other slopes in the region had become unstable, making monitoring the region essential.

Concerns have been raised over a newly formed barrier lake upstream from Gyirong county that was formed by the landslide, which CCTV said on Friday was holding the equivalent of 1,000 Olympic swimming pools of water.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore’s blueprint for economic success: plan, but be prepared to adapt
item.description:
In the discussion on Hong Kong’s first ever five-year plan, much ink has been spilled on the merits of a planned economy. The most recent example of this was Anthony Rowley’s commentary that cited Singapore as an example of a highly successful planned economy.

Unfortunately, he misrepresents what planning in Singapore is about. There are lessons that Hong Kong can draw from how the Singapore government navigated a changing environment – but not the ones Rowley highlights.

It is quite understandable why an observer would view Singapore as a planned economy. After all, signs of order are all around. Nearly 80 per cent of Singaporeans live in public housing; the city is well-designed, green, and manicured. Clearly, this is a city that has been meticulously planned and engineered for decades.
item.content:encoded:
In the discussion on Hong Kong’s first ever five-year plan, much ink has been spilled on the merits of a planned economy. The most recent example of this was Anthony Rowley’s commentary that cited Singapore as an example of a highly successful planned economy.

Unfortunately, he misrepresents what planning in Singapore is about. There are lessons that Hong Kong can draw from how the Singapore government navigated a changing environment – but not the ones Rowley highlights.

It is quite understandable why an observer would view Singapore as a planned economy. After all, signs of order are all around. Nearly 80 per cent of Singaporeans live in public housing; the city is well-designed, green, and manicured. Clearly, this is a city that has been meticulously planned and engineered for decades.

Above all, Singapore’s politics is carefully managed by a ruling party that has been in power since 1959, and political dissent is often constrained by a paternalistic state.

But the idea of the Singapore economy as a top-down, dirigiste and planned one is a caricature at best. While various government agencies in Singapore engage in planning (loosely defined), the city state has never had five or 10-year plans, nor set production targets the way the Eastern bloc countries and China did.

Policies, not plans

Singapore’s first finance minister and deputy prime minister Goh Keng Swee was openly disdainful of socialist planning, saying that “planning as we know it has a limited value. Economic policy is more important”.

In economic policy, perhaps the most important difference between the Singapore economy and Hong Kong’s is the role of the state in industrial development.

Since the establishment of the Economic Development Board (EDB) in 1961, the Singapore state has promoted manufacturing as one of the key engines of the economy. Even today, manufacturing output comprises an astonishing 19 per cent of Singapore’s GDP, compared with less than 1 per cent in Hong Kong.

The EDB – or any other economic agency – has never produced five-year plans, so that cannot be the reason for Singapore’s success in industrialisation and industrial upgrading. But thanks to industrial policy, Singapore is a key node in global value chains in various high value-added industries such as electronics, petrochemicals, precision engineering, and pharmaceuticals and biotech to name a few.

The lesson from Singapore here is that five-year plans are much less important than specific policies that drive industrial diversification and upgrading.

A plan is simply a declaration of intent; whether that intent becomes reality depends on the right policies being formulated and how they are implemented. It is also quite common for governments to come up with bold visions and ambitious intents; what is much rarer is the capacity to execute change effectively.

With industrial policy, this means ensuring sound macroeconomic fundamentals and having the right microeconomic tools – such as tax incentives, foreign labour allowances, vocational training and worker upgrading programmes – to develop the desired industries.

But none of this was static or unchanging: external shocks and changing domestic conditions often necessitated changes to Singapore’s economic policies in ways that no five-year plan can foresee.

Quick to adapt

A second common error is to mistake the precision of the plan for its validity or quality. Even in a free-market economy like Hong Kong’s, there is a fascination bordering on obsession with setting precise targets or key performance indicators (KPIs) for government. The logic is that since much of what government does not lend itself easily to market metrics, targets or KPIs impose the necessary discipline on government.

This obsession is not always healthy. A target may be very precise, but it could also measure the wrong thing. This is not to diminish the value of planning, but to emphasise the importance of adapting quickly to changing conditions.

Being large bureaucracies, governments are often creatures of habit; their behaviours do not change quickly or easily even when circumstances require them to do so.

You just start it and hope for the best

Goh Keng Swee, Singapore’s first finance minister

When asked in 1992 if he had started out with a master plan in mind, Goh replied: “I had no initial vision. You just start it and hope for the best.” In many respects, Singapore’s economic success was the result of constant adaptation and improvisation.

For example, Singapore’s original economic plan was import-substitution industrialisation. This was one of the motivations for Singapore to join the newly established Malaysian federation in 1963 – to create a common market.

When Singapore separated from Malaysia in 1965, the plan was clearly no longer workable. Singapore adapted quickly and embraced export-oriented industrialisation, laying the foundations for the highly globalised economy it became a decade or so later.

Another example of adaptation was the practice of adjusting Central Provident Fund (CPF) contribution rates as a macroeconomic stabilisation tool. Singapore has, on various occasions, adjusted employer contribution rates in response to changes in macroeconomic conditions – lowering them to maintain cost competitiveness when faced with negative demand shocks, and raising them to deal with wage and inflation pressures.

Pay attention to process

Finally, the real value of a plan lies in the process rather than the plan itself.

A five-year plan is limited in at least two ways. First, the relatively short time horizon means that it is almost inevitable that the plan would be a collection of (achievable) goals that the various parts of the government have already set for themselves. It is unlikely to contain much that departs from existing priorities.

Second, because the emphasis of a five-year plan is to come up with specific deliverables, it is unlikely to catalyse a creative (re-)imagination of the future. Five-year plans are usually linear extrapolations of present trends, with targets adjusted marginally upwards to reflect the government’s enthusiasm in new areas – such as artificial intelligence.

Governments often overestimate their ability to change things in the short term but underestimate it over the long term. This bias informs Singapore’s approach to planning. Because much of what a government does on a routine basis is short term, the two main forms of planning that the Singapore government undertakes adopt a much longer time horizon. The emphasis is also on long-term strategy rather than near-term deliverables.

In city planning, for instance, the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s concept plan is reviewed once every decade and covers a time horizon of 50 years. Meanwhile, its master plan guides the city’s physical development over the next 10 to 15 years.

Since the turn of the century, the city state has also embraced scenario planning as a way of thinking (creatively) about the future.

Unlike five-year plans, the main goal of scenario planning is not to come up with a single plan for government with specific goals, targets or KPIs. Neither is scenario planning meant to produce predictions or forecasts. Instead, it is to generate distinct, plausible stories about the future (even if they seem improbable), question long-held assumptions, and surface the challenges and opportunities in the various scenarios.

Unlike five-year plans that are based on a particular view of the future, scenario planning is a much more divergent process that aims to anticipate various possible futures.

More recently, the Singapore government has expanded its capabilities in what it calls “futures thinking”.

It set up a Centre for Strategic Futures about a decade ago to “build a strategically agile public service ready to manage a complex and fast-changing environment”. The centre’s logo, with a black swan embedded, reflects its ambition to develop the government’s foresight and its ability to adapt.

This idea of planning as thinking creatively about the future is about as far as one can get from the world of five-year plans.

item.title: [SCMP] Small state, big agenda: Singapore prepares to steer Asean through crisis
item.description:
Every bloc needs a chair capable of getting things done – and Southeast Asia watchers say that description fits no country better than Singapore.

The city state will get the chance to prove it in the bloc’s 60th anniversary year, after it takes the Asean helm from the Philippines on January 1.

Speaking at Singapore’s National Day Rally on August 22, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the world was becoming more fractured and dangerous – one that the city state would have to “endure and survive for many years to come”.
item.content:encoded:
Every bloc needs a chair capable of getting things done – and Southeast Asia watchers say that description fits no country better than Singapore.

The city state will get the chance to prove it in the bloc’s 60th anniversary year, after it takes the Asean helm from the Philippines on January 1.

Speaking at Singapore’s National Day Rally on August 22, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the world was becoming more fractured and dangerous – one that the city state would have to “endure and survive for many years to come”.

“Our response cannot be to retreat and turn inward,” Wong said, calling for the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations to deepen integration “to create a more effective single market”.

A litany of headaches stand in the way of that ambition, from Myanmar’s civil war to an unresolved Thailand-Cambodia border row, simmering South China Sea tensions and keeping a distracted United States engaged with the region.

But if any country can rise to the challenge, it is Singapore, according to Thitinan Pongsudhirak, a professor of political science and international relations at Chulalongkorn University in Bangkok.

There was a joke among regional observers, he said, that Singapore should chair Asean every year, because “it is the most equipped despite its small size”.

Technocratic leadership

Singapore last chaired Asean in 2018, launching a smart cities network, spearheading efforts against transnational cybercrime and terrorism, and helping negotiators agree on a single, shared draft for a South China Sea code of conduct.

Analysts expect a similar chairmanship style this time around: efficient, unglamorous and results-driven.

“Compared with the Philippines, whose position as a South China Sea claimant gives it greater urgency on maritime security, Singapore is more likely to act as an honest broker and focus on institutional follow-through and economic integration,” said Joanne Lin, senior fellow and Asean Studies Centre coordinator at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

I would expect Singapore’s chairmanship to be more technocratic and implementation-oriented

Syaza Shukri, political scientist

A similar contrast can be drawn with Malaysia’s recent stewardship, according to Syaza Shukri, an associate professor of political science at the International Islamic University Malaysia.

“I would expect Singapore’s chairmanship to be more technocratic and implementation-oriented than some previous chairmanships, such as Malaysia’s, focusing more on normative and diplomatic agenda,” she said.

Singapore tended to emphasise deliverables, Syaza said, though its effectiveness would still depend on its ability to build consensus among member states.

Its greatest impact, in her view, will come in economic integration, trade resilience, energy and connectivity.

An economically fragmented bloc was more vulnerable to pressure from major powers, she said. “In that sense, Singapore’s economic agenda and its geopolitical agenda are really two sides of the same coin.”

‘Tangible effects’

Sharon Seah, principal fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, points to a scheme launched under Indonesia’s 2023 chairmanship as a concrete integration success: an interoperable QR code payment system linking the bloc’s national banks that is now working with WeChat, the Chinese super-app used by over a billion people for messaging, social media and mobile payments.

“Singapore can try to take this idea further with key Asean trading partners and promote a systems interoperability that can help millions of Asean small and medium-sized enterprises,” she said.

“This will be a very tangible effect of Asean payment systems integration.”

Lin sees another opening on trade: Singapore could push for a less fragmented regional response to US tariff pressures by cutting non-tariff barriers, simplifying customs and rules of origin procedures, and coordinating responses to trade diversion and transshipment concerns.

“I don’t think Singapore can solve Asean’s major crises, but it can try to sustain momentum, preserve common principles and leave Asean better coordinated and more resilient,” she said.

Underpinning this is decades of institutional muscle memory. As a founding member, Singapore has the bureaucratic capacity and personnel to manage the bloc’s machinery, not just chair its meetings.

“There is no doubt among the community of Asean observers that Singapore possesses strong agenda-setting powers and has able personalities who can steer the organisation at the various levels,” Seah said – borne out in this year’s State of Southeast Asia Survey, in which 31.3 per cent of respondents named Singapore the strongest leader on the bloc’s key challenges.

Conflicts of interest

For all the promise of economic statecraft, Singapore’s chairmanship will also be judged on harsher metrics – and few loom larger than Myanmar.

For Thitinan, success hinges on how the city state handles Myanmar’s civil war and what he calls its “civilian-disguised government after a bogus poll”.

Elections held between December and January were widely criticised as a junta-engineered sham to legitimise coup leader turned president, Min Aung Hlaing.

“If Min Aung Hlaing is readmitted after gaining recognition from Laos, Thailand, and Cambodia … then leaders of major dialogue partners might not join Asean-related summits next year,” Thitinan said, adding: “Min Aung Hlaing is Singapore’s chief challenge.”

Asean barred Myanmar’s generals from high-level meetings after the 2021 coup, but has since signalled willingness to welcome them back into the fold.

Singapore’s chairmanship would also be measured against the ongoing Thailand-Cambodia border row and South China Sea tensions, Thitinan said – as well as its ability to draw “the US back into the Asean fray in order to balance out China”.

On the South China Sea, Syaza said Singapore’s status as a non-claimant state cut both ways: no territorial stake made it a plausible broker of dialogue, but that same distance limited how far it could speak for claimant states like the Philippines and Vietnam.

Should the long-stalled Asean-China code of conduct for the disputed waterway remain unresolved by the end of the Philippines’ term, “Singapore could inherit the task”, she said.

No less consequential will be energy security. Asean’s heavy reliance on Middle Eastern oil and gas was laid bare this year by the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran, spotlighting the need to move away from fossil fuels.

“Asean needs to fast track the green energy transition,” said Pou Sothirak, a former Cambodian ambassador and now a senior adviser at the Cambodian Centre for Regional Studies, calling for the “practical adoption of renewable energy, including stronger and smarter grid interconnectivity”.

Like every Asean chair before it, Singapore will ultimately need to build consensus among member states with divergent interests to achieve its ambitions.

“Singapore’s unique convening powers will be tested in the year ahead,” Seah said.

item.title: [SCMP] India-China ties are warming, the time to capitalise is now
item.description:
When Ajit Doval met China’s top diplomat Wang Yi in June, New Delhi’s national security adviser called China and India “partners, not rivals” and said a stable relationship “serves the common interests of both sides”.

Wang, for his part, called for the two countries “to accelerate the resumption of dialogue mechanisms and promote exchanges” in trade, finance and other fields.

These warm statements were a sharp departure from the adversarial tone that had bedevilled ties since Chinese and Indian troops clashed at Galwan in the summer of 2020.
item.content:encoded:
When Ajit Doval met China’s top diplomat Wang Yi in June, New Delhi’s national security adviser called China and India “partners, not rivals” and said a stable relationship “serves the common interests of both sides”.

Wang, for his part, called for the two countries “to accelerate the resumption of dialogue mechanisms and promote exchanges” in trade, finance and other fields.

These warm statements were a sharp departure from the adversarial tone that had bedevilled ties since Chinese and Indian troops clashed at Galwan in the summer of 2020.

Before Galwan, Beijing and Delhi had been actively trying to repair a relationship frayed by frequent, low-level border clashes. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and China’s Xi Jinping met for a summit in Mamallapuram – a historic Indian port city with a long history of Buddhist exchanges with China – in October 2019, having already met in Wuhan the year before. But Galwan swept all that away.

It took five years of diplomatic and military negotiations to change the tone of the relationship again, culminating in a Modi-Xi summit on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation gathering in Tianjin last August.

That thaw has now provided an opportunity to revive the India-China Strategic Economic Dialogue (SED), the mechanism launched in 2011 by Manmohan Singh and Wen Jiabao that produced six rounds of talks before 2019.

India originally pushed for the SED to address its ballooning trade deficit with China. The dialogue’s working groups focused on six key areas: infrastructure (including Chinese investment in high-speed rail and railway modernisation), energy conservation and environmental protection, policy coordination, pharmaceuticals and hi-tech cooperation in AI, mobile technology and other areas.

The last meeting, in September 2019, ended on an upbeat note, with Delhi stating that the SED had “emerged as a crucial mechanism to facilitate bilateral trade and investment flows, and enhance economic cooperation”.

The big question now is whether it still can. The answer is probably yes, even though the world has changed dramatically since 2019. Disruptions to the multilateral trading system caused by US President Donald Trump’s tariffs and Washington’s weaponisation of trade, energy and finance have hurt China and India both.

But a revived SED would need a wider ambit in this newly fractured world and some long-standing issues still need to be addressed.

China must convincingly address Indian concerns about its aggressive trade and industrial policies, while India must clear the air regarding Chinese questions over targeted foreign investment restrictions.

India should also look at the trade deficit issue from a holistic perspective. A trade relationship defined by higher imports is not, on its own, detrimental. India has a trade deficit with partner countries like Japan and South Korea, for instance, but has secured export-oriented investment from them.

Hence, if India can grow its own manufacturing and export sectors, Chinese imports can become an asset rather than a liability. As Delhi expands export-oriented manufacturing – with the India-assembled iPhone, for example – it may well need to import more components and machinery from China, not less.

Vietnam shows how this can work: its trade deficit with China reached US$115 billion in 2025, up from US$83 billion the year before. Over the same period, its exports to the United States climbed from US$137 billion to US$194 billion. Imports and exports, in other words, can rise together.

The SED could help achieve such an outcome, steering Chinese capital into India’s export-led manufacturing. Delhi is already, albeit very cautiously, exploring the possibility of Chinese investment in non-sensitive sectors and its finance ministry has suggested export-oriented Chinese investment as a way of dealing with the trade imbalance.

With production costs rising at home, Chinese manufacturers may well find a lower-cost Indian base attractive – particularly as a springboard into South Asian, African and Middle Eastern markets. Handled well, such investment would let Chinese imports feed into greater Indian exports, creating mutually beneficial economic synergy.

India was once counting on the huge American consumer market to power its growth, but US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau made clear in March that Washington had learned its lesson, telling an audience in Delhi: “We are not going to make the same mistakes with India that we made with China 20 years ago.”

Washington was not “going to let you develop all these markets, and then, the next thing we know, you are beating us in a lot of commercial things”, he said at this year’s Raisina Dialogue in the Indian capital.

In this new, fractured world, India needs a new strategy to reach out to non-Western markets.

Harvard Professor Meg Rithmire and co-author Peter Cowhey have argued that the US should try to work with China to re-industrialise itself. If that logic holds for America, it holds for India too.

Closer economic cooperation with China could also open new markets in the Global South. There’s no doubt that most Global South countries would welcome closer cooperation between China and India, as it could help strengthen the world economy and improve the functioning of multilateral economic and financial institutions.

A new positive China-India economic synergy could profoundly help the wider Global South.

The time has clearly come for policymakers in both countries to understand that major win-win possibilities exist. If they both accept this, a revived SED can be more meaningful than the earlier rounds of sectoral dialogues.

That means returning to an earlier logic that characterised the bilateral relationship, based on the understanding that a pending resolution of the border issue and “peace and tranquillity” along the Line of Actual Control would allow the wider relationship to move forward.

The tone of ties has already shifted. The time to act has, decisively, arrived.

Sanjaya Baru is Distinguished Fellow, United Services Institution of India. He was adviser to Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and Director for Geo-economics & Strategy, International Institute of Strategic Studies. This article was published in coordination with the Asian Peace Programme (APP), an initiative to promote peace in Asia, housed in the NUS Asia Research Institute.

item.title: [SCMP] How the Philippines missed a Korean gambling racket worth US$3.8 billion
item.description:
The Philippines spent years dismantling Chinese-linked gambling compounds in dramatic, headline-grabbing raids.

But all the while, and with far less scrutiny, South Korean syndicates were building a parallel industry worth billions of US dollars – one that a spate of recent arrests suggests is still very much intact.

The most recent involved a 29-year-old Korean woman named Kim Young-sun, who authorities allege ran a network of 23 illegal online betting websites out of offices in Pasay and Quezon City that raked in an estimated 5.33 trillion won (US$3.8 billion) between November 2018 and this year.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines spent years dismantling Chinese-linked gambling compounds in dramatic, headline-grabbing raids.

But all the while, and with far less scrutiny, South Korean syndicates were building a parallel industry worth billions of US dollars – one that a spate of recent arrests suggests is still very much intact.

The most recent involved a 29-year-old Korean woman named Kim Young-sun, who authorities allege ran a network of 23 illegal online betting websites out of offices in Pasay and Quezon City that raked in an estimated 5.33 trillion won (US$3.8 billion) between November 2018 and this year.

Her arrest, announced on Monday, offered a rare glimpse into an underworld that has apparently thrived for years in the shadow of the much louder scandal surrounding Chinese-linked Philippine offshore gaming operators, or Pogos.
