For almost a decade, Pogos dominated the headlines. Compounds linked to Chinese syndicates were exposed for human trafficking, torture and fraud on a scale so shocking it triggered a congressional inquiry, presidential intervention and, eventually, a permanent ban.

But while investigators trained their attention on those operations, an analogous Korean criminal economy was expanding largely unnoticed. Kim’s arrest and a related case unsealed by police in Seoul just weeks earlier suggest this economy had grown far larger than most realised.

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency disclosed on August 12 that it had uncovered an illegal gambling operation using websites featuring child sexual abuse material to lure users to betting sites.

The syndicate behind it, traced to Pasay City and active from August 2019 until earlier this month, generated an estimated 47.6 billion won in revenue, while affiliated betting sites handled some 4.7 trillion won in wagers.

Two suspects, one already the subject of an Interpol Red Notice, were arrested and referred to prosecutors for alleged violations of child-protection and anti-pornography laws.

Taken together, the arrests sketch the outline of an industry hiding in plain sight: sophisticated, long-running and largely untouched by the Philippines’ anti-Pogo enforcement drive.

Hidden in plain sight

“The Chinese were sticking out like sore thumbs,” said Winston Casio, who until December served as a deputy director of Manila’s Presidential Anti-Organised Crime Commission (PAOCC).

“There were low-hanging fruits to be plucked … that worked to the Koreans’ advantage.”

Pogos – the formerly legally licensed offshore gambling firms that multiplied under former president Rodrigo Duterte – became the public face of the issue after President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr shut them down in 2024, citing links to organised crime, trafficking, fraud and money laundering. Lawmakers made the ban permanent a year later.

The accompanying raids were harrowing. PAOCC-led operations in 2023 and 2024 unearthed evidence of torture chambers and human trafficking inside Pogo compounds that fuelled investigations – including into former town mayor Alice Guo, who was sentenced to life in prison in November for her role in setting up a scam centre in Bamban, Tarlac province.

Meanwhile, Korean networks barely registered: PAOCC managed just three raids on operations linked to South Korean nationals between 2023 and last year.

Chinese and South Korean syndicates operated in similar ways, but had different specialisms, Casio said, with Korean operations tending to focus on rigged betting websites.

“They hide behind the veneer of legitimate ball games – for example, during the World Cup, Euro Cup or the NBA Finals, but the games are pre-recorded or rigged … unlike the Chinese where the scams were rooted in investment and pig-butchering scams,” he told This Week in Asia.

Korean crime networks in Southeast Asia do not operate as an extension of the region’s more deeply embedded Chinese triads, yet they are far from strangers, according to experts.

“Korean gangsters called jopok or kangpae have been running independently from triads for years, although they do work together in Southeast Asia when it’s helpful or they need to source drugs, launder money or run scams,” said Jeremy Douglas, deputy director of operations at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. “Gaming and scams are no different.”

Bora Park, a research fellow at the Institute for National Security Strategy in Seoul, went further, suggesting that many Korean gambling rings in the Philippines had “close ties to China from the very beginning”, often forming part of multinational operations rather than being composed solely of Korean nationals.

Predating Pogos

Analysts who spoke to This Week in Asia said Korean-linked illicit gambling operations predated the Chinese-run Pogos that multiplied to more than 300 licensed firms at their peak.

Criminal groups began migrating to the Philippines in the 2000s alongside legitimate investors, entrepreneurs and other members of the Korean diaspora, Douglas said.

Casio added that many Korean-linked operations were remnants of once-legitimate businesses that benefited from infrastructure and networks established years earlier.

Alexander Ramos, former executive director of the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Centre in the Philippines, dates the sector’s origins to the mid-2000s, when he said Korean operators ran legitimate gambling businesses within special economic zones before some splintered off into illegal operations.

Song Bong-gyu, an assistant professor at Hansei University who has tracked Korean organised crime since 2007, said the appeal of the Philippines was obvious from the start.

“Establishing operations overseas made it possible to distance themselves from Korean law enforcement while continuing to target customers in South Korea,” Song said, adding that illegal gambling operations targeting Korean nationals were already running out of the Philippines by 2014.

When the Pogo boom arrived under Duterte, it gave Korean syndicates new infrastructure to plug into. Pre-existing networks converged with Pogo-era offices, staff and payment systems, before later scattering again into smaller, harder to trace units, according to Song.

“Over time, the Philippines developed personnel, technological expertise, office and residential facilities, telecommunications infrastructure, payment channels and local intermediaries that could support offshore online gambling operations,” he said.

“Large compounds may disappear, but criminal operations can become smaller, more dispersed and less visible, while the networks connecting them remain extensive.”

The ‘balloon effect’

For her part, Park expressed scepticism that Korean organised crime was independently colonising Southeast Asia.

She argued it was far more likely that Korean operators had simply plugged into existing local or Chinese-affiliated networks that were already active in the region.

After the Philippines’ Pogo ban took hold in early 2025, Park said many Chinese-linked groups initially retreated to neighbouring countries or even to China – only for some to then move back again.

Cho Je-seong, a research fellow at the Korean Institute of Criminology and Justice, has a name for this pattern: the “balloon effect”, in which enforcement pressures squeeze criminal activity into new shapes rather than eliminating it.

“There can also be an organisational dimension to this process, in which a larger organisation becomes fragmented into several smaller groups or networks as enforcement pressure increases,” he said.

Even small cells would often run several gambling websites at the same time, Cho said, with dedicated teams for illegal bank accounts, recruitment, site maintenance and money laundering.

Last year’s passage of the law formally criminalising Pogos, building on Marcos’ executive order a year earlier, had lulled the Philippine public into a false sense of security, Casio said.

“Because of the anti-Pogo law, people think that the Pogo problem is already gone from the Philippines,” he said. Kim Young-sun’s arrest suggests otherwise.

item.title: [SCMP] Inside Thailand’s bid to wire the world’s AI revolution
item.description:
In the rush to build an AI future, semiconductors are the silicon rock stars that soak up all the applause. Yet behind the curtain, an unglamorous stagehand is doing much of the heavy lifting.

Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the copper-laced panels inside every mobile phone, car key fob, digital camera and data-centre server rack on Earth. Without them, even the most advanced AI chip would be useless, unable to process even a single line of code.

This year alone, more than 1 million square metres (10.8 million sq ft) of PCBs will roll out of WellTek Electronics’ factory in Ayutthaya – just one company’s contribution to Thailand’s scramble for an edge in the global tech supply chain.
item.content:encoded:
In the rush to build an AI future, semiconductors are the silicon rock stars that soak up all the applause. Yet behind the curtain, an unglamorous stagehand is doing much of the heavy lifting.

Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the copper-laced panels inside every mobile phone, car key fob, digital camera and data-centre server rack on Earth. Without them, even the most advanced AI chip would be useless, unable to process even a single line of code.

This year alone, more than 1 million square metres (10.8 million sq ft) of PCBs will roll out of WellTek Electronics’ factory in Ayutthaya – just one company’s contribution to Thailand’s scramble for an edge in the global tech supply chain.

“They are essential to our daily life. They are in all electronics you are using,” said WellTek founder Jennifer Deng, who established the Thai subsidiary of her China-based Jiangxi Welgao Electronics in Ayutthaya two years ago.

Thailand is now Southeast Asia’s No 1 producer of PCBs – often described as the nervous system of modern electronics, channelling essential signals through increasingly complex arrays of semiconductors, resistors and capacitors – and the fifth largest in the world.

Deng’s US$75 million WellTek plant, built in under a year, is the first of two planned for Ayutthaya, a major Thai industrial zone once dominated by Japanese carmakers and global electronics giants, now being rewired for the artificial intelligence age.

Circuitous success

Malaysia may lead the field in lucrative semiconductors and Vietnam in electronics assembly, but PCBs give Thailand its competitive advantage in Southeast Asia’s race for tech relevance.

Its rise in this niche owes as much to the trade wars triggered by Washington as it does to the smart timing of Thai authorities in welcoming global companies seeking new bases away from the tariff line of fire.

“The market demanded movement to Thailand,” Deng told This Week in Asia from WellTek’s Ayutthaya headquarters, where workers in crisp company polo shirts hustled down corridors beneath posters bearing the mantra “Conscience and Altruism”.

Over the next few years, Deng not only wants to build a second factory but treble output to more than 3.6 million square metres (38.8 million sq ft) of PCBs per year.

Thailand’s existing PCB industry gave it a head start over rivals, she said, explaining that “Europeans and Americans all requested we are outside of China, and our main partners are here in Thailand.”

Narit Therdsteerasukdi, secretary general of Thailand’s government-run Board of Investment, told an investor forum on Wednesday that the country was at a “turning point”.

Investment in the PCB and electronics component sector topped US$10 billion over the past three years, he revealed, calling this proof of how Thailand should pivot its economy.

“We need to restructure our economy … and the electronic industry, especially PCBs, is a very good example [of how to do it],” he said. “The key question is where do we go from here?”

For Narit, the country’s future growth depends on climbing the value chain, backed by a higher-skilled workforce trained for the AI age.

Printed fortunes

PCBs are a rare success story in a decade of patchy industrial policy that has left Thailand a regional growth laggard.

Many of the ideas floated to accelerate growth through new manufacturing chains and a splurge of foreign investment have been delayed, watered down or scrapped entirely on contact with the reality of delivering big infrastructure projects in a politically febrile kingdom.

Trade dispute and fuel-price spikes from distant wars have further hurt an economy that expanded just 2.4 per cent last year – a relative crawl compared with Vietnam’s 8 per cent.

Yet around 60 per cent of all new investment into Southeast Asia’s PCB industry has flowed into Thailand since 2023, according to the Thailand Printed Circuit Association.

Phutana Daoruang, the association’s general manager, said Thailand already had the PCB infrastructure, built up by a dozen or so Taiwanese firms, when Donald Trump’s first presidency fired the starting gun on companies fleeing US tariffs.

Thailand’s location and logistics networks, tax breaks, industrial estates and skilled workforce allowed the new factories to plug straight into electronics clusters like Ayutthaya, with the upgraded deep-sea port at Laem Chabang – a two-hour drive away – providing a maritime gateway to China.

“We pitched to compete with Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam as the fundamental infrastructure was already here,” Phutana told This Week in Asia.

“Thailand is quite suitable, we are quite strong in logistics and electricity supply is stable – especially compared with Vietnam and Malaysia.”

There are now around 50 PCB companies in the country, forming a sector that meets a modest 5 per cent of world demand but is eager to capture more of a global market forecast to reach US$100 billion in the coming years.

The ambition is to export eight to 10 times more PCBs than Thailand currently does – reaching roughly US$18 billion to US$25 billion in trade volume and a 20 per cent global market share.

Lofty as that sounds, it may not be impossible given the trillions of dollars flowing into data centres that need increasingly complex layers of PCBs.

“It’s quite complicated and uses very specialised material,” Phutana said of PCB manufacturing. “Thailand has the fundamentals to do it.”

Running hot

AI has changed the stakes for PCB manufacturers. A PCB destined for use with an AI accelerator card – roughly the size of a sheet of A4 paper – is a very different beast from the boards that are found inside car key fobs.

Densely layered with winding copper traces that resemble an illuminated cityscape from above, these boards must survive extreme heat and power loads while shuttling vastly more data at far higher speeds, providing the physical foundations for the AI chips crunching numbers across the region’s data centres.

Thailand has attracted billions of US dollars of data-centre investment in recent years on the promise of booming AI demand – so much, so fast that the capital is arriving well ahead of the physical buildout of centres themselves.

But data centres are voracious consumers of water and electricity while creating comparatively few jobs, and domestic critics argue that beyond a handful of landlords, Thailand risks getting the environmental costs without the economic rewards.

Delta Electronics Thailand, the local arm of the Taipei-headquartered “grid to chip” manufacturer that became the first company on the Thai stock exchange to be valued above US$100 billion in February, is now eyeing a bigger prize – the power and cooling systems that keep those centres humming.

In the Thai electronics world, Delta is the gatekeeper to the big data-centre contracts – and as it grows, Thailand and its PCB makers are desperate to keep it on side.

“Thailand is moving beyond cost competitiveness towards higher-value industries,” Delta said in a statement, pointing to “advanced engineering talent, energy infrastructure readiness and supply chain depth” as the areas that, with “continued progress” and “pro-business policies”, could give the country a lasting regional edge.

Not everyone shares that confidence. Analysts the world over have grown increasingly nervous about an AI investment bubble and what its bursting might do to countries that have calibrated their industrial strategy on the boom continuing.

Even Delta admits to being “mindful” of “tariff uncertainty, engineering talent gaps, supply chain constraints, intensifying competition in AI infrastructure” and the difficulty of scaling manufacturing “while maintaining quality and profitability”.

Down on the factory floor, the constraints are more immediate. PCB manufacturing demands “a crazy amount of water each day”, according to Thailand Printed Circuit Association chief Phutana – and it needs to be “high purity”, competing directly with the needs of households and other industries.

“The next wave of investment is there. Everyone in AI servers and data centres is looking for new land to expand their facility.” he said. “The customers cannot wait.”

Layered on top of water constraints is a supply squeeze on laminates – the non-conductive, rigid base material that forms the physical foundation of circuit boards – and essential chemicals, a knock-on effect of the US-Israel war on Iran disrupting imports.

Thailand’s Board of Investment says it is exploring ways to free up more water and power, but critics argue the country is sprinting ahead of its own capacity to sustainably keep pace.

Somnuck Jongmeewasin, research director at environmental monitor and advocacy group EEC Watch, said automation had killed the jobs case for hosting PCB plants at all.

Relocation incentives meant most equipment was imported, he said, with little technology transfer or upskilling of local workers – turning Thailand into an “assembly line” for foreign capital rather than a genuine beneficiary.

“The factories that come here don’t use as much labour as they used to,” he said. “If they come from Chinese capital, they barely hire Thai workers at all. Blue collar [workers] are Myanmar, white collar are Chinese.”

Despite the scepticism, there is a more hopeful reading – one rooted less in job numbers than in opportunity.

Thailand’s education system produces precious few science, technology, engineering and mathematics graduates each year and PCBs may be one of its rare growth industries suited to hiring them.

“Thailand faces a severe shortfall in meeting the surging demand for PCB and electronics workers,” said Panisa Harnpathananun of the National Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation Policy Council in Thailand.

She estimated the sector would need roughly 225,000 high-skilled workers over the next five years, against the around 1,100 electronics engineers Thai universities produced in 2024.

“This deficit is driven by an ageing population and a structural educational mismatch,” Panisa said.

Plans are afoot to close that gap, including a “sandbox” scheme to fast track engineering degrees and proposals to retrain redundant car industry workers for PCBs and semiconductors.

In a country short on other engines of growth, Panisa said PCBs might offer “the most critical opportunity and the strategic careers” its graduates were likely to find.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong Science Park celebrates 25 years of innovation and growth
item.description:
A particular kind of energy settles over Hong Kong Science Park on a weekday morning: researchers, deep in conversation, cross footbridges with laptop bags slung over shoulders; engineers transport prototypes between buildings, hunting for the next set of testing conditions; the air is rich with the buzz and hum of a community that has, over a quarter of a century, grown from reclaimed land at Pak Shek Kok into the largest start-up incubation platform in the city.

Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) kick-starts its silver-jubilee celebrations this year, and that industrious atmosphere is precisely what its new chairman, Cordelia Chung, wants people to understand about what has been built here. Not a laboratory, not a gadget: an ecosystem driving growth – one she intends to carry into its next phase.

Chung took up the chairmanship on July 1, arriving with a résumé that speaks of more than two decades inside one of the largest technology companies in the world. At IBM, she held senior leadership roles and steered the mainland China, Hong Kong and Asean markets, served as the vice-president and general counsel for Asia-Pacific, and was appointed to the IBM chairman and CEO’s Global Strategy Council as its first Asian female executive, contributing to worldwide direction setting across more than 140 countries. Her international background – having lived and worked in Tokyo, Singapore, Shanghai, Beijing and Hong Kong – brings a broader outlook.
item.content:encoded:
A particular kind of energy settles over Hong Kong Science Park on a weekday morning: researchers, deep in conversation, cross footbridges with laptop bags slung over shoulders; engineers transport prototypes between buildings, hunting for the next set of testing conditions; the air is rich with the buzz and hum of a community that has, over a quarter of a century, grown from reclaimed land at Pak Shek Kok into the largest start-up incubation platform in the city.

Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) kick-starts its silver-jubilee celebrations this year, and that industrious atmosphere is precisely what its new chairman, Cordelia Chung, wants people to understand about what has been built here. Not a laboratory, not a gadget: an ecosystem driving growth – one she intends to carry into its next phase.

Chung took up the chairmanship on July 1, arriving with a résumé that speaks of more than two decades inside one of the largest technology companies in the world. At IBM, she held senior leadership roles and steered the mainland China, Hong Kong and Asean markets, served as the vice-president and general counsel for Asia-Pacific, and was appointed to the IBM chairman and CEO’s Global Strategy Council as its first Asian female executive, contributing to worldwide direction setting across more than 140 countries. Her international background – having lived and worked in Tokyo, Singapore, Shanghai, Beijing and Hong Kong – brings a broader outlook.

She is no stranger to HKSTP, either, as her tenure on the board of directors, from 2017 to 2023, will show. Among Chung’s long list of achievements, receiving the Medal of Honour from the Hong Kong government in 2024, for her role in propelling the city’s innovation and technology (I&T) development, is arguably one of the most meaningful.

It is that blend of corporate governance and lived experience in a future-focused sector that shapes Chung’s vision for HKSTP, along with her sense of service to the community, instilled early on during her formative years at a convent school, which guides her intentionality to empower and enable talents.

China’s 15th five-year plan outlined high hopes for the continued advancement of Hong Kong’s I&T industry as an international hub for science and technology, and for it to deliver results. But Chung does not reach for a single headline figure to convince the audience of her ambition, instead framing her philosophy around four qualities: breadth, depth, height and strength.

“Hong Kong’s economy has relied heavily on finance and service industries, but facing global challenges, industrial transformation is now imperative. What we’re currently looking for is the breadth of I&T. We want to fully integrate I&T into traditional industries in order to expand Hong Kong’s industrial base,” she says, explaining that expanding talent development, nurturing that passion early and planting the seeds will provide a clear pathway for the next generation.

Once breadth is established, depth comes into play. “Besides pursuing advanced technology, we also aim for a wide application of technology,” she says, pointing to the investment in AI computing capacity as the base for something broader than any one company’s product road map. “It offers hope for transformation to traditional industries that have reached a bottleneck.” She counts off some of Hong Kong’s foundational economic pillars: “Financial services, construction, real estate, education – all of them can be pushed forward with technology, and it can be applied to so many different disciplines.”

Height, the third quality, is where Chung’s own international career shines through most clearly. Hong Kong’s unique East-meets-West positioning must be leveraged to “proactively attract businesses and talent from around the world. At the same time, we must lead the world by helping local and mainland Chinese I&T ventures expand to global markets”.

Last but not least, strength describes the pace and density she wants HKSTP to sustain. “It’s easier to create synergy when talent, capital and different resources are highly concentrated,” Chung says. Bumping into experts from different fields while walking through the park’s corridors and campuses encourages exchange and intellectual confluence. Removing friction at each stage of a company’s growth and creating a support network to match innovators with investors allows the start-ups to have the “sprint energy” to break through and thrive.

Chung’s vision is grand, and to understand her framing of the next chapter, it helps to trace how HKSTP arrived at this one.

Its roots stretch back to the 1970s, when the first of three industrial estates – in Tai Po, Yuen Long and Tseung Kwan O – was established, starting a lineage that eventually produced the Hong Kong Industrial Technology Centre Corporation in 1993.

It was not until 2001 that the government consolidated these assets under the HKSTP umbrella as the city’s flagship innovation and technology body, with the Hong Kong Science Park at Pak Shek Kok as its centrepiece.

With a quarter of a century under its belt, that foundation has grown into a multi-location operation spanning around 240 hectares (593 acres) of dedicated infrastructure. With a network of more than 210 investors and over 500 public- and private-sector partners, HKSTP credits these relationships with keeping talent, technology and capital moving through its community.

In the past eight years alone, HKSTP has demonstrated rapid acceleration, raising more than HK$170 billion (US$21.7 billion) in funding for its start-ups, with its Corporate Venture Fund leveraging private capital at a ratio of roughly one to 13. Under Chung’s predecessors, the number of companies based in the park rose from around 600 to more than 2,600, 14 unicorns were nurtured and 23 start-ups went public. HKSTP counts more than 26,000 professionals from 26 markets among its ranks, including success stories such as SenseTime and Lalamove, all built and scaled within its own ecosystem.

From its origins as an industrial asset manager, the evolution of HKSTP into a global technology catalyst has been defined by game-changing milestones. Following Hong Kong Science Park’s opening in June 2002, early operations focused on building research and development (R&D) capacity across four pillars: electronics, biotechnology, precision engineering and IT. Back then, Hong Kong’s technology scene was primarily designed to serve as an innovation engine for the city and the Pan-Pearl River Delta, reimagined in 2019 as the Greater Bay Area.

An iconic symbol of this ambition arrived in 2010. Following Charles Kao Kuen’s Nobel Prize win the previous year for groundbreaking achievements in fibre optics, HKSTP named its central landmark – the striking ovoid Charles K. Kao Auditorium, affectionately dubbed the “Golden Egg” – in honour of Hong Kong’s own laureate, inspiring generations of local talent.

In 2019 came the announcement of InnoHK, a flagship government initiative enabling research collaborations in artificial intelligence, robotics and healthcare with top global universities, while 2021 saw the repositioning of the three traditional industrial estates in Tai Po, Yuen Long and Tseung Kwan O as modern InnoParks.

It was a pivotal era that culminated in a historic visit by President Xi Jinping, in 2022, cementing the park’s role in the national innovation agenda.

HKSTP’s momentum has only accelerated. It extended its physical footprint with a Shenzhen branch in Futian district the following year and, in 2025, the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou Innovation Cluster was ranked No 1 in the world.

If Chung supplies the vision for the road ahead, HKSTP CEO Terry Wong Ping-sau is responsible for the daily mechanics of getting there. Wong has more than 30 years of international executive experience across advanced mobility, smart cities, infrastructure and energy, including in markets such as Australia and Saudi Arabia, but he describes his own first year in the role as a process of listening intently before acting.

“I spend a large amount of time almost every day meeting stakeholders, including universities, the government, start-ups, corporations, partnerships and investors,” he says, adding that he celebrated his one-year anniversary at HKSTP in much the same way. In fact, that instinct for stakeholder management is not so different from the discipline required to deliver an infrastructure project, despite the subject matter. Big budget, small budget, international, or local matters not. “We have to have a strategy, be clear about what we want to achieve, and work together so that big teams share the same goal.”

What has changed is the expanded terrain that HKSTP now covers, a point that dovetails with Chung’s own emphasis on breadth as a strategic priority. “We have a broad technical arena,” says Wong. “Market development, AI and robotics – it’s so broad, no one can say they’re an expert in all of this.”

But there is a method to the madness of managing that range. HKSTP has organised its support around four pillars that play to Hong Kong’s natural advantages: life and health technology, AI and data science, green technology and advanced manufacturing. Support is calibrated to a company’s stage of growth, moving from early incubation, global connections and talent scouting through to business development, early capital and elite programmes, as well as venture-capital networks designed to help mature firms expand abroad. Wong describes this as a journey “from ideation to IPO”, spanning over 20 initiatives, including funding, proof-of-concept support, business matching and market access.

Central to delivering that support is Inno.OS, the corporation’s own platform, blending hardware, software and services to help companies build value. Physical infrastructure is equally important. Beyond Hong Kong Science Park, the three InnoParks, dedicated to advanced manufacturing, offer plug-and-play production facilities that let companies move quickly from R&D into commercial output. A GreenTech Hub focuses on sustainability, and a new I&T facility, InnoPole, has been announced at the San Tin Technopole, in the Northern Metropolis area of the New Territories, where Chung has separately been appointed to the board of the dedicated company overseeing the site.

Successful support systems must also consider the well-being of the innovators at the heart of progress. InnoCell, a 17-storey smart-living and co-creation space next to Hong Kong Science Park, was built to house the talent on which the ecosystem depends. It embodies what HKSTP describes internally as a “Work, Live, Play, Learn” philosophy: proximity between researchers, engineers and entrepreneurs, whether in a laboratory or a shared kitchen, produces the kind of chance encounter that formal programming cannot manufacture. InnoCell is a physical expression of the same principle Chung raises when she talks about strength: put enough talent and capital within walking distance of one another, and ideas begin to take shape.

Nowhere is that philosophy more apparent than in life and health technology. More than 350 companies within the HKSTP ecosystem are involved in such fields as drug discovery and digital health. PanopticAI, a start-up founded by Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) alumni, has developed a camera-based monitoring solution capable of reading vital signs, including heart rate, blood pressure and respiration rate, from little more than a short video clip. PanopticAI won clearance from the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for contactless pulse and respiratory rate measurement on its mobile application, making it the first Hong Kong company to secure such approval for a piece of software as a medical device. Early adopters now include Gleneagles Hospital Hong Kong and healthcare firm Bupa.

Another example is Koln 3D, a Hong Kong Science Park company that has become the first medical metal 3D-printing manufacturer in the city, producing patient-specific body implants used in reconstructive surgeries as far afield as Central Asia and Europe. Its AI-powered technology can accurately tailor-make bone replacements and 3D models.

Starting out in 2013, Koln 3D has since expanded its production into the Greater Bay Area and Switzerland, and partnered with hospitals in Singapore, France and Kazakhstan – exactly the kind of internationalisation Chung and Wong say they want to accelerate across the Hong Kong Science Park portfolio.

Meanwhile, Lalamove, an on-demand delivery platform that grew from a local start-up within Hong Kong Science Park into a unicorn that operates in 17 markets across Asia, the Americas and the Europe, Middle East and Africa region, tells the story of scale centred on international expansion.

Founded in 2013, Lalamove, formerly known as “EasyVan”, joined HKSTP’s incubation programme early on to connect with technology partners and unlock investments that accelerated its development. Within 18 months, the company received two major capital injections and expanded to mainland China and other Asian markets. In April, it successfully tested its low-altitude-economy logistics solutions in complex urban environments, flying a cargo-carrying drone from Hong Kong Science Park, over Tolo Harbour, to the Mars Centre in the Tai Po InnoPark.

Positioning Hong Kong as a connector is an instinct that runs through HKSTP, supported by its own cross-border work. HKSTP presents itself as a two-way avenue for Hong Kong and mainland Chinese innovators seeking to expand internationally, while also helping overseas companies enter the Greater Bay Area, mainland China and beyond. Its Shenzhen branch has attracted more than 90 innovation companies, helped raise over 800 million yuan (US$119 million) in funding and supported more than 170 companies moving northbound into the mainland and 80 moving southbound into Hong Kong.

“Whatever we do, the market here is too small, anyway,” says Chung. “We need to have that broader, connective outlook.”

HKSTP says its Global Connect programme has brought together more than 8,000 stakeholders, advisers and innovators, while its Global Mixer programme has taken more than 200 partner companies to over 20 exhibitions in more than 10 countries, from Las Vegas to Dubai to Singapore.

“We can provide what we call a one-stop service,” says Chung. “If you have an idea, we can incubate you, we can give you money. When we think you’re doing a good job, we can help you accelerate. We can introduce investors, lawyers, bankers, tax consultants, accountants – the full suite of things that you need to really grow your business. If what you do is something that can be produced, you can actually land in one of our InnoParks and do the pilot production there and test it out.

“It’s about building the bridge, making sure people are connected, making sure that the people who have the ideas meet the people who can make it happen.”

She explains that the park’s bridging ability can “support the scale and eventual maturity of the entire I&T landscape in Hong Kong. We’re ready; the infrastructure is ready. We’re not going from zero to one, we’re [going] from one to 10 or one to N”.

For companies coming from different starting points, Wong notes, the support required is rarely identical. “For companies from mainland China, their main objective is to expand overseas, and they already have good products that are selling in China.” What HKSTP offers is help understanding global regulatory standards and linking them with the right industry players. Newer, earlier-stage companies tend to need more fundamental support: introductions to researchers, help refining a prototype, or access to corporate partners willing to run pilot trials. “Instead of doing it on their own, the people in our park get access to different stakeholders,” Wong says. “We proactively curate the people they actually need.”

Chung brings the governance experience and the outward-facing conviction to argue that Hong Kong’s next phase depends on breadth of talent, depth of adoption, height of ambition and strength of concentration. Wong brings the operational discipline to turn that framework into an organisation whose real product is connective tissue: the funding relationships, the mentorship networks and the physical proximity that let Hong Kong’s researchers and entrepreneurs turn ideas into products, and products into global businesses.

For an organisation that has spent 25 years building that infrastructure, both physical and relational, Chung’s four-part vision reads less like a slogan and more like a checklist for the next page. Breadth, so that more of Hong Kong’s economy and more of its young people have a stake in the outcome. Depth, so that the technologies built here change how entire industries operate. Height, so that Hong Kong’s position between mainland China and the rest of the world becomes a genuine advantage. And strength, so that the density of talent and capital already gathered keeps generating the kind of collaboration no five-year plan can fully script in advance.

Chung feels confident about the future because she has seen first-hand the path that lies ahead and where it can lead, during her years as a board member of HKSTP. “When I first joined, the start-up population here was around 600. Now, we have over 2,600. It has really grown. But is it enough? I don’t think it’s enough. So, that is one thing that I want to steer: for us to become much more energetic in this area,” she says. “In the last 10 years, 20 years, we have created a solid foundation. Now, we can take it to the next level.”

Much can change in the next 25 years. In fact, the chairman is counting on it. Chung muses on the next chapter with good humour: “I have to think of my own age, if I still have the ability to …” She trails off, deep in thought, imagining the possibilities.

“In 25 years’ time, I hope that the various science parks in the entire Greater Bay Area will be truly integrated. With laws and regulations completely streamlined, HKSTP will be the largest innovation cluster globally,” she smiles. “A day at Hong Kong Science Park will look like being in the leading science and technology hub in the entire world: a SuperPark.”

HKSTP kicks off its 25th anniversary on August 31 with its “Together to Next” prelude celebration, honouring the visionaries, partners and innovators of the I&T community. To register for the event, click here

item.title: [SCMP] Tanker, transporter, controller: China’s Y-20 family expands its Pacific reach
item.description:
When six Chinese heavy transport planes entered European airspace in April 2022, it was not just their cargo that drew international attention.

Bound for Serbia, the Y-20 aircraft had flown thousands of kilometres from China carrying components of the Chinese-made FK-3 surface-to-air missile system.

A second wave of six aircraft followed, bringing the operation to 12 sorties in what was then China’s biggest overseas airlift involving the strategic cargo plane.
item.content:encoded:
When six Chinese heavy transport planes entered European airspace in April 2022, it was not just their cargo that drew international attention.

Bound for Serbia, the Y-20 aircraft had flown thousands of kilometres from China carrying components of the Chinese-made FK-3 surface-to-air missile system.

A second wave of six aircraft followed, bringing the operation to 12 sorties in what was then China’s biggest overseas airlift involving the strategic cargo plane.

Coming just weeks after Russia invaded Ukraine, the delivery raised concerns among European capitals about Belgrade’s growing military ties with Beijing. But the operation also revealed something significant about Chinese capabilities: the People’s Liberation Army could now use its own heavy transport aircraft to move military equipment from East Asia deep into Europe.

At the centre of that capability was the Y-20 Kunpeng, China’s first domestically developed heavy military transport.

Four years on, the aircraft is evolving into something considerably more versatile. China has introduced an improved version powered by domestically produced engines, confirmed that the airframe can switch between transport and aerial-refuelling roles, and is using it as the basis for a new airborne early-warning aircraft.

What began as China’s answer to a shortage of strategic airlift is becoming a family of support aircraft that could help the PLA move forces further from home and sustain and coordinate combat aircraft deeper into the western Pacific.

China’s home-grown heavy airlifter

China formally launched its large transport aircraft programme in 2007, with the Xian Aircraft Corporation leading development.

The first Y-20 flew in January 2013 and entered PLA Air Force service in July 2016, giving Beijing an indigenous heavy airlifter after years of mostly relying on imported Russian Il-76 aircraft.

The platform’s development was driven in part by Beijing’s difficulty in acquiring additional Russian Il-76 transports and Il-78 tankers, according to Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist in Chinese military aviation and author of several books on the subject.

Designed to fill that strategic void, the Y-20 can carry a maximum payload of roughly 66 tonnes, with an estimated range of about 3,700km (2,300 miles) at that load. But the Serbia mission highlighted how refuelling stops along the route could extend the airlifter’s reach far beyond its range on a single flight.

One of the programme’s most important changes has come under the wings, however.

The original Y-20A uses Russian D-30KP-II turbofan engines. The newer Y-20B instead uses four domestically produced WS-20 high-bypass turbofans.

The WS-20 offers greater thrust and better fuel efficiency than the D-30, although reliable public figures quantifying the resulting gains in range or payload are not available. More broadly, replacing Russian engines gives China greater control over the production and future development of an aircraft increasingly central to its long-range aviation capabilities.

Rupprecht estimates that around 90 Y-20A-family transports and tankers were operational by August 2025, while close to two dozen Y-20Bs were in service or awaiting delivery.

From transport to tanker

The Y-20 has also helped China address another constraint on its ability to project air power: aerial refuelling.

China has developed a dedicated tanker derivative, the YY-20A, which allows combat and other aircraft to fly further and remain airborne longer – an increasingly important capability as PLA operations extend deeper into the western Pacific and across the South China Sea.

Its growing utility was on show during joint exercises with Egypt in August, when a YY-20A was photographed refuelling an Egyptian Air Force Rafale – a rare example of a Chinese tanker supporting a foreign-made combat aircraft.

But rather than relying solely on dedicated tankers, China is now adding greater flexibility to the Y-20 fleet itself.

State broadcaster CCTV confirmed earlier this month that the Y-20B could switch between transport and aerial-refuelling missions by installing additional fuel tanks and removable refuelling equipment.

Rupprecht argues that the evidence points towards the Y-20B becoming a common multi-role tanker-transport platform rather than China maintaining entirely separate production lines for B-model transports and tankers.

Such an arrangement could allow commanders to shift aircraft between two critical tasks – moving troops and equipment or refuelling combat aircraft – as operational requirements changed. It would also allow the PLA Air Force to generate additional tanker capacity from its transport fleet when required, rather than relying entirely on dedicated tanker aircraft.

That flexibility could be particularly valuable during sustained operations further into the western Pacific or over the South China Sea.

However, no operational Y-20B has yet been publicly observed fitted with the complete tanker configuration. Rupprecht assesses that the necessary fuel-transfer systems and wiring may already be incorporated into production aircraft even when the external refuelling equipment is absent.

Seeing further from shore

Yet the platform’s evolution extends beyond transport and aerial refuelling. The Y-20B is also providing the basis for the KJ-3000 airborne early-warning and control aircraft, which has been undergoing flight testing since late 2024.

As PLA combat aircraft expand their operational reach, the KJ-3000 is intended to solve another problem: greater range matters little without the ability to detect threats, track targets and coordinate operations across an expanding battlespace.

The KJ-3000’s large dorsal radar is designed to provide airborne surveillance and command-and-control capabilities that could complement or eventually replace China’s ageing KJ-2000 fleet, which is based on the Russian Il-76.

Its development highlights a broader consequence of the Y-20 programme: China now has a domestically produced large-aircraft platform that can be adapted for specialised roles, further reducing its reliance on imported airframes.

That capability is becoming more important as Beijing asks the PLA to operate further from home. A Taiwan conflict could require sustained high-intensity operations while potentially confronting US and allied forces across the western Pacific, while the South China Sea presents another vast operating area.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries, including the United States – Taiwan’s main international backer, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

item.title: [SCMP] Mainland Chinese firms share risks to deliver Northern Metropolis success: analysts
item.description:
Mainland Chinese enterprises will play a key role in developing Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis by sharing financial risks and helping align the megaproject with national strategy, according to real estate and political advisers.

Their analysis followed the award of the blueprint’s first pilot area in Hung Shui Kiu to HSK New Development, a consortium led by five mainland giants and local developer Sino Land on Monday.

Pledging an investment of HK$16.8 billion (US$2.14 billion), the consortium will develop sites totalling 10.5 hectares (25.9 acres) at a low land premium of HK$1.03 billion. It beat the only competitor, a stand-alone bid from Henderson Land Development.
item.content:encoded:
Mainland Chinese enterprises will play a key role in developing Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis by sharing financial risks and helping align the megaproject with national strategy, according to real estate and political advisers.

Their analysis followed the award of the blueprint’s first pilot area in Hung Shui Kiu to HSK New Development, a consortium led by five mainland giants and local developer Sino Land on Monday.

Pledging an investment of HK$16.8 billion (US$2.14 billion), the consortium will develop sites totalling 10.5 hectares (25.9 acres) at a low land premium of HK$1.03 billion. It beat the only competitor, a stand-alone bid from Henderson Land Development.

The mainland contingent comprises four state-backed developers – China Overseas Land & Investment, China Merchants Land, China Resources Land (Overseas) and CTG Investment – with decades of experience, alongside e-commerce and technology titan JD.com.

Jeffrey Lam Kin-fung, chairman of the board of directors of the Hung Shui Kiu Industry Park Company – a government vehicle created to drive the district’s development – noted that pooling top players across real estate, construction and hospitality would accelerate development.

“Each of the six companies has a special role to play, which will contribute to the holistic development of the Northern Metropolis,” he said.

While analysts attributed the participation of mainland heavyweights to national priorities, technical expertise and familiarity with the local market, real estate advisers stressed that future tenders would require greater flexibility and longer bidding windows to encourage more competition.

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said mainland firms would emerge as key players in the Northern Metropolis, a 30,000-hectare mega development close to the city’s border with the mainland set to be transformed into an economic powerhouse and housing hub.

“Beijing has encouraged mainland Chinese companies to participate and help transform and upgrade Hong Kong’s industry development. They also have more experience in promoting and planning new quality development forces,” he said, referring to China’s growth model focused on technological breakthroughs and industrial upgrades.

“While Chinese firms can help Northern Metropolis development better align and serve national development strategies, they can also organise their businesses in Hong Kong, the mainland and overseas.”

He added that it was unrealistic to expect a major influx of investment from the West into the Northern Metropolis amid geopolitical tensions, noting that Western countries too needed investments for development.

Lau Chun-kong, chairman of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors’ land policy panel, said the consortium had “formidable financial strength” and an edge across a range of services.

He noted that Sino Land had solid cash flow in Hong Kong’s real estate sector to support the pilot area in Hung Shui Kiu, which is envisioned as a future high-end professional services and logistics hub.

Under the tender terms, HSK New Development will carry out extensive site formation across the 10.5-hectare area, retaining three residential plots totalling 2.6 hectares to deliver more than 3,000 private flats.

According to the consortium, the residential sites will feature over 100,000 sq ft of commercial space, incorporating smart retail concepts and unstaffed supermarkets.

The master plan prioritises natural ventilation and optimal sunlight exposure, backed by renewable energy installations and advanced carbon-reduction technologies.

All parking spaces will provide electric vehicle charging capabilities alongside smart access control and automated parking systems, while individual homes will be equipped with smart systems driven by artificial intelligence (AI).

The consortium will construct a smart logistics hub on a one-hectare enterprise and technology (E&T) plot, with JD.com required to operate at least 15,300 square metres (161,458 sq ft) – roughly 30 per cent of the gross floor area – within 55 months.

The facility will also feature hi-tech logistics operations, including autonomous delivery systems.

The consortium will return two E&T plots and a government, institution or community site to the authorities by 2028 after completing site formation works.

It will also develop a 1.44-hectare open space and build a footpath and a pedestrian street for the government in phases by 2030-33.

Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at Colliers, noted that pooling diverse capital sources mitigated risk, following the local property market downturn.

“Eventually, it is a relatively long-term project … It involves [industry], residential and infrastructure development. Having various sources of capital and having companies to supplement one another can minimise the risks,” she said.

Lee also said she believed mainland firms would play a key role in future pilot projects, noting that the four state enterprises had long operated in Hong Kong while JD.com had steadily built up its local presence.

She said established players had a stronger grasp of the local market than newcomers, while geopolitical factors also worked in their favour.

“A long-term investment in Hong Kong by American and European businesses remains an uncertainty given the geopolitical developments in recent years,” she added.

To accommodate the needs of different enterprises, Lee suggested that the government could allow phased industry development in future pilot area projects.

She noted that nascent enterprises might require smaller floor areas while technology firms would be reluctant to share facilities with other competitors.

Hannah Jeong, head of valuation and advisory services at CBRE Hong Kong, highlighted that while the land premium was relatively low at HK$1.03 billion, the estimated development cost was HK$16.8 billion, due to requirements to form extensive sites and build facilities beyond residential homes.

She noted that while the model remained financially viable, profit margins would be slim.

“The residential profits are expected to fund and support the broader innovation-focused development,” she said.

She suggested lengthening the tender period for future pilot areas beyond six months.

“Given the complexity of these developments and the need to combine technology operators, investors and residential developers, the market requires adequate time to establish the right partnerships and formulate viable business models,” she said.

Jeong said that some enterprises had earlier expressed interest in the pilot area but were unfamiliar with the tendering process, noting that mainland firms often had slower decision-making processes.

She also urged the government to promote tenders more actively to non-local companies.

The government is expected to roll out pilot areas in the future innovation hub in San Tin and the border commerce district in Fanling North, though updated tender dates for the projects – originally set for 2025 and 2026 at the earliest – have yet to be announced.

Additional reporting by Jess Ma

item.title: [SCMP] Singaporean who filmed couple on rooftop and demanded sex, cash gets jail
item.description:
A man who hid behind some plants to film a couple having extramarital sex at a rooftop garden in Singapore later used the video to threaten the woman while asking for sex and cash.

When the police began investigating, the offender asked the woman to drop the case, even approaching her sister at a supermarket.

Despite this ongoing investigation, the man targeted another couple having sex in a parked car and took a photograph of them before confronting them.
item.content:encoded:
A man who hid behind some plants to film a couple having extramarital sex at a rooftop garden in Singapore later used the video to threaten the woman while asking for sex and cash.

When the police began investigating, the offender asked the woman to drop the case, even approaching her sister at a supermarket.

Despite this ongoing investigation, the man targeted another couple having sex in a parked car and took a photograph of them before confronting them.

On Tuesday, Mohammad Sharulnaim Miswan, a 33-year-old Singaporean, was sentenced to two years and 10 months’ jail, along with three strokes of the cane.

He pleaded guilty to three charges which include putting a person in fear of harm to commit extortion, obstructing justice and wrongful confinement.

Another two charges were taken into consideration.

In sentencing, the judge told Sharulnaim that his actions had been most hurtful to his wife, who wept in court with a newborn baby in her arms.

Addresses and names of the victims were redacted from court documents due to gag orders protecting their identities.

At about 1am on January 15, 2024, Sharulnaim walked past a 35-year-old woman and a 39-year-old man at the rooftop garden of a multi-storey car park.

Suspecting they might engage in sexual acts as the man was touching the woman, Sharulnaim hid behind some plants to catch them in the act.

He took five videos of the pair having sex, capturing their faces in some of the clips and moving to another spot at one point for a better view.

Months later on May 6, 2024, the woman took her son to a clinic and was waiting to see the doctor when she was approached by Sharulnaim.

He introduced himself and asked if she was married and whether the boy with her was her son.

The woman’s turn at the clinic was next and she took her son to see the doctor. While the woman was waiting to collect medication, Sharulnaim approached her again.

He said he had a video of her having sex on the rooftop and showed her a screenshot, getting her to agree to meet him in his car to discuss it.

In his vehicle, Sharulnaim told the woman that he wanted to post the video online.

She pleaded with him not to do it, saying her son had special needs.

Sharulnaim dropped the woman and her son off, exchanged numbers and continued to communicate with her on how to settle the issue.

He said he intended to report the video to the police or make it go viral. The woman offered him S$300 (US$236) but he said it was “too low”.

Sharulnaim told her that if she was charged with an offence relating to the video, she faced months in jail and a fine of up to S$5,000.

He then sought S$2,000 and later S$1,500, but the woman could not afford either sum.

Sharulnaim then asked for S$1,000 and for the woman to have sex with him. He said he could pick her up and they could have sex at a car park, after which he would delete the video.

The woman refused the sex request and agreed to pay him S$1,300 by the following day. However, on the advice of the man in the sex video, she lodged a police report.

Unaware of this development, Sharulnaim sent the woman a photograph of a police station, saying he was going to lodge a report.

When the woman did not reply, Sharulnaim called the man in the sex video and repeated the threat.

The man felt threatened and said he would pay S$1,000 as the woman had only S$300. He pleaded with Sharulnaim to leave her alone because she had a young son and mother to take care of.

No payment was ultimately made and the police arrested Sharulnaim. While his statement was being recorded, he learnt that he was being investigated for putting a person in fear of harm to commit extortion.

Months after this, in September 2024, Sharulnaim approached the woman’s sister in a supermarket and said he had an explicit video of her sister.

The woman was also present but did not speak to him until Sharulnaim approached her. He asked her to tell the investigation officer that she no longer wished to pursue the case.

To placate him, the woman said she would consider it. She refused to take down Sharulnaim’s new number and instead told the investigation officer about what happened.

Sharulnaim saw the woman with her sister and son at the supermarket again the following month and begged the woman to drop the case.

He asked for forgiveness, saying he was the sole breadwinner and that his parents and wife had learned about what happened. He claimed that he wanted to kill himself.

He also asked the woman to tell the police they were family, even though they were not. His friend had told him that this might help get the case dropped.

He also offered gifts and financial help to the woman if she let the matter go.

The woman’s sister lodged a police report that same day.

While the case was ongoing, on February 25, 2025, Sharulnaim came across another couple having sex in a parked car at a multi-storey car park.

He took a photograph of them before knocking on the window and gesturing to them to step out.

Lying that he was a former police officer, Sharulnaim asked the pair in their 20s for their ages and schools.

He said he had taken a video of them having sex and said he would lodge a police report, scaring the man.

Sharulnaim said he wanted to lodge a police report against them and that they would be fined for engaging in such acts in public.

The couple tried to leave and walked away, but Sharulnaim drove his vehicle and cornered the pair.

He rolled down his window and insisted that the man leave while he took the woman home.

The woman said her home was nearby and she would walk, but Sharulnaim insisted. He locked the doors and drove off, complimenting the woman on her looks and asking why she was in a relationship with her boyfriend.

When Sharulnaim came to the woman’s home, he saw her boyfriend waiting there for her and said he would not let her alight until her boyfriend left.

He told the woman she should not be with her boyfriend because she was too pretty for him.

Eventually, he unlocked the doors and let her go. She later lodged a police report and Sharulnaim was arrested again.

Deputy public prosecutor Niranjan Ranjakunalan sought two years and 11 to 13 months’ jail for Sharulnaim, along with three strokes of the cane.

Sharulnaim has prior convictions for theft and desertion from civil defence, among other charges.

Defence lawyer S Balarumugan said his client had a daughter and a month-old baby. He said he was also financially supporting his aged parents, who had medical conditions.

He said his client apologised to the victims for the ordeal he caused and assured the court he would be “more responsible” in future.

District Judge Samuel Wee allowed Sharulnaim’s wife to stay in the courtroom to hear sentencing remarks instead of leaving to tend to her crying baby.

He told Sharulnaim that his actions were premeditated and planned.

“You know the hurt it has caused your family,” said Judge Wee. “I would say … [it] has been most hurtful to your wife. Despite that, she’s still here today.”

Sharulnaim’s wife began to break down in the courtroom, surrounded by family.

The judge asked Sharulnaim to look at him as he was talking and told him about the consequences of his actions.

“Because of what you did … your children are going to grow up for a short period of time without their father,” Judge Wee said.

“And your wife, who has already had to bear the brunt of your very hurtful conduct, is going to be the one continuing to care for them while you are away.”

He asked if Sharulnaim had anything to say to his family, to which the man said he had already spoken to his wife and was grateful that she had stayed by his side.

The judge then reminded him to think about what he did while in jail and be clear on what he wanted for his future and his family on his release.

He allowed Sharulnaim time to speak to his various family members before being taken to jail. He said goodbye to his baby through a hole in the glass.

For putting a person in fear of harm to commit extortion, he could have been jailed for between two and five years and caned.

For obstruction of justice, he could have been jailed for up to seven years and fined.

For wrongful confinement, he could have been jailed for up to three years and fined.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Anwar traded reform for power. Now Umno wants it all
item.description:
The roar from thousands of People’s Justice Party (PKR) delegates gathered at a grand convention centre in Melaka last weekend exuded all the confidence expected of a party leading Malaysia’s government.

The past three years have been the culmination of more than two decades of struggle for PKR, with it finally achieving its long-held goal of installing leader Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and wielding the power to push through reforms.

Yet beneath the confident facade lurks a ruling party now scrambling to find its way.
item.content:encoded:
The roar from thousands of People’s Justice Party (PKR) delegates gathered at a grand convention centre in Melaka last weekend exuded all the confidence expected of a party leading Malaysia’s government.

The past three years have been the culmination of more than two decades of struggle for PKR, with it finally achieving its long-held goal of installing leader Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and wielding the power to push through reforms.

Yet beneath the confident facade lurks a ruling party now scrambling to find its way.

PKR’s victory in the 2022 general election came at the cost of the very reforms it had promised to deliver, as Anwar had little choice but to negotiate compromises with erstwhile rivals, including former ruling party Umno, to steady his administration. Those trade-offs did not go unnoticed.

Anwar’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, of which PKR is a founding and principal member, has suffered a series of bruising defeats across three state elections since November – and whatever platform the prime minister gave a once-deflated Umno has turned the party into the greatest threat to his rule.

Staring down the possibility of being turfed out of Putrajaya after just one term, PKR members are left wondering how to reverse the trend, especially as surging Malay nationalist sentiment carries a resurgent Umno forward.

“The delegates are all confused. They need clear direction,” a senior party leader told This Week in Asia, speaking anonymously due to the sensitivity of the matter.

“Before, it was about coming to power and raising Anwar as prime minister. Now what?”

Senior members who attended last weekend’s congress pointed to a disconnect between Anwar, his party’s top leadership and the rank and file, who have been left without a common purpose to rally around.

That gulf became apparent during Anwar’s opening speech at the congress last Saturday.

Delegates gave only a lukewarm response as their party president and prime minister listed out, at length, his administration’s successes in bolstering growth and investment numbers.

It was only when Anwar touched on the multibillion-ringgit scandal at the Tabung Haji pilgrim fund – made public last month – that the crowd roared to life, with some delegates passionately demanding retribution against Umno, the party in power when the alleged offences occurred.

That reaction offered the clearest indication yet that the prime minister and PH need to coalesce around a clear message if they hope to slow Umno’s momentum, and that of its nascent partnership with the opposition Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS).

“You see Umno and PAS talking about uniting the ummah [Muslim faithful], and claims that [PKR coalition partner] DAP is out to wrest power from the Malays. It’s simple messaging that people can easily understand,” the senior PKR leader said.

When comparing investments and other economic indicators, Anwar scored higher than past leaders, he said. “But the people here don’t understand all that. You need to present things using simple language.”

House of cards

The problems trace back to November 2022, when Anwar was named prime minister by former king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah on condition that he form a unity government that included allies and rivals alike, to avoid a hung parliament.

The arrangement threw a lifeline to Umno, which had just suffered its worst electoral outing, winning fewer than 30 of parliament’s 222 seats.

From there, Anwar has been accused of setting aside his reform agenda and steering his government rightward, mirroring the previous Umno administration’s penchant for cracking down on sexual minorities and free speech in a bid to win over a Malay-Muslim majority suspicious of his motives.

Despite growing outrage from long-time supporters, the prime minister enjoyed a period of relative political stability over the first half of his five-year term, as economic growth and foreign investment hit record highs.

But that proved to be merely the calm before the storm.

The first salvo was fired in the Sabah state election last November, when Anwar’s PH coalition was all but wiped out. Hardest hit was the Democratic Action Party (DAP), the largest party in Anwar’s federal coalition, which lost every seat it contested.

Over the past two months, PH’s tenuous grip on power has truly sunk in, as it suffered back-to-back defeats at the hand of fellow federal partner, Umno.

Umno cruised to an extended supermajority in the southern state of Johor in July, then struck an informal alliance with Islamist rivals PAS to wrest control of Negeri Sembilan state from PH earlier this month.

The losses in the three state elections were the first tangible signs that Anwar and PH were in real trouble, after years of complaints from civil society groups and PH’s own support base about the lack of reforms following decades of promises.

Wong Chen, a three-term MP who quit PKR this month after being unceremoniously removed from a government post and cut off from his constituency fund, said the current trend pointed to PH losing the next national poll, which must be held by February 2028 at the latest.

If they don’t quickly reform in the last few months that they have, then they won’t even be able to win enough support

PKR defector Wong Chen on his former party

Wong, who later joined fellow former PKR leader Rafizi Ramli’s Bersama party, said the recent string of electoral losses proved that Anwar’s personal popularity was not enough to guarantee PH’s survival against Umno and PAS.

“They have to start accepting the fact that if they don’t quickly reform in the last few months that they have, then they won’t even be able to win enough support to be a strong opposition,” Wong said.

The losses did trigger a response from Anwar. Last weekend, he pledged that the government would proceed to repeal the controversial University and University Colleges Act 1971 – which student activists have long said stifles freedom of speech and expression – and fulfil promises to impose a two-term limit on the prime minister and separate the powers of the attorney general and public prosecutor.

But those pledges may amount to little if they only translate into legislative change, according to Timothy Wong, a senior analyst with government affairs consultancy BowerGroupAsia.

“There needs to be real action behind institutional reforms rather than relying solely on legislation to convince the majority,” he said.

“They will need to do more to convince a politically fatigued electorate, especially urban and middle-class voters who are feeling increasingly disenfranchised by the country’s politics.”

Complicating matters further is Anwar’s continued reliance on Umno, which long-time Malaysia watcher James Chin says has every reason to sabotage the prime minister’s reform push, leveraging its cabinet positions – and the budgets that come with them – to bolster its own electoral chances.

“If you want to do real deep reforms, you have to inform the cabinet. And of course Umno, which has a lot of ministers in cabinet, will try to sabotage it or not agree to it, so you’re stuck,” said Chin, a professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.

“He [Anwar] knows deep down inside that Umno is plotting to win the next election and replace him as prime minister.”

Cracks in PH

Anwar caught a break, of sorts, last weekend, when delegates at DAP’s own convention voted decisively to remain within the governing coalition, after months of speculation the party might walk away.

But that lopsided vote belied the seething dissent within DAP’s ranks over how Anwar has managed the ruling coalition – especially his perceived favouring of Umno.

“Instead of bringing the coalition partners together, what has he done? He has divided us, pitted one against the other and empowered Umno. We cannot afford to ignore that,” DAP leader Sangeet Kaur Deo told her party’s convention.

“We cannot run away from the fact that today, under our government, Malaysia is more divided on racial lines than ever before. We cannot deny that there are scandals relating to corruption that have escalated during the time that we have been in power.”

Within PKR itself, the complaints are just as pointed. Some argue Anwar’s political instincts have curdled into self preservation.

His decision, in closing the party congress last Sunday, to announce an extra 222 million ringgit (US$54.6 million) in annual constituency allocations for MPs – money used for everything from pothole repairs to cash handouts for the needy – struck many grass-roots members as besides the point.

It did nothing to address the growing anger over stalled reform, critics say – with no explanation offered either for why three PKR MPs seen as loyal to Rafizi had their own allocations slashed.

Rafizi quit PKR after losing the deputy presidency to Anwar’s daughter, Nurul Izzah, in a contest he claimed was rife with nepotism.

Nurul Izzah has since stepped back too, beginning what the party has called a “leave of absence” to pursue her studies after serving her final days as her father’s deputy at the congress.

The extra funding fits a pattern: over the past two years, Anwar has pushed to increase cash handouts and maintain costly fuel subsidies despite the strain on public coffers, in a bid to win broader support.

One grass-roots leader offered a warning from history. “You can’t keep giving people freebies and expect them to love you. Look at what happened during BN’s time,” he said, invoking the Umno-led Barisan Nasional coalition that lost power in 2018 at the height of the 1MDB corruption scandal despite its own cash-handout scheme. “They still lost. We are doing exactly the same thing now.”

These internal rifts may not trigger an outright collapse of PH, but analysts warn that pressure from DAP and PKR supporters will keep mounting as long as Anwar prioritises political stability and his relationship with Umno over the reform agenda.

“The bigger danger is not PH formally breaking apart, but becoming increasingly hollowed out as an electoral alliance,” said public policy adviser Kamles Kumar, associate director for Malaysia at strategic advisory group Asia Group Advisors.

“If electoral losses continue, the question will increasingly shift from whether PH can stay together to whether staying together still benefits each component party.”

And the next test for PH is not far off. The Melaka state election, which must be called by February next year, is already looming and the Umno-led BN – which holds 21 of the state assembly’s 28 seats – has signalled its terms for any future deal: PH can have a shot at the seven seats BN does not currently control, but nothing more.

The bigger danger is not PH formally breaking apart, but becoming increasingly hollowed out

Kamles Kumar, public policy adviser

According to one Melaka-based PKR grass-roots leader, the party leadership is seriously considering the offer, even if it means accepting a subordinate role to Umno.

Yet this appears badly out of step with sentiments on the ground. “The top are talking about negotiating with BN, but we’ve already seen what happened in the two past state elections. On the ground, people are already sharpening their knives,” the insider said.

“As far as the grass roots are concerned, we have two choices. Fight and lose, or not do anything and die [politically].”

Anwar has promised party delegates he will listen: to their opinions, their suggestions and even their criticism.

For a party that spent 20 years fighting to put him in power – and is now watching that power slip through its fingers – the question is no longer whether he hears them.

It is whether, after everything, just listening will be enough.

Additional reporting by Iman Muttaqin Yusof

item.title: [SCMP] How to be a good tourist; a guide for the modern traveller
item.description:
From Tenerife to Thessaloniki, demonstrators’ chants and roadside graffiti alike say, “Tourists go home”, although sometimes in rather stronger language.

Around the world, the residents of “must-see” destinations can no longer see each other for the crowds, and increasingly view tourists less as benefactors and more as a bane. Local authorities are responding ever more robustly to their complaints.

To drink alcohol in certain Amsterdam streets now attracts a fine of €95 (US$110), while in the village of Varenna, on Italy’s Lake Como, it’s twice as much for wearing swimwear away from the beach.
item.content:encoded:
From Tenerife to Thessaloniki, demonstrators’ chants and roadside graffiti alike say, “Tourists go home”, although sometimes in rather stronger language.

Around the world, the residents of “must-see” destinations can no longer see each other for the crowds, and increasingly view tourists less as benefactors and more as a bane. Local authorities are responding ever more robustly to their complaints.

To drink alcohol in certain Amsterdam streets now attracts a fine of €95 (US$110), while in the village of Varenna, on Italy’s Lake Como, it’s twice as much for wearing swimwear away from the beach.

Not far away, in seaside Portofino, the introduction of no-loitering zones has effectively put an end to selfies, unless you’re a professional narcissist and the income to be expected from sponsors or followers is greater than the potential €275 (US$317) penalty for blocking traffic.

However, much of the globally growing ill will is not about bad behaviour but merely about numbers.

Destinations that have seen many long-term rental properties turned into more profitable short-term accommodation for tourists are introducing strict regulations (British Columbia) or banning Airbnb and its ilk altogether (Barcelona).

Local satisfaction is crucial to success, but if the visited are unhappy, so are the visitors.

Tourists discover soaring head taxes, 90-minute queues and compulsory advance-purchase tickets with a timed entry, and that the quiet stroll between two pretty mountain villages they have come back to enjoy for a second time now has an entrance fee and one-way-only traffic, and yet is still a conga line.

Individual residents, municipal authorities and national tourism bureaus alike declare that they don’t dislike tourists, and don’t want to discourage them, but they do want to choose the visitors they get.

An official online Tokyo travel guide, How to stay safe and be respectful in Tokyo at night, has little to say about safety in what anyway ranks as one of the world’s least dangerous cities. Instead, it explains how not to offend locals by littering, or by drinking or smoking in public.

But if the Japanese are too polite to say straight out, “Don’t come unless you obey the rules”, José Antonio Donaire, Barcelona’s commissioner for sustainable tourism, feels no such restraint. He wants to restrict visitors to no more than the 15.7 million the city hosted in 2025, and he wants half of those to be cultural tourists – presumably people who swoon at the sight of Joan Miro’s surrealist art or Antoni Gaudi’s soaring Sagrada Família rather than their 15th Estrella Damm lager of the day.

In terms of accommodation capacity, all tourists may be equal, but some are more equal than others. These regulations, fines and fees suggest a definition of good tourists: it’s those who stay longer, spend more with local businesses, respect the needs of residents, do not congregate all in one spot and neither dive into historic fountains (€500/US$576 fine in Rome) nor indulge in drunken caterwauling at 3am (€140/US$161 in Amsterdam).

However, concentrating on attracting good tourists will still not solve the problem of volume, and some destinations are looking to spread the load.

Japan has offered some international visitors free domestic flights to destinations beyond the well-worn Tokyo-Kyoto-Osaka trail that two-thirds of them take.

Spain’s new policy is to encourage visitors to avoid the summer peak, and to look beyond the supply of sun, sea, sand and potential sexual partners along its crowded Mediterranean beaches towards the equally sun-baked sleepy villages of the interior.
