While Hemrajani said the effectiveness of Meta’s new safety protocols “remains to be seen”, she called the latest developments “a turning point” that were likely to spur other governments into demanding change.

Elina Noor, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said the Meta settlement showed “there is more to be done in holding Big Tech accountable for a range of harms”, affecting children in particular.

But she said the picture was complicated by the fact that many of the same companies being pressed to pay billions in damages were also providing technical expertise and underwriting capacity-building efforts to help the region fight scams.

Yesterday’s rules

Asean’s existing digital cooperation mechanisms were not built around platform accountability, focusing instead on phone calls and SMS.

The bloc’s current guidelines “expressly exclude scams conducted through social media and OTT services such as WhatsApp”, said Alejandro Reyes, chief strategic officer of non-profit organisation AI Safety Asia, referring to services delivered directly to users over the internet.

“Yet much of the problem has shifted onto precisely those platforms,” he told This Week in Asia.

As an example, Reyes pointed to Singapore, where social media accounted for roughly 30 per cent of scam cases last year, with messaging apps responsible for another 23 per cent.

Digital governance analyst Hafizh Nabiyyin said Asean leaned too heavily on scam prevention and non-binding guidance, such as public education campaigns or knowledge-sharing exercises, rather than holding platforms to account.

This was a function of the bloc’s non-interference principle, consensus-based decision-making approach and tendency to take “a middle-ground position”, he said.

Even if it expanded its guidelines to cover platform accountability more explicitly, “they would just be guidelines and not regulations or legislation”, Hemrajani said.

Asean was not the European Union and it could not feasibly introduce comparable legally binding rules for Big Tech companies, she added.

‘Coalition of the willing’

If bloc-wide legislation is seemingly off the table, then what can Asean do?

Existing regional frameworks set baseline measures, backed by information sharing and joint investigations, for individual members to adopt.

Asean’s Guideline for Digital Platform Regulation, for instance, recommends that member states verify the identity of all online sellers on digital platforms.

When Taiwan adopted a similar measure, it saw scam advertisements drop sharply as a result, said David Lam, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, digital economy and technology policy.

“As effective as this measure is, however, Asean leaves it to member countries to individually enforce it,” Lam said.

Enforcement, not ambition, is where the region keeps stumbling. Malaysia’s social media licensing requirements – later codified under its Online Safety Act – were largely ignored or rejected by social media companies when first introduced.

Meta had also reportedly ignored Philippine requests to take down deepfake videos of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr used to promote an investment scam, Lam said.

Collective bargaining power against Big Tech platforms could be consolidated via an Asean-wide framework, Noor argued, enabling the bloc to take on companies “whose market valuation and even annual revenue rival Southeast Asian economies”.

But she said the obstacles to enforcement were numerous. Not only are these the same companies that underpin much of the region’s digital economic growth, member states also have differing exposure to online harm and uneven levels of digital maturity.

On top of that is the ever-present risk of US trade retaliation against governments seen as targeting American tech firms unfairly.

Yet at least a subset of Asean member states clearly wanted tougher Big Tech regulation, Lam said, driven by the twin pressures of scams and child safety.

He pointed to Project Nexus – a regional instant-payments system built by a founding group of countries around binding operation standards, with the door left open for others to join later – as a template for how a “coalition of the willing” might operate on platform accountability too.

Reyes said pushing platform accountability up the Asean agenda would fit “naturally with Manila’s stated priorities on digital transformation and protecting vulnerable groups”.

But as chair, the Philippines is merely a convenor.

“The chair cannot impose a regional regulatory regime,” he said. “There is no Asean equivalent of an EU legislature and regulator imposing and enforcing a single platform law across the region.”

A more realistic ambition, Reyes said, would be establishing a “common regional floor” of shared minimum standards on scam advertising, account verification, fraud reporting, evidence preservation, child safety and cooperation with law enforcement.

“If the Philippines wants to lead this at Asean, the question is not only what regional framework it can broker, but what enforceable obligations it is prepared to put in place at home,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Beyond Amsterdam: Amersfoort’s 15th century charm lies in its canals, cafes and tourist-free calm
item.description:
It would be odd to visit the Netherlands without spending time in Amsterdam, the canal-laced city of slender, leaning houses in patterned brick with their toothy stepped gables, famous for its Rembrandts and Van Goghs, and for action-movie speedboat chases along its waterways and under narrow humpbacked bridges.

Some visitors are attracted less by this culture than by the city’s cheerful open-mindedness; sex workers on display in windows among everyday shopping in a central red-light district and marijuana that was available in cafes for decades before deregulation became fashionable anywhere else. It’s also pleasant just to take a canal-side bench with a lunch of pickled herring, stroopwafels, or chips with peanut-butter sauce, and watch the boats and bicycles go by.

However, faced with up to 20 million tourists a year, the city’s 950,000 residents would increasingly like you to consider alternatives, or at least to spread out a bit. It’s not as if the Netherlands’ culture and history stop dead at Amsterdam’s periphery. Within a short train ride (the only kind here; anything more will take you to Belgium or Germany), there are what seem like little bits of Amsterdam that have broken off and floated away. These also have centuries-old tottering houses, ancient churches, canals and the same generally welcoming atmosphere, but each with its own individual style.
item.content:encoded:
It would be odd to visit the Netherlands without spending time in Amsterdam, the canal-laced city of slender, leaning houses in patterned brick with their toothy stepped gables, famous for its Rembrandts and Van Goghs, and for action-movie speedboat chases along its waterways and under narrow humpbacked bridges.

Some visitors are attracted less by this culture than by the city’s cheerful open-mindedness; sex workers on display in windows among everyday shopping in a central red-light district and marijuana that was available in cafes for decades before deregulation became fashionable anywhere else. It’s also pleasant just to take a canal-side bench with a lunch of pickled herring, stroopwafels, or chips with peanut-butter sauce, and watch the boats and bicycles go by.

However, faced with up to 20 million tourists a year, the city’s 950,000 residents would increasingly like you to consider alternatives, or at least to spread out a bit. It’s not as if the Netherlands’ culture and history stop dead at Amsterdam’s periphery. Within a short train ride (the only kind here; anything more will take you to Belgium or Germany), there are what seem like little bits of Amsterdam that have broken off and floated away. These also have centuries-old tottering houses, ancient churches, canals and the same generally welcoming atmosphere, but each with its own individual style.

Amersfoort, for example, was once made prosperous by beer and textiles, as well as its location on the navigable Amer river, later renamed the Eem, but now is a backwater half an hour away from Amsterdam by frequent train. It’s a concentrated and walkable pocket of Dutch culture ancient and modern, best viewed not as a checklist of sights but as a souvenir-shop-free town where ordinary life goes on in a historic setting. Wandering is a pleasure in itself.

From Amersfoort Centraal station, it’s a 15-minute walk to the largely pedestrianised Old Town and a landmark that can be seen from some distance away, the 98-metre (321 feet) Gothic Onze Lieve Vrouwetoren, or “Tower of Our Lady”. This solitary finger of reddish brick, built in the 15th century, its accompanying chapel long vanished, rises in steps that change to carved grey stone topped with a shining golden cockerel. From the top, if you can manage the 346-step climb, there are views over the town centre’s labyrinth of narrow streets. But there’s as much pleasure in relaxing with something restorative at a cafe, bar or restaurant in the small square at its base, taken while listening to the sound of the bells reverberating around the ancient facades as the tower’s clock strikes the quarter-hour, the half-hour or the hour.

In one corner of the square, the 16th century Kapelhuis (“Chapel House”) is a reminder of when Amersfoort was a major destination for pilgrims, attracted by a supposedly miracle-working stone statue of the Virgin Mary that once perched here. But the continuing survival of the seemingly flimsy stepped frontage, its brickwork in herringbone and circular decorative patterns, seems miracle enough.

A little further down the narrow Lieve Vrouwestraat is antiquity of a more domestic nature, in a pair of equally diminutive half-timbered houses that also date from the 16th century, framed in stridently red-painted wood, with dark green shutters.

Carry on and the road swings to the left to follow the route of the original city wall along a parade of further ancient housing of particular bricky dignity, walls bulging in some places and studded with the plates of the tie beams holding the buildings together, large ground-floor windows opening onto the thin streets. Dormers with hoists suggest the impossibility of getting furniture up or down steep interior stairs. Many are muurhuizen, or “wall houses”, built in the 15th and 16th centuries on the route of the 13th century city wall using some of its remains. The expanding town had replaced the earlier defences with a larger ring, some of whose impressively fortified water gates still stand.

These narrower streets intersect those of regular shopping – shoes, a pharmacy, a bustling bookshop with plenty in English – and cross short and sturdy bridges over tree-lined canals that reflect the ancient frontages alongside. Wandering visitors may happen upon the small, covered 17th century fish market, an 18th century synagogue or fragments of the original city wall. And if they are in need of a souvenir, there’s the Mondriaanhuis.

Amersfoort may be short on Rembrandts or Van Goghs, but the town was the birthplace of Pieter Cornelis Mondriaan, more famously known as Piet Mondrian (1872-1944), the master of a grid-like abstraction whose style was picked up and absorbed into the fashion of Saint Laurent and Moschino. The house in which the painter was born shows nine earlier figurative pieces that only hint at the abstraction that was to come, although there are many works by contemporaries clearly influenced by the artist’s later work. A shop sells attractively “Mondrian-ised” merchandise.

The finest wall house is the Groot Tinnenburg, which was built before 1414. It was part of the original city wall and connected to a substantial water gate now replaced by a simpler bridge. Still privately owned, and currently up for sale (yours for a rumoured €2.65 million/US$3.08 million), its great mass, towering stepped gables, smart red shutters and location right on a canal make it perhaps Amersfoort’s most photogenic spot, although various water gates compete for that title, too.

The gate once attached to the Groot Tinnenburg was rendered redundant by the construction of the Monnikendam, on the second wall, here close to the route of the first. Both protected the water supply and defended the city from waterborne assault where several streams combine to form the Eem.

A blank-faced bridge, its flatness relieved only by arrow slits, the Monnikendam connects two squat brick towers capped with witches’ hats of grey slate, the canal passing under an arch low enough to make standing boatmen duck.

Walk anticlockwise from the Groot Tinnenburg along the outer bank of a city-circling canal, this section known as the Zuidsingel (“South Canal”), and you’ll discover that several wall houses have long gardens reached rather romantically by private bridges.

A clockwise stroll takes you past a small cobbled bridge leading to the Thieves’ Tower, part of a wall house that functioned as a prison from 1434 to 1889, and on to the Kamperbinnenpoort, the only gate from the first city wall to have been preserved, at least partially. Its tall towers, standing over the high road entrance, seem like a version of the Monnikendam that’s been over-fertilised and has bolted skywards.

The carving of a windmill and assorted greenery over the ornately framed entrance to a stolid 19th century building here, De Snuif Molen (“Tobacco Mill”; now an Asian grocery store), is a reminder of a later source of revenue for the town. And continuing round to the north, the white-painted Prattenburg house, with a tall, dark-red octagonal tower poking from a steep-sided roof, was once the home and warehouse of a Jewish tobacco dealer.

Turning south towards the town centre quickly brings you to the Kanunnikenhuisje, another pocket-sized Gothic brick frontage, from 1520, once home to the priests of the Sint-Joriskerk (“St George’s Church”) opposite. It’s now home to the Tante Cor cafe, with seats outside from which to watch people pass by on their way to market while sipping the Dutch version of coffee with extra milk – the koffie verkeerd, or “wrong coffee”.

The medieval Sint-Joriskerk is on a different scale from anything seen since the Tower of Our Lady, with triple steep roofs running its length over nave and aisles, having expanded over time to absorb its formerly external spire-topped tower, which now shoots up unexpectedly from within one roof. There’s carved stone around the entrances but the whole is otherwise domesticated by being constructed of the same materials as the rest of the town, and even more so by having had businesses glue themselves to the church’s outer wall on all sides.

These include the rectangular Butter Market hall, which opens onto De Hof square and is supplemented at weekends by a cluster of stalls, all family bustle and with nothing made for tourists. It offers the aromas of fresh baking, waffles and other hot snacks wrapped in gingham paper, and vast wheels of orange cheese.

Examining the facades around the square reveals signs of historical trade; the painted head of a helmeted figure with gaping mouth that protrudes from one of them suggests this was long the site of a pharmacy.

Proceeding northwest down Havik, following the canal of the same name along the city’s north side, you’ll pass substantial former merchants’ houses to arrive at the Museum Amersfoort. Reached across the canal by its own little bridge, the museum occupies three former wall houses in striking striped brick, linked to form a labyrinth of small spaces containing displays that tell Amersfoort’s history. Within are early landscapes of the city when its first wall was intact, a table model of its historic layout and local treasures such as the keys to the city that French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was too busy to accept when he passed through in 1811.

The museum explains the city’s relationship with water, the Eem having been used not only for shipping but also to provide fresh water, vital for both drinking and the development of the brewing and cotton-cloth industries that financed the town’s growth. But the only river that rises within the Netherlands, to drain into the ocean not far to the west, presents something of a threat to Amersfoort’s future, providing a channel for flooding as sea levels rise, and if dykes fail.

The best exit from the Old Town is through the nearby Koppelpoort, the most substantial of the city’s remaining gates, uniquely dominating both land and water approaches to the town. Built around 1425, it’s a string of octagonal towers and connecting buildings frowning forbiddingly over roadway and waterway alike.

From here, the railway station is a 15-minute walk away, but by now, it’s clear that Amersfoort isn’t just a side trip from Amsterdam; it’s an ideal base from which to explore the larger city and the rest of the region. Its central location, also on a major railway junction, makes access to the rest of the Netherlands easy. For now, it’s quiet and relaxed. The accommodation is relatively cheap and likely to become more competitive still as Amsterdam places further limits on short-term holiday rentals.

Perhaps the day-tripping should be done the other way.

item.title: [SCMP] Making tracks through China’s past and present
item.description:
“Peking wore the green lace of spring, its thousands of willows and imperial cypresses making the Forbidden City a place of wonder and enchantment,” American journalist Edgar Snow wrote of Beijing in 1936.

Ninety years later, strolling before the vermillion ramparts of the Forbidden City, it’s clear that Beijing’s mass conversion to electric vehicles has rendered the city not only cleaner than it has been of late, but also quieter – allowing Zhongshan Park to bloom much as Snow described.

Snow’s description was included in his wartime account of a journey to Yanan, Red Star Over China (first published in 1937), his destination then being the base of the Chinese Communist Party. But the city has made headlines much more recently, with the December opening of the Xian-Yanan high-speed railway taking the length of China Railway’s operational network past the 50,000km (31,070 miles) mark.
item.content:encoded:
“Peking wore the green lace of spring, its thousands of willows and imperial cypresses making the Forbidden City a place of wonder and enchantment,” American journalist Edgar Snow wrote of Beijing in 1936.

Ninety years later, strolling before the vermillion ramparts of the Forbidden City, it’s clear that Beijing’s mass conversion to electric vehicles has rendered the city not only cleaner than it has been of late, but also quieter – allowing Zhongshan Park to bloom much as Snow described.

Snow’s description was included in his wartime account of a journey to Yanan, Red Star Over China (first published in 1937), his destination then being the base of the Chinese Communist Party. But the city has made headlines much more recently, with the December opening of the Xian-Yanan high-speed railway taking the length of China Railway’s operational network past the 50,000km (31,070 miles) mark.

It took Snow more than two days to cover the 1,000km (621 miles) from Beijing to Xian by rail, but China’s 21st century public transport will make my own pilgrimage to Yanan, with some history-imbued detours along the way, far smoother.

With tickets bought online, I set my sights first on Jinan, the capital of Shandong province, located on the upper reaches of the Yellow River and 400km (249 miles) to the south of Beijing.

At the massive, oval-domed Beijing South station, I board a G-class train that makes light work of the Central Plain, rocketing across an area the size of Paraguay characterised by undulating wheat and rapeseed-flower fields. It takes just over two hours to reach the far side of the mighty Yellow River, a reminder that Beijing was one of the few ancient Chinese cities that were not fed by the “mother river”.

Jinan’s urban district stands to the south of the river. First impressions upon arrival at dusk are of a typical second-tier city composed chiefly of modern high-rises strung together by flyovers. My mood isn’t much improved by the hotel I pre-booked, which is located down a gloomy Shizhong district alley, past street-side barbecue joints populated by drunks, with electrical wires dangling overhead and between adverts for spas and KTV (karaoke television) lounges. The labyrinth of hotel corridors has tobacco-stained carpets and room service comes courtesy of R2-D2-like robots.

Morning illuminates Jinan in a better light.

A short walk leads to Wulongtan (“Five Dragon Pond”), a classical garden comprising several natural springs. It was mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals, the official chronicle of the state of Lu (1042BC-249BC), which existed here before the unification of China under Qin Shi Huang.

Bamboo-lined pathways lead between concave-roofed pavilions and goldfish ponds sprinkled with water lilies. Some park-goers are writing classical verses in calligraphic characters on the ground with giant brushes dipped in water, while a group of aunties practises a traditional sword dance beside a man who, unfazed by their music, drifts through the elegant postures of tai chi.

Wulongtan is one of several public gardens fed by spring water that dominate Jinan and help explain its motto, splashed on numerous billboards: “City of springs, no worries for people”.

To the north, the Jinan Baili Huanghe Scenic Area flanks the south bank of the Yellow River, which, in truth, is more of a coffee colour. Here, elders stretch while courting couples watch the sunset from viewing points along the river’s edges. Farmers still cultivate the muddy riverbanks, using nutrient-rich loess soil that has flowed down from Shaanxi province to feed rows of green vegetables, as they and their ancestors have done since the dawn of Chinese civilisation.

Following the riverfront path eastwards leads to the Luokou Yellow River Railway Bridge. Conventional rolling stock still uses this century-old, German-built viaduct, which was completed in 1912.

Also of German vintage in Jinan are a few villas, a colonial-era post office and the former station house on the Jiaoji Railway – Shandong’s first railway, which connected with the port of Qingdao.

Jiaoji Railway Station, which now houses a museum, was completed in 1915 and built in early European Renaissance Revival style. It is distinguished by a prominent central colonnade beneath a large clock. The line itself has been modernised and no longer leaves from the station-turned-museum, but from Daminghu station, near Daming Lake Park.

Unfortunately, the art nouveau Jinan Railway Station depicted in the museum, and which stood 500 metres (1,640 feet) from Jiaoji station, came to be regarded as “a symbol of colonialism” and was replaced by an unexceptional building in 1992. It’s from here that I depart for Taian, just a 20-minute hop away by high-speed rail.

Taian would be an unremarkable provincial city were it not for a mountain considered so sacred for so many centuries, it has assumed the status of a god.

Mount Tai is the easternmost of China’s nine Daoist peaks, attracting up to a million pilgrims a year, who attempt to follow the emperors’ journey 8km (five miles) up the mountainside, paying homage to Heaven and Earth, at the summit and foot of the mountain, respectively.

I set out early to beat the crowds, but my 6am hotel alarm call is not early enough; everyone else has made the same calculation. It’s not so much a hike, then, as a communal walk along stone steps carved out of the mountainside as far back as Qin times, some two millennia ago.

Amid cypress trees and gushing streams, every rock we pass has been inscribed with poetic verse and it becomes apparent that the passage from the First Heavenly Gate to Jade Emperor Peak owes its glories – the temples and pavilions – to the patronage of the imperial court.

Past the Immortal Bridge, a natural formation of three huge boulders, the ascent to the Nantian Gate, some 1,500 metres (4,920 feet) above sea level, funnels hundreds of walkers between two walls of rock. Almost everyone is grasping the handrails as they haul themselves upwards at this point, cries of “jia you” (“add oil”) ringing out as pilgrims encourage one another to keep going.

There’s more than a sense of achievement to reward those who make it to the top of the mountain, where Tianjie (“Heaven Street”), a tourist strip with plenty of restaurants, awaits hungry hikers.

Unashamedly, I take the cable car back down to Earth, and the following day, I take the morning train to Kaifeng, in Henan province. There’s no fast service between the two cities, so I’m relegated to a second-class bunk in a half-full carriage, a sign that conventional rail might be dying out in the age of high-speed.

My fellow passengers are all tall northerners, their skin cracked by the sun of the high latitudes. Men in leather jackets and tightly fitting shirts walk back and forth along the gangway at 20-minute intervals, to find somewhere to smoke; women fondle their Xiaomi phones. Over seven hours of rail travel, there’s little to do but meditate on China’s heartland passing gently by while sipping tea and dipping into Red Star Over China.

Kaifeng is depicted in one of China’s great masterworks, Along the River During the Qingming Festival, a 12th century scroll painting that hangs in Beijing’s Palace Museum, as the Forbidden City is officially known, and reveals the bustling street markets and classical architecture of the capital of the Northern Song dynasty (960-1127) in its imperial heyday. The view from my taxi suggests the contemporary prefecture-level city is a few centuries past its prime: Soviet-style tenements jockey for space with modern towers, all of which appear to have adopted a colour code inspired by the muddy waters of the Yellow River.

The roads are the domain of e-bikes and e-trikes, which buzz like hornets around a nest within the refurbished city walls that frame the former capital.

In the middle of an anarchic roundabout stands the Drum Tower – three layers of green-tiled roofs atop a grey-brick foundation, the result of a complete 2013 rebuild – looking regal amid the shabby storefronts and chain hotels of downtown Kaifeng. At night, the eaves of the tower are illuminated with LED lights as it becomes the focus of a market. Hundreds of carts are pushed from side streets, to congregate around the tower, and from them issue the hissing and sizzling of cooking oil, with notes of garlic, ginger and pork fat, as diners feast on crispy wheat cakes and mutton noodle soup.

Kaifeng might not ooze the kind of laid-back prosperity I experienced in Jinan, but what it lacks in polish, it makes up for with heritage.

From the Old Town’s central access, Shudianjie (“Bookshop Street”), where some time-honoured book vendors are still in business, it’s easy to walk to some of the chief attractions, including the Shanshangan Guild Hall, a social hub established by northern merchants in the late 18th century.

Flanked by its own mini drum and bell towers, the hall has traditional roofing, the eaves of which have been decorated with lively scenes from the lives of travelling merchants and other wood carvings. One, in the Eastern Hall, depicts a man being dragged along the ground by his horse; others show golden bats, a symbol of luck, beneath animals and birds frolicking among bunches of grapes.

A 10-minute walk away, the Buddhist Daxiangguo Temple is still populated by robed monks 1,500 years after its founding. Watching the faithful prostrate themselves before Arhat statues at the back of the Main Hall, I’m reminded that train travel in China can be as much about time as it is space.

Kaifeng’s principal reminder of its Northern Song heyday is the 1,000-year-old Iron Pagoda, which towers 56 metres (184 feet) over the northeastern corner of the walled city. It is not made of iron but earned its name from the patterned glazed Buddhist tiles on its exterior, which give the tower the russet tones of rusted iron.

Despite Kaifeng’s plethora of historical marvels, it’s the tumble-down backstreets, where the rhythms of life remain unchanged by China’s high-speed dash towards a neon-hued future, that are hardest to bid farewell to when I depart from Kaifeng North station, bound for Xian.

Snow was received by the Kuomintang governor of the city when he visited Xian. I’m met with crowds pushing onto Metro Line 2, eager to get to the walled city centre. Yet, on emerging from Zhonglou station, which lies beneath the Bell Tower, it is impossible not to be impressed with what was, after all, the capital of 13 dynasties. Xian has the panache of somewhere that mattered, and mattered for a very long time – a self-confidence evident in the swagger of its denizens as well as the power architecture: the enormous Soviet-style Bell Tower Hotel, facing the Bell Tower; the “twin Tang towers” to the south of the city – the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda and Small Wild Goose Pagoda; the enormous walls and the broad boulevards that stitch it all together. Everything is on a scale that is only really rivalled by Beijing.

Having scarcely encountered another foreigner since leaving the capital, it’s something of a culture shock to witness legions of Western tourists, most of whom are taking advantage of the 30-day visa exemption policy to strike Qin Shi Huang’s Terracotta Army off their bucket list.

There again, Xian was the capital of the cosmopolitan Tang dynasty (618-907) and long served as the eastern gate to the Silk Road. This multicultural history is reflected in the Tang-era Great Mosque, which stands off a narrow, covered alley filled with vendors of tourist tat. One of the largest mosques in China, it was established in 742, although heavily restored during the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), and integrates Arabic features into a familiar Chinese design. Attracting mostly religious tourists from Central and Southeast Asia, the mosque’s tranquillity stands in contrast to the adjoining Muslim Quarter, which gets my vote for the finest street food in East Asia.

After braving the throngs several times for bowls of biang biang noodles, barbecued naan bread and persimmon doughnuts, I feel sufficiently energised to complete my railway quest.

Snow travelled north through fields of opium poppies that “nodded their swollen heads, ready for harvest, along the newly completed motor road” before sleeping “in a filthy hut […] with pigs and donkeys quartered in the next room”. I, on the other hand, cruise across the Loess Plateau at 250km/h (155mph) in an air-conditioned carriage.

The Yan River, a major tributary of the Yellow, bisects Yanan. The waterway and city are best viewed from Pagoda Hill, atop which stands the 44-metre (144 feet) Baota Pagoda, an octagonal brick tower that dates back to Tang times. Most of Yanan’s other tourist sites recall events that took place 90 years ago.

I taxi to the Date Garden, which was the site of the Communist Party Secretariat from October 1943 to March 1947. As well as various war bureaus, the former residences of officials, including Mao Zedong, Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi and Zhou Enlai, are located in the grounds of this erstwhile warlord’s manor, their humble furnishings still decorating their yaodong (“cave houses”), as earth-sheltered dwellings still common in Shaanxi province are called.

Concluding that to truly appreciate Yanan, I too should sleep in a cave, I consult a taxi driver parked outside the Date Garden, who takes me to Jingjiawan Village, where enterprising locals have converted family cave homes into guest houses.

A bright-eyed, middle-aged man, Xiao Zhang, greets me in the courtyard of the Old Yanan Cave Dwelling Hotel before showing me to my cavern for the night. Snow recounts sharing a kang, a traditional northern bed, with rats. But my kang has an electric blanket, while my cave is equipped with a widescreen television, an en suite bathroom and even voice-activated lights.

After a nap and a shower, I’m told to find an alfresco table on the edge of a cliff overlooking a large valley, a dramatic landscape of windblown yellow soil that has created steep ravines divided by deep gullies. The land here is rich in nutrients and has been cultivated for centuries, a history evident in crumbling terraces that were abandoned in the late 20th century as farmers emigrated to work in east-coast factories.

Lao Zhang, the family patriarch-turned-chef, takes my order and brings me a Wusu beer, with which I toast my journey back in time, from capital to cave.

item.title: [SCMP] Xi is in Bishkek for SCO summit. How does bloc fit China’s Eurasian strategy 25 years on?
item.description:
As Washington’s strategic focus shifts and energy and grain supply disruptions continue to unsettle the Middle East, Beijing’s expanding presence across Central Asia is expected to be in focus as Kyrgyzstan hosts the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit this week.

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s presence in Bishkek is expected to put the spotlight on whether the increasingly diverse grouping can move beyond diplomatic signalling, according to analysts. The SCO’s 25th anniversary summit was also expected to offer crucial clues to Beijing’s ambitions for a more multipolar Eurasia at a time of shifting regional power dynamics, they said.

The meetings over Monday and Tuesday are themed as “25 years of the SCO: together for sustainable peace, development and prosperity”. They are expected to focus on regional security, connectivity, energy and digital cooperation, while also addressing wider challenges including Iran, Afghanistan and food security.
item.content:encoded:
As Washington’s strategic focus shifts and energy and grain supply disruptions continue to unsettle the Middle East, Beijing’s expanding presence across Central Asia is expected to be in focus as Kyrgyzstan hosts the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit this week.

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s presence in Bishkek is expected to put the spotlight on whether the increasingly diverse grouping can move beyond diplomatic signalling, according to analysts. The SCO’s 25th anniversary summit was also expected to offer crucial clues to Beijing’s ambitions for a more multipolar Eurasia at a time of shifting regional power dynamics, they said.

The meetings over Monday and Tuesday are themed as “25 years of the SCO: together for sustainable peace, development and prosperity”. They are expected to focus on regional security, connectivity, energy and digital cooperation, while also addressing wider challenges including Iran, Afghanistan and food security.

China-Central Asia goods trade hit a record US$106 billion last year, according to Chinese government data, making Beijing the largest trading partner of the five countries combined for the first time.

Li Lifan, an expert on Russia and Central Asia at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, said the SCO and Central Asia held special significance for Beijing.

“As global competition intensifies between the US-led West and the emerging Global South amid a fractured international order, Beijing has placed greater weight on the SCO and Central Asia as a whole,” Li said, adding that “by deepening engagement and aligning more closely with Central Asian partners, China seeks to build common ground and present a more united front”.

“Through the SCO, China can project power and influence aspects of the global order,” he said, noting that the group’s expansion showcased China’s diplomatic appeal and influence.

In China’s diplomatic hierarchy, the United Nations ranks as the highest-level platform, while the SCO follows as the most important regional body.

Founded in 2001 by China and Russia, the now 10-member Eurasian security and economic forum brings together four Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan – and also newer entrants Belarus, India, Pakistan and Iran. Turkmenistan is the only non-SCO member in Central Asia but often attends summits as a guest nation.

Zhu Yongbiao, director of the Centre for Afghanistan Studies at Lanzhou University, said security remained Beijing’s top priority in Central Asia, not only along its western border but across the wider region, including the protection of key connectivity projects.

“I believe China’s primary interest in Central Asia is security, that is, ensuring a peaceful and stable neighbourhood,” he said.

Regional security is expected to feature prominently on the Bishkek agenda, according to Li, with Afghanistan, intelligence sharing and counterterrorism cooperation among the main concerns.

The potential for instability spilling over from Afghanistan, combined with Kyrgyzstan’s own security priorities, gives those discussions added weight.

While the China-Central Asia trade figure reflects the rapid expansion of commercial ties, Zhu cautioned against overstating the region’s economic weight.

He said Central Asia’s limited population and economic scale, as well as “overstated claims” about its mineral and energy resources, meant the region accounted for a relatively small component of China’s overall foreign trade.

Zhu emphasised that the region’s true strategic value stemmed from its geography – sitting next to China’s western border in Xinjiang, and serving as a critical bridge between China, Russia, the Middle East, South Asia and Europe.

Infrastructure is a central focus of the SCO, highlighted by the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway. Now under construction after two decades of negotiation and recent clearance from Russia, the line would create a pivotal trade artery, connecting China with Central Asia and onwards to the Middle East and Europe while plugging into an overland trade link to Afghanistan.

Li cautioned that security would remain a major challenge for the railway, as the route passes through difficult terrain and long tunnels vulnerable to terror attacks.

“Protecting this ‘steel lifeline’ is critical, as it is seen as China’s gateway to Central Asia and the Persian Gulf,” he said.

As a local saying goes: We wear Moscow’s armour, but our heart beats in Urumqi

Li Lifan, Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences

The railway is part of a wider effort to develop alternative routes, such as the “Middle Corridor” linking Central Asia and the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus, Turkey and Europe. Potential routes through Iran could provide additional access to the Persian Gulf and South Asia, but remain at the planning stage because of sanctions on Iran and regional instability.

Zhu said these projects were driven by demand from Central Asian and other states, rather than by Chinese strategy alone.

“Central Asian states, South Asia and Iran all seek stronger links, making connectivity inevitable,” he said. “China’s involvement adds momentum, enhances cooperation, improves quality, and accelerates the development of related routes.”

Energy and food security are also emerging as important non-traditional security concerns for the SCO, Li added, citing fuel disruptions linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine and the impact of climate change on harvests.

Iran’s protracted conflict with the United States will also be closely watched, given the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz for both energy and grain shipments.

Meanwhile, China’s expanding economic and technological role has raised questions about its ties with Russia, which remains the region’s principal security partner.

“Central Asian economies increasingly lean on China for trade, investment, infrastructure and technology, while Russia retains military bases, security arrangements and deep political and cultural ties,” Li said.

“As a local saying goes: ‘We wear Moscow’s armour, but our heart beats in Urumqi [capital of Xinjiang].’”

Yun Sun, director of the China programme and co-director of the East Asia programme at the Stimson Centre, noted that the SCO had also served as a mechanism for managing China-Russia relations, and that its limited practical achievements reflected the geopolitical and economic differences among its members.

“Some people call it a ‘nothing burger’. But conflict prevention and management of potential animosity are also of significant value,” she said.

China’s messaging through the SCO might also evolve now that strategic pressure from Washington had eased, Sun added, saying: “This year is the first time for a decade that China does not face a dire threat on the US front.”

She noted that while Beijing previously leveraged the SCO partly to help counter US pressure, its fundamental goal – demanding global governance reform and a “more just and reasonable international order” – remained unchanged.

Li, however, cautioned that the SCO’s role in the US-China rivalry should not be overstated.

“Central Asian states tend to pursue their own interests and resist taking sides. China has framed cooperation as open and inclusive, generally refraining from pressuring Central Asian governments to ‘choose sides’,” Li said. “Their approach is best described as hedging.”

Central Asian leaders deliberately exploited great-power rivalry to preserve strategic autonomy, resisting pressure to align fully with Russia or any other power, he added.

Meanwhile, the US has been stepping up engagement with Central Asia, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio expected to visit all five former Soviet states soon after the SCO summit.

Last November, Trump hosted the leaders of the five Central Asian nations in a “C5+1” summit at the White House to sign multibillion-dollar trade and critical mineral supply chain deals.

In recent weeks, the US has pressed dozens of countries including Kazakhstan to “choose sides” in artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation. There is even talk of inviting Trump to the region, underscoring Washington’s growing interest.

Uzbekistan has approached the US about joining Pax Silica, its flagship initiative on AI supply chains, a month after it signed up for China’s own global grouping, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Kazakhstan – the first Central Asian nation to sign up to Pax Silica – joined Waico in July.

Artyom Lukin, a professor at Russia’s Far Eastern Federal University, had a more sceptical take on the SCO’s practical impact.

“I think the SCO can’t be regarded as an efficient organisation delivering tangible results,” he said. “It’s definitely a talking shop in the first place and in the second place as well. I think almost everyone understands this reality.”

However, that does not make the organisation irrelevant.

As Lukin put it: “The SCO does have a certain value as a forum for multilateral dialogue of Eurasian powers as well as a venue for diplomatic signalling.”

item.title: [SCMP] Trita Parsi on why US air strikes strengthened Iran’s hand and failed to trigger a revolt
item.description:
Trita Parsi is co-founder and executive vice-president of the Quincy Institute, a Washington-based think tank. He is an expert on US-Iranian relations, Iranian foreign policy and the geopolitics of the Middle East. He has written four books on US foreign policy in the Middle East, with a particular focus on Iran and Israel. Born in Iran, Parsi moved to Sweden with his family as a child and then to the United States as an adult.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

What is your take on US President Donald Trump’s so-called economic D-Day on Iran? Some mainland Chinese and Hong Kong companies are implicated in the new secondary sanctions. Can Trump achieve his goals with these measures or will they backfire? What results will these sanctions bring?
item.content:encoded:
Trita Parsi is co-founder and executive vice-president of the Quincy Institute, a Washington-based think tank. He is an expert on US-Iranian relations, Iranian foreign policy and the geopolitics of the Middle East. He has written four books on US foreign policy in the Middle East, with a particular focus on Iran and Israel. Born in Iran, Parsi moved to Sweden with his family as a child and then to the United States as an adult.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

What is your take on US President Donald Trump’s so-called economic D-Day on Iran? Some mainland Chinese and Hong Kong companies are implicated in the new secondary sanctions. Can Trump achieve his goals with these measures or will they backfire? What results will these sanctions bring?

Trump’s D-Day sanctions will either fail to squeeze Tehran very hard and not much happens, or they will be hard-hitting and then the question is whether Iran counter-escalates or surrenders. And the pattern so far is really clear: Iran fears capitulation much more than escalation.

And given that [US Treasury Secretary Scott] Bessent has not listed any clear demands, Tehran will interpret the purpose of D-Day as a measure to force its surrender.

So instead of this leading to an end to the conflict, it will just start another round of the escalatory cycle.

What is your take on the latest developments regarding the US-Israel war on Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and the feasibility of the proposed Oman-Iran deal? We have seen contradictory signs from the Trump side, while Iran is raising even more demands. When will this escalation end?

Unfortunately, I don’t see any end in sight right now. Despite the fact that [Iran and the US are] not necessarily far away from each other on some of the core issues on the strait, there still seem to be a couple of things in the talks that have dramatically reduced confidence and trust between the two sides, and that’s already in a scenario in which trust clearly has been in very limited supply.

So, I do fear that in the near future we will not see any positive developments and, unfortunately, there is a risk of a further return to more conflict despite the fact that the conflict so far has been so tremendously non-constructive. It has not given the United States any additional benefit. We may still end up in another round of fighting.

Given reports of a drain on US ammunition, are military conflicts still possible?

They are still possible. It’s just that it will become riskier because what happens is that the US is running out of ammunition which it can fire from a long distance. In the next round of fighting, we may end up seeing that the US uses more aeroplanes that will have to fly into Iranian airspace and fly at lower altitudes, which will increase the risk for the US. And as a result we may see more aeroplanes getting shot down, and things of that nature.

What is the prospect of the Strait of Hormuz reopening, and under what circumstances could it happen?

Unfortunately, the prospect at this point seems very limited, but for it to open up it’s important to recognise that, even short of a deal, we may end up in a scenario in which some traffic will increase because both the Iranians and the Americans have a need for there to be traffic.

Iran is also suffering from the fact that the strait is closed. So, this is not pain only on one side.

So, the strait may still be blocked in name but some kind of traffic may still go through – even though the parties will not admit it?

Yes, but it would be very limited. It would not be near normal levels.

Five months into the war, what has changed in Iran politically and socially, and what has changed in its influence in the region?

Iran’s influence in the region, arguably, has increased. At least its leverage has increased and, I think, a lot of countries are now of the view that this war has clearly not only failed but has also led to a scenario in which the Iranians have really survived an attack that almost no other country in the region would be able to survive.

They have been attacked by two nuclear-weapon states and they have essentially come out on top. This is not something that any other country in the region could easily have done. And as a result, their deterrence [against] the other states has increased, and their leverage has increased internally.

However, [while] the population is accepting that this is a war situation, they can only accept that for a period of time. They cannot accept a war situation for months, dragging into years.

Now, of course, this was an aggression against Iran. They see this as a war of defence, which gives the government an amount of time in which the internal situation will be somewhat stable, despite shortages and economic problems.

But if this goes on for more than a year and if there’s a perception – and I’m not saying that perception exists right now – that the Iranian government itself is an obstacle to a resolution, then you will start seeing a lot of anger and sentiments internally in the country welling up.

It’s also important to recognise that the government has a lot of problems with the larger population. Those problems are now secondary because there’s a war. But once the war is over, these problems are going to come back. They haven’t gone away. They have not been resolved.

And if this war goes on for too long and the population is suffering, that’s going to add to some of these challenges. But for now, it’s safe to say that the government’s internal position is stronger than it was six months ago.

And in some ways, the war may have saved the Islamic Republic just as much as Saddam Hussein’s invasion of Iran in 1980 did. He thought he was going to overthrow the Iranian government, but he ended up saving the Iranian government. The revolution was still new. They had not consolidated their power, but because of the external threat, they did consolidate that power. They did manage to get control of the internal situation.

Iran was facing some of the worst protests in decades. And then [this year] this attack comes and the country unites against an external threat. And in that way, the attack may have saved the Islamic Republic.

Six months ago, huge protests took place and young people seemed to be very angry with the government. Are you saying the government’s control over the population has been strengthened because of the war?

It has been strengthened because there’s a war and people are concerned about their security. When the US is bombing critical infrastructure, refineries and simultaneously saying that they’re trying to destroy the country and an entire civilisation, at this point it becomes clear this is not a war against a government. This is a war against the country as a whole, and that works in the favour of the government.

Before the US and Israel started bombing Iran, Trump called for people to revolt against the government. And now it seems he is pushing the people closer to the administration because of the bombing?

Absolutely. And it shows you the foolishness of this war and the massive miscalculation.

What is your take on the Mecca defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan? Analysts say it is a sign these countries no longer view the US as a security guarantor for the Arab states. What will the Middle East look like if this perception persists?

First of all, that is absolutely correct. This is a manifestation of the fact that a lot of countries in the region have lost faith in the American security umbrella, in its efficiency and reliability. They have seen that the security umbrella is ineffective against Iran and at the same time the American side is unwilling to really defend these countries from Israel.

So, they have to look for alternatives and this is just going to be one of many things that I suspect will happen, and these are initial reactions. They may not end up becoming the end state.

This pact also is explicitly said to be open. Additional countries can be added to it. It can go in that direction if the Iranians play their cards wrongly in this long-standing American effort to contain and isolate Iran, which has been the organising principle of American foreign policy in the region and was driven by American hegemonic desires.

The US’ desire for hegemony in the region, which necessitated isolating Iran, may now be replaced by a regional desire for the same goal, meaning that the impetus will come from regional states that will seek to isolate and contain through a pact that isolates and encircles Iran because of a perception of threat. This would be a very bad development for the Iranians. It ultimately would be a very bad result for the region because the real conclusion that should be drawn is that you can’t contain or isolate Iran.

That policy inevitably led to this war. And if you try that policy again, but without the US, the result will nevertheless likely be the same. It will just lead to another conflict.

And we see that pattern in other bloc formations as well. Bloc formations are supposed to create stability, but oftentimes they make a long-term conflict more likely. What this can end up becoming, however, is the beginning step. It’s an embryonic agreement. Its end destination and objective is undecided and it may move towards becoming a larger regional security arrangement, not just a bloc between three countries, which ideally would be an inclusive security order [taking] inspiration from Asean. That would be much better for the region as a whole, and it would be based on creating economic integration and interdependence between the states in the region.

That possibility is still there because this pact does not preclude it. But it can lead to a scenario in which this pact eventually becomes an obstacle to that vision.

What is the likelihood of Iran becoming a regional power? If Iran somehow gets the US to lift some of the sanctions, will it become a regional power?

Iran already is a regional power. The question is, is the region accepting Iran’s role as a regional power or is its role as a regional power contested?

Iran needs to have a role that is commensurate with its geopolitical weight. And that is where diplomacy really comes in, and where the Iranians have to play their cards very cleverly and effectively and not rely entirely on hard power.

Because if you rely too much on hard power, all you do is convince your neighbours that you are a threat and their reaction will be to try to balance you.

How will China’s influence and role in the Middle East change as new dynamics and a new order are created in the region? And how will China’s relationship with the Gulf States and Iran change?

Let’s first review what China has done in this war so far. China has really stayed out of this conflict, it has not taken sides.

There is a revelation on the Iranian side that China was not hostile to Iran, of course, but China did not come to Iran’s aid in a very significant way.

Yes, there may have been some intelligence sharing et cetera, and that may not have been unimportant, but that’s very different.

There have been two main orientations in Iran: one that favoured orienting Iran towards the West; and the other one favoured leaning towards China and Russia. But both schools have been proven wrong. The first because a deal with the US was not possible, and the second because neither Russia nor China supported Iran meaningfully in the war.

The conclusion is that Iran is alone. Iran has always been alone. It doesn’t mean that it doesn’t have friends, but it doesn’t have security pacts. Those strategic relations do not translate into security pacts.

And as a result, it has to stand on its own [two feet]. And in some ways, that makes Iran’s outlook very similar to that of China. China is looking at itself similarly – it does not extend security pacts.

The Iranians, as a result, are going to invest more, not to say that they’re going to walk away from China at all. On the contrary, they’re going to continue to invest in China relations, but with a clearer idea of what that relationship is. It is not a security relationship or a pact in which they can rely on Chinese support for their defence.

Instead, it will be that Iran will have to invest in the region. It will invest in its forward defence, meaning its reliance on the Houthis, on Hezbollah and other groups, and then try to see how it simultaneously can improve relations with its regional neighbours.

But the forward defence is a protection not against its neighbours. It’s a protection against the US and Israel.

Hezbollah is Iran’s first line of defence against an Israeli attack. Israel only attacked when Hezbollah was weak. When Hezbollah has been strong, the Israelis have been more careful about attacking Iran.

However, China has played its cards very well. It has stayed out of this conflict. It has not done anything to deliberately damage the US. It has not taken advantage of this to undermine the US. The US is doing enough to undermine itself – China doesn’t need to.

At the same time, China has also realised that, yes, it always had a balance between its relationships with Iran and Saudi Arabia. But now China has realised that Iran is much stronger – not that Saudi Arabia isn’t but Saudi Arabia is dependent. Iran is independent. Iran alone defeated Israel and the US.

Saudi Arabia, even with the help of the US, could not defeat the Houthis. And China’s perspective in the long term is to have very good relations with the countries that have the ability to provide stability in specific regions. And there, the outcome of this war has put Iran in a different light from Beijing’s perspective.

How will Beijing’s relationship with the Gulf countries change, and how will these countries view Beijing? Because some may expect China to act to relieve or mediate the situation, but it has not.

Beijing’s strategy so far has been very smart. It has not entered into any alliance with other states. It’s doing the opposite of the US. The US cannot help itself but get involved in everyone else’s conflict, whereas China very wisely stays out.

But China is going to see an effort by the other GCC [Gulf Cooperation Council] states to become as close to China as possible economically to make sure that any future potential conflict between Iran and any GCC states would have a deep impact on China economically and, as a result, China would have a greater need for not necessarily getting involved militarily, but to get involved diplomatically.

China has an ability that the US doesn’t have here. Everyone trades extensively with China. No one can afford to have a bad relationship with China because of economic reasons. And as a result, China can come in as a diplomatic force because everyone wants to make sure that they don’t move themselves too far away from China.

The GCC will be hoping that China will get involved diplomatically and that it will feel a self-interest to get involved diplomatically because of economic reasons.

Why did Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reject Trump’s Gaza proposal, and how will the US relationship with Israel change? Trump is under a lot of pressure internally, with Israel blamed for dragging the US into this war.

There is a tremendous amount of frustration in the White House with Israel. Israel dragged the US into this war. We’re also seeing that Netanyahu is willing to say no to Trump. The Trump administration has not pushed back hard against Netanyahu on this issue, and there have even been statements saying that Netanyahu was faced with an election and, as a result, this is a sensitive period.

If this was happening under the Biden administration, it would have gone out of its way to blame Hamas when Israel rejected a peace deal. We saw that repeatedly. Israel kept on rejecting peace deals, undermining peace deals, and the Biden administration protected Israel by blaming Hamas. The Trump administration did not do that this time. Everyone knows it’s Netanyahu who rejected this proposal.

I find that interesting.

Has Hamas been weakened so much that it’s hard to say it is Hamas any more?

No, I don’t think so because it was the same situation before, and Hamas, even though it is weakened, still has some agency. So one could easily have done it back then as well.

What we have seen is that Trump, even though he doesn’t put consistent pressure on the Israelis, is willing to go out and blame Israel and push back hard against Israel at times. It tends to be very temporary, but he has shown that willingness. Whereas the Biden administration had a policy in which they wanted to see no daylight between Israel and the US. And by that, allow the Israelis to completely set the agenda.

Are you suggesting there is reduced US backing of Israel?

We may end up seeing a significant distance between the two countries. The Israelis were very unhappy about the signing of the MOU [memorandum of understanding, by the US and Iran in June] and if the MOU had succeeded, and it still may, it would have led to a scenario in which there would have been a crisis in US-Israeli relations.

How will Trump’s dealings with the Middle East, especially the war with Iran, affect the midterm elections?

There’s going to be a general unhappiness because of inflation, gas prices, food prices, directly resulting from this. You’re already seeing that in some primaries, the US relationship with Israel has become a very hotly contested issue and the race is almost reduced to whether a candidate is in favour of the war, in favour of Israel, in favour of what Israel did in Gaza, or against it.

This is very unusual. And it’s showing how things are changing in a very dramatic way in the US. But for these specific midterms, the Republicans are going to suffer defeats. Some members of Congress may come out and blame Trump and the war explicitly, either to save themselves or, if they lose, out of anger and frustration, because many of them are not just angry about the war. They are angry because they see that Trump does not care what happens to Republican members of Congress.

He does not seem to be particularly concerned about this and as a result they’re facing an end to their careers politically because of what Trump has done and Trump does not do anything to support them. So, there’s a feeling of betrayal and abandonment. It’s very hidden right now but beneath the surface it festers.

Will that increase the risk? Will that prompt Trump to take even more radical actions if there are failures in the midterms?

There is a risk that after the midterms that Trump – because he has more difficulties in Congress – will become even more radical in his conduct. This is one of the potential miscalculations the Iranians are making in which they think the punishment of Trump in the midterms would be satisfactory to them, which perhaps on an emotional level it would be, but it can also lead to a scenario in which he increasingly does not care about certain constraints, and certain norms and guardrails.

Look at how his behaviour changed after he lost the election in November 2020. Between November 2020 and January 2021, Trump considered some very radical options. One of them, which was actualised, was the protests on January 6, [an] attempt at a takeover, but he was also contemplating war with Iran during those two months as a way of staying in power. You may end up seeing a scenario in which the midterm elections and a loss will make him more radical.

item.title: [SCMP] Is the Irtysh River the choke-free Arctic shipping gateway that China needs?
item.description:
As conflicts around the world highlight the vulnerability of global shipping lanes, China and Russia are reportedly weighing the possibility of turning a vast river into an inland cargo route to the rest of the world.

At the heart of this ambition is the 4,248km (2,640-mile) Irtysh River, which originates in China’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region and runs through Kazakhstan before flowing into Russia’s Ob River and ending in the Arctic Ocean.

To China, this river-to-sea shipping route could offer inland access to the resource-rich and strategically important Arctic.
item.content:encoded:
As conflicts around the world highlight the vulnerability of global shipping lanes, China and Russia are reportedly weighing the possibility of turning a vast river into an inland cargo route to the rest of the world.

At the heart of this ambition is the 4,248km (2,640-mile) Irtysh River, which originates in China’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region and runs through Kazakhstan before flowing into Russia’s Ob River and ending in the Arctic Ocean.

To China, this river-to-sea shipping route could offer inland access to the resource-rich and strategically important Arctic.

More importantly, unlike traditional maritime chokepoints like the Malacca and Bering straits, the route could avoid Western naval blockades, foreign coastguard surveillance and sanctions by the United States, according to observers.

Shipping through the Arctic – the so-called Northern Sea Route – was long impractical due to the thick ice that covered the sea for much of the year. But warming temperatures have gradually made the passage more viable, raising China’s interest in the route.

That interest has been compounded by geopolitical tensions.

Zhao Long, a senior research fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz were raising prospects for alternative shipping routes.

“Both overland transport corridors and maritime shipping lines are facing the impacts of geopolitical conflict and the spillover effects of these conflicts are increasingly long-term and pronounced,” Zhao said.

“Therefore, any potential solution that offers additional route options will inevitably gain momentum.”

An added advantage is the amount of time saved. Voyages along the Northern Sea Route could go from China’s Ningbo port to Felixstowe in Britain in 20 days, compared to 40 days via the Suez Canal.

Chinese freight companies are already seeing the potential. Earlier this month, Chinese carrier Sea Legend Line launched a regular weekly container service along the route, the first of its kind using the Arctic Ocean.

Alexei Likhachev, head of Russia’s state atomic energy corporation Rosatom, which manages the Northern Sea Route, said that more than 30 shipments were expected along the route this year. That is up from 14 in 2024 and 24 in 2025, according to news agency Interfax.

Likhachev said shipments between Chinese and Russian ports accounted for nearly 15 per cent of all cargo traffic along the route, adding that freight between the two neighbours via the Arctic Ocean “should reach 20 million tonnes by 2030”.

But China’s access to the route now relies on the Bering Strait, making it a potential chokepoint for Beijing – and Moscow – in the event of an American blockade launched from Alaska.

Separating Russia’s Chukchi Peninsula from the Seward Peninsula of Alaska, the Bering Strait is the only marine gateway between the Arctic and Pacific oceans. At its narrowest point, the strait is only about 85km wide.

During the Cold War, both the US and Soviet Union fortified their sides of the strait, which was often transited by submarines collecting intelligence.

Marc Lanteigne, a professor with The Arctic University of Norway, said the militarisation of the Arctic had been revived in recent years and that the US was now monitoring Alaskan waters more closely.

Since 2015, Chinese and Russian navies have carried out regular patrols in the Bering Strait. In July 2024, for the first time, Chinese and Russian strategic bombers flew over the area, prompting the North American Aerospace Defence Command to scramble US F-16 and F-35 fighters alongside Canadian CF-18s to intercept the formation.

In October 2024, the China Coast Guard entered the Arctic Ocean through the strait in a joint drill with their Russian counterparts for the first time, an operation that Chinese observers said at that time had effectively expanded the coastguard’s far-seas operational range.

This activity has raised alarm in the US.

In July last year, US President Donald Trump signed a budget bill with almost US$25 billion in extra coastguard spending, including almost US$9 billion for new icebreakers and US$300 million for new facilities in Alaska.

When the Chinese research icebreakers Xuelong and Xuelong 2 passed north through the US exclusive economic zone and over the extended North American continental shelf in the Bering Sea last month, they were watched closely by both Canadian and the US coastguards for days.

This proximity to the US “is why the Northern Sea Route passing through the Bering Strait is never safe geopolitically”, according to Artyom Lukin, a professor of international relations at Far Eastern Federal University in Vladivostok.

“If China wants an assured access to the Arctic Ocean, it needs to solve the Bering Strait dilemma. A corridor along the Irtysh River, via China itself, Kazakhstan and Russia, is one obvious solution.”

Zhao said that while passing through the Bering Strait remained the most economical option, developing the Irtysh River made sense for contingencies.

“If extreme situations arise – such as a total blockage of the strait making it unnavigable, whether due to natural causes, political reasons or security factors – then obviously, you still have a backup plan.”

If China wants an assured access to the Arctic Ocean, it needs to solve the Bering Strait dilemma

Artyom Lukin, Far Eastern Federal University

While landlocked Kazakhstan has long sought to develop the Ob-Irtysh system, the vision gained momentum in 2024 when the country revealed a concrete plan to develop the route.

Then last year Kazakhstan approved a blueprint to develop shipping on the river system.

Speaking last month at a Russia-Kazakhstan cooperation forum held beside the Irtysh in the city of Omsk, Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow and Astana were working together on plans for the river and aiming “to strike a balanced approach between increasing freight transport, developing water resources and preserving the river’s ecosystem”.

Batyrbek Musin, an adviser to the board for development at Pavlodar River Port on the Irtysh, said the three nations were actively considering the new transport corridor.

“This strategic issue can take the form of a ‘Water Silk Road’,” Musin said on the sidelines of the forum, according to news portal Russia’s Pivot to Asia.

The Chinese government has not made any statement on the proposed route.

Kazakhstan hopes to expand its shipbuilding, repair and port facilities to support heavy freight on the Irtysh. The goal is to increase its annual cargo traffic to an estimated 2.5 million tonnes, from the 1.5 million tonnes today.

Russia, meanwhile, has designated the Ob-Irtysh system as part of its planned Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor, a broader strategic project aimed at creating shipping routes beyond the reach of Western sanctions.

Zhao, in Shanghai, said this project could link Russia’s vast Siberian heartland with the Chinese market.

“This aligns with Russia’s need to reduce its transport dependence on Europe under Western sanctions, while also fitting into its broader foreign policy pivot.”

But turning the river into a major trade artery will not be easy.

Navigating the river system would mean overcoming the harsh Siberian winters that freeze the waterway for up to six months a year, possibly limiting commercial shipping to a narrow summer window.

Meanwhile, seasonal low water levels and heavy silting also create shifting sandbars, which would require huge dredging capacity so that large cargo barges would not run aground.

As part of its cooperation with Russia, Kazakhstan launched its first dredger, the Irtysh-2503, in April.

In addition, getting cargo to and from China’s densely populated coast to remote Xinjiang – especially in the quantities required to make the river route worthwhile – would require further infrastructure investment.

Lanteigne said that in expanding infrastructure along the Irtysh River, authorities would also need to balance preserving the waterway as a source of fresh water.

Another key challenge for the project would be navigating China and Russia’s subtle tug of war for influence in Central Asia.

“Astana has been seeking to diversify its regional friends, including China as well as in the Caspian region, while Russia has been trying to maintain its traditional role as a security guarantor in Central Asia.”

Lukin said that making the Irtysh route navigable would require enormous investment and the renewed political support of the three countries.

“The total costs could be in the tens, and even hundreds, of billions of dollars. Only China has the resources on such a scale.

“But will it commit such huge investments to the project that mostly runs through the territories of Russia and Kazakhstan? Undertaking the Irtysh project requires a whole new level of trust and closeness between China, Russia and Kazakhstan.”

item.title: [SCMP] Vietnam’s move to end executions for drug trafficking sparks debate in region
item.description:
Vietnam is seeking to end executions for drug trafficking under a draft revision to its Penal Code, a notable shift in a country with one of Southeast Asia’s toughest anti-drug regimes.

The proposal, presented to lawmakers last week, would remove trafficking from Vietnam’s list of capital crimes. Last year, Hanoi kept the offence on the list during an earlier round of death penalty reforms.

If passed, the revised law would leave capital punishment for four crimes: treason, murder, terrorism and illegal narcotics production.
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam is seeking to end executions for drug trafficking under a draft revision to its Penal Code, a notable shift in a country with one of Southeast Asia’s toughest anti-drug regimes.

The proposal, presented to lawmakers last week, would remove trafficking from Vietnam’s list of capital crimes. Last year, Hanoi kept the offence on the list during an earlier round of death penalty reforms.

If passed, the revised law would leave capital punishment for four crimes: treason, murder, terrorism and illegal narcotics production.

For years, several Southeast Asian governments have treated serious drug trafficking as a crime that warranted the death penalty. However, some countries have re-examined their laws, leading to amendments.

Malaysia ended mandatory death sentences in 2023. Singapore retains the death penalty for the most serious trafficking offences in which the legal thresholds are exceeded for quantities of various controlled drugs.

The issue has led to debates on whether capital punishment still has a place in society, whether judges should have the discretion in sentencing, and how governments can disrupt the drug trade without the death penalty.

Hanoi’s gradual reforms

Vietnam’s proposal is not an abrupt departure from capital punishment but the latest step in a long-running, incremental recalibration, according to Hai Thanh Luong, a Vietnamese criminologist at Griffith University in Australia.

Luong described Hanoi’s approach as “retentionist-but-reductionist”, referring to the state’s steady narrowing of offences punishable by death and retaining the punishment for exceptionally serious crimes.

He said the proposal to remove the death penalty for drug trafficking reflected gradual political and legal reforms, doubts over whether executions could suppress drug supply and Vietnam’s deeper integration into global legal and diplomatic frameworks.

“The strongest driver [is] Vietnam’s gradual legal and political reforms rather than a sudden ideological shift,” Luong said.

The proposal would still allow the death penalty for illegal narcotics production, drawing a distinction between manufacturers – seen as more central to sustaining the drug trade – and traffickers.

Luong said the changes would not have a major impact on drug availability. “Drug markets quickly adapt by replacing arrested individuals and shifting routes,” he said.

When asked about the different treatment of drug traffickers in Vietnam, Malaysia and Singapore, Luong said that the three countries viewed deterrence, social order and the state’s role in punishment differently, even as they faced similar challenges of curbing drug flows.

Singapore’s approach

While Singapore retains capital punishment for the most serious drug trafficking cases, it incorporates a broad anti-drug strategy that includes enforcement, education and rehabilitation.

Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam has said Singapore’s policy aims to prevent the harm caused by drugs, while imposing severe penalties on traffickers who bring substantial quantities into the country.

The city state’s Ministry of Home Affairs said a 2024 survey of 12,000 respondents in six regional cities found that 84.2 per cent believed the death penalty deterred people from trafficking substantial amounts of drugs into Singapore.

About 82.5 per cent considered the death penalty a more effective deterrent than life imprisonment, according to the survey.

Shanmugam has said the government would reconsider the policy if evidence shows that abolition helps or that the death penalty does not help. Until then, he said, Singapore would “hold the line”.

The death penalty is not a certainty under Singapore’s anti-drug laws, as they take into account the role played by convicted individuals in an offence.

Eugene Tan, an associate professor at Singapore Management University’s Yong Pung How School of Law, said offenders convicted of trafficking above the prescribed thresholds could receive life imprisonment if they had acted only as a courier.

They also had to obtain a certificate from the public prosecutor confirming they had provided substantive help to the authorities in disrupting trafficking activity.

Couriers whose abnormality of mind had substantially impaired their mental responsibility could also be sentenced to life imprisonment without a certificate, Tan said.

Tan explained that the framework allowed courts to differentiate between degrees of moral blameworthiness, while retaining zero tolerance against serious offences.

“The shift to the discretionary death penalty regime should not be misconstrued as letting up on serious crimes such as drug trafficking,” Tan said.

This Week in Asia has contacted Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs for comment.

Malaysia’s sentencing shift

In 2023, Malaysia announced that it was abolishing the mandatory death sentence for drug trafficking, leaving courts to choose between execution and life imprisonment.

Ngeow Chow Ying, a Malaysian lawyer and deputy convenor of the Anti-Death Penalty Asia Network, said the change led to a sharp fall in new death sentences.

Citing Amnesty International figures, she said Malaysian courts imposed 38 new death sentences in 2023, 24 in 2024, and 15 in 2025.

For drug trafficking cases, “courts now weigh aggravating and mitigating factors to decide between death and life imprisonment”, Ngeow said.

Mitigating factors could include an offender playing a lower-level role such as a courier or mule, the type of drugs involved and an early guilty plea, Ngeow explained.

“Appellate courts, for instance, have commuted death sentences to life imprisonment for young or first-time couriers caught with substantial drug quantities, in recognition of their limited role in the operation,” she said.
