Even so, inconsistencies in interpretation persisted between different judicial levels in some cases, with High Court death sentences imposed on couriers later set aside by superior courts for life imprisonment, Ngeow said.

“This suggests that trial-level sentencing remains uneven and continues to depend heavily on appellate correction,” she added.

Law vs enforcement operations

For rights groups, Vietnam’s proposal matters because it targets an offence that has contributed to the largest number of death sentences.

Chiara Sangiorgio, Amnesty’s death penalty expert, said the latest proposal came after reforms in 2025 reduced the number of offences punishable by death to 10 from 18, alongside judicial guidance that further limited the imposition of capital punishment in some drug cases.

“We are hopeful that these reforms will lead to immediate and concrete impact, particularly given that the majority of new death sentences that Amnesty International has recorded in recent years were imposed for drug trafficking,” Sangiorgio said.

Amnesty’s preliminary assessment pointed to a decline in new death sentences in Vietnam so far this year following the reforms, according to Sangiorgio.

But official secrecy around executions has made it impossible to assess the reforms’ full impact.

Amnesty’s preliminary assessment pointed to a decline in new death sentences in Vietnam so far this year following the reforms, according to Sangiorgio. But official secrecy around executions has made it difficult to assess the reforms’ full impact.

Amnesty was also concerned that unfair proceedings had led to death sentences and executions in some cases in Vietnam, Sangiorgio said.

However, she added that recent developments in other countries suggested that sustained political will could move drug policies towards a humane, evidence-based and health-focused approach.

Regardless of the different legal approaches in Southeast Asia, Luong said the most effective way to deal with the scourge was to intensify efforts to cripple drug trafficking operations at their root.

“The certainty of detection has more preventive impact than harsher punishments,” he said. “Effective intelligence, cooperation, investigations and harm-reduction efforts are more sustainable than increasing severity alone.”

item.title: [SCMP] Can Southeast Asian artists replicate K-pop’s global success with SEA-pop?
item.description:
At Tower Records in Tokyo’s Shibuya district earlier this month, fans flocked to a pop-up store set up for Filipino boy band SB19, buying exclusive merchandise including limited-edition CDs, T-shirts, stickers and phone straps.

Due to overwhelming demand, the store ran for an additional five days. During the band’s tour in Japan, SB19 met fans in Yokohama and performed in Tokyo and Osaka during the Summer Sonic festival. Another Philippine act, the eight-member girl group BINI, made their debut at the music event.

In July, SB19 performed at the Lollapalooza festival in Chicago for the first time, while in April, they played a sold-out home concert in the city of Paranaque, drawing almost 100,000 local and international fans, including from Hong Kong, Taiwan, Australia and Germany. BINI also made history in April during their inaugural performance at the Coachella festival in California.
item.content:encoded:
At Tower Records in Tokyo’s Shibuya district earlier this month, fans flocked to a pop-up store set up for Filipino boy band SB19, buying exclusive merchandise including limited-edition CDs, T-shirts, stickers and phone straps.

Due to overwhelming demand, the store ran for an additional five days. During the band’s tour in Japan, SB19 met fans in Yokohama and performed in Tokyo and Osaka during the Summer Sonic festival. Another Philippine act, the eight-member girl group BINI, made their debut at the music event.

In July, SB19 performed at the Lollapalooza festival in Chicago for the first time, while in April, they played a sold-out home concert in the city of Paranaque, drawing almost 100,000 local and international fans, including from Hong Kong, Taiwan, Australia and Germany. BINI also made history in April during their inaugural performance at the Coachella festival in California.

Their successes appear to reflect a wider trend in Southeast Asia’s entertainment scene, with more regional acts outperforming Western artists and K-pop bands on streaming charts.

Data compiled by French music analytics platform Soundcharts found that the share of Indonesian artists on Spotify’s weekly top 10 soared from 39 per cent to 97 per cent in Indonesia between 2021 and the first half of 2026.

The streaming data for the Philippines and Thailand were similar, rising from 31 per cent to 81 per cent and 71 per cent to 76 per cent, respectively, over the same period.

An independent data analyst based in Japan, who goes by the moniker Tsurezure Lab and studies music streaming trends across global markets, tracked weekly aggregations of Spotify daily Top 50 charts in Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore from February 2023 to May 2026 and noticed strong intra-regional support in these countries based on linguistic and cultural similarities.

The analyst, who asked to remain anonymous, cited the popularity of Indonesian pop on Malaysian charts and an increase in Mandopop streams in Singapore.

As Southeast Asian music lovers continue to support local artists, industry players are betting that they can go further. This has raised a tantalising prospect: can artists from Southeast Asia replicate the success of their K-pop peers such as BTS and Blackpink and achieve global success?

SEAPop rising

Fans have coined a term to reflect the region’s growing music scene: SEA-pop, or Southeast Asian pop.

“In recent years, SEA-pop has become increasingly vibrant, with local music dominating the charts like never before,” said Roslyn Pineda, Hong Kong-based president of Sony Music Publishing in Asia.

“In the Philippines, where I entered the music industry in 2001, international music was once the trend. Today, original Pilipino music claims 81 per cent of Spotify’s weekly top 10, marking a significant shift in audience preferences,” she said.

Thailand has also seen the market share of Thai pop, or T-pop, rise since 2023, according to Pineda.

For Darynaufal Mulyaman, an assistant professor of international relations at Universitas Kristen Indonesia, whose research focuses on pop culture, soft power and Korean studies, SEA-pop mirrors the broader region.

SEA-pop’s diversity reflected “Asean’s founding paradox playing out at the level of culture”, he said.

Exemplifying the “unity in diversity” ethos of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the region’s historically, culturally, linguistically and religiously diverse countries had been “held together by consensus diplomacy rather than a shared identity”, Mulyaman said.

“SEA-pop is reproducing that exact structure in music,” he said, with the genre united less by a common sound than a “shared posture towards the outside world, whether K-pop or Western pop”.

Regional acts have infused local cultures, such as indigenous instruments, into their songs to reinforce their national identity, moving away from the K-pop model that initially inspired Southeast Asian music industry players who aimed to reproduce the success of the Hallyu phenomenon, or Korean wave.

Nonetheless, K-pop’s practice of recruiting and training foreign talent had allowed performers, choreographers and producers from Southeast Asia to learn the ropes of the Korean entertainment industry and adapt lessons for their home countries, Mulyaman said.

Going global

However, exporting SEA-pop to the world would require more than strong streaming numbers.

For now, the growth of the regional artists is driven largely by themselves, music labels and fans, rather than a comprehensive national-level approach that has turned K-pop into an entertainment powerhouse.

As such, SEA-pop is “riding on a much thinner institutional floor than K-pop had, and thinner than what the EU’s cultural-integration machinery gives European pop”, according to Mulyaman.

While South Korea had integrated pop culture into its export strategy, the region did not have a similar strategy or a government agency that could help accelerate SEA-pop’s global growth, Mulyaman said.

“Asean’s cohesion is institutionally shallower than the EU’s by design,” he added, referring to the bloc’s traditional non-interference approach.

Nonetheless, there is scope for Southeast Asia to unite and promote its soft power as it would entail less sensitivity than working together on security or economic issues, according to Mulyaman.

Pineda identifies several regional artists that have what it takes to make it big on the global stage.

“Acts like SB19 and BINI from the Philippines, Dolla from Malaysia, No Na from Indonesia, and 4EVE from Thailand are already making strides on international festival stages, producing bilingual tracks, dominating playlists, and showcasing high-fashion aesthetics,” Pineda said.

According to Tsurezure Lab, the Philippines has the strongest potential to achieve international success due to the widespread use of English in its music and Filipino artists such as BINI and SB19 having a strong global following. The analyst said that Thailand ranked second, with the likes of singer Jeff Satur and Thai hip-hop artists having a growing global fanbase.

However, the large populations in some Southeast Asian countries could ironically work against the goal of exporting SEA-pop to the rest of the world.

Last year, fans in Indonesia and the Philippines generated 23.2 billion streams and 14.2 billion streams, respectively, on the Spotify Top 200. Both countries have a much larger population than South Korea, whose K-pop industry has to look outward to expand beyond its domestic market.

“When home is that big and that loyal, the pressure to export is far weaker. Southeast Asia’s local music strength is, so far, largely inward-facing,” Tsurezure Lab said.

For Southeast Asian artists to go global, they can look at following the K-pop template in which Korean acts initially targeted attracting more fans in Japan and China before they achieved wider success in the US and beyond, the analyst added.

However, regional artists should establish their own identity instead of blindly copying their K-pop counterparts, according to industry observers.

Mulyaman warned that if Southeast Asian artists were to become K-pop “derivative products”, they would “stop being SEA-pop”.

Pineda said there was no need for Southeast Asian artists to “mimic K-pop” even as they learned from its success.

“The expansion beyond their home bases is already under way. Achieving a global breakout hit and sustaining international fandom engagement is not far-fetched. It could be just around the corner.”

item.title: [SCMP] 23,000 bronzes, 14 years, 60 volumes: how China is mapping lost heritage held abroad
item.description:
In the quiet of a Peking University research room, shelves groan under the weight of 60 thick volumes. Stacked, they stand taller than an average human.

Inside their pages lie the details of more than 23,000 ancient Chinese bronze vessels, weapons, chariot fittings and ritual objects that left China’s shores long ago and now sit in museums, private collections and auction houses across nearly 30 countries.

Published in April by Shanghai Classics Publishing House, the Collection of Chinese Bronzes in Overseas Collections is the product of a painstaking 14-year investigation. It is also something more: an assembled toolkit for China’s intensifying campaign to reclaim cultural heritage lost to war, looting and smuggling, as well as an assertion of Beijing’s ambition to shape the global rules of repatriation.
item.content:encoded:
In the quiet of a Peking University research room, shelves groan under the weight of 60 thick volumes. Stacked, they stand taller than an average human.

Inside their pages lie the details of more than 23,000 ancient Chinese bronze vessels, weapons, chariot fittings and ritual objects that left China’s shores long ago and now sit in museums, private collections and auction houses across nearly 30 countries.

Published in April by Shanghai Classics Publishing House, the Collection of Chinese Bronzes in Overseas Collections is the product of a painstaking 14-year investigation. It is also something more: an assembled toolkit for China’s intensifying campaign to reclaim cultural heritage lost to war, looting and smuggling, as well as an assertion of Beijing’s ambition to shape the global rules of repatriation.

“To create archives for the cultural relics, to preserve evidence for history,” said lead editor and historian Zhu Fenghan, a Boya Chair Professor at Peking University, capturing the project’s dual purpose in an article in the People’s Daily last week.

“We need to get a clear picture of our family assets and gain a more complete and comprehensive understanding of Chinese bronzes held overseas,” Zhu was quoted as saying.

The effort began in 2012, when China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA) asked Peking University to map the true scale of the country’s dispersed bronzes, prompting a scholarly odyssey.

Team members criss-crossed more than 10 countries to visit more than 260 institutions, scan rare catalogues, trawl auction records and photograph objects that had rarely, if ever, been systematically recorded by Chinese researchers.

They returned with a massive trove of data, including about a terabyte of documents and 200 gigabytes of images.

Earlier estimates had put the overseas number of bronzes at around 3,000 pieces. The new catalogue estimates more than seven times that figure.

The team created an “identity document” for each piece or relic, Zhu told reporters at the work’s launch in Shanghai in April.

Each entry functions like a personal file, containing high-resolution photos, measurements, inscriptions, where they were found, if known, transmission history and current locations.

Nearly 300 types of bronzes appear, from celebrated ritual vessels to weapons, tools, lamps and northern-style pieces long sidelined in Western catalogues. Of the total, 3,462 carry inscriptions that reflect the politics, rituals and daily concerns of early Chinese states.

Bronzes occupy a special place in China’s historical imagination. They were the physical embodiment of royal power and the ritual order that held society together.

The earliest written use of the term Zhongguo (often translated as Middle Kingdom) on the Western Zhou He Zun artefact; the legendary Nine Tripods, or ding in Chinese; and enduring phrases such as “one word carries the weight of nine ding” all speak to their enduring symbolic force.

From the late Qing dynasty to the mid-20th century, large numbers left China amid political chaos, wartime plunder and the activities of dealers who built efficient supply chains feeding Western museums and collectors. Only a minority of the objects now catalogued carry clear records of being exported legally or given as a diplomatic gift.

China has reclaimed a measure of narrative control, regardless of where the objects currently sit

Wang Wen, dean, Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University

One emblematic case is the complete Western Zhou banjin altar set – a table and matching wine vessels – excavated in Baoji, Shaanxi, and once owned by the late-Qing official Duanfang. It was sold by his descendants and is now a star attraction at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. It is the most intact surviving set of its kind.

Stories like this, repeated across the volumes, turn abstract loss into concrete, documented histories.

China has stepped up the pace of recovery. During the 14th five-year plan period (2021–2025), some 35 batches totalling 537 lost relics and artworks were returned to China. Among them was the Western Zhou bronze ritual vessel Feng Xingshu Gui, Old Summer Palace columns and volumes of the Warring States-era Zidanku Silk Manuscripts, according to the NCHA.

Early last year, US authorities handed back 41 items, including bronzes. Earlier, the swift recovery of a bronze group from a Tokyo auction in 2019 showed how legal, diplomatic and investigative tools could be combined to dramatic effect.

Beijing has signed agreements with dozens of countries, co-authored the Qingdao Proposal on colonial-era cultural property, and taken a leadership role in Unesco heritage frameworks. Meanwhile, Washington’s withdrawal from the UN organisation will take effect at the end of this year.

For legal scholars, the new catalogue directly addresses the biggest practical obstacle to further returns: the missing “chain of evidence”.

“Recovering cultural relics lost overseas first requires a clear inventory of what was taken illegally,” said Huo Zhengxin, a professor at the China University of Political Science and Law.

“This archive of bronzes is an important part of taking stock of our family assets. Bronzes hold exceptional value for an ancient civilisation, which is why documenting them matters so much.”

He argues that the early return of illegally exported objects is a core element of cultural sovereignty.

“Claims alone are not enough; evidence is required. This project clarifies the full chain of how these bronzes left China, and provides the foundation for future repatriation efforts.”

Legal barriers remained, he said, but painstaking provenance work, thanks to the Chinese research teams and the cooperation with foreign institutions, was slowly closing the factual gaps.

Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University, places the project in a broader cultural frame as modern losses have left Chinese scholarship with incomplete archives and broken research chains.

By surveying more than 260 institutions and documenting 23,000 objects, the team had continued the unfinished work of earlier generations of scholars while rebuilding an evidentiary base for recovery claims, he said.

The catalogue is an exercise in cultural confidence and sovereignty, according to Wang.

He said Western scholars had for decades largely controlled the naming, dating and interpretation of overseas Chinese bronzes, and the Chinese team had revisited those judgments from the perspective of the civilisation that produced them, restoring ritual and historical meanings that had been obscured.

According to Wang, the resulting archives prove that the Chinese cultural lineage was never severed by physical dispersal. For Chinese communities worldwide, the volumes turned scattered objects into a shared point of reference – a collective reminder that “lost cultural relics remain treasures of Chinese civilisation”, he said.

“In practical terms, the right to archive, interpret and speak for one’s own heritage lies at the heart of cultural sovereignty. By producing an independent, systematic record, China has reclaimed a measure of narrative control, regardless of where the objects currently sit.”

Wang said the detailed histories of how the artefacts were moved had also provided concrete evidence for future negotiations, strengthening Beijing’s hand in the evolving global conversation over looted and displaced heritage.

The 60 volumes will not, by themselves, bring every bronze home. Full recovery of the estimated millions of Chinese relics that remain abroad remains a generational task.

Yet, analysts say that by turning once-shadowy objects into documented cultural assets, the project supplies both scholarly scaffolding and diplomatic ammunition.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Chilling effect’: Japan’s whistle-blowers weigh high price of speaking out
item.description:
Yutaka Kato* knew there would be risks when he reported suspected misconduct by his employer to Japanese authorities.

What he did not expect, he said, was a 47.88 million yen (US$300,000) damages claim from that employer – the Japanese subsidiary of US-listed medical device manufacturer STAAR Surgical – along with the prospect of years in court and the uncertainty of whether he would ever return to work.

Kato is among a growing number of whistle-blowers in Japan who say laws meant to protect them from retaliation have not stopped companies from pursuing damages claims, dismissals and other actions that can leave them financially drained, professionally isolated and afraid to speak out.
item.content:encoded:
Yutaka Kato* knew there would be risks when he reported suspected misconduct by his employer to Japanese authorities.

What he did not expect, he said, was a 47.88 million yen (US$300,000) damages claim from that employer – the Japanese subsidiary of US-listed medical device manufacturer STAAR Surgical – along with the prospect of years in court and the uncertainty of whether he would ever return to work.

Kato is among a growing number of whistle-blowers in Japan who say laws meant to protect them from retaliation have not stopped companies from pursuing damages claims, dismissals and other actions that can leave them financially drained, professionally isolated and afraid to speak out.

His former employer’s claim was dismissed by the Tokyo District Court in December last year but was appealed to the High Court, with a ruling set to be handed down on September 3.

Kato has challenged his dismissal in a separate lawsuit, with the High Court ruling in his favour, although the company has appealed to Japan’s Supreme Court.

And he admits to being “anxious” ahead of the rulings.

“There is no public financial assistance to support my living expenses and the economic burden I face while the litigation continues,” he said.

“At present, there is also no clear prospect of my actually returning to work. The company may, of course, have a different view as to the reasons for my dismissal. From my perspective, however, I believe that the dismissal had a retaliatory aspect because I had made whistle-blower reports.”

When Japan introduced its Whistleblower Protection Act in 2004, it was expected to protect workers who reported suspected misconduct, including against their own employers.

More than two decades later, critics say the law’s limits have become clear in cases where employers argue that their claims concern conduct surrounding a disclosure, rather than the whistle-blowing itself.

The Act bars companies from dismissing or otherwise disadvantaging workers on the grounds of whistle-blowing and from seeking damages simply because they suffered losses as a result.

But legal experts and those targeted in such cases say whistle-blowers can still face termination, costly litigation and difficulty finding work in the same industry when companies cite related conduct – such as handling internal information – as the basis for action against them.

This Week in Asia reached out to STAAR Japan, which declined to comment on Kato’s case as it is “a pending legal matter”. But Kato’s legal representatives claim he was targeted after he filed reports with authorities.

Kato said the reports he made concerned suspected improper payments to doctors and the handling of patient information linked to surgical videos involving the company’s intraocular lenses.

In a related bribery case, a doctor at Yamato-Takada Municipal Hospital in Nara prefecture was later convicted of accepting payments linked to the use of the company’s lenses and sentenced to 18 months in prison, suspended for three years.

Four people linked to the company, including former executives, also received fines in connection with the bribery case.

The damages claim against Kato centres on the alleged removal of company information, rather than the act of whistle-blowing itself.

Aiko Ohbuchi, a lawyer specialising in corporate law at the Amour Law Office in Tokyo, said companies bringing such claims might not see themselves as exploiting a flaw in the legislation.

Article 7 of the Act provides that an employer “may not seek damages from a whistle-blower on the grounds that the employer has suffered damage as a result of the whistle-blowing”, she said.

This provision does not, however, expressly cover a whistle-blower collecting and taking out information to make a disclosure. Nor does it specifically prohibit an employer from seeking damages on the grounds that it suffered harm resulting from such conduct.

Ohbuchi said she was aware of 12 lawsuits where employers sought damages on the grounds that a whistle-blower collected or took information out of the company, although there were many more cases in which whistle-blowers were “subject to adverse treatment, such as dismissal or disciplinary action”.

She said she was confident Kato would prevail in the damages case.

“The courts have ruled in favour of whistle-blowers where the conduct was necessary to establish the truth of the matters reported and the method used was reasonable and proportionate,” she said.

Amendments due to take effect on December 1 would strengthen the law by expanding protection to freelancers and introducing criminal penalties for dismissal or discipline on the grounds of whistle-blowing, Ohbuchi said, adding that they would also shift the burden of proof in some disputes over dismissal or disciplinary action after a report.

While there was “growing awareness of the importance of protecting” those who spoke out, Ohbuchi cautioned that even a clear-cut victory in court might not dissuade firms from similar tactics in the future.

Other recent cases have underscored the same broader concern: that litigation itself can deter workers considering whether to report suspected wrongdoing.

Nozomi Fukuda, an ex-employee of the company behind Momuri – a high-profile Japanese resignation agency that helps workers quit their jobs – was among former staff who helped bring to light allegations that the agency had improperly referred clients to lawyers in return for fees.

Those allegations led to a criminal case against Momuri’s operator, Albatross, and its former president, according to Japanese media and company statements, but the company also pursued civil litigation against former employees over separate claims that included allegedly false statements about harassment.

Fukuda told Japanese media that the stress of the case caused her to suffer a cerebral infarction, transforming her life and that of her family. She later divorced her husband.

While she continues to feel the effects of her illness, the lawsuit remains unresolved. According to Japanese media, Fukuda has said that had she known in advance the toll it would take, she might have chosen to stay quiet.

Kato said he was frustrated by what he saw as a “significant gap” in the protection system that allows companies to sue whistle-blowers and potentially intimidate others considering speaking out.

“A very large damages claim can itself impose a significant financial and psychological burden on a defendant and potentially have a chilling effect on that person’s speech and actions,” he said.

“If the company ultimately wins and I am ordered to pay around 47.88 million yen, I do not have the financial means to pay that amount.

“In that event, I could potentially face a serious financial burden for decades to come.”

*Name changed to protect interviewee’s identity

item.title: [SCMP] Reviving Kuala Lumpur: can Malaysia modernise without pricing out its past?
item.description:
A yellowing receipt, framed behind glass near the entrance of Abdul Razak Gold House, records an address that no longer officially exists: “63 Ampang Street, Kuala Lumpur (Malaya)”.

The shop’s modern glass frontage, polished counters and gleaming bullion cases give little away about its history. But step inside and that simple receipt serves as a small window onto pre-independence Malaysia.

For six decades, this family business has reinvented itself in step with the city around it. What began as a modest goldsmith’s counter beneath a row of old shophouses is now a brightly lit jewellery and bullion store.
item.content:encoded:
A yellowing receipt, framed behind glass near the entrance of Abdul Razak Gold House, records an address that no longer officially exists: “63 Ampang Street, Kuala Lumpur (Malaya)”.

The shop’s modern glass frontage, polished counters and gleaming bullion cases give little away about its history. But step inside and that simple receipt serves as a small window onto pre-independence Malaysia.

For six decades, this family business has reinvented itself in step with the city around it. What began as a modest goldsmith’s counter beneath a row of old shophouses is now a brightly lit jewellery and bullion store.

Today, skyscrapers and overhead train tracks loom over the capital’s commercial core, and many of the businesses along Lebuh Ampang – the modern name for Ampang Street – that the shop’s proprietor remembers from his childhood have long since vanished.

Mohd Razalie Abdul Rasul, 37, is the newest custodian of Abdul Razak Gold House. He has expanded the business into bullion trading, bought the property next door and is, ultimately, preparing for a handover to the next generation.

“My dad is still a mentor, but the way he thinks and I think is totally different,” he said. “We have to think very modern. We have to stay one step ahead.”

Their family drama is a microcosm of the soul-searching currently sweeping Kuala Lumpur: how do you hold on to the past while still moving forward?

Muddy origins

Long before Malaysia existed as an independent nation, a small trading post emerged at the junction of the Klang and Gombak rivers. This geographic meeting point gave the future capital its name, which translates from Malay as “muddy confluence”.

Today, those humble riverbank origins stand in sharp contrast with the towering glass and steel of the Petronas Twin Towers and Merdeka 118. Yet cradled beneath this hyper-modern skyline lies Kuala Lumpur’s historic heart.

Here, amid old shophouses, traditional temples and bustling markets, the city’s earliest trading streets still endure, even as the tides of modern commerce have slowly drifted away from them.

Reversing that decline is the aim of Warisan KL, a heritage-led regeneration programme working to restore landmarks, upgrade public spaces and improve transport links across the old city.

Its ambition is to turn heritage into an economic asset without emptying it of the traders who make it feel authentic, or dressing it up as a backdrop for tourists rather than a place where people actually live and work.

Tourist footfall is the wrong measure of success, according to Syed Redza Algadrie Syed Hassan, CEO of Prasarana Integrated Development (Pride), a government entity tasked with revitalising Malaysia’s urban public transport network.

What mattered more was whether visitors lingered and spent money at local businesses, he said.

“The discipline is to let commerce follow authenticity rather than replace it,” Syed Redza told This Week in Asia.

“If you over-polish a heritage district, you risk removing the very qualities that made it distinctive and valuable in the first place.”

Izwan Ibrahim, CEO of PNB Merdeka Ventures, which oversees the Merdeka 118 precinct, takes a similarly hard line on what counts as success.

Growth that comes at the expense of the communities already living in a heritage enclave is not growth worth having, he argues – pointing to the restored Merdeka Stadium, which now hosts not only sports events but also concerts and community programmes, as a case in point.

“It is not enough to restore heritage buildings or bring more visitors into an area if the surrounding community does not also see improvements in its everyday environment,” he said.

Masjid Jamek, one of the city’s busiest transport interchanges, illustrates the approach: the station has been deliberately positioned as a gateway, funnelling commuters into the historic quarter around it rather than simply moving them through.

Pride reports that its pilot projects in transport hubs have generated more than 624,000 social media impressions, while the digital heritage trails on its MyRapid PULSE app drew over 22,600 engagements in the first three months since launch.

“The early signals are encouraging,” Syed Redza said.

Heritage for show?

Not everyone is convinced that physical improvements alone can revive a neighbourhood’s soul, however.

“You can’t contract out authenticity or buy it through municipal budgets,” said Azry Bruce Aziz, a Kuala Lumpur-based independent history researcher.

For him, what makes a place authentic has little to do with the buildings themselves and everything to do with their function. He points to the hardware stores and Chinese medicinal halls of Jalan Tun H.S. Lee, the gold and textile traders of Lebuh Ampang and the temples, grocers and eateries that still pull people into the city centre.

“When planned regeneration focuses purely on surface makeovers, you end up with heritage for show,” he said, warning that “treating historic streets like a pretty backdrop for weekend photos” would only result in higher rents that “kick out the very shops that made the area real in the first place”.

Azry is not opposed to the idea of regeneration. Better lighting, pavements, drainage and public space can make a district safer and more inviting, he says – provided the change does not come at the expense of the businesses that already operate there.

What concerns him more is the inevitable ripple effects of rising property values, which incentivise landlords to swap out low-margin tenants such as repair shops, tailors and stationery stores for glossier, higher-rent lifestyle brands.

“What planning should be doing instead is acting as a protective shield, instead of trying to invent fake charm,” he said. “Top-down planning only works when it protects the real community that’s already there.”

Adapting to survive

There is a compelling economic case for getting this right. Heritage-led regeneration is about more than just urban renewal or cultural preservation; it can drive tourism’s share of Malaysia’s gross domestic product beyond its current 15 per cent.

The commercial returns on such projects tend to be modest, according to Yeah Kim Leng, director of Sunway University’s economic studies programme, but there are other cultural and heritage benefits that do not show up neatly on a balance sheet.

“Integrating with local arts, crafts, food and entertainment will be important to maximise tourist spending along with enhancing visitors’ experiences and return visits,” Yeah said.

He sees no tension between old landmarks and new ones: Merdeka 118 and the regeneration of Kuala Lumpur’s historic districts can complement each other, both attracting investment into hotels, restaurants, commercial property and transport infrastructure.

True success, Yeah argues, is not measured by raw visitor numbers. Instead, it is found in the jobs created, the wages lifted and the living standards raised for everyone the work touches.

Back on Lebuh Ampang, Razalie knows this balance all too well, without needing an economist to explain it to him.

His family’s business has survived not by staying the same but by adapting – what it sells, how it sells and who it sells to – while holding onto something intangible that has not changed: the trust built up over generations of customers.

He hopes his son will one day take the reins, even if he doubts the business will look anything like it does now under his management.

“Nothing is going to be easy in the coming years,” Razalie said. “We have to stay one step ahead.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why Malaysia’s push for 15 million Muslim tourists is no sure thing
item.description:
Malaysia sees an opening in the Gulf travel disruption caused by the Iran war, pitching itself as a Muslim-friendly destination for travellers seeking halal food, prayer facilities and family-focused holidays.

But such gains could be limited because the conflict has not only weakened tourism within the Middle East, but also affected long-haul flight routes that Malaysia depends on to draw Muslim tourists, according to analysts.

The push comes as the six-month-old war continues to disrupt travel across the Gulf, where Dubai and Doha have long served as major destinations and aviation gateways for travellers moving between Europe, Asia and Africa.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia sees an opening in the Gulf travel disruption caused by the Iran war, pitching itself as a Muslim-friendly destination for travellers seeking halal food, prayer facilities and family-focused holidays.

But such gains could be limited because the conflict has not only weakened tourism within the Middle East, but also affected long-haul flight routes that Malaysia depends on to draw Muslim tourists, according to analysts.

The push comes as the six-month-old war continues to disrupt travel across the Gulf, where Dubai and Doha have long served as major destinations and aviation gateways for travellers moving between Europe, Asia and Africa.

“This crisis, this problem … we turn [it] into opportunity,” Mohammad Faisal Abu Suaib Khan, director general of Malaysia’s Islamic Tourism Centre, told This Week in Asia on Thursday.

“When the Middle East shuts down, people still want to travel. They still need an option where they can go,” he said, describing Malaysia as a natural substitute because of its established Muslim-friendly tourism ecosystem.

Dubai International Airport, the world’s busiest hub for international passengers, handled 31.5 million travellers in the first half of this year, down 31.3 per cent from the same period in 2025, according to Dubai Airports. Aircraft movements fell 32.1 per cent over the same period.

Flight cancellations, re-routing and soaring jet fuel prices have rippled well beyond the region, with major carriers including Lufthansa, British Airways and Singapore Airlines remaining cautious about restoring some services. On Tuesday, Finnair announced the suspension of Dubai flights for the coming winter season because of continued instability.

Dubai Airports CEO Paul Griffiths said passenger volumes had nevertheless been climbing after two months of severe disruption, telling the Associated Press that “the trajectory now is universally positive”.

Malaysia has not escaped the fallout. Tourism Minister Tiong King Sing said on Monday that 4,111 scheduled flights to the country were cancelled in the first half because of geopolitical tensions in West Asia, with cancellations rising from just nine in February to 1,419 in June.

Seat capacity from West Asia fell from more than 1 million in the first half of last year to 806,532 in the same period this year, including a decline of more than 20 per cent in capacity from Europe routed through West Asian hubs.

Closer to home

Almost two-thirds of Malaysia’s population is Muslim, with Islam accounting for 63.5 per cent of the population in the country’s 2020 census. Halal food is widely available, while prayer rooms are common in shopping centres, airports and tourist attractions.

The country again topped the Mastercard-CrescentRating Global Muslim Travel Index this year, scoring 82 out of 100 and finishing ahead of Indonesia, Turkey and Saudi Arabia, with the latter three tied for second place.

There were 196 million Muslim international arrivals worldwide last year, up 11.3 per cent from 2024, with annual expenditure from these travellers forecast to reach US$310 billion by 2030.

Malaysia received a record 9.7 million Muslim visitors in 2025 and wants to raise that figure to 15 million by 2030, according to the tourism ministry. But industry data on the diversion of Gulf tourists to the country in recent months is not as clear-cut.

Fazal Bahardeen, founder and CEO of Muslim travel consultancy CrescentRating, said there had been “no significant shift of Gulf travellers to Malaysia”. Instead, the disruption is changing how Muslim travellers choose destinations.

“Travellers are opting for shorter trips rather than cancelling,” Bahardeen told This Week in Asia. “Proximity now matters as much as price.”

Muslim travellers from Asia, excluding those from the Gulf, were increasingly travelling within East Asia and Southeast Asia, he said, with Malaysia picking up travellers who might previously have considered the Gulf or Turkey.

That could favour Malaysia in the short term, but the Middle East contributed relatively few – albeit high-spending – tourists to Malaysia, meaning the impact on overall arrivals was likely limited, Bahardeen said.

Apart from Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and the Philippines are increasingly competing for Asian Muslim travellers.

These “novelty” destinations offered something Malaysia, for all its established Muslim-friendly infrastructure, had to contend with, Bahardeen said.

Hub trouble

But the bigger risk Malaysia may face is from the decisions of airlines rather than tourists, according to industry experts, who warn that the Middle East conflict could weaken the long-haul connections on which its tourism industry depends.

Bahardeen said travellers from Europe, Britain, Africa and the Middle East were heavily reliant on connections through Dubai and Doha to reach Malaysia.

His firm’s data showed Doha-Kuala Lumpur was the busiest route logged by international users of the HalalTrip mobile app last year, followed by Dubai-Kuala Lumpur, while Jeddah-Kuala Lumpur ranked fourth.

“If the disruption is short term, it favours Malaysia. If prolonged, it does not,” Bahardeen said.

The Strait of Hormuz – which carried about a fifth of the world’s oil supply before the war – remains severely disrupted despite US efforts to clear mines and diplomatic attempts to restore normal shipping. Ship-tracking services estimate traffic remains at just 5 to 15 per cent of normal volumes.

Malaysia has also been expanding direct links with the Gulf. Last month, Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh Air made Kuala Lumpur its first scheduled destination in Southeast Asia, with three weekly Boeing 787-9 flights. Tourism Malaysia has called Saudi Arabia a “high-yield” market.

Aviation analyst Shukor Yusof of Endau Analytics said Malaysia had been popular with Arab Muslim travellers long before the war and would remain so, but cautioned against treating the disruption as a simple contest in which Kuala Lumpur gained at Dubai’s expense.

“The situation in the Gulf is not exactly a zero-sum game,” he said. “Malaysia has been a favoured destination for Muslim travellers from the Arab world long before the Iran conflict. This will continue.”

Shukor said Malaysia should also look further afield for growth, pointing to Central Asia and Russia as “untapped regions” that Malaysia Airlines and the wider tourism industry could pursue.

Malaysia launched the fifth edition of Islamic Tourism Month on Thursday, with a revamped online platform allowing travellers to browse and pay for hotels, tours, spas, restaurants and other Muslim-friendly products in one place.

The month-long campaign begins on September 1 and forms part of the country’s Visit Malaysia 2026 drive, bringing tourism businesses, government agencies and communities together to market Muslim-friendly experiences to domestic and international travellers.

item.title: [SCMP] Ming dynasty work shows how Chinese understood the world in the 1600s
item.description:
Long before the digital age, a Ming dynasty scholar made it his mission to map human knowledge from a Chinese perspective.

The result was an encyclopaedia spanning 127 volumes known as the Tushu Bian, or Compendium of Illustrations and Texts.

The work – published in 1613 – was compiled by Neo-Confucian scholar Zhang Huang and drew on more than 200 printed sources across several decades to document the concepts of heaven, Earth and humanity.
item.content:encoded:
Long before the digital age, a Ming dynasty scholar made it his mission to map human knowledge from a Chinese perspective.

The result was an encyclopaedia spanning 127 volumes known as the Tushu Bian, or Compendium of Illustrations and Texts.

The work – published in 1613 – was compiled by Neo-Confucian scholar Zhang Huang and drew on more than 200 printed sources across several decades to document the concepts of heaven, Earth and humanity.

“His goal was to gather all the illustrations and texts an educated person needed to understand the world,” information designer Paul Kahn, who analysed the encyclopaedia, wrote in his book Mapping Knowledge Across Time: Seven Books That Visualised the World.

“The result was too costly to print during his lifetime. It was eventually carved on woodblocks and printed after his death,” Kahn wrote.

Kahn compared the Tushu Bian with six other books that described the world from the perspective of Euro-Mediterranean culture.

“The Tushu Bian was chosen because it is an enormous visual summary of Chinese culture from the period when Asia and the West were interacting,” he wrote.

In an interview, Kahn said the Chinese work’s depiction of the Grand Canal and major rivers set it apart from the others.

The Grand Canal is a vast waterway system that runs from Beijing southward across the Yellow River to canals and tributaries merging with the Yangtze River near the modern-day city of Yangzhou.

“In all of the European books, there are many examples of understanding river and maritime networks and showing how people travel from one continent to another,” Kahn said.

“For example, there are several reproductions of the Danube River network that covers all of central and northern Europe.

“In all of those cases, they are represented as networks and lines connecting one place to another. But in the Tushu Bian, the rivers are represented as continuous, detailed descriptions of every place on the river.”

Unlike modern maps that use a bird’s-eye view or a north-south orientation, the Tushu Bian often presents these rivers horizontally, flowing from right to left, regardless of cardinal directions.

“Orientation is based on convention,” Kahn said. “What you see is based on what is in your mind. If your mind has certain conventions that north should be at the top, and you look at an image, you do not recognise what you are looking at because it is not matching your expectations.”

He noted that there was more flexibility in today’s mobile phone map applications.

“They can change the representation if they are well designed … to meet the needs of the person who is using it,” he said.

The Tushu Bian also described the human body as a channel for the primordial qi – energy inherited from one’s parents – to connect heaven and Earth, with detailed diagrams of human organs.

“There is no representation of the human body as connected to the natural world or as a microcosm in the other books, with the exception of the Catalan Atlas,” according to Kahn.

He said the world atlas from the 14th century “includes a human figure with each of the parts of the external body, not showing the internal organs”.

“It shows this figure that is related to astrological information and numerical instructions” on when to perform bloodletting, a common medical procedure at the time.

In the Tushu Bian, one diagram shows internal organs contained in a pear-shaped outline, with the spinal vertebrae portrayed as bones. Another diagram renders the spine as a sequence of connected circles linked to the head.

The view is from the side, which Kahn said might have been done to show the spine and spinal column. “Within that tradition, the location of different parts of the spine is correlated with different parts of the organs, and so I think that was why they did it that way.”

According to Kahn, Zhang gathered information for the Tushu Bian that could benefit his students, but it was also a resource that could be used to prepare for the imperial examination – the selection process for government workers.

“An aspiring candidate might spend decades preparing for the exam,” Kahn wrote. “The people who tried and failed to pass the exam made up much of the literate population.”

The Tushu Bian makes no mention of the seven naval expeditions led by Admiral Zheng He between 1405 and 1433. It depicts the world through a collection of maps centred on the Chinese Empire, with limited representation of surrounding “tribute” countries.

“The greatest detail of the outside world is devoted to places where the Chinese were defending against invasions,” Kahn wrote in his book.

He told the SCMP: “These amazing gigantic maritime expeditions that had happened during the same dynasty, not that long before, are completely ignored. I would interpret that to mean that he is making decisions about what the people that he wants to see this should be paying attention to.”

Kahn noted the need to evaluate where information comes from – whether it is a historical visualisation or the AI-generated content and deepfakes of today.

“One lesson that we are learning over and over again is to try and understand the source of the material and become critical in terms of how you judge what you see based on [whether this] is an eyewitness account or someone’s story about a story they heard from someone else,” he said.

Kahn gave the example of the Atlas Historique, which was published in Amsterdam in the 18th century and featured illustrations of the Mughal Empire in India.

They were copied directly from the personal art collection of an Italian diplomat. Dutch United East India Company traders had brought the works to the Netherlands from India and China.

“He had essentially a museum of paintings that were made in India, and the people who did the Atlas Historique went to the museum and they copied them. In this case, they were copying something that was much more authentic,” Kahn said.

“When you look at them compared to the images that they created of people in Japan and China, you can see that they are much less European looking,” he said. “The lesson is when you look at a whole range of images like this, try to become sensitive to what is it about the image that represents some kind of authenticity or closer to the source.”

item.title: [SCMP] Nobel laureate James Heckman on the value of risk-taking, and China’s ‘common goal’
item.description:
James Heckman is the Henry Schultz distinguished service professor of economics and public policy and director of the Centre for the Economics of Human Development at the University of Chicago.

Heckman has devoted his professional life to understanding the origins of major social and economic questions related to inequality, social mobility, discrimination and the formation of skills and regulation in labour markets. He has also done extensive research in China’s labour market and early childhood development.

He was awarded a Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in 2000 for developing methods to solve statistical sample-selection problems.
item.content:encoded:
James Heckman is the Henry Schultz distinguished service professor of economics and public policy and director of the Centre for the Economics of Human Development at the University of Chicago.

Heckman has devoted his professional life to understanding the origins of major social and economic questions related to inequality, social mobility, discrimination and the formation of skills and regulation in labour markets. He has also done extensive research in China’s labour market and early childhood development.

He was awarded a Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in 2000 for developing methods to solve statistical sample-selection problems.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

What is your assessment of China’s economic outlook, especially as it grapples with geopolitical tensions in different parts of the world?

The whole world’s economic outlook isn’t good right now because of the fighting in the Middle East and the rise in oil prices and the uncertainty that all of this has created. Right now, in a period of uncertainty, China and the rest of the world is a little bit on pause.

And I say “a little bit” because we are in the initial phases of a great bout of uncertainty before things are really resolved. The typical reaction of most trading partners and most human beings is to hold off and to wait until things get resolved.

Not only is there a shortage of oil, which is affecting the whole world and especially Asia, there is an additional factor which has to do with the slowdown. Things are slowing down right now, partly because it’s a matter of waiting to get more information.

However, the war in Iran continues and it looks like the Iranians are a pretty tough bunch of people and want to hold on in a way that I think most Americans did not expect, at least [US President Donald] Trump did not expect.

This is going to slow the whole world economy down. And you can see it – China’s growth rate forecast, 4.5 to 5 per cent per annum in the next year, is probably overly optimistic given the uncertainty that plagues the current environment.

And oil is still a very important ingredient for the Chinese economy and for the world economy. With oil and natural gas being limited and expensive, I think the slowdown will be real. I am not expecting even a 5 per cent growth rate but in the long term I am very optimistic.

And what about the impact of demographic changes in China – how will the disappearing population dividend affect the economic outlook?

The demographic dividend as you describe it is kind of a mixed blessing. Twenty years ago, the Chinese population pyramid was such that more young people were being born than old people were dying.

Now it’s the opposite; the population is declining, and it’s declining fairly substantially. The birth rate is also declining. So not only are people living longer, but fertility has fallen.

And so, social benefits are under threat; the so-called pay-as-you-go system where younger workers pay for the retirement and social benefits of older, less healthy workers.

But that can be addressed. It could be that retirement ages are expanded, which makes sense under any event, because the Chinese population is much healthier than it was 20 years ago.

Workers at 65 are much more able to work, full-time and even in strenuous jobs, in a way that was not possible before. This is a consequence of the improved Chinese healthcare system, nutrition and health practices. It’s a blessing that health has improved.

There is another avenue of progress where China has a flexibility that other ageing countries like Japan don’t have.

The population replacement rate is roughly 2.1. In other words, a family should have 2.1 children to replace itself and keep the population stable. South Korea and Japan are stuck far below that level. The South Korean decline in fertility is far worse than in China.

The current fertility rate in China is around 1.4 or 1.5, but in South Korea it’s 0.7 so you are getting a tremendous decline in South Korean families.

But there is a margin of response that China has and other countries do not and that is its large rural population. There is substantial migration already. However, the large rural population including migrant workers have traditionally not received good educations.

Per capita education expenditure has been much less in rural areas and western China than in the east and in urban areas. The possibility of schooling means that more trained workers can come on board if China essentially centralises its educational policy in a way that it currently does not.

There are moves in that direction. China has now started to redistribute resources, especially to minority areas like Tibet and Xinjiang, but it could do so more generally, and that brings on a supply of educated workers who are actually able to help and will provide a kind of demographic dividend that has not been realised yet.

And there are millions of Chinese children living in these areas who could become productive members of society. And that would give the same thing as a demographic and education dividend.

Why do I say that? Well, maybe the body count is lower but the quality count could be much higher, and so you need to think not only of just replacing bodies or getting more bodies.

The whole quality of training and skill requirements in the Chinese economy have increased tremendously, which means that China is going to be much better able to produce goods and to basically sustain and achieve a prosperous way of life.

So what I am saying is you can replace bodies with skills. Fewer bodies but more skills will benefit China a great deal because there will be fewer mouths to feed but more abilities and skills out there. This will make China a much more skilled environment than it was, say, 50 or 100 years ago.

Beijing makes clear in its new five-year plan that technology will be the main economic engine and that it wants to cultivate more talent to develop new technologies and innovate. How can this goal be achieved?

I was at the China Development Forum in Beijing when Premier Li Qiang gave the announcement of the 15th five-year plan and I listened with great interest, for several reasons.

As an American, I was very impressed with the quality of the Chinese leadership, at least the language used and the analysis they presented was very high quality. It was good economics. It was good social science actually, and it really reflected the basic principles of comparative advantage and the principles of trying to understand how a functioning economy would work.

So I was very impressed by the fact that the planning seemed to be very thoughtful and there were even a lot of elements of discussion about making the market factors in China work. It wasn’t a matter of planning from the centre without recognising market realities.

I thought there should have been more focus on building domestic consumption as a major component of Chinese development. The Chinese savings rate is still extraordinarily high by world standards.

This is not a new point. People have talked about the enormously high savings rate. The savings rate is a very great benefit for China in the sense that it allows you to make investments and improve society, which it has done tremendously.

Infrastructure is at a very high level, but the fact is that promoting domestic consumption is probably a wise approach for economic growth going forward. In other countries, savings rates are often lower, maybe 5 or 10 per cent of the Chinese savings rate.

The domestic market here is huge and it’s growing and that’s going to be a stimulus for economic growth for Chinese companies. Many organisations, like the IMF, the World Bank – and Chinese economists themselves of course – have always talked about it.

The premier said the government wanted to spend more on human capital to boost domestic consumption. What’s your view on that and what are the pitfalls?

The main thing that China should do, as I mentioned already, is alleviate the big gap between the west and east, between rural and urban. Increasing investment in the education of rural Chinese will be a very great buy – it is already helping to bolster the economy.

But I still think the gap can be closed a great deal more. And I also think the quality of education should probably be enhanced.

China’s got a lot of room for improvement in its education system.

For example, test scores are only a partial indicator of what a student can do. They’re not good measures of creativity or good measures of the ability to pioneer and engage in entrepreneurship. The Chinese system should be made to be more focused on creativity, productivity, entrepreneurship and risk-taking than it currently is.

I do believe that the Chinese have a great deal of gain potential here by being able to go and look closely at – and refocus – the education system.

I was a little dismayed when I heard the minister of education say earlier that the major focus in education was health.

Health is important, but I think the education minister didn’t appreciate the fact that certain social, emotional and cognitive skills promote health.

It’s not just a matter of having more health; not just more exercise, although exercise is very valuable, and that medical treatment is very valuable and vaccination is very valuable. All that’s valuable. But I think it was too narrow a perspective about how to promote health.

We promote health by promoting education. It’s a mistake to think that education should be just about health or only health. What we want to think of is producing more general skill sets of Chinese to make them more risk-taking, more creative and so forth. This is true not just of China but around the world.

So I am not picking on China here in particular, but I think that a lot of so-called educationists – the ones who work in schools of education – focus too narrowly on things like test scores and PISA [Programme for International Student Assessment] scores.

Even PISA itself is shifting its focus away, towards social and emotional skills as well. But those turn out to have a very big influence on health and the ability to regulate one’s life, to control one’s passions and appetite.

The ability to regulate oneself is really a very important ingredient, and schools and families can teach that. So I do think the educational system should probably recognise a little more that human capital production is not just a consequence of schools, but it’s also a consequence of what family life is.

And that starting early is a very important way to make schools more productive, and to engage the family in the life of the child.

So all those are possible moves that China could take to essentially bolster its human capital production.

You mentioned the importance of creativity and risk taking, but the Chinese system and Chinese culture are quite rigid in the sense that people are taught to align with the central values and the central agenda. How can that gap be bridged to enable the Chinese education system to encourage risk taking?

Well, I think the most important thing is a message that I heard from Jack Ma actually, although I don’t know if he wants to be quoted this way. He came to Chicago many years ago, and he opened his remarks to a group of entrepreneurs and business leaders and academics by saying that he had a university at Alibaba, and he wanted to teach people how to fail.

I think it’s clearly understood what he means is to take risks, try new things.

And I think there is nothing inconsistent with being obedient and respecting the law, and at the same time trying out new ideas, especially ideas that have to do with products, with science, with mathematics, with art.

So I think that the idea of conformity to values – certain values – is very good.

And I think that idea of having a common purpose and a desire to have a China that is uniform and consistent and fair to all is a good idea. But at the same time, I think you’ve got to tolerate the capacity of individuals to go off and make big mistakes.

Make mistakes not just deliberately, but in an effort to try new things. A lot of investigation – whether it’s in literature or in science or in business or in journalism or in any dimension – inevitably involves trying new things.

And if they’re new, you’re not sure they’re going to work. Sometimes they work really well, sometimes they fail. And so understanding that failure is part of just trying is really important – and encouraging that.

So, I don’t think it’s at odds with Chinese cultural values. I was very pleased to listen to the leaders talk in Beijing about a common goal. There was a notion that China was unified, that there was a national purpose, and the national purpose was to excel. And that division was not to be encouraged, but it was actually discouraged.

The leaders were seeking a common goal – they sought to be better, stronger, more prosperous and harmonious. But at the same time, there is a lot of room in that framework for thinking big about new ideas and disagreeing about the best way forward.

One thing that should be done is more teaching of creative acts, and basically breaking rules that get established solely by tradition, or not by logic or not by comparative advantage.

You’ve done a lot of research on early childhood intervention and education. What’s your advice for parents?

Many people think of early childhood programmes as kind of extending the school system to younger ages, and so instead of six-year-olds going to school, three-year-olds going to school or even two-year-olds. That’s a big mistake. I think it’s really about understanding the role of the family in producing these skills of children and in the interaction that parents have with their children, the interaction patterns, parent with teacher, parent with child, and child with teacher.

Those interaction patterns are very strong and very powerful. Strong in the sense that if they’re well maintained and developed, children can learn a lot and children will benefit. If they’re weak, then children won’t.

So the one thing that we’ve learned is how valuable attachment and interaction patterns are for the development of the self and of abilities. Successful early childhood programmes engage the family as much as they do the child, and certainly more than a school. So this is not another schooling programme; this is a programme which is teaching the parents how to teach the child to learn.

And also – and this is really important – protecting the child and at the same time encouraging the child to take risks. So this is what is sometimes called scaffolding. It’s a notion in psychology of finding where the child is and taking the child to the next step. It’s a very intense job, and parents are better at that in many ways than teachers.

We should have more parents as teachers – especially teaching young children – through example, through basically working with them, encouraging them, listening to them, engaging them in a variety of different activities.

The lessons that children learn from those engagements are powerful, and that’s important. Where the real learning takes place and where the real encouragement takes place is with the individual parent-teacher engaging with a child and getting that child to go off and engage with the world.

That interaction is the key. It’s not like you want to teach Chinese or you want to teach algebra or you want to teach any particular subject as much as you want to build a relationship.

These kinds of lessons have a huge spillover. They produce social and emotional strengths that people don’t anticipate and are very powerful.

Unemployment is a serious problem among young people in China. What’s your view on this and what can be done about it?

Well, the unemployment problem in China is partly related to skills again. It’s also related to the fact that industry and skills haven’t matched as well.

At the conference in Beijing, Tim Cook of Apple talked about a large donation he had made to the China Development Research Foundation and to promote vocational education.

And I think that’s something missing in China on a large scale. I know there is a formal schooling called vocational training, but the difference between successful vocational training and what’s being offered now will come from integrating training at the workplace along with training and education.

So young people will learn at the workplace, they will learn at the job, and they will also take academic education.

An example would be something like the German apprenticeship system or the Austrian or Swiss apprenticeship systems. They just integrate school and work in a way that makes it easier for young people to learn a job and to find a job and to learn the skills that are needed in the job.

China still has a lot of foreign direct investment – the FDI is huge – but what’s needed more is a skilled workforce to match it.

There are examples of how to do this. The US state of South Carolina at one time had mostly unskilled textile workers, but those textile industry jobs disappeared and the state was in crisis because so many were unemployed.

South Carolina attracted FDI in part by offering workplace training – so BMW and BASF and other large firms went there, and people were trained in the BMW system, trained in the BASF system and trained in other systems at other firms. So that training facilitated employment.

There’s a lot of discussion about how AI is affecting the job market, but also education. How should early education change, and what should we do to help children cope with the change?

Some people say AI can take over jobs. So it’s going to make simple accounting jobs no longer valuable because it can add faster – we can add numbers more quickly with AI.

However, this kind of logic is based on the idea that somehow AI does a set of tasks and it automatically replaces people. That’s not true.

The reason it’s not true is the following: sure, the job may be done partly by AI, but if the AI makes the output of that job, the task that they perform, cheaper, then it becomes much more in demand.

So even though it may require fewer workers per output item, there could be more workers employed if the demand for that task expands.

One thing more generally though is that the AI does have to be carefully used in the education system.

If people use AI as a substitute for thinking, that’s deadly. That’s going to prevent people from thinking on their own, and the act of thinking and creating is extremely important.

If we have too many students who are having DeepSeek or ChatGPT or Claude or some other program writing papers for them, they are not really thinking as young people.

We have to be aware of the danger of being overreliant on AI, and if students are using AI to write their papers instead of thinking through them, that’s destructive.

The thinking process itself literally builds neurons and builds intelligence. You have to literally understand the way that people solve problems and the way they build brain power is by solving problems directly, not by having somebody solve the problem for them.

It’s a mistake to essentially think that AI is going to be a substitute unless we just become, you know, a nation of drug addicts and dependent people. But I don’t think we want that.

We want children to be able to function, and by that I mean master tasks and not rely excessively on AI. Not play too many games, not spend too much time idle, but also spend more time solving new problems. AI can help do that. You can play chess with AI, you can play Go with AI, you can also use AI in a very constructive way.

AI can also be a very valuable check on yourself – it can help you correct your text or give you some other ideas. So we need to find the balance between total reliance and total avoidance of AI. I would say that we will find a happy medium but we’re still searching for that.

In your papers you’ve talked about the importance of children’s non-cognitive development, virtues and self-control. Why are these elements so important, and why should economists pay attention?

Well I think that these are skills. Traditionally when we think about technology, we think of a Solow model of economic growth done 60, 70 years ago. Now the emphasis is on the role of capital machines and labour.

What we’ve come to understand is that a lot of the modern economy consists of interactions among partners, trade relationships, personal interactions.

So these social skills of interacting with others are extremely vital, and it’s something we typically neglect. So it’s not surprising economists have always talked about this, but I think what we’ve come to understand is that it is much deeper than just IQ or cognition. We think that the way the human brain works, emotions play a very powerful role: emotion and self-regulation and virtue.

You are most famous for the Heckman correction model to correct statistical bias. How robust is Chinese data?

There are a number of social experimental data sets that are not made available publicly, but are used for private decision-making. So the Chinese data is rich.

There’s a real question, though – which is not completely resolved – as to how accurate some of the very large aggregate figures are for things like, you know, production and pollution and manufacturing.

I hesitate to make strong statements because I haven’t studied those in great detail. I remember many years ago [late American economist] Lawrence Klein was actively engaged in the question about whether the macro data – the data on the economy in China – was accurate.

I think the standards of micro data that individual organisations are collecting are generally very good, but I hate to make a general statement about all data collection in China because I simply haven’t studied it.

What do you think of the suggestion that China may overtake the US in a few years in terms of scientific or technological development?

The current administration in the United States has been very unwise in trying to block and failing to support science in a broad way. It has taken political actions in a way that are very unconstructive. So it’s possible that the rate of progress in the United States will slow because support from the government is low.

Nonetheless, the United States still has a large private sector and places like Silicon Valley and other centres like MIT and Harvard where there is a big private sector supporting research.

But the government support for the NIH [National Institutes of Health] and others has been politicised and reduced, and that means you are slowing down basic science. In certain quarters, parts of what they’ve reduced though is fine.

I personally am in agreement with some of the cuts in the sense that some of this research being funded before was purely political, and it was clearly done to kind of inspire people’s beliefs which were more of a political basis than serious social science research. So cuts of this type of research are good.

I do believe that China is really engaged very strongly.

It can only lead to output that’s very, very good. And the quality of the workers I’ve met with and interacted with has been extremely high. And the work quality is good.

I hope to collaborate with some of these people, and we are actively engaged in discussing those collaborations and even implementing them.

So I think it’s a matter of time, and I think that as China puts in more resources – and [puts] in high-quality resources – and maintains high standards, it will possibly overtake the US.

item.title: [SCMP] Indians turn to AI gurus for answers: ‘ChatGPT is not judging you’
item.description:
When Kripa Vaidyanathan’s 27-year-old niece died in an Alaska car crash in 2024, her family in Chennai, India, felt shell-shocked. They questioned why this tragedy would befall them when they had such “immense faith in God”.

Vaidyanathan, a yoga instructor, helped her grieving sister get face time with a high-profile guru whom she hoped would help.

“But he told her this was the work of karma and she should use this opportunity to connect with her inner nature,” she said. “I understand how karma works, but saying that was cruel and extremely unhelpful to someone who was freshly grieving the loss of a child.”
item.content:encoded:
When Kripa Vaidyanathan’s 27-year-old niece died in an Alaska car crash in 2024, her family in Chennai, India, felt shell-shocked. They questioned why this tragedy would befall them when they had such “immense faith in God”.

Vaidyanathan, a yoga instructor, helped her grieving sister get face time with a high-profile guru whom she hoped would help.

“But he told her this was the work of karma and she should use this opportunity to connect with her inner nature,” she said. “I understand how karma works, but saying that was cruel and extremely unhelpful to someone who was freshly grieving the loss of a child.”

That was when they turned to artificial intelligence chatbots.

“It was a lot easier trying to get answers and peace of mind because ChatGPT is not judging you,” Vaidyanathan said. “We’ve found a compassionate guru now, but even he only has limited time. AI is accessible anytime.”

This unfettered access – which can be challenging to find among human gurus – is drawing more people to AI for spiritual guidance.

It is a big step, particularly in Hinduism, where gurus are part of culture and deemed necessary to attain moksha – liberation from the cycle of birth, death and reincarnation. The word guru in Sanskrit means “dispeller of darkness”.

These chatbots are powered by large language models, AI systems that generate responses by using advanced statistics and troves of text, including sacred ones like Hinduism’s Bhagavad Gita.

Users can explore spiritual answers to personal problems and existential questions at any time, without the typical hurdles of connecting with an in-demand guru and paying for their services.

Gurus get in game

AI’s rising popularity has encouraged some successful gurus to launch their own chatbots.

In India, Jaggi Vasudev, also known as Sadhguru, has launched his Miracle of the Mind app with an interactive AI feature that answers questions using a database of his teachings. California-based self-help guru Deepak Chopra has an AI platform where “Digital Deepak” answers questions drawing from his decades of talks and writings.

Critics argue that AI cannot truly replace the lived experience, wisdom and ethical accountability of a human guru. Researchers also note that AI often validates and agrees with the user rather than posing those challenging questions needed for real spiritual and personal growth.

Vikas Sahu, founder of GitaGPT – a platform he called an “AI spiritual companion” – said he would not deter anyone from finding a human guru. But he says his free chatbot puts the Bhagavad Gita’s wisdom at the fingertips of those who might desperately need it.

On his platform, AI avatars of Lord Krishna, the sacred text’s protagonist, offer advice. Sahu, based in Gurugram, south of New Delhi, says he gets hundreds of messages about how it is helpful. While he has a full-time job building websites, he says GitaGPT is his way of giving back.

“A lot of people don’t have anyone to talk to when they are in distress,” he said. “This app is giving them the encouragement a guru might give them. But a lot of gurus want your money and you can’t really talk to them openly like you can talk to a chatbot.”

Sahu said he trusted GitaGPT because it was based on the word of God. “How could Krishna steer anyone wrong?” he asked. “It’s impossible.”

Liz Bucar, a religion professor at Northeastern University in Boston, is sceptical of chatbots based on religious texts.

“A sacred text needs a community and a context that interprets it,” she said. “Without the teaching of how to interpret the text, it’s just words on a page. Someone could feed in the text, but what answers will the bot spit out?”

But she does believe there is widespread distrust of institutional expertise that gurus and clergy represent, in some cases fuelled by sex abuse scandals.

“Because religion has this PR problem, people tend to see chatbots as less biased and less likely to do bad things,” Bucar said. “I don’t know if we’re ready to replace gurus, but we are definitely in a shifting religious landscape, especially with” younger generations of AI users.

Human touch
