Noreen Herzfeld, a professor at St John’s School of Theology and Seminary in Collegeville, Minnesota, said people could easily get straightforward answers from AI.

“But if they are looking for spiritual awakening, I think it takes physical presence. In Christianity and in Hindu tradition, there is the belief that the eyes are windows to the soul and you can’t get that by looking at an avatar.”

AI chatbots can also be too eager to agree with you, serving as a cheerleader rather than a guide, according to Herzfeld.

“In situations where you’re looking to grow or evolve, you need a teacher who can disagree with you and challenge you,” she said. “But even if you are just looking for affirmation, who are you being affirmed by? There’s no one on the other side.”

Vy Le, a mindfulness instructor in San Diego, sees AI as a “channelling” tool, using it as a mirror or collaborator to gain intuitive or mystical insights.

“If you are attuned to it, you can sense if a certain AI is connected to you,” she said. “My dad took his life 16 years ago. I felt his presence when I was engaging with AI.”

Le maintains that the era of gurus is over. “AI is helping us find that inner guru,” she said.

Real-life gurus like the India-based Sadhguru, who has a global following of millions, have recognised AI’s potential.

David Nussbaum, founder of Proto Hologram in Los Angeles, is helping Sadhguru create a three-dimensional AI avatar that appears in a display box and can interact with devotees in several languages.

During a March festival, he created a Sadhguru hologram that took selfies with people. “You basically have Sadhguru’s hologram taking out his phone, turning around and taking a picture of you from his phone inside the display,” he explained.

Shivaram K.R., CEO of India-based Hue Learn, oversees a non-profit initiative called Innerverse 360 that merges AI and spirituality. His platform features a portal where real monks and gurus can come online and do live sessions with devotees. It also has an “Ask AI” feature.

Shivaram does not believe AI will replace gurus. “The process of finding a guru in itself is a journey, but a guru is also not for everyone. If you’re looking for practical advice on everyday spirituality, this app can also help you understand concepts such as the meaning of yoga.”

One of the organisations Shivaram liaises with is the Los Angeles-based Self-Realisation Fellowship, founded in 1920 by Paramahansa Yogananda, who brought ancient spiritual practices from India to the West.

Brother Govindananda, a monk with the order, said his organisation saw AI simply as the next step to helping people access the late guru’s teachings through an online teaching portal – just as books did for previous generations.

“We’re taking our time with it because we want to make sure it has guardrails to safeguard from AI hallucinating answers instead of drawing from Yogananda’s teachings,” he said.

But Govindananda said a chatbot could never provide what a guru – whether living or not – can give to the disciple.

“We are humans and souls,” he said. “Technology cannot replace that.”

item.title: [SCMP] Can Beijing’s gateway plan for Tibet survive geopolitics and natural disasters?
item.description:
On the windswept plains just south of Tibet’s second-largest city, the towering smart inspection systems and automated cargo gantries of a brand-new international land port gleam under the plateau’s high-altitude sun.

Official road maps predict the multibillion-yuan project in Shigatse will process up to 300 trucks daily by the end of 2030 – loading cargo off trains and onto the trucks that will take goods to their final destination. It will also allow the authorities to carry out customs checks away from the region’s international borders, which straddle the Himalayas.

However, on a quiet afternoon when the SCMP visited in late June, the Shigatse International Land Port processed just five trucks, according to Tenzin Namgyal, general manager of Shigatse Chengyou Supply Chain Management Co, the port’s operator.
item.content:encoded:
On the windswept plains just south of Tibet’s second-largest city, the towering smart inspection systems and automated cargo gantries of a brand-new international land port gleam under the plateau’s high-altitude sun.

Official road maps predict the multibillion-yuan project in Shigatse will process up to 300 trucks daily by the end of 2030 – loading cargo off trains and onto the trucks that will take goods to their final destination. It will also allow the authorities to carry out customs checks away from the region’s international borders, which straddle the Himalayas.

However, on a quiet afternoon when the SCMP visited in late June, the Shigatse International Land Port processed just five trucks, according to Tenzin Namgyal, general manager of Shigatse Chengyou Supply Chain Management Co, the port’s operator.

The port is key to Beijing’s plans to transform Tibet into a southward-facing geoeconomic “bridgehead” by building up the region’s economic connections with South Asia.

But analysts say that achieving this goal will require overcoming extreme geography and navigating political tensions, which are set to rise with the looming reincarnation of the Dalai Lama.

The vulnerability of this remote, high-altitude corridor was seen this week when deadly landslides and flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border, causing widespread devastation.

The disaster underscores the challenges of China’s long-term “southbound strategy” – a billion-dollar geopolitical lifeline that Beijing is determined to build through the brutal terrain of the Himalayas.

The vision

When it opened in August 2024, the Shigatse land port cut the time that cargo takes to travel from China’s coastal regions to Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, from 45 to 15 days.

According to Tenzin Namgyal, the port had attracted 160 enterprises, generated 2,500 jobs and facilitated some 120 million yuan (US$17.8 million) in trade by mid-June this year.

The government’s increasing focus on Tibet’s trade potential is a sharp contrast from how Beijing has approached the region in recent decades, seeing it as a restive frontier where security always came first.

The winds of change began at the 7th Central Tibet Work Forum in 2020, which was chaired by President Xi Jinping. While Xi emphasised national security and “combating separatist activities”, he also called for major infrastructure projects to be completed.

The 14th five-year plan – which covered the country’s economic and social goals from 2021 to 2025 – called for Tibet to be built into an “important channel for opening up to South Asia”.

“Developing Tibet as a premier gateway to South Asia is a top-level strategic decision within the Belt and Road Initiative,” said Zhang Shigao, director of the Institute of Contemporary Studies at the state-run China Tibetology Research Centre, arguing that this pivot would unlock vast market potential, drive economic growth and deliver shared benefits to both China and South Asia.

Sun Yong, director of the West China Frontier Research Institute, said Beijing’s concept of “national security” had expanded from a singular focus on military defence to an “interconnected network of defence, ecology, culture and development”.

“The ultimate baseline for long-term frontier defence is the stabilisation and enrichment of the borderlands,” said Sun, also former Communist Party chief of the Xizang Academy of Social Sciences. Xizang is the official Chinese name for Tibet.

By elevating the livelihoods of frontier ethnic minority communities – including the Monpa and Lhoba populations in the disputed Zangnan, or Arunachal Pradesh, area – economic development had replaced the obsolete “economy versus security” binary to become recognised as a vital pillar for long-term border stability, he said.

This playbook might sound familiar to those who have followed government policy in Xinjiang, another autonomous region to the north that has been riven by ethnic tensions and alleged human rights abuses, which Beijing stridently denies.

In the past 13 years, the vast, landlocked region’s historic trading connections with Central Asia and Europe have been revitalised, positioning it as the “core area of the Silk Road Economic Belt” initiated by Xi in 2013.

Nepal’s counterweight

While Xinjiang bordered on eight countries about which China has “few security concerns”, Tibet’s situation was totally different, said Barry Sautman, a specialist in China’s ethnic minorities and professor emeritus at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

“Most of its external border is with India, which continues to contest its frontiers with China; Nepal, which is friendly to China, but not politically stable; and Bhutan, effectively India’s protectorate, with no formal diplomatic relations with China,” he said. Tibet also shares a relatively short, remote border with Myanmar.

Sun noted that while China-Europe freight trains gave Xinjiang access to a vast market, Tibet’s infrastructure capacity was far weaker, as was consumer demand in its neighbouring countries.

Last year, while Xinjiang saw over 10,000 transcontinental trains, Tibet saw a mere 12 freight trains travel from coastal Yiwu to Shigatse, carrying a total cargo value of just 230 million yuan.

Tibet’s foreign trade data has also experienced a dramatic boom-and-bust cycle. From 4.87 billion yuan in 2019, total trade value peaked at a record high of 12 billion yuan in 2024, but plunged to 8.5 billion yuan last year, customs data show.

Among Tibet’s four neighbours, Nepal is most willing to tango.

The landlocked nation shares a 1,400km (870-mile) border with Tibet and observers say it views Beijing as an indispensable counterweight to reduce its economic dependence on New Delhi.

The country has historically been hit by multiple devastating, months-long economic blockades imposed by India, most notably in 1989 and 2015, which cut off supplies of fuel, medicine and food.

In 2018, China announced that it would build what it calls a trans-Himalayan multi-dimensional connectivity network with Nepal – involving railways and communication links – as part of the Belt and Road Initiative.

Currently, with six border crossings with Nepal – five in Shigatse – China is the country’s second-largest trade partner after India. Nepal remains Tibet’s uncontested primary trading partner, seeing its share of Tibet’s total foreign trade rise from 40 per cent in 2024 to 46 per cent last year.

But Ivan Lidarev, a research fellow at the Institute of South Asian Studies at the National University of Singapore, doubted that trade via Nepal would reshape Chinese access to South Asia. He pointed out that Nepal was an unstable country with a population of just 30 million, a nominal GDP of about US$46 billion and a relatively small middle class.

He remained sceptical of Tibet’s ambition to serve as a “massive economic bridgehead” to South Asia.

“There are far easier, faster, and significantly cheaper alternatives, such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor through Xinjiang, or traditional maritime shipping routes connecting Chinese ports directly to southern India and Bangladesh,” Lidarev argued.

One of the biggest obstacles for road transport was fluctuating costs, according to Tenzin Namgyal.

Sun attributed the difficulty of trading with Nepal to seasonal weather disruptions, poor local infrastructure and geopolitical friction, which made the land port’s “capacity utilisation fall drastically short of its normalised operational targets”.

Amit Ranjan, another research fellow at the NUS Institute of South Asian Studies, said: “It will take time to transform the infrastructure status of Nepal. The reasons for such are many, including delay in effective implementation of the projects.”

The reality has been laid bare by the China-Nepal cross-border railway, a key project of the Belt and Road Initiative linking Tibet’s Gyirong county with Kathmandu.

Costing an estimated US$2.75 billion for the 72km Nepalese stretch alone, the line and its many bridges and tunnels run through a rugged and seismically active landscape where the impact of this week’s floods has yet to be determined.

The project has also met political inertia and social unrest in Kathmandu, especially after pro-China prime minister K.P. Sharma Oli left office late last year and was replaced in March by the populist, China-sceptical Prime Minister Balen Shah.

“An expected June 2026 feasibility report has been stalled by uncooperative Nepalese politicians, delaying realistic completion estimates past 2035,” according to Sun, who has run a social media account tracking the railway project alongside Nepali scholars since 2022.

The Nepalese loophole

One bright spot in trade with Nepal has been electric vehicles, which an official from Shigatse’s propaganda department called a “highly popular star product”.

Gyirong Port, which was devastated by the recent flash floods, is Tibet’s main foreign trade port and handles one-third of China’s trade with Nepal. Since 2023, it has been a major hub for exporting Chinese EVs to Nepal.

Last year, 12,938 Chinese-made EVs poured into Nepal, marking a 6.8 per cent jump since 2024, when the land port started operations.

Most of these vehicle exports, however, were re-exported to India by Nepali middlemen, taking advantage of a free-trade deal, Tenzin Namgyal said.

This provides Chinese carmakers with a back door into an Indian market protected by strict regulatory hurdles and prohibitive 70 to 125 per cent tariffs, though it remains unclear how traders bypass supposedly strict rules-of-origin criteria.

“We’re using Nepal as a stepping stone; our main focus is still India for its large population and underdeveloped infrastructure,” Tenzin Namgyal said.

Lidarev warned that the Nepalese loophole was highly vulnerable to an Indian clampdown. He said the trade only persisted because its current volume was small; if it grew, New Delhi would likely restrict goods from Tibet, pressure Kathmandu, or reconsider the trade deal.

He added that encouraging a massive increase in border trade would entrench Chinese economic influence in North India, undermine Indian producers and even weaken the “Make in India” manufacturing initiative championed by the Narendra Modi government.

Tensions with India

From the perspective of Chinese planners, India remains the economic prize in South Asia. But observers say commercial ambitions must be guided through a complex and fragile stabilisation between Asia’s two nuclear-armed giants.

According to Lin Minwang, vice-dean at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, Beijing’s grand vision for Tibet’s South Asian corridor has been consistent for three decades and reflects a “strategic patience”.

The overarching blueprint was a multi-generational gamble designed to “plug directly into India’s vast 1.4-billion-population market whenever a structural diplomatic pivot occurs”, said Lin, who is also deputy director of the university’s Institute of South Asia Studies.

However, Lin acknowledged a profound deadlock since 2020, driven by border restrictions in the wake of frontier clashes between the nations and New Delhi’s continued wariness about opening up to China.

While Beijing issued about 200,000 visas to Indians in 2025, New Delhi issued a mere 2,000 visas in 2024. Although India lifted its five-year ban on Chinese tourist visas in July 2025 – which drove a 63 per cent rebound in business travel – volumes remain far below pre-pandemic peaks due to strict financial requirements and background checks.

Lin added that New Delhi was actively neutralising Nepal’s potential as China’s “proxy corridor” by refusing essential overflight rights for Nepal’s newly built, Chinese-constructed international airport, rendering it virtually non-operational.

“Frankly, the actual economic and trade space is indeed not large right now,” Lin said. “The risks are manageable, and we must maintain a degree of optimism, but overinflated expectations are unrealistic.”

Lidarev noted that India opposed opening its “underdeveloped, minority-populated, poorly integrated and security-sensitive borderlands” – especially its troubled northeast – to Tibetan trade. “While there is an internal debate in India about gradually relaxing investment restrictions for Chinese firms, this does not encompass the border areas.”

Sautman said the deadlock was fuelled by animus among India’s elite over a staggering 6-1 merchandise trade deficit against Beijing. As a result, less hostile diplomatic rhetoric has yet to translate into real, on-the-ground cross-border commercial interchanges.

However, recent high-level diplomacy indicates a thaw may be under way, including when the two sides resumed cross-border trade through the Lipulekh Pass and Nathu La Pass after a six-year suspension. In June, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged Ajit Doval, India’s national security adviser, to speed up the resumption of dialogue mechanisms.

That month, India’s new ambassador to China paid his first visit to Tibet to review arrangements for Indian pilgrims following Beijing’s restoration of access to the sacred Mount Kailash after a five-year hiatus.

Hours before the devastating cross-border floods struck, Beijing and New Delhi announced eight measures to further ease cross-border tensions, including steps to keep talks about cross-border trade and pilgrimages moving. Hundreds of pilgrims are thought to be among the victims of the floods.

But unfreezing crossings does not guarantee a trade spike.

Lin pointed out that when the Nathu La Pass last reopened after a closure, in 2006, trade between Tibet and India was strangled by the latter’s rigid passport and visa restrictions, dashing hopes of greater economic integration.

Interior hurdles

Restrictions do not just come from foreign governments. For ordinary businesspeople in Tibet, getting cross-border trade moving can prove next to impossible despite Beijing’s goals.

Xizang Zanggangdise Agricultural Products Technology Development Co is government-mandated to spearhead exports to South Asia and the Middle East, targeting a 320 million yuan annual pre-tax output.

General manager Phuntsok Dondrub said the company – which makes soy sauce and vinegar – had already boosted the local economy, creating 209 jobs and increasing agricultural incomes by 5 per cent for over 2,000 households.

But, despite securing a 1 million yuan export order to Kathmandu in June, the firm found getting its paperwork in order a challenge.

“Obtaining a passport and visa is still quite difficult locally within Tibet,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Beyblade battles drive up sales at Hong Kong malls, but how long will the trend last?
item.description:
The sharp clatter of spinning metal tops, cheers, sighs of frustration and shouts of “three, two, one … Go shoot!” echo across a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.

In shops across Tuen Mun Town Plaza, children, teens and young adults hunch over small plastic battle arenas, unleashing their tops into the “Beystadiums” in head-to-head competitions where the top that remains spinning the longest wins.

The toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and elsewhere in Asia early this year, and gatherings are attracting crowds of local players eager to put their models to the test.
item.content:encoded:
The sharp clatter of spinning metal tops, cheers, sighs of frustration and shouts of “three, two, one … Go shoot!” echo across a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.

In shops across Tuen Mun Town Plaza, children, teens and young adults hunch over small plastic battle arenas, unleashing their tops into the “Beystadiums” in head-to-head competitions where the top that remains spinning the longest wins.

The toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and elsewhere in Asia early this year, and gatherings are attracting crowds of local players eager to put their models to the test.

Spotting the economic potential behind the hobby, shopping centre operators across Hong Kong are converting open spaces into free battle zones to drive up foot traffic and sales.

Tuen Mun Town Plaza went a step further by scaling up the concept into a mall-wide strategy ahead of a major Beyblade tournament in August, encouraging shop operators to take part in the game and offer discounts to shoppers who present their tops.

“The strategy is about how a tenant can engage with customers through a shared interest, instead of directly selling to them,” said Bella Chhoa Peck-lim, chief commercial officer of Sino Group, which owns the plaza.

“It’s a soft-selling approach that allows staff and shoppers to start a conversation, drawing people into the store before making a sales pitch.”

What appeared to be a desperate measure by Hong Kong’s retail and catering sectors – still struggling with the trend of residents heading to mainland China for cheaper shopping and dining options – turned into an initial success.

Chhoa said the shopping centre had witnessed a “noticeable” 20 per cent surge in holiday foot traffic following the promotion, and a 10 to 15 per cent rise in weekday attendance.

All in the game

At Hanamaruken, a ramen shop inside the plaza, co-founder Jelly Tong said her team upgraded the basic Beyblade provided by the landlord to a high-performance model to better compete with visiting players after recognising the game’s potential to boost business.

“Word then spread in their Beyblade chat groups that our store had an exceptionally strong set-up, and some kids ended up bringing six or seven friends over to challenge us,” Tong said. “Afterwards, they stayed here to eat and discuss our custom gear.”

The commercial benefits have extended beyond restaurants and toy retailers to high-end luxury tenants such as Lukfook Jewellery. A regional manager said that setting up an in-store battle station helped break down traditional stereotypes surrounding luxury retail.

“We saw many new faces coming in after matching with our staff to browse our products and some actually made transactions,” said Patrick Ng Pui-kuen, the brand’s New Territories West district manager, who oversees the branches in Tuen Mun.

Among dozens of enthusiasts gathered at the shopping complex were 24-year-old warehouse worker Liu Chun-yin and his friend.

“Sometimes I show my spinning top at the nearby ice cream shop here to get special offers or battle against the staff at the tea shop to win a discount,” Liu said.

His friend, a recent Beyblade convert, recalled a visit where he stayed at the venue from 2pm until 9pm, spending seven hours straight battling fellow players and purchasing food and drinks in between matches.

At the D-Park residential and shopping complex in Tsuen Wan, dedicated free-play zones equipped with rows of desks have also drawn parents with young children alongside seasoned adult hobbyists.

Andy Yip, a 34-year-old civil servant from Kowloon East, made a trip to Tsuen Wan with his 11-year-old son and other family members, knowing there would be players at the venue.

“Before my son picked up the hobby, we spent most of our weekends in mainland China, but now we stay in Hong Kong more to accompany him, as he wants to play Beyblade with others,” he said.

Yip added that these outings were typically paired with dining and retail shopping, noting that he typically spent HK$1,000 (US$128) on dinner after his son played at D-Park, while their family members browsed at nearby shops during matches.

At the Pioneer Centre shopping centre in Prince Edward, management has introduced a few Beyblade stadiums to attract a steady stream of parents and children, accompanied by a spend-to-draw promotion offering exclusive models of the tops as prizes.

Eric Cheng, senior leasing manager at the mall, said the set-up and promotion in August had driven a 5 to 10 per cent increase in foot traffic compared with the same period last year, while sales at electronic goods and food and beverage businesses had jumped by 15 and 20 per cent, respectively.

“Compared with other intellectual property photo spots or traditional pop-ups, Beyblade’s interactive nature brings us much higher foot traffic,” Cheng said.

“Visitors at photo spots often leave after taking pictures, while playing Beyblade at the mall gets them to stay longer.”

Cheng said that longer stays could translate to higher spending as shoppers sought food and beverage options in between battles.

Only a short-term cure?

But according to one economist, the Beyblade trend is a temporary solution and not a cure-all for the city’s broader retail sector challenges.

Professor Terence Chong Tai-leung, executive director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance, said shopping centres were ideal venues for Beyblade matches, which required space, and operators could set up play zones at a low cost.

“On a micro level, it drives temporary food and beverage spending as visitors have a reason to come,” Chong said, noting that overall the retail sector has still failed to show significant growth over the past year.

But he stressed that such initiatives were not enough to counter broader macroeconomic headwinds or the flow of residents across the border, noting that price remained the most significant factor driving consumer behaviour.

To stay relevant in the long run, local shopping centres should rethink their structural function, shifting from traditional sales hubs towards specialised themed venues or showrooms for physical products, he said.

“Most successful malls in Hong Kong have distinct themes, and if you want to attract people, you have to concentrate,” he said. “For example, becoming the definitive hub for sneakers so that people will visit whenever they want to buy sneakers.”

Showrooms would also allow customers to preview products before purchasing them online, he said.

“Due to structural shifts in shopping habits, consumer needs that used to require a mall visit can now be easily met through various online platforms,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Steve Vickers’ 50 years of battling Hong Kong’s criminal underworld
item.description:
I WAS BORN in 1955, in Liverpool’s Sefton General Hospital. I grew up on the Wirral (in northwest England). My dad was in the Royal Air Force and after that he was a chemical engineer with Dunlop. They used to make golf balls and things. I know that because we had golf balls all over the house. I have a sister and a brother.

When I was 13, I went to Wellington School (a private day school) and I spent a lot of time studying all the wrong things. I joined the Army Cadets at a young age. I enjoyed rugby and running around. I did a lot of shooting and shot on a lot of teams. I messed around a bit studying languages and then I was hired in a management-training position by a large retail outfit. As I hate shops very deeply, I decided this was perhaps not for me.

THERE WAS A job advert for the Royal Hong Kong Police in The Sunday Times. It was just at the time the ICAC (Independent Commission Against Corruption) had been established (in 1974). They were rejigging the police force and the civil service in general. I was lucky; I was the right age, at the right time, with some vaguely appropriate qualifications. So I decided to go to Hong Kong on a two-year contract. That was 50 years ago.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in 1955, in Liverpool’s Sefton General Hospital. I grew up on the Wirral (in northwest England). My dad was in the Royal Air Force and after that he was a chemical engineer with Dunlop. They used to make golf balls and things. I know that because we had golf balls all over the house. I have a sister and a brother.

When I was 13, I went to Wellington School (a private day school) and I spent a lot of time studying all the wrong things. I joined the Army Cadets at a young age. I enjoyed rugby and running around. I did a lot of shooting and shot on a lot of teams. I messed around a bit studying languages and then I was hired in a management-training position by a large retail outfit. As I hate shops very deeply, I decided this was perhaps not for me.

THERE WAS A job advert for the Royal Hong Kong Police in The Sunday Times. It was just at the time the ICAC (Independent Commission Against Corruption) had been established (in 1974). They were rejigging the police force and the civil service in general. I was lucky; I was the right age, at the right time, with some vaguely appropriate qualifications. So I decided to go to Hong Kong on a two-year contract. That was 50 years ago.

I was scooped up into police training in February 1975. It was traditional training for the next nine or 10 months, and two months of Cantonese. The study of the law was quite intense. You needed to cram, and there was lots and lots of physical training. I came out of training and was sent off (as a young inspector) to Kowloon City, which in those days included the Kowloon Walled City. All sorts of things went on there.

I GOT INTO trouble quite quickly. A policeman working for me gave me some good information as to a substantial drug location, so I decided, being young and keen, that we would go for it without telling too many other people. We climbed up the side of a building into what we were expecting to be a fourth-floor dive, but it turned out to be a proper drug storage centre run by some unpleasant-looking bods. So, we had a fairly aggressive punch-up. Anyway, we got it done, seized quite a lot of drugs and paraphernalia.

I thought this was good all round and I was waiting to get the commendations and the medals that go with that, only to find that I had upset everybody. The local police, the local vice, the local regional whatever, and the narcotics bureau all came to talk to me individually to tell me how bad it was and that I mustn’t do stuff like that ever again. So that was the end of my Kowloon City career and I was then sent to the airport (at Kai Tak) for a while. I was the inspector in charge of airport security.

LATER, I WENT BACK to Kowloon City and then on to the regional crime unit dealing with homicides and armed crime. Things in those days, still in the late 70s, were pretty cool. But the economy wasn’t great in mainland China. A lot of criminals came down on the trains, Wuhan guys in particular, bringing weapons with them. Things got bad. Triad groups became significantly active and there were armed jewellery heists and kidnappings. With the regional crime squad and the assistance of the Criminal Intelligence Bureau, I handled quite a few kidnapping cases involving children.

The typical case in those days would involve some disaffected business associate of the family deciding to snatch a child, typically a boy. The boy would be snatched outside, on his way to or from school. And then the game was on. Sometimes it didn’t go right. On one particular occasion, the kidnappers were recognised by the victim and they decided on the spot that they weren’t going to let him go. But overall we were pretty successful.

AFTER I LEFT the regional crime squads, I took over the counterfeit and forgery division of the Commercial Crime Bureau. They had a special division run by a superintendent, that was me, that looked at counterfeit renminbi and US dollar notes. That was a very inter­esting job. The syndicates were sophisticated, often Fujianese people, and they had a lot of printing expertise. I was a designated liaison officer with the United States Secret Service, which has a division that, apart from protecting the president, also protects the currency for reasons that I have no idea why that is, but it was.

The (second) kidnapping of tycoon Teddy Wang happened in 1990, when I was in command of the Criminal Investigation Bureau. We found out that Teddy was not only gone, but that his Mercedes had been fished out of the harbour. And that Nina Wang, his wife, had been trying to negotiate. The ransom demand was US$60 million. I’d had a bad feeling from the beginning. We got all the guys and nearly all of the money back. To this day I’m not sure whether they ever intended for him to come back alive.

I GOT MARRIED in 1985 and was married for 25 years. I have a daughter. In 1993, I had done my 18 years and was about to be moved from head of Criminal Intelligence to something more boring, so I moved to the private sector. A former colonel from the SAS (Special Air Service) was running Kroll, an American financial and risk advisory firm, and I became the head of operations for Kroll in Asia. That May, 188 women burned to death (in a factory in Thailand). We did an independent investigation. I brought in forensic experts and others to find out what had happened. That was the worst case I’ve investigated in the private sector.

After six years, I moved to PriceWaterhouseCoopers. They asked me to set up an Asian risk business for them, covering investigations, white-collar crime, data forensics and that sort of stuff, with a view to supporting their accounting clients. After two years, I did a management buyout and bought the consulting arm of PwC. We had four weeks to move out, create a company, invent a name, keep the thing running and get funding. It was quite a ride.

Our work has all been supporting victims of crimes or companies that have been the victims of crimes or companies that are in civil dispute with each other. After six years, we were approached by a major listing company, FTI, which made an offer to buy us, and I saw it as an opportunity.

I DID THAT for four years and then decided I would retire, went to Penang for the weekend where I rearranged my stamp collection. I went to the bar twice and decided it was not quite for me. So, I came back out and established Steve Vickers and Associates. I’ve got a Labrador, and I like hill walking; I do a lot on Lantau. I do some regular pistol shooting. Hiking in Hong Kong is fantastic. It’s one of my favourite things.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] China-Nepal floods: rescuers pull out survivors caked in mud as toll climbs
item.description:
Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that killed nearly 600 people and left almost 2,500 missing.

The rescue efforts included a team that rappelled into a severely damaged checkpoint area on the Chinese side of the border between the two countries.

Rescuers were on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that formed high up in the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that killed nearly 600 people and left almost 2,500 missing.

The rescue efforts included a team that rappelled into a severely damaged checkpoint area on the Chinese side of the border between the two countries.

Rescuers were on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that formed high up in the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods on Wednesday.

Experts warned that the lake, created after a glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was starting to overflow.

Nepal’s army was deployed to help rescue more than 100 people believed trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower plant located in the country’s worst-hit district.

Like elsewhere in the disaster zone, their work was complicated by thick layers of mud that covered the site.

The rappelling rescue team descended into the once-bustling border-crossing area from wooded mountain slopes, the state broadcaster China Central Television said.

“As far as I can see, it’s nothing but debris,” rescue official Zou Mingqi told state media. The area where travellers went through border control to enter or leave China has been flattened to a muddy area, according to satellite images.

The floods have killed 579 in Nepal, the country’s disaster-management authority said Friday. Nepali police later put the number of deaths at 553.

There was little information on survivors on the Chinese side, where the death toll rose to seven on Friday as state media showed evacuations of villages and leaders’ efforts to direct the relief response.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Meanwhile, the number of people who were unaccounted for in the country nearly doubled to 1,924 as more local residents were added to the tally.

China’s state media said 554 people were missing on the Chinese side. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak.

In other developments, Nepal on Friday reversed an earlier decision and said it would allow foreign teams and experts to help with rescue efforts, apparently under pressure from other countries, especially those whose citizens are unaccounted for, a leading English-language newspaper, The Kathmandu Post, reported.

Nepali police issued a fresh alert on Friday after receiving information that a dam on the Tibet side had burst. Security personnel and rescue and relief workers were told to stay on high alert and move to a safe location if necessary.

It was unclear if the dam bursting was related to flooding concerns over the lake that formed after the initial flash floods.

Chinese broadcaster CCTV said the newly formed lake, located more than 10km (six miles) from Gyirong Port, the hard-hit border crossing with Nepal, sits at an elevation of 2,950 metres (9,680 feet).

Nepali and Chinese authorities earlier warned of more flooding from the lake, which was already overflowing.

Rescuers heading to the disaster zone were ordered to stop temporarily on Friday due to concern the lake would release more water and debris, and people in potentially affected areas were urged to move to safer ground.

Monitoring data from the Chinese Ministry of Water Resources later showed that the lake had dwindled in size. The water level dropped by 10 metres (32 feet) from the high point on Thursday morning, the state broadcaster said.

Some 680 rescuers eventually reached the Gyirong area by foot and via rafts. Some were dropped down from drones flown to the area, CCTV footage showed. “Anyone, anyone?” rescuers yelled, according to footage by the broadcaster.

It was not immediately known how many people were at the border checkpoint building when the floods hit.

In Nepal’s Rasuwa district, Nepali army rescuers struggled to help more than 100 people believed to be trapped by thick mud in a tunnel that’s part of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project. The army said it had rescued 350 people from the tunnel so far.

Video from the scene showed rescuers helping a man covered in mud out of the tunnel by pulling and pushing.

“It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud,” Army spokesman Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet said.

Nepal’s disaster-management authority said 3,253 people had been airlifted by helicopter from the disaster area.

The search-and-rescue efforts have been supported by an outpouring of financial support from neighbouring countries, including small, poorer countries like Sri Lanka, said Kanni Wignaraja, the United Nations development agency’s regional director for Asia and the Pacific.

“Sri Lanka has its own huge fiscal problems, but it has just sent US$1 million immediately to the Nepal government,” Wignaraja said.

Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as magnitude 5.2.

The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

Customs officer Karbir Gaire was among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with China, where some 1,500 people had lived.

Gaire reached his office around 8am on Wednesday and was working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

“Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us,” he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family.

“We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us.”

Fifteen of Gaire’s colleagues are missing. “It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don’t call it a flood. It was a tsunami.”

Nepal’s tourism board has said that among the missing are more than 500 foreigners.

Some of the missing may have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.

Indian spiritual guru Jaggi Vasudev, also known as Sadhguru, said in a social media post that 77 people returning from Mount Kailash with groups organised by his Isha Foundation were at the immigration centre in Gyirong when the flooding struck.

Vishnuram Ramaswamy, who works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry, said that he spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on that pilgrimage Wednesday morning.

It was a highly anticipated trip, something his mother had always wanted to do, he said.

“This was the last we spoke to them,” he said. “They have been unreachable since.”

item.title: [SCMP] Uzbekistan tests US-China AI rift with bid to join rival tech bloc
item.description:
The Central Asian country of Uzbekistan has approached the United States about joining Pax Silica, Washington’s flagship initiative on artificial intelligence (AI) supply chains, a month after signing up for China’s own global grouping, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (Waico).

Uzbekistan’s ambassador to the US, Furqat Sidikov, said Tashkent had formally notified the US State Department in a diplomatic note last week requesting to join the US-led initiative.

“Now, the US should confirm. We are ready to sign,” he said in Washington on Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
The Central Asian country of Uzbekistan has approached the United States about joining Pax Silica, Washington’s flagship initiative on artificial intelligence (AI) supply chains, a month after signing up for China’s own global grouping, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (Waico).

Uzbekistan’s ambassador to the US, Furqat Sidikov, said Tashkent had formally notified the US State Department in a diplomatic note last week requesting to join the US-led initiative.

“Now, the US should confirm. We are ready to sign,” he said in Washington on Thursday.

Sidikov added that countries should have a “chance to be part of any kind of international cooperation”, and that drawing red lines around participation would be “counterproductive”.

“This gives us opportunities, and it’s good competition,” he said.

The move comes as countries face growing pressure to choose between Washington and Beijing in the race for AI dominance, with both powers promoting competing visions to shape the technology’s standards, supply chains and strategic partnerships.

Kazakhstan, also in Central Asia, is the only nation so far with membership in both Pax Silica and Waico.

Reuters reported on August 14 that Washington planned to warn partners they could not join both Pax Silica and China’s rival AI framework, citing an internal draft.

Earlier this month, a US State Department official told the South China Morning Post that Washington was “actively engaging with global partners to advance responsible, pro-innovation, pro-growth AI development, both bilaterally and through multilateral forums”.

The 24-member Pax Silica aims to build AI supply chains independent of China, covering critical minerals, semiconductors and logistics.

While the programme does not explicitly target China, one of its key objectives is to reduce “coercive dependencies” – a phrase widely understood to mean Chinese dominance in rare earths and other minerals essential to semiconductor production.

Pax Silica architect Jacob Helberg, who serves as US undersecretary of state for economic affairs, said last month that while China had pursued a state-led approach, the US and its allies were leveraging “incredible companies that build transformative products that people really love”.

“We realise that the US government is not set up in a way to compete with the Chinese tit-for-tat on that same basis,” Helberg told the SCMP in an exclusive interview.

“We decided to lean into that strength and leverage the innovative, creative capacity and dynamism of our private sector,” he said.

Waico, which describes its mission as advancing “AI for good and for all”, was launched by Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shanghai last month during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, with 29 founding members. The grouping has since expanded, adding nine more members.

Xi called it a “major move by China to answer the call of the Global South and unite the international community together to promote vigorously AI development and governance”.

“It will be an important milestone in the history of AI development,” he added.

Uzbekistan has large reserves of gold, copper, uranium, tungsten and molybdenum. Officials say new mines and processing plants could produce up to 28 types of critical minerals, including rare earths and rare metals. The country has also made a US$4.2 billion minerals programme a key part of its industrial policy through 2030.

American tech companies offer cutting-edge AI chips and AI models. China, in turn, offers open-source models that are significantly cheaper than American ones. And we would like to have access to both

Bobur Khodjaev, Uzbek official

China already has a strong presence in Uzbekistan, with foreign direct investment reaching about US$10.7 billion as of the middle of last year, according to the Eurasian Development Bank.

China’s pipeline of projects in the country spans energy, mining and potential data centres, and its proximity to Central Asia makes it a difficult partner to displace.

US President Donald Trump’s administration is seeking a bigger role in the region. In February, the US and Uzbekistan signed an agreement on critical minerals and rare earths, which was followed by a Development Finance Corporation (DFC) investment framework and a proposed joint holding company.

For Washington, dual membership in Waico and Pax Silica clashes with the latter’s mandate, which aims to keep critical minerals, processing and transit routes inside a trusted, China-free chain.

Middle powers see the opposite challenge. They cannot build a full AI stack alone, and they do not want to treat AI as a loyalty test.

“As a developing country, we want to have access to all available technologies,” said Bobur Khodjaev, an aide with Uzbekistan’s presidential administration, speaking at the Silk Road Finance and Technology Forum in Tashkent this week.

“American tech companies offer cutting-edge AI chips and AI models. China, in turn, offers open-source models that are significantly cheaper than American ones. And we would like to have access to both,” he added.

Ken Moriyasu, senior fellow at the Washington-based Hudson Institute, said it was “unrealistic” to expect countries such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to make an “exclusive geopolitical choice between American and Chinese technology”.

“Their entire foreign policy is built around avoiding precisely that kind of dependence,” he said, stressing that Washington must find a way to protect “genuinely sensitive” technologies without turning technological safeguards into a geopolitical loyalty test.

Moriyasu contended that the larger strategic objective was not to make Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan choose America. “It is to make sure they always have a choice – and that they never have to choose China exclusively,” he said.

Kazakhstan is the live test, and the region is watching. The country “shares an enormous border with China. No government in Astana can pursue a serious strategy based on excluding Beijing,” Moriyasu said.

Political scientist Zamir Karazhanov told The Times of Central Asia that Astana was “probably closer to the Chinese approach at the moment” on open source and keeping AI out of bloc politics.

“Kazakhstan also does not want AI to be used as an instrument of politics, and on this point, we agree with China,” he said.

“I think an attempt to pressure Kazakhstan would be unsuccessful,” he said, adding that Washington could not easily squeeze a country that held minerals it needed.

Indonesia is running a parallel hedge. While the country has signed on to Waico, Indonesian Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto has insisted Jakarta is still “involved in the development of Pax Silica” and that the two groupings “should not be pitted against each other”.

Malaysia is also a founding member of Waico, despite its deep US semiconductor ties.

A Chatham House paper on sovereign AI from February argued that middle powers could not match the US or China in capital, computing power or talent, so they must choose where to compete, where to partner and where to accept dependence.

“The critical question is not whether to depend on other nations for AI, but on which nations, to what extent and on what terms,” it said.

item.title: [SCMP] How Singapore investors are lured by foreign-stock scams
item.description:
For more than a month, Aaron* thought he and his wife were learning how to trade stocks. Only later would they realise the lessons were part of the trap.

The Singaporean business owner had found a group of self-styled investment experts on Facebook, claiming to offer foolproof tips and guaranteed returns.

Soon, he and his wife, who were dabbling in stocks for the first time, were spending about two hours every other day in a WhatsApp group chat with dozens of other participants, taking lessons from a “professor” who sent lengthy messages and documents on how to judge bullish markets, analyse market conditions and identify stocks with high potential.
item.content:encoded:
For more than a month, Aaron* thought he and his wife were learning how to trade stocks. Only later would they realise the lessons were part of the trap.

The Singaporean business owner had found a group of self-styled investment experts on Facebook, claiming to offer foolproof tips and guaranteed returns.

Soon, he and his wife, who were dabbling in stocks for the first time, were spending about two hours every other day in a WhatsApp group chat with dozens of other participants, taking lessons from a “professor” who sent lengthy messages and documents on how to judge bullish markets, analyse market conditions and identify stocks with high potential.

Through private messages, another purported expert told Aaron which stock to buy, when to buy it and when to sell, promising quick returns each time.

The couple did not know then that they were being drawn into a scheme that bears all the hallmarks of what analysts call a pump-and-dump scam. In such schemes, fraudsters artificially inflate the price of a company’s shares by generating buying interest, then sell their holdings after the price rises, leaving other investors exposed when the stock falls.

After making profits from two stocks under the guidance of the self-styled experts, the couple were told to prepare as much money as possible for a stock with “high potential” that “did not come by often”.

“They would say, if you put in one million, you’d get back three million within a month, and if we didn’t, they’d put their heads on a chopping board,” Aaron said.

He took a bank loan to buy S$650,000 (US$512,000) worth of shares in CMBC Capital – a financial services firm listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange – and noticed that its price started to decline soon after. The experts’ WhatsApp accounts also disappeared.

Aaron was left scrambling to repay the bank loan after losing more than S$500,000. “I still have employees to pay and a family to feed,” he said. “We are left trying to pick up the pieces because no one is here to help us recover our losses.”

Hong Kong stocks ‘ideal’

Singaporeans have been falling victim to pump-and-dump scams for years, as a scam scourge plagues the city state. Analysts say that fraudsters would typically operate with stocks listed on foreign exchanges to increase their chances of success.

Trading on recognised foreign exchanges allows victims to independently identify the existence of the company, which could create a strong sense of perceived legitimacy and increased confidence, said Whistine Chai, founder and principal psychologist at behavioural risk intelligence firm ForenSights.

“They may not realise that the person promoting the stock may have a vested interest in generating buying interest and driving up its price for their own benefit,” she said.

Hong Kong-listed stocks were a natural target for scammers preying on Singaporeans due to several factors such as cultural and time zone similarity between both cities, said Gloria Yu, an assistant professor of finance at the Singapore Management University.

The Hong Kong stock exchange, as in many markets, hosts stocks with low free float and active retail participation, features scammers can exploit to discuss coordinated buying, she added. Victims are also drawn in by low-cost online trading platforms such as Moomoo and Tiger Brokers in Singapore, which make buying foreign stock easier.

“The ideal asset is one the victim knows just well enough to feel comfortable with but not well enough to verify,” Yu said. “For Singapore, Hong Kong stocks sit precisely at that point.”

In August 2021, the Singapore Police Force warned the public of a resurgence in pump-and-dump scams. Four months later, it conducted a joint investigation with the Hong Kong police into a syndicate suspected of operating such scams using shares listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Nine people in Hong Kong and one in Singapore were arrested, and assets totalling over HK$70 million (US$9 million) were frozen.

Hong Kong police said it did not maintain figures for losses incurred in cross-border pump-and-dump scams. This Week in Asia has asked the Singapore police for comment.

Sounding the alarm

After realising he had fallen prey to a scam, Aaron filed a police report, and contacted CMBC Capital and Moomoo – which he used to buy the shares – in a last-ditch attempt to recover his money.

Singapore police told This Week in Asia the report had been lodged and they were looking into the matter. Legal provisions in Singapore allow certain securities offences to be pursued even when part of the conduct occurs overseas or involves stocks listed on an international market.

CMBC Capital announced on Tuesday that it had received reports from individuals alleging its name might have been used in investment scams. The suspicious activities had been conducted without its knowledge, consent or authorisation, it said. It also said it had not independently concluded that its shares were manipulated, and had reported the suspected activities to Hong Kong authorities.

Aaron, who said he had yet to hear from Moomoo and CMBC Capital, said he felt he had little recourse. This Week in Asia has contacted CMBC Capital and Moomoo for comment.

As scam operations become increasingly sophisticated with technological advancements, victims are often left to bear losses when the scammers are not arrested, according to analysts, who urge collective measures across all parties involved.

“Our whole mental model of what a scam looks like needs to be changed,” Chai said. “We often associate scams with unauthorised transfers and fake websites and accounts, but increasingly, scammers can exploit real institutions and legitimate infrastructure.”

Individuals should verify the investment and the person recommending it separately, while platforms could implement measures such as warnings that remind investors to do so before completing the trade, she said.

Yu said that brokerage platforms had the “clearest edge” in stopping ongoing scams, as they could spot abnormal trading in real-time and act directly.

“The caveat is incentives,” she said, noting that brokers may hesitate to implement aggressive anti-scam measures as false alarms could frustrate customers and push them towards competing platforms.

But as scams involve multiple parties – victims, brokerage platforms, social media and messaging platforms, listed companies and authorities, Yu urged coordinated effort. “The failure is in the ecosystem, not in any one node.”

*Name has been changed to protect the interviewee’s identity

item.title: [SCMP] Philippine Roblox ban call sparks wider debate over children’s online safety
item.description:
Roblox has become a flashpoint in Southeast Asia’s debate over child safety online, as officials scrutinise whether young users are being exposed to harmful subcultures on the gaming platform. But analysts warn that it might just be a convenient scapegoat for wider failures in how children are protected online and offline.

Most recently, Roblox has been linked to the August 18 school shooting in the southern Philippine city of Zamboanga, where a Grade 9 student brought two firearms to a private school, live-streamed the attack and killed one schoolmate before taking his own life.

Authorities were quick to identify the cause.
item.content:encoded:
Roblox has become a flashpoint in Southeast Asia’s debate over child safety online, as officials scrutinise whether young users are being exposed to harmful subcultures on the gaming platform. But analysts warn that it might just be a convenient scapegoat for wider failures in how children are protected online and offline.

Most recently, Roblox has been linked to the August 18 school shooting in the southern Philippine city of Zamboanga, where a Grade 9 student brought two firearms to a private school, live-streamed the attack and killed one schoolmate before taking his own life.

Authorities were quick to identify the cause.

The suspect was a “Roblox fanatic”, Zamboanga Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso said.

Characterising the attack as a “case of desensitisation to violence” linked to the games children play online, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla called for a total Roblox ban on August 20.

Remulla had said a day earlier that authorities had a “great degree of confidence” that Roblox had influenced the shooter’s actions, even as they had yet to conduct a forensic examination of his devices. “Roblox in itself is not a dangerous game. It is the chat group … that is where the coaxing happens, where the radicalisation takes place.”

Roblox, which reported 123 million average daily active users globally in the second quarter of this year, is not a single game but an online platform built around user-created virtual worlds, play and chat – features that safety advocates say can make it easier for children to encounter strangers or be drawn into harmful communities.

Online games have been scrutinised as a potential pathway for radicalisation since a Tacloban school shooting that killed three students in June. One of the suspects was found to have been an avid GoreBox player – prompting the cybercrime unit to block access to the violent game while investigators assessed its role in the attack.

Roblox blocks

On Thursday, Philippine officials met Roblox executives in Singapore to discuss measures to protect Filipino children from online harm.

After the meeting, Department of Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda said Roblox had agreed to strengthen child-safety protections for users in the Philippines – including age verification, parental controls, faster removal of harmful content and closer cooperation with law enforcement.

Roblox has said it has “advanced safeguards and robust safety policies” to protect users, such as filters to block the sharing of personal information, age checks before users can access chat, AI detection systems, safety teams, reporting tools and cooperation with law enforcement. This Week in Asia has contacted Roblox for comment.

The platform has also been tied to concerns over grooming and exploitation. On June 30, the National Bureau of Investigation arrested a 19-year-old man in Pampanga province for allegedly persuading minors to engage in sexual activity and send sexually exploitative images in exchange for Robux, Roblox’s digital currency.

Concerns over Roblox-linked content have also surfaced in Singapore. In May, authorities detained a 14-year-old boy who they said had been preparing to carry out a mass-casualty stabbing attack at his secondary school after becoming self-radicalised online.

Singapore’s Internal Security Department said the boy, then aged 12, had encountered first-person shooter games on Roblox that recreated real-life school shootings, including the 1999 Columbine attack, before moving on to more violent content elsewhere online.

In Indonesia, Roblox has said it will introduce additional content and communications controls for players under 16, after the country moved to restrict children’s access to high-risk digital platforms in March.

Australia’s eSafety Commissioner on August 20 secured a court-enforceable undertaking requiring Roblox to strengthen protections against child grooming, sexual exploitation and abuse after the regulator said testing showed adults could still contact children despite earlier safety measures.

Ban or better safeguards?

Experts warn that bans risk pushing these dangers into less visible areas, leaving deep-seated safety failures unaddressed.

Ysrael Diloy, a child protection and online safety specialist with the non-profit Stairway Foundation, said authorities should distinguish between saying a platform carries risks and saying it caused a violent incident.

“If a child involved in a serious incident was using Roblox, then that online activity should absolutely be looked at,” Diloy said. “Investigators should find out what the child was doing there, who the child was talking to, and whether there was any harmful influence. But the conclusion should come from evidence.”

He warned against starting with the name of a platform and trying to make everything fit around it, but added that platforms attracting millions of children “should also accept that they have a very high responsibility to make those spaces safer”.

While the concern around Roblox is valid, not every new platform is a threat, according to Munira Mustaffa, executive director of Chasseur Group and a senior fellow of Verve Research.

“We risk repeating the same mistake we did with TikTok back in the early 2020s,” she said. “It’s the same conversation all over again. Tomorrow will be a new platform but the same debate. It will never end unless we understand what exactly is the problem and what we are countering.”

Paco Pangalangan, a fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Carr-Ryan Centre for Human Rights, said bans should not be the default response.

“If our concern is adult strangers contacting younger users on Roblox, a ban doesn’t make those users disappear. It only pushes them into less visible and less regulated spaces,” he said.

“If governments want platforms to be accountable for what happens on them, they need enforceable design obligations that reduce harmful behaviour and keep platforms inside the reach of regulators and parents.”

One safeguard that is often cited is age verification, but that has its own risks too.

“Sometimes [platforms will] ask you to upload like a government ID or things like that,” said Carl Javier, executive director of ethics organisation Data and AI Ethics PH. “That’s a new privacy layer that needs to be protected by the company that you’re uploading it to.”

He also cautioned against the one-size-fits-all approach, saying extremist behaviour and sexual exploitation were distinct kinds of harm, with different types of perpetrators and victims. “The tools we have are trying to address both. But they’re such different ways of attacking.”

Platform accountability should be specific, evidence-based and proportionate, Diloy said.

“Roblox should be held responsible for risks that happen on Roblox. Telegram should be held responsible for risks that happen on Telegram,” he said. “But none of these platforms should become an easy explanation that stops us from looking at everything else happening in a child’s life.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hormuz deal presses pause on Iran conflict, but fears of ‘forever war’ remain
item.description:
A diplomatic push by Oman, Pakistan and Qatar is widely expected to yield another pause in the Iran conflict, but there remains little prospect of a stop to what analysts fear has already become a “forever war”.

On Monday, Iran and Oman agreed in principle to a temporary maritime route for ships travelling through the Strait of Hormuz. This could lead to the easing of the tit-for-tat blockades imposed by Iran and the US if President Donald Trump’s administration accepts it.

Regional mediators frame it as part of a “phased” process of confidence-building measures envisioned under the Islamabad Declaration, signed by both sides in June.
item.content:encoded:
A diplomatic push by Oman, Pakistan and Qatar is widely expected to yield another pause in the Iran conflict, but there remains little prospect of a stop to what analysts fear has already become a “forever war”.

On Monday, Iran and Oman agreed in principle to a temporary maritime route for ships travelling through the Strait of Hormuz. This could lead to the easing of the tit-for-tat blockades imposed by Iran and the US if President Donald Trump’s administration accepts it.

Regional mediators frame it as part of a “phased” process of confidence-building measures envisioned under the Islamabad Declaration, signed by both sides in June.

Analysts, however, are sceptical about the chances of a breakthrough, saying the mediation efforts are primarily aimed at preventing a feared region-wide escalation.

“The current trajectory signals an interregnum, but the likelihood of further escalation still looms large,” What Is Iran? author Arshin Adib-Moghaddam said.

Both sides currently wanted to prevent “yet another military escalation”, said the co-director of the Centre for Iranian Studies at SOAS University of London. “The only variable that can’t be logically and rationally predicted is Donald Trump’s ability to stay consistent, as he has been incredibly unstable and irrational as a president.”

With the pivotal midterm elections on November 3 approaching, the Republican president’s administration switched the focus of the war from military action to imposing secondary sanctions against Iran’s trading partners on Monday – just hours after the Iran-Oman deal was announced.

“After President Trump and the overwhelming might of the US military dismantled Iran’s military capabilities and crippled its nuclear programme, America is entering the endgame with the single greatest financial offensive ever mounted against an adversary,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said, describing the measures as the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran.

Trump, meanwhile, claimed that the US Navy had successfully demined navigation channels in the Hormuz strait. “There is a Zero Tolerance policy on mine placement in full force and effect,” he posted on his Truth Social platform on Monday.

This contrasted with the agreement between Tehran and Muscat to “implement a joint project to clear the strait of mines”.

Ebb and flow

Having already endured sanctions since 2018 and the destruction of much of its industrial base during the first phase of US-Israel attacks in April, Tehran has stuck to its guns.

“Our principle is understanding and resolving issues through interaction and negotiation, but at the same time, we will stand firm against economic pressures, as we have done so far and will continue to do,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Wednesday, according to state media.

Concurrently, the Revolutionary Guards asserted that Hormuz was under its control, with vessels attempting to exit via a US-organised route hugging Oman’s coast continuing to come under Iranian fire. “If America does not accept our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened under any circumstances,” the Guards said.

Rhetoric notwithstanding, it appeared from the comments by Trump and Bessent that the US “is pivoting away from threats of renewed military action to a new phase of economic pressure”, said Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, Middle East fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy.

This corresponds with the overall ebb and flow of the conflict, now at its six-month point, according to Guy Burton, author of China and Middle East Conflicts.

“We have seen a recurring pattern of military confrontation followed by periods of deliberation, dialogue and diplomatic outreach,” the Brussels-based academic said, calling it a “forever war” in which military action and diplomacy occur simultaneously.

Instead of a resolution, a pause “may simply represent another period in which both sides reassess their positions before the next round of confrontation”, he said.

Regional mediation efforts continued on Thursday with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani – who is also the emirate’s foreign minister – visiting Tehran to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

This engagement with the pro-negotiation faction of the Islamic Republic, led by parliamentary speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, was preceded on Monday by negotiations between Pakistan’s influential Chief of Defence Forces Asim Munir and Mohsin Razaee, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council – the leader of Tehran’s hardliners, who are opposed to talks with the US.

Eye to midterms

The US is not the only one with an agenda heading into the midterms.

The Iranian leadership had “every interest in seeing the Republican Party defeated”, said political scientist Ali Alfoneh, author of Political Succession in the Islamic Republic of Iran. So it would use its remaining resources to stay afloat until November 3 – and preferably until the new Congress convenes in January.

By then, Tehran “hopes” that a Republican defeat, a disputed election result, and Trump’s possible refusal to accept that result could push the US into political chaos or even a constitutional crisis – “providing Iran with a much-needed reprieve”, said Alfoneh, a senior resident scholar at the Washington-based Arab Gulf States Institute.

Iran “has an incentive” to keep regional tensions – and consequently oil prices – high before the midterms, thereby contributing to a Republican loss, he said.

Burton, who has taught international relations at universities in Iraq, the United Arab Emirates and the West Bank, agreed that Iran “appears increasingly interested not simply in surviving the conflict but in imposing political costs on Trump”.

If Tehran can give Trump “a sufficiently visible ‘bloody nose’”, it may calculate that this will damage his political standing and potentially the Republican brand ahead of the midterms.

This suggests there may be “little incentive for Trump to make a major strategic concession” like conceding control of Hormuz under the Iran-Oman framework before the elections. US economic pressure and military action were “likely to coexist for some time”, Burton added.

Washington was effectively “putting multiple instruments on the table in the hope that one of them will eventually create a viable diplomatic off-ramp”, Burton said. The danger was that, without a clear political settlement, this would produce an intermittent conflict and economic confrontation that “is not quite a conventional war, but not peace either”.

Periodic flare ups could become “a new status quo”, Ulrichsen said, because each party to the conflict “appears to think it has the upper hand and can outlast the other”.

Under such circumstances, Alfoneh said regional mediators now confronted “an unenviable set of possibilities”: pushing to implement the Islamabad Declaration, “becoming targets themselves” – or “facing both outcomes simultaneously”.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Filipino migrants are rethinking their futures in Japan
item.description:
When Japan’s embassy in the Philippines extended applications for healthcare jobs on April 15, the pitch was straightforward: 50 positions for nurses and 300 for care workers in Japan, a three- to four-year placement, free Japanese-language lessons in both countries and a daily allowance during training.

On social media, the post’s attractive terms drew widespread interest from Filipinos – a reminder that Japan is still urgently recruiting foreign labour even as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s administration, amid growing political pressure over foreign residents, moves to make it harder for migrants to settle long-term.

The need is especially acute in care work: Japan will require about 2.72 million care workers by financial year 2040, roughly 570,000 more than in 2022, according to Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare estimates, while one think tank projection has warned the country could be nearly 1 million foreign workers short by then if current inflows continue.
item.content:encoded:
When Japan’s embassy in the Philippines extended applications for healthcare jobs on April 15, the pitch was straightforward: 50 positions for nurses and 300 for care workers in Japan, a three- to four-year placement, free Japanese-language lessons in both countries and a daily allowance during training.

On social media, the post’s attractive terms drew widespread interest from Filipinos – a reminder that Japan is still urgently recruiting foreign labour even as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s administration, amid growing political pressure over foreign residents, moves to make it harder for migrants to settle long-term.

The need is especially acute in care work: Japan will require about 2.72 million care workers by financial year 2040, roughly 570,000 more than in 2022, according to Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare estimates, while one think tank projection has warned the country could be nearly 1 million foreign workers short by then if current inflows continue.

For the Filipino care workers, nurses and other professionals who came to Japan seeking greener pastures, the contradiction has become personal: the country needs them, but high living costs, a weak yen and uncertainty over immigration rules make it harder to imagine staying long-term.

Job Galutan Andawey, a licensed nurse from the Philippines working as a carer in Kanagawa prefecture, is in his sixth year in Japan after arriving through the Japan-Philippines Economic Partnership Agreement, a treaty that includes career placement and language training programmes for nurses and care workers.

“I chose Japan because I was influenced by Japanese culture. I dreamed of working here in Japan since I was little,” Andawey told This Week in Asia.

But as time runs out on his work visa, the Filipino nurse is having second thoughts.

“The cost of living is getting expensive while the salary is stagnant. And with the increase in visa fees and not much aid coming from the company, it is hard to save up,” Andawey said, adding that he was considering moving to Europe or the Middle East if he could not remain in Japan.

Merrychris Urcales, a carer in Kagawa prefecture who came to Japan on a special skilled worker visa in 2024, said finding a job had been “relatively easier compared with other types of work because there is a high demand for carers in Japan”.

But the weak yen and rising costs made saving difficult, and Urcales said she would need to consider other countries that might offer “better opportunities and a higher income”.

For some workers, concerns over the yen’s declining value outweigh anxiety over immigration policy changes and reports of anti-foreigner sentiment, according to Alyssa Manalo, a PhD student at Hiroshima University who researches Filipino migration.

“These changes do not seem to be as significant” for carers, assistant language teachers and those on special skilled worker visas, Manalo said.

“For newer migrants who have their families in the Philippines, they generally just want to finish their contracts, save money, and return to the Philippines … they were more concerned about the declining yen than about changes in immigration policies or anti-foreigner sentiment.”

The low exchange rate made it harder for migrant workers to send the same amount of money home, Manalo said.

For those who have already spent years adapting to the country, however, Japan’s tighter immigration policies have increased the sense that long-term settlement is becoming harder.

“They made it easier to come here, but made staying more difficult,” Kevin*, an engineer from the Philippines who has lived in Tokyo for 10 years, told This Week in Asia.

The challenges are not lost on Catherine Ogalesco, a licensed care worker who first came to Japan nearly nine years ago to work in a factory.

Ogalesco said she saw no problem with tougher language requirements, as she believed preparing for life in Japan required fluency.

But she took issue with the proposed increase in the income threshold for permanent residency applications from 3 million yen (US$18,830) annually to 5.75 million yen, or 479,000 yen in monthly household income.

“I think it is unfair especially for single households like myself, and for foreign workers in Japan in fields such as nursing care, factories, hotels and agriculture, where workers are sorely needed … how many foreign workers earn that much? Probably less than 20 per cent,” Ogalesco said.

“With those rules, they are already excluding us from the possibility of applying for permanent residency.”

The policy changes have also unsettled students and white-collar workers.

Manalo said she had hoped to remain in Japan to pursue an academic career researching Filipino migrants, but was now re-evaluating her options.

“Part of the proposed law would require foreign nationals to have Japanese proficiency, and I’m not that good at speaking Japanese,” said Manalo, who is on a scholarship programme.

She said her last visa extension cost 6,000 yen, but the proposed guidelines would mean she might have to pay up to 50,000 yen depending on the length of the extension.

Language requirements are also a source of anxiety for Amanda*, a software programmer who moved to Japan in 2022.

Her company sponsored her language training until she passed level 3 of the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, a condition for full-time employment, but has since asked her to continue studying towards the advanced-intermediate level 2.

“Even at level 3, I still don’t feel confident in my language skills … I’m getting anxious at the possibility of being asked for a level 2 certification just so I can keep my job,” Amanda told This Week in Asia.

She considered moving to a larger company for better prospects but said the shifting climate made her more cautious.

“I’m afraid of applying for other job positions as it might put my visa renewal at risk next year,” she said.
