Despite the policy changes, foreign residents described reports of rising anti-immigrant sentiment as the views of a minority amplified by the political climate, rather than a universal experience.

“I live in a rural area of Japan, and I have not experienced any forms of racism or discrimination. As long as you follow Japanese etiquette and rules, I personally don’t think Japanese people will say anything bad to you,” Manalo said.

Ogalesco remains undeterred by the changing rules. “Even with the changes, I would still choose to stay and work here in Japan. Here, I feel safe and financially comfortable.”

Manalo is hopeful that Japan’s growing reliance on foreign workers will push the government to reconsider its approach as the country continues to grapple with labour shortages and an ageing population.

“Japan is already becoming more dependent on foreign workers, particularly in sectors such as caregiving, construction and agriculture,” she said.

“At some point, Japan needs to be more open to migrants, especially in care-related work where the demand for workers will continue to grow.”

*Names changed to protect interviewees’ identities

item.title: [SCMP] US base dispute hangs over Japan’s Okinawa governor election
item.description:
Okinawa’s governor election next month is set to be a major test of whether Japan’s ruling party can win over voters from a prefecture that has long opposed its security agenda and the heavy US military presence on its islands.

A victory by Genta Koja, the Liberal Democratic Party-backed candidate, would likely help smooth ties between Okinawa and Tokyo and weaken resistance against the planned relocation of the US Marine Corps’ Futenma base within the prefecture, according to analysts.

Such an outcome would boost efforts by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s LDP to convince Okinawans that closer cooperation with Tokyo can deliver stronger economic support.
item.content:encoded:
Okinawa’s governor election next month is set to be a major test of whether Japan’s ruling party can win over voters from a prefecture that has long opposed its security agenda and the heavy US military presence on its islands.

A victory by Genta Koja, the Liberal Democratic Party-backed candidate, would likely help smooth ties between Okinawa and Tokyo and weaken resistance against the planned relocation of the US Marine Corps’ Futenma base within the prefecture, according to analysts.

Such an outcome would boost efforts by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s LDP to convince Okinawans that closer cooperation with Tokyo can deliver stronger economic support.

The LDP is preparing to go all out to support Koja in the election scheduled on September 13, according to Japanese media reports.

The ruling party hopes the 42-year-old will replace incumbent governor Denny Tamaki, an independent politician backed by the All Okinawa coalition, which includes the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan and the Social Democratic Party.

Koja, a former vice-mayor of Naha, the capital of Okinawa, is also backed by other parties including Komeito and the Democratic Party for the People.

“We’ll help Koja realise his election pledges with all our strength,” said Yasutoshi Nishimura, chairman of the LDP’s election strategy committee, at a rally for Koja’s candidacy in Urasoe, a city in Okinawa, on August 20.

Announcing his policy agenda on August 14 in Naha, Koja pledged to double prefectural income and achieve an average economic growth rate of 7 to 8 per cent over his four-year term.

However, he did not mention the controversial project to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma base to the Henoko district in Nago city.

The relocation has dragged on for years due to fierce opposition from residents, who demand that the base leave Okinawa rather than move to another part of the prefecture. They say that Okinawa bears an unfair burden of hosting the most American military facilities in Japan.

Japan is seeking the relocation to reduce safety and noise hazards in a densely populated urban area, while keeping the US military presence in Okinawa.

Raymond Yamamoto, an associate professor at Aarhus University, said the election centred around Okinawa’s relationship with the central government.

Tamaki represents the continuation of the All Okinawa coalition, which has resisted the relocation and challenged Tokyo’s security agenda.

“Koja, by contrast, is backed by the LDP and seeks to restore a more cooperative relationship with the central government,” Yamamoto said.

“His candidacy can be seen as an alternative to Tamaki’s confrontational approach towards Tokyo.”

Yamamoto noted that the LDP had struggled to win the Okinawan governorship for over a decade. The last time a candidate backed by the LDP won an election in the prefecture was in 2010, when Hirokazu Nakaima, a businessman and former public servant, won re-election.

The US military presence in Okinawa has become increasingly important for Japan as it seeks to boost its defence of its southwestern islands amid rising regional tensions, according to Yamamoto.

“A victory would send a strong national signal that the LDP has returned to political dominance under Takaichi’s leadership,” Yamamoto said.

Ra Mason, an associate professor of international relations and Japanese foreign policy at the University of East Anglia, said given the LDP’s tactics to “win at all costs” in local elections, Koja could potentially unseat Tamaki.

With half of the facility in Henoko having been built, the “damage” was already done, said Mason, author of Okinawa: Great Power Competition and the Keystone of the Pacific, with the issue having been “relegated to a symbolic struggle”.

“An LDP-affiliated prefectural governor will likely serve to enable further fortification and militarisation of the Okinawan islands and the Ryukyu Island chain,” Mason said.

Okinawa is the largest island of the Ryukyu Islands, a chain stretching southwest from Kyushu to Taiwan.

One of the biggest challenges Koja faces is whether he can persuade Okinawans that his links to the LDP will lead to higher investment in the prefecture that benefits ordinary citizens living there, instead of just large companies, according to Mason.

“[These entities] have historically sucked profits back to stakeholders on the Japanese mainland.”

Consistently ranking last among Japan’s 47 prefectures for annual average income, Okinawa has almost double the mainland’s unemployment rate and the highest rate of non-regular employment.

Benjamin Ascione, a lecturer at Waseda University’s Graduate School of Asia-Pacific Studies, said these indicators would favour Koja, who had argued that closer cooperation with Tokyo could deliver greater economic benefits.

Ascione said the LDP was in a strong position in the election as it had devoted significant time and resources to win over voters, adding that Koja had a good chance of winning given that legal opposition to the Henoko relocation plan appeared to have run its course, with Okinawa losing almost all its lawsuits against Tokyo over the move.

“This significantly alters the significance of a vote for Tamaki as he no longer has an effective legal mechanism to prevent the central government from proceeding with the Henoko plan,” he said.

The fragmentation of the All Okinawa coalition opposing the relocation and the shift in attention towards cost-of-living issues would also put Koja in good stead, Ascione said.

“Even if Tamaki wins, he would have a visibly weaker and more divided coalition,” he added.

Calling it premature to call Koja the clear favourite, Ascione said: “The race remains competitive, with neither candidate having established a decisive lead.”

Okinawa hosts about 25,000 American service members across 31 US military facilities, making it a key hub for Washington’s power projection in the Pacific. Japan and the US have been holding talks on cost-sharing to maintain the American military presence in the country.

Having Okinawans on board over the US military issue would help soothe tensions between the prefecture and Tokyo, according to Ascione.

“However, from an alliance-management perspective, the effect would be primarily symbolic as it would not fundamentally alter Washington’s broader demands on Japanese defence spending and burden-sharing,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] How typhoons and extreme weather could undermine Taiwan Strait combat readiness
item.description:
The record heat and extreme weather seen across East Asia this summer have prompted warnings that climate change will be an increasing challenge for military planners focused on potential flashpoints such as the Taiwan Strait.

Besides the risks to both troops and equipment, typhoons and other storms could also damage critical infrastructure and disrupt training, as well as divert personnel and resources towards emergency relief.

Although militaries may be able to adapt in peacetime, they may have less flexibility in times of war, where extreme weather could have a direct impact on combat operations.
item.content:encoded:
The record heat and extreme weather seen across East Asia this summer have prompted warnings that climate change will be an increasing challenge for military planners focused on potential flashpoints such as the Taiwan Strait.

Besides the risks to both troops and equipment, typhoons and other storms could also damage critical infrastructure and disrupt training, as well as divert personnel and resources towards emergency relief.

Although militaries may be able to adapt in peacetime, they may have less flexibility in times of war, where extreme weather could have a direct impact on combat operations.

Armed forces are adapting to the challenge in different ways.

For example, Japan and the United States have formally incorporated climate risk into their assessments of force readiness, bases, equipment and supply chains, while Taiwan has folded climate-related disasters into its mobilisation and resilience planning.

The Philippines is expanding facilities under its defence cooperation agreement with the US, some of which are specifically designed to strengthen its disaster response and ability to carry out humanitarian relief operations.

Meanwhile, mainland China’s public response has focused heavily on tactical adaptation.

This summer, mainland Chinese forces continued testing how extreme heat affected their operations.

For example, in the southern region of Guangxi, a People’s Armed Police unit pushed drones to their limits in high temperatures, according to China Military Online.

Meanwhile, a People’s Liberation Army Air Force unit analysed how personnel and equipment performed in high temperatures and explored specialised maintenance procedures for extreme conditions.

Environmental factors are already imposing real-world trade-offs.

Earlier this month, Typhoon Dolphin hit Okinawa at a time when US forces at Kadena Air Base were carrying out a readiness exercise.

The approaching typhoon, which prompted the evacuation of more than a million people in eastern China, meant personnel had to prepare helicopters and tankers for the storm while simultaneously supporting the readiness exercise.

The previous month, a series of typhoons struck mainland China, causing widespread flooding across vast swathes of the country that prompted the PLA to send personnel, vehicles and other equipment to help with relief efforts.

Typhoons have also repeatedly disrupted Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang exercises. They forced parts of the 2023 and 2024 drill to be cancelled or halted prematurely, while Typhoon Danas diverted some forces towards disaster recovery at the start of the 2025 edition.

Extreme conditions also have a direct impact on both servicemen and women and the uncrewed systems that play an increasingly important role in modern warfare.

The US Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine has found that as well as having a physical impact, heat stress can also impair cognitive functions such as attention and memory.

Meanwhile, Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said planners would have to account for different conditions when deciding what equipment to use.

“For example, the cheap componentry and light weight of many smaller variants of unmanned systems make them susceptible to extreme temperatures and high winds,” Bosack said.

Storms can also sharply curtail military activity. When Typhoon Gaemi struck Taiwan in July 2024, the PLA aerial activity around the island fell from 22 aircraft in the July 2023-24 period to zero for three consecutive 24-hour periods, before flights resumed.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland.

Most countries, including the US, Philippines and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but many are opposed to any attempt to take it by force.

The impact of extreme weather on military operations would be amplified in wartime, when commanders may not be able to wait for conditions to improve.

Several analysts highlighted the ways in which it could affect any large-scale assault on Taiwan, where tensions with the mainland have been steadily rising.

In 2020, a peer-reviewed Chinese study found statistically significant long-term increases in wind speeds and significant wave heights in the Taiwan Strait, based on simulations covering 1988 to 2017.

“While improvements in PLA capabilities may have reduced some of these seasonal constraints, they have not eliminated the underlying physical challenges,” said Christopher Sharman, director of the China Maritime Studies Institute at the US Naval War College, speaking in a personal capacity.

PLA amphibious forces, he added, were working to improve their ability to operate in poor weather, at night and under other degraded conditions.

Sherri Goodman, secretary general of the International Military Council on Climate and Security, pointed to modernised amphibious brigades, larger amphibious ships, civilian vessels and improvements in transport and logistics as examples of how Chinese capabilities had evolved.

But Goodman, a former US deputy undersecretary of defence for environmental security, also warned that while better capability could widen a weather window, “it does not eliminate the window”.

K. Tristan Tang, a non-resident fellow at the National Bureau of Asian Research, said extreme weather would affect forces on both sides but the impact would probably be greater on the PLA because it would have to project and sustain forces across the strait.

“Severe weather would not necessarily make those operations impossible, but it could reduce their effectiveness and make coordination considerably more difficult,” Tang said.

For Goodman, the scale of the operation presents a further problem. Moving a large force would require not only troops and vehicles but also a continuing flow of fuel, ammunition and other supplies across contested waters and onto beaches or through ports.

“An invasion is not won by getting the first troops ashore. It is won by sustaining them,” she said.

James Holmes, a professor at the US Naval War College, argued that harsher conditions could favour Taiwan as the tactical defender, provided its own military remained operational.

“Anything that afflicts the aggressor only enhances that advantage,” he said.

Taiwan would face vulnerabilities of its own. Tang said that damage to the island’s ports or airfields could seriously hamper its operations, although it could also deny the PLA infrastructure it might hope to use after securing a foothold.

Goodman offered a broader qualification, arguing that the effects would depend on where vulnerabilities emerged across the different forces involved and their ability to recover.

“Climate change does not automatically favour one side. It imposes costs and creates vulnerabilities across the battlespace,” she said.

“The important question is where those vulnerabilities occur, how concentrated they are and how quickly each side can recover from them.”

That shifts the question from exposure alone to how well militaries can absorb disruption. Measures such as redundancy, dispersal, hardened infrastructure, rapid repair and alternative logistics routes could help forces continue operating when parts of their networks are damaged.

“Resilience is not simply disaster preparedness. It is warfighting capacity,” Goodman said.

“The military that can fight through disruption – and recover fastest from it – will have an advantage.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why Chinese media says US historians are giving ‘ammunition’ to separatists
item.description:
China has stepped up its offensive against a US-born school of thought on China’s last imperial dynasty, accusing it of providing “theoretical ammunition” for attempts to divide the country.

The denunciation comes as online debates over the Qing dynasty (1644-1911) continue to give rise to inflammatory rhetoric, and as Beijing’s ethnic policies and historical narratives are increasingly becoming an arena for international political competition.

An article published by the state-run China Ethnic News last Monday warned that New Qing History was “seriously eroding the historical foundations of the community for the Chinese nation in the real world” and should be “forcefully refuted”.
item.content:encoded:
China has stepped up its offensive against a US-born school of thought on China’s last imperial dynasty, accusing it of providing “theoretical ammunition” for attempts to divide the country.

The denunciation comes as online debates over the Qing dynasty (1644-1911) continue to give rise to inflammatory rhetoric, and as Beijing’s ethnic policies and historical narratives are increasingly becoming an arena for international political competition.

An article published by the state-run China Ethnic News last Monday warned that New Qing History was “seriously eroding the historical foundations of the community for the Chinese nation in the real world” and should be “forcefully refuted”.

That marked the latest broadside in a two-year campaign by the outlet to attack the loosely defined scholarly movement, which began to take shape in the late 1980s.

Rather than being an organised movement with a unified doctrine, New Qing History refers to a broad revisionist approach to understanding how the Manchu-led Qing managed both China’s Han majority and the many other ethnic groups under their rule.

Scholars taking this approach have drawn on Manchu-language sources to question the long-held assumption that “Sinicisation” – the idea that conquerors of China and even neighbouring peoples were transformed by Chinese culture, often portrayed as a spontaneous and largely one-way process – was the only explanation.

They also draw on anthropological and sociological perspectives to explain the Manchu rulers’ relations with Tibetan religious leaders, Mongolian chieftains and Turkic elites in Xinjiang.

The China Ethnic News article reiterated several criticisms that Chinese historians have long levelled at New Qing History, including accusations that the approach undermined the Qing’s historical status as a truly Chinese dynasty.

It said historians were “fracturing the integrity of the Chinese nation” by treating frontier regions under Qing rule such as Mongolia and Xinjiang as separate units from China’s interior.

The piece argued that this “erroneous view of history” could lead to “multiple real-world harms” amid the complex international political environment.

“By deconstructing the Qing’s territory into ‘pluralistic modules’ and denying the historical affiliation of frontier regions and China, New Qing History is effectively providing ‘theoretical ammunition’ for various separatist forces,” warned the authors Li Defeng and Zhang Yide from Inner Mongolia University.

For at least a decade, Chinese scholars have explicitly or implicitly accused New Qing History of being part of an “academic intrigue” aimed at dividing China.

In the article, Li and Zhang said that New Qing History could be traced back to theories advanced by scholars in imperial Japan who argued that Manchuria and Mongolia were not part of China.

In a since-deleted interview with Chinese digital outlet The Paper, Georgetown University professor James Millward argued that the allegations that New Qing History was part of an anti-China conspiracy were a “misunderstanding”.

He added that the movement’s purpose was to refine the scholarship of earlier historians – such as John K. Fairbank – on topics such as the tribute system, Sinicisation and the idea of China as the civilisational centre.

In a 2017 interview with The Paper, Ding Yizhuang, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), praised the school’s focus on Manchu-language sources and acknowledged its value in inspiring research in China.

“As for whether the ‘New Qing History’ has some political agenda or even a conspiracy behind it, I think we should first … at least understand what they are talking about before criticising it. Only then can such criticism be convincing,” she said.

However, at an academic symposium in 2019, Ding said that “New Qing History is an American thing, not our thing” and rejected any affiliation with the movement.

Liu Xiaomeng, another CASS scholar, wrote in a piece published in 2012 that New Qing History had helped to move research from an excessively Han-centric approach and set a higher bar for Chinese scholars working in the field.

However, Liu also warned that denying the Qing dynasty was part of Chinese history would inevitably push the school towards an extreme position.

Over the past few years, the debate has become more politically charged as Beijing has sought to reshape the relationship between ethnic minorities and the state – such as through the recently enacted Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which some observers have described as providing a statutory mandate for assimilation.

In an academic research guideline issued in 2024, the National Ethnic Affairs Commission – a central government agency overseen by the Communist Party’s United Front Work Department – called for resistance to a range of “erroneous historical views”, including New Qing History.

The criticism of New Qing History also comes as Beijing steps up efforts to build a “Chinese intellectual system in philosophy and social sciences” capable of explaining China’s practices to the outside world without what officials describe as the monopoly or distortion of Western concepts and narratives.

Monday’s article said New Qing History applied modern Western theories of the nation-state to China’s long-standing model of a “unity in diversity” Chinese nation, while using concepts such as “empire” and “colonialism” rooted in European historical experiences to describe centuries of two-way interaction among different regions of China.

The Chinese government began compiling an official history of the Qing in 2002, with the project originally expected to take little more than a decade. But it remains unfinished, a potential sign of the political sensitivity surrounding the period.

“New Qing History has produced a lot of books and many arguments. We need to catch up. A complete rebuttal cannot be built on just one or two articles,” read one comment below Monday’s article.

Rebuttals of New Qing History perspectives have not exclusively been aimed at foreign scholars – the movement has found support among some fringe Chinese nationalists.

Some influencers – often labelled “Han chauvinists” – have blamed China’s backwardness compared to Western powers and its descent into a “century of humiliation” in modern times on the Manchu rulers’ takeover of the Han-dominated Ming dynasty.

They portrayed the Manchus as foreign “barbarians” who colonised China and stalled its civilisation.

That echoes New Qing History’s approach of treating the Qing as more than simply another Chinese dynasty and comparing it with the Mughal and Ottoman empires.

The view reached a peak in popularity in the second half of last year before being rebuked by state media, but its supporters remain active online today.

item.title: [SCMP] More Hong Kong consumers allege coercive beauty sales in wake of Opatra crackdown
item.description:
More consumers in Hong Kong have come forward to allege aggressive sales tactics across the beauty sector, including credit card abuse, unwanted physical contact and pressure to buy costly products, on the back of a crackdown on the local operations of a UK-based brand.

Legal experts warned that such practices could breach the Trade Descriptions Ordinance, which prohibits harassment, coercion and misleading conduct used to pressure consumers into making purchases they otherwise would not have made.

Non-consensual physical contact could also trigger additional criminal liability, they added.
item.content:encoded:
More consumers in Hong Kong have come forward to allege aggressive sales tactics across the beauty sector, including credit card abuse, unwanted physical contact and pressure to buy costly products, on the back of a crackdown on the local operations of a UK-based brand.

Legal experts warned that such practices could breach the Trade Descriptions Ordinance, which prohibits harassment, coercion and misleading conduct used to pressure consumers into making purchases they otherwise would not have made.

Non-consensual physical contact could also trigger additional criminal liability, they added.

Following the arrest of two managers at the Hong Kong operator of UK-based beauty chain Opatra London over coercive sales practices, its company secretary resigned, while customs officers continue investigating six customer complaints involving disputed sums between HK$1,800 (US$230) and HK$100,000.

Customs said that the number of complaints had risen to 25 as of Thursday and an investigation was under way.

Opatra’s headquarters in the United Kingdom said on Friday that it and the Hong Kong distributor had agreed to suspend operations.

The brand’s four Hong Kong branches – two in Sha Tin, one in Yuen Long and one in Causeway Bay – have suspended operations since the controversy flared up about a week ago.

Now, more victims have detailed alleged aggressive sales tactics they have encountered while shopping for beauty products.

For 22-year-old university student John*, it took just a few seconds to be dragged into what he described as a “beauty trap” on the busy Hankow Road in Tsim Sha Tsui in May.

Outside a Lionesse shop, John said he was approached by a saleswoman who handed him a “free sample”.

He said the woman told him he had “dark eye circles” before applying an unidentified skincare product directly to his face. Concerned about a possible skin reaction and caught off guard by the ambush, John said he agreed to enter the shop.

Once he was seated, John said staff applied another liquid, claiming it was a HK$1,560 deep cleanser. They then showed him the “dirt” removed from his skin in a mirror in an attempt to persuade him to buy the product, he said.

John said he was then hurried into signing an electronic form, with the signature box enlarged to the point that he could not read the contract terms, including a “no refunds” clause.

Instead of handing over the product, the saleswoman then directed him to a free facial and bombarded him with questions about his age and employment status, along with two other staff members, John said.

Under pressure, he agreed to purchase a HK$30,000 annual facial package, but explicitly requested an instalment plan capped at HK$2,500 a month due to his credit card limit, he said.

John alleged that one of the salesmen took his card and made multiple attempts to process transactions exceeding HK$2,500.

Bank records showed five unsuccessful attempts, he said, for HK$30,000, HK$8,440, HK$5,000, HK$7,500 and, finally, HK$2,500. He said the bank immediately blocked the card because of the suspicious activity.

He said he ultimately paid HK$2,500 via PayMe to a merchant named “Vertex Innovations Limited” so he could leave the shop.

When he sought a refund through the Consumer Council, Lionesse’s management denied allegations of high-pressure sales practices, arguing that the open shop environment meant he could have “left immediately”, John said.

The company said the failed transaction records reflected standard authorisation procedures between the bank system and the merchant terminal and did not constitute improper sales practices. It declined to provide a refund, instead offering to exchange products of the same value.

In response to queries from the South China Morning Post, Apex Retail, which manages Lionesse in Hong Kong, declined to comment on individual allegations or circumstances that did not involve identifiable customer matters.

Recalling the experience, John said: “I’m just a student. The incident put immense psychological pressure on me and forced me to waste a lot of time organising bank records, payment details and relevant documents to file a complaint.”

He added: “I never intended to get involved in beauty services, but this experience made me realise how dark and manipulative beauty sales could be.”

He is now seeking a chargeback of HK$4,060 from the bank.

Company registration records show the directors of Apex are Ozel Barnos, Eli Vaknin, Sagi Vardi, Yogev Itzhak Vardi and Yinon Avraham Vardi.

The company website, which has become inaccessible, said it started as an Israeli family business and now had about a dozen shops in the city, under the brands of Earth, Napara, Privilege Boutique, Avinichi, Dualsonic and more.

Another firm to come under scrutiny was The Mineral Boutique, a brand under Beauty Express Group that has at least five branches in major shopping centres.

A 42-year-old clerk surnamed Wong alleged that similar tactics were used when a saleswoman applied a product directly onto her skin without permission at the Log-on shop in Festival Walk, Kowloon Tong, in June.

Wong said the saleswoman claimed the product could only be removed using a specialised device inside the counter area.

Once inside, Wong alleged, staff repeatedly grabbed her hand when she tried to pull away and cornered her while attempting to sell her high-value products, alongside a store manager.

Wong said that when she tried to leave, the saleswoman replied: “What is there left to think about? You’ve already seen the results.”

Wong said the remark prompted her to leave immediately and then file a formal complaint with City’super, the parent company of Log-on.

In a response to Wong, City’super said it had investigated the incident, reiterated that aggressive sales tactics were strictly prohibited and offered her a gift box.

City’super told the SCMP that it had received two customer “comments” about the counter’s services in the past year, as well as “a limited number of comments or complaints” over the past five years.

It said all cases had been investigated and handled through established procedures.

Asked whether such complaints influenced lease renewals, City’super declined to comment on specific contractual arrangements.

“We evaluate business relationships and commercial arrangements based on a range of factors including compliance with applicable laws and regulations, operational requirements, customer feedback and other relevant considerations,” it said.

Beauty Express Group declined to comment on the complaint, citing a lack of sufficient information to identify the customers involved.

It told the SCMP that it did not tolerate aggressive sales practices, non-consensual physical contact or any conduct that compromised a customer’s ability to make a free and informed purchasing decision.

The group’s directors include Aviad Ben Ezra and Baruch Szerer. Other brands under the group include Telosin, Premier by Dead Sea, Gratiae and more.

Lawyer Eric Chan Pak-ho said the tactics used on the student could constitute an offence under the Trade Descriptions Ordinance. However, the key question was whether sales staff had used “harassment, coercion or undue influence” to persuade John to agree to each purchase.

Chan added that concealing no-refund policies could increase the company’s legal liability.

Under the law, practices that significantly impair a consumer’s freedom of choice or conduct and cause them to make a purchase they would not otherwise have made are considered an offence.

Commercial lawyer Kenix Yuen Pui-kwan said that applying beauty products to a consumer’s skin might not, in itself, breach the ordinance.

“However, if that conduct forms part of a broader sales strategy involving harassment, coercion or undue influence, it may be relevant,” Yuen said.

Depending on the nature of the physical contact, other criminal issues could also arise, she cautioned.

Dr Amos Cheung, a clinical psychologist registered with the Hong Kong Psychological Society, said falling victim to high-pressure sales tactics did not mean a person lacked intelligence.

Such tactics were carefully engineered to exploit human vulnerability and bypass rational reasoning, he said.

Offering free samples could make shoppers feel indebted and reluctant to refuse invitations to enter a store, while applying products to someone’s face without consent could also help identify customers who were more susceptible to manipulation, he said.

Sales representatives could exaggerate imperfections in shoppers’ appearance in ways linked to their self-esteem and sense of self-worth, pushing them towards “emotional reasoning”, Cheung said.

“Such feelings of fear, anxiety and restlessness could impact your rational reasoning process and push you into a state of emotional reasoning,” he said.

He added that compliments could also lower customers’ guard by making sales staff seem friendly and trustworthy.

“If you are unsure about a store’s sales tactics, do not visit it alone,” he said.

“It’s important to be alert to words intended to trigger unnecessary anxiety, shame and panic, and prepare your response, such as ‘I never purchase out of impulse. I will think about it.’ Then, leave immediately.”

*Name changed at interviewee’s request

item.title: [SCMP] From Perth to pyramids: Hong Kong’s Graham Elsom on a lifetime of travel and adventure
item.description:
I WAS BORN in Perth, in Western Australia, in 1945. During the second world war, my father was with the military in an administrative position and left Australia in 1940 on the first troop-ship that departed. This was the Empress of Japan, a converted Canadian Pacific liner. I have one brother, Ross, who’s two years younger. We moved to Melbourne a few years later, and my mother and I flew down on one of the first commercial passenger flights. My brother and I went to Canterbury Primary School and later to Scotch College, which was a private Presbyterian boys’ school. There was a lot of demand for places there and my exam results had not been nearly good enough to get in, and I somehow realised my mother was disappointed. I’d got 37 per cent in one French exam, so I worked hard and later scored 87 per cent, which got me into the school. I joined in 1958 and left in 1962.

BY THE TIME I was 12, I had already developed a passionate desire to travel and knew I wanted to get into the travel business. I avidly collected and read travel brochures, and whenever I saw an ocean liner tied up at Station Pier, I was so envious. I wanted to go where those ships were going. In 1962, I got my first job, at Thomas Cook & Son on Collins Street, which was the ritzy street in Melbourne, commonly known as the “Paris end”. I was an assistant messenger and in charge of the brochure rack, which I found mesmerising with all those brochures and destinations, especially in those days.

MY FATHER HAD come out of the army and was working for Esso, the petroleum company, and his job moved to Sydney. So, I left Thomas Cook. In Sydney, I joined the Dutch shipping company Royal Interocean Lines. The company was headquartered in Hong Kong and had quite a substantial travel agency here. I was brought over to take over the travel branch in 1976, and I’ve been here ever since, so 50 years.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in Perth, in Western Australia, in 1945. During the second world war, my father was with the military in an administrative position and left Australia in 1940 on the first troop-ship that departed. This was the Empress of Japan, a converted Canadian Pacific liner. I have one brother, Ross, who’s two years younger. We moved to Melbourne a few years later, and my mother and I flew down on one of the first commercial passenger flights. My brother and I went to Canterbury Primary School and later to Scotch College, which was a private Presbyterian boys’ school. There was a lot of demand for places there and my exam results had not been nearly good enough to get in, and I somehow realised my mother was disappointed. I’d got 37 per cent in one French exam, so I worked hard and later scored 87 per cent, which got me into the school. I joined in 1958 and left in 1962.

BY THE TIME I was 12, I had already developed a passionate desire to travel and knew I wanted to get into the travel business. I avidly collected and read travel brochures, and whenever I saw an ocean liner tied up at Station Pier, I was so envious. I wanted to go where those ships were going. In 1962, I got my first job, at Thomas Cook & Son on Collins Street, which was the ritzy street in Melbourne, commonly known as the “Paris end”. I was an assistant messenger and in charge of the brochure rack, which I found mesmerising with all those brochures and destinations, especially in those days.

MY FATHER HAD come out of the army and was working for Esso, the petroleum company, and his job moved to Sydney. So, I left Thomas Cook. In Sydney, I joined the Dutch shipping company Royal Interocean Lines. The company was headquartered in Hong Kong and had quite a substantial travel agency here. I was brought over to take over the travel branch in 1976, and I’ve been here ever since, so 50 years.

I ABSOLUTELY loved Hong Kong from day one. The cargo side of the shipping company imploded because they turned their ships into pallet-carrying ships and should have waited a little longer and turned them into container ships. My predecessor had taken a lot of the travel clients, so I had the thankless job of trying to find customers. I was based in Prince’s Building, in Central. We were trying to sell to firms (corporate travel-organisation packages) and Leighton Asia, the big construction firm, was one of my earliest accounts.

IN 1978, I opened my own travel agency, Concorde Travel, which occupied two floors in On Lan Street, in the heart of Central. I believe we prospered because we were known for being able to put together truly exotic itineraries. Clients, especially civil servants, would spend a few days at home, then go off on a genuinely exploratory trip to some exotic locations. I loved putting these trips together. I ran the agency for 39 years and closed it in 2016. For someone who wanted to travel, I’ve lived a charmed life. I would go to travel-industry meetings and would be invited to a destination for a few days, all expenses paid. Because I was my own boss, I would extend my stay and travel elsewhere.

IN 1981, I WENT to Egypt for what was a highlight of my life. During the war, when my father was posted to the Middle East, he had climbed the Pyramid of Menkaure. Nearly 40 years later, I started to climb it. The stone blocks were enormous and you had to hoist yourself up. I gave up and went back down. But as I walked away, I felt so ashamed. So, I started again. When I did reach the top, I could see the shadow of the pyramid below. Then, all of a sudden, a young fellow came out of the shadows and I was scared stiff. All he wanted was to take my photograph for a fee of US$1. These days, it is, of course, illegal to climb a pyramid.

IN THE 1970s AND 80s, a favourite destination from Hong Kong was the Philippines. I remember when the Philippine Plaza hotel opened, in 1976. (It was located in Metro Manila, and later known as the Sofitel Philippine Plaza Manila, and closed in 2024.) I flew down when it was new. I was having a beer there and, when I went to pay the bill, the waiter said, “Why don’t you stay another five or 10 minutes as the first lady is going to walk past.” So, I paid up and went over to have a look at a great big tent that had been erected for a gala lunch. Inside, there were hundreds of people sitting at tables. I was one of the only foreigners standing at the back. Imelda Marcos was sitting up on the stage and she started to sing. Afterwards, she told her minders to wait and walked along the back of the tent, came up to me and said hello.

INITIALLY, I LIVED on Bowen Road. I first visited Cheung Chau in 1976, soon after I’d arrived. The managers of the other travel agencies wanted me to be introduced and they chose Cheung Chau for the occasion. The nature of the industry is such that we must all sell each other’s products, whether they be airlines, shipping companies, tour operators, resorts, hotels or whatever. It was important that we all knew each other. As we arrived in the Cheung Chau harbour, I noticed a small block of flats being constructed on top of the hill, clearly with a spectacular view. I bought one and am still there, 50 years later. The other travel agents thought I was insane – back then, it was a weekender-only place. Now, I’m proud to say I am Cheung Chau’s second-longest gweilo resident.

IN 1993, I WAS attending a travel-industry meeting in Fortaleza, in northeast Brazil, when this fancy-looking fellow came up to me offering a luxury trip up the Amazon. My friend and I were expecting it to be a five-star vessel, but it turned out to be a basic wooden fishing boat, with just two bunks. I opted to sleep in a hammock with the crew on deck. We knew not to swim in the river, because of the piranhas. If there is any blood in the water, piranhas will come in masses. But when the anchor chain got tangled up in the propeller, our “luxury tour” host just dived in. We were horrified. So, we dived in as well.

ONE TRIP I’LL never forget was to St Helena, where I saw Napoleon’s grave, in 1983. St Helena now has an international airport, which has killed all the romance. Before, it was isolated. I’d spent four days sailing there from the coast of Africa, from Walvis Bay in Namibia. I consider this to be one of the most moving moments in my travels: sitting in silence in this valley with Napoleon, all alone. Of course, he had been dug up and moved to the spectacular Les Invalides in Paris in 1840, but being in that solitude with someone so great was wonderful.

I’VE SET UP a website, Graham’s Heritage Hotels, where I provide information on hotels that are unique, historic, atmospheric and have a story behind them. So, it can also be for armchair travellers. This can be either a luxury residence or a monastery where you sleep on the floor. Many people really want luxury. But I don’t mind if it is five-star or three-star – it’s about the adventure.

FOR MY NEXT TRIP, I want to go to Kunming (in Yunnan province), where you can do a day trip on an old train that’s used by the villagers. It carries ducks and vegetables and will cost you two yuan (HK$2.30). Actually, I probably shouldn’t tell you about it.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Ready player 3: India offers Asean a US-China alternative
item.description:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.
item.content:encoded:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.

“That’s the main reason why we decided to sign up on short notice,” she said of the Indusfood expo, held in Greater Noida at the start of this year.

“With India having a bigger population than China … and a lot of them are vegetarian, we thought they’d be more open to those types of food ingredients.”

Sheentaro’s products were previously showcased at the China-Asean Expo in Nanning and Cordero said the reception was so positive that “when this opportunity in India came about, we said ‘let’s try it again’”.

Southeast Asian nations are increasingly looking to India as an alternative market, arms supplier and technology partner as China and the US vie for regional influence.

India is more than happy to oblige, observers say – though it also knows its limits. It cannot out-trade China, nor can it supplant America’s security umbrella. What is offers instead is room to manoeuvre, free of the demand to choose sides.

That message travelled to Manila last month, where India’s foreign minister, S. Jaishankar, used Asean-led meetings to press the case for deeper cooperation, calling it the only way to “de-risk and diversify”.

He spoke of energy security and food security, and how precarious both had become. Neither these nor public health could be taken for granted in this new “era of volatility and disruption”, Jaishankar said, identifying maritime trade as a further source of anxiety.

A more stable and secure future was in reach, he said, but only by working together: an animating theme of India’s Act East Policy, launched 12 years ago to forge stronger economic, strategic, and cultural ties with Southeast Asia and the broader region.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi were also in the Philippine capital last month for talks with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations on the South China Sea, supply chains and security – a reminder of how much great-power rivalry still shapes regional diplomacy.

The economic dimension of India’s engagement push was on full display earlier in July, when Delhi hosted talks on upgrading the Asean-India Trade in Goods Agreement, a decade-old free-trade pact that officials say no longer reflects current realities.

Two-way trade came in at US$128 billion in the 2025-26 financial year, according to India’s Commerce and Industry Ministry – respectable, but only a fraction of the US$1 trillion and change that China did with the bloc.

Analysts say India’s strategy appears to be centred around pairing diplomacy with trade, defence exports and maritime cooperation, offering Southeast Asia a third option beyond the US-China binary.

It is best described as “a search for mutual wins”, according to Arvind Raj, a geopolitical analyst and associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ Centre for Multilateralism Studies in Singapore.

A more multipolar neighbourhood would give Southeast Asian nations more choices and more room to hedge, he said – as India, in turn, secured a larger foothold in a region that it had long courted from the margins.

Summitry to substance

For years, India’s Asean diplomacy has been heavy on the ceremony, but light on the delivery.

“Asean sits at the centre of India’s Act East Policy on paper, but for most of the past decade the relationship ran on summitry rather than substance,” said Oorja Tapan, a doctoral researcher of international politics at Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi.

Analysts say the clearest evidence of how that dynamic is beginning to change can be seen in the region’s expanding arsenals.

During a three-day state visit last month, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi sealed a deal for Jakarta to buy BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles – jointly developed by India and Russia – making Indonesia the third Southeast Asian buyer after Vietnam and the Philippines.

A separate deal for Jakarta to acquire India’s Astra air-to-air missiles was also signed.

Pooja Bhatt, an associate professor of international relations at India’s O.P. Jindal Global University, calls such defence cooperation “not only part of increasing trade with Asean but also a form of strategic signalling” – proof that Delhi can deliver hardware, not just handshakes.

India wanted to become Southeast Asia’s “resident partner”, Tapan said, offering “capability without a formal alliance demand attached” and without asking the region to choose sides.

Pairing defence exports with renewed free-trade negotiations showed that Delhi wanted to be seen as “a dependable partner offering security cooperation, technology-sharing and balanced regional influence”, said Shristi Pukhrem, a visiting fellow at the India Foundation think tank and director of its Act East Centre.

Foreign policy researcher Joanne Lin concurred that weapons sales alone would not be enough to anchor the relationship.

India’s relevance depended on it delivering across “trade, maritime security, connectivity, tech and supply chains”, said Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and visiting scholar at the MIT Centre for International Studies.

“This is why India is trying to address concerns over trade imbalance, rules of origin and possible re-routing of Chinese goods through Asean, while Asean looks forward to market access with fewer barriers.”

Beyond US-China?

Ultimately, India’s pitch boils down to optionality.

Delhi is not seeking “supremacy in Asean”, according to Abhishek Sharma of the Observer Research Foundation think tank in the Indian capital, but rather is trying to advance its own trade interests while pushing for a stronger, more secure – and more multipolar – Indo-Pacific region.

This framing allowed the South Asian nation to cast itself as an independent pole, distinct from both Beijing and Washington and without the associated baggage, said Sharma, a junior fellow with the foundation’s strategic studies programme.

Lin agreed that India functioned as an additional option for Asean rather than a direct replacement for either the US or China.

India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner

Joanne Lin, foreign policy researcher

“They are looking for partners that can widen their strategic space without forcing them into rigid alignments,” she said of Southeast Asian nations. “India’s strategic autonomy, multi-alignment and Global South positioning resonate with Asean’s own instinct to diversify partnerships and preserve room for manoeuvre.”

In Tapan’s telling, India “lowers the cost of hedging” for the region, due to it being “aligned enough with the West to be useful, [but] non-aligned enough that buying Indian missiles doesn’t read in Beijing as joining a containment bloc”.

Still, Lin was careful not to overstate Delhi’s diplomatic standing within the region.

India “is not yet in the same league as China or the US” in terms of Southeast Asia’s “perceptions of influence”, she said.

“China remains deeply embedded economically, while the US remains central to security calculations. India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner, useful, non-coercive and increasingly visible, but still needing stronger economic delivery.”

‘Some way to go’

India still had “some way to go” to match the scale of Chinese capital, trade volume and state-driven speed, said Bhatt, the international-relations professor.

China’s trade with Asean was about eight times higher than India’s last year – a gulf that does not look likely to close any time soon.

But Delhi’s diplomacy need not be based on countering China alone.

India and Asean spoke “a common language of non-alignment” and shared “a common belief in the Global South”, Bhatt said.

Soft-power advantages bolster India’s appeal, according to Pukhrem, pointing to Delhi-funded restoration work at heritage sites such as Cambodia’s Angkor Wat and Vietnam’s My Son temples as evidence of outreach that “builds soft power rooted in shared civilisational ties rather than transactional influence”.

Tapan agreed that it was not a case of “India vs China’s clout, but India raising the price of Chinese dominance”.

The recent BrahMos sales had demonstrated regional appetite for Indian weapons systems, she said, further pointing to demand for naval hardware, generic pharmaceuticals and digital public infrastructure “that no Chinese product can substitute”.

Tapan also identified India’s growing appeal as a “China plus one” destination for companies looking to diversify supply chains.

“None of this beats a trillion dollars of trade. But Asean’s operating logic is hedging,” she said. “The realistic question is whether India can be indispensable in the places where China is either unwelcome or absent.”

Lin cautioned against India defining its Asean engagement purely in oppositional terms.

“Asean does not want to be treated as a theatre for India-China rivalry,” she said, adding that Delhi could make the most impact by helping the bloc diversify supply chains, build maritime capacity and strengthen digital and health cooperation.

“India’s broader influence will depend on whether it can also deliver in areas that matter to Asean’s economic and development priorities,” Lin added.

item.title: [SCMP] Brazil’s rare earths will not loosen China’s magnet grip this decade, researchers say
item.description:
Brazil will not be able to make rare earth magnets from its own raw materials before 2032, the coordinator of the country’s main magnet pilot plant said on Wednesday, leaving China’s near monopoly on the technology intact for years to come.

Andre Luis Pimenta de Faria, who runs the plant for Senai, the research and training arm of Brazil’s national industry confederation, told a public policy panel at Exposibram, the country’s largest mining congress, that first batches could come by the end of 2028, but only using imported inputs.

“If we look at the full picture of everything needed to produce a permanent magnet, we are talking about a more distant horizon, maybe 2032–2035,” Faria said.
item.content:encoded:
Brazil will not be able to make rare earth magnets from its own raw materials before 2032, the coordinator of the country’s main magnet pilot plant said on Wednesday, leaving China’s near monopoly on the technology intact for years to come.

Andre Luis Pimenta de Faria, who runs the plant for Senai, the research and training arm of Brazil’s national industry confederation, told a public policy panel at Exposibram, the country’s largest mining congress, that first batches could come by the end of 2028, but only using imported inputs.

“If we look at the full picture of everything needed to produce a permanent magnet, we are talking about a more distant horizon, maybe 2032–2035,” Faria said.

The plant runs on Asian process technology chosen when it was designed, and buys abroad the processed ore it feeds into its furnaces, Faria said.

Brazil also makes no electrolytic iron, a high-purity input very different from the ore it ships overseas, despite being one of the world’s two largest iron ore exporters.

Pablo Cesario, chief executive of the Brazilian Mining Institute, called even that timetable optimistic and put the average gap between a proven reserve and first production in Brazil at 17.2 years.

“This is a 10 or 15-year game. And in those 10 or 15 years the others are running too,” he said.

The contest over Brazilian ore

Those timetables matter because permanent magnets made from rare earths drive the motors in electric vehicles, wind turbines, industrial robots and precision weapons, and China produces roughly 90 per cent of the world’s rare earth permanent magnets.

In April 2025, Beijing imposed export controls on seven medium and heavy rare earths and the magnets made with them, disrupting supply to carmakers in Europe, the United States and Asia.

Brazil holds the world’s second largest rare earth reserves after China, and the contest over who gets access to them has already reached the presidential campaign.

Ronaldo Caiado, then governor of the state of Goias and now a presidential candidate, signed a critical minerals memorandum with Washington in March, and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva accused him and other opposition figures of preparing to “sell Brazil”.

The state is home to Serra Verde, which says it is the only miner outside Asia producing the full set of magnet rare earths at scale, and in April the American company USA Rare Earth agreed to buy it for US$2.8 billion.

The transaction could redirect the mine’s output from Chinese refiners to American ones.

That contest is a fight over ore rather than over industry, because Brazil refines almost nothing of what it mines and has no commercial magnet plant of its own.

Asked by the South China Morning Post whether Brazil could diversify its partners while Beijing controls the processing technology, and whether the alternative was alignment with China, Cesario said he had put that question directly to Chinese officials.

“They are open to us. They do not see us as enemies, they see us as partners,” he said.

Faria added the export restrictions were a strategy Brazil had to work around rather than protest against.

“We can kick and scream, we can cry, but it is a strategy of the Chinese government,” he said, arguing the disruption had pushed manufacturers worldwide to look for suppliers outside China.

A bill stuck in the Senate

Brazil has no legal framework for converting any of that demand into binding contracts.

The bill written to supply one has been stuck since May, when the lower house approved it and sent it to the Senate, where it stalled amid friction between Lula and Senate president Davi Alcolumbre. Senators are expected to take it up during a week of priority votes starting on Monday.

If approved, this legislation would create a national critical minerals policy and a fund to guarantee financing for mining projects, but the fight is over a third element, a council attached to the presidency.

Mining companies say the proposed council would have a say over offtake agreements – the long-term supply contracts that underpin mine financing – and over changes in company ownership. Cesario said that leaves too much discretion in the hands of the executive. Mining companies say the proposed council would have a say over offtake agreements

“If we scare off foreign investors, or any other investor, the sector locks up,” Cesario said.

Those powers would land hardest on Chinese companies, which have been taking stakes in Brazilian lithium and rare earth projects. If the council carries them, Brasilia would hold a veto over supply deals and over future acquisitions of the sort agreed at Serra Verde.

Where the industry fears too much state control, the foreign ministry complains of too little direction.

Mauricio Lyrio, its secretary for climate, energy and environment, told the panel in a recorded message that Brazil faced “almost a universal courting” from countries seeking rare earth partnerships, and that it had no framework for deciding which offers to accept.

Until it has one, Lyrio said, Brazil should “pick the ideal partner for each individual mineral rather than react to proposals from abroad”, citing what he called the country’s ecumenical diplomatic tradition.

That approach is already being tested away from both Washington and Beijing.

Luis Gonzaga Trabasso, who coordinates Magbras – a magnet project involving 28 companies and seven research institutes – said the group was bidding into a European raw materials partnership programme, with talks under way with Germany, Sweden, Switzerland and Norway.

Jorge Boeira, an analyst at the Brazilian Industrial Development Agency, said none of those routes changes the underlying arithmetic, because the gap Brazil is really trying to close is one of planning time.

Beijing “set up a government office dedicated to rare earths in 1975, decades before anyone treated the sector as strategic”, Boeira said.

“They had 50 years to build the chain they dominate today, in mining, in refining and downstream,” the analyst added.

Faria borrowed that same date to place Brazil on the clock. “We are setting up the framework now because we know we have potential,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Himalayan glacier collapse hits crucial China-Nepal trade route as casualties mount
item.description:
The catastrophic flash floods and mudslide that devastated the Gyirong Port crossing along the China-Nepal border on Wednesday have dealt a heavy blow to China-Nepal trade and imperilled Kathmandu’s push to cut reliance on Indian transit routes.

However, if Beijing and Kathmandu are to proceed with ambitious infrastructure projects, they are expected to take environmental factors into consideration and adjust their construction methods accordingly, one expert said.

Chinese officials confirmed three deaths and said more than 500 people, including 260 foreign nationals, remained missing on Thursday. Nepal said more than 900 people were missing, including 517 foreigners, and at 5pm Thursday its official death toll was 359.
item.content:encoded:
The catastrophic flash floods and mudslide that devastated the Gyirong Port crossing along the China-Nepal border on Wednesday have dealt a heavy blow to China-Nepal trade and imperilled Kathmandu’s push to cut reliance on Indian transit routes.

However, if Beijing and Kathmandu are to proceed with ambitious infrastructure projects, they are expected to take environmental factors into consideration and adjust their construction methods accordingly, one expert said.

Chinese officials confirmed three deaths and said more than 500 people, including 260 foreign nationals, remained missing on Thursday. Nepal said more than 900 people were missing, including 517 foreigners, and at 5pm Thursday its official death toll was 359.

China’s Ministry of Natural Resources said on Thursday that the deadly mudslide was initially triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse inside Nepal that rapidly evolved into a high-velocity debris flow.

According to Guo Zhaocheng, a senior engineer at the Aero Geophysical Survey and Remote Sensing Centre under the ministry, the collapsing ice rushed down the channel at high speed, swept up vast glacial moraine, or scraped rock, and evolved into a debris flow before hitting Gyirong Port and surging downstream into Nepali territory.

Gyirong Port serves as the strategic anchor connecting China and Nepal. It handled nearly 30 per cent of total trade volume between the two in 2024, and is a primary overland entry point for Indian pilgrims travelling to Tibet. Some 280 Indian pilgrims remain missing after the disaster, according to India’s foreign ministry.

Gyirong is one of three international gateways along the 1,415km (879-mile) Himalayan frontier between Nepal and China, where it operates alongside Purang and Zhangmu to handle both passenger travel and cross-border commerce.

All six major overland crossings on this border lie within China’s Tibet autonomous region, with the other three functioning exclusively as commercial trade points.

“This massive mudslide has severely affected Gyirong port and will inevitably hit trade between China and Nepal hard,” said Liu Zongyi, director of the Centre for South Asian Studies at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies.

“Nepal imports far more from China than it exports, so its dependence on the Chinese economy remains significant.

“Establishing road and rail links with China is essential for Nepal if it wants to alter its economic trajectory and geopolitical landscape,” Liu said, highlighting the broader stakes for Kathmandu.

“To transform itself from a landlocked country into a land-linked one, connectivity with China is indispensable.”

At the centrepiece of these infrastructure ambitions is the proposed China-Nepal railway, which is currently undergoing feasibility studies. Designed to extend from Shigatse through Gyirong directly to Kathmandu, the megaproject aims to drastically reduce transit times and freight costs across the Himalayas.

Zhang Li, deputy director of the Fudan Institute of Belt and Road & Global Governance, said the disaster would cause short-term disruptions to the operation of Gyirong Port, the preliminary geological survey work for the China-Nepal railway, and the cross-border movement of materials and personnel.

However, “they will not change the overall direction of China-Nepal connectivity and cooperation”, he asserted.

“On the contrary, they will prompt both sides to adopt more refined and meticulous approaches in railway route selection, disaster monitoring and early warning systems, as well as the disaster-prevention standards for the China-Nepal power interconnection project.”

Yet the physical realities of the terrain present formidable obstacles.

Liu cautioned that the rail link remained a long-term plan. “The geological conditions along the route are extremely difficult. If the railway is built, it would have to rely heavily on tunnels.”

“These projects are strategic and especially significant for Nepal, as they are crucial for reducing its dependence on India. If construction proceeds in the future, environmental factors will be taken into account and construction methods adjusted to make them more scientific and more rational,” Liu said.

In a push to boost trade with China, the Nepalese government has pledged to start construction on the Tokha-Chhahare Tunnel.

Connecting Tokha in Kathmandu to Chhahare in Nuwakot, the project lies along the vital Kathmandu-Rasuwagadhi transit corridor and could cut bilateral transport costs by up to 50 per cent, according to local media.

Expanding cooperation beyond transit, the two countries are also working to construct a 16km, 220kV power transmission line connecting Nepal’s Chilime region to Gyirong. The landmark initiative is designed to enable two-way electricity trading and optimise seasonal grid balance.

China’s deepening footprint along the Himalayan crest continues to draw scrutiny from India – Nepal’s largest trading partner by a wide margin – which strongly opposes the railway initiative.

New Delhi’s fears that a modern rail and road link stretching from Tibet to Kathmandu brings Chinese logistics closer to the Siliguri Corridor – the narrow, strategic strip of land connecting mainland India to its northeastern states.

By using landlocked Nepal’s economic reliance on Indian transit routes, New Delhi has historically deployed formal and informal restrictions to maintain geopolitical leverage.

Providing Nepal with an alternative overland trade route through China threatens to undermine India’s historical transit monopoly and diplomatic clout over Kathmandu.

The disaster follows a recurring pattern of environmental shocks along the fragile corridor.

In July last year, a glacial lake outburst about 35km upstream in Tibet sent a wall of water surging down the Bhotekoshi River, destroying the Nepal-China Friendship Bridge at Gyirong, halting border traffic for months and leading to 17 deaths.

Researchers from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), alongside partner organisations in Nepal and China, are assessing whether a high-altitude ice-rock avalanche was the initial trigger for the disaster.

“The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time most probably triggered by an ice avalanche [that] blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist for ICIMOD, said in a statement.

According to the US Geological Survey and preliminary assessments by earth scientists, the disaster could have been triggered when a collapsing glacier set off a violent chain reaction that caused a powerful surge of water and debris down narrow mountain gorges into the valley.

Meanwhile, earth scientists are issuing cautions about climate-driven destabilisation of the high Himalayas.

The United Nations reported that Nepal has lost nearly a third of its ice cover in just over 30 years, with glacial loss accelerating 65 per cent faster over the past 10 years than the previous decade.

Rising temperatures are actively thawing the region’s permafrost – the centuries-old frozen soil and rock anchoring the steep mountain faces. As the structural binder thaws, massive rock and ice formations will become unstable, turning routine slope failures into catastrophic torrents downstream.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Strong signal’: South Korea raises rates again to fight inflation, rising home prices
item.description:
South Korea’s central bank has raised interest rates for a second straight month, with analysts saying its semiconductor boom has given policymakers room to confront inflation, a weak won and rising home prices, but at the cost of a deeper squeeze on indebted households and small businesses.

The Bank of Korea (BOK) lifted its benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage point to 3.0 per cent on Thursday, a month after an identical increase took it to 2.75 per cent in July.

The latest move brought the rate to its highest level since February 2025 and signalled a central bank willing to accept some damage to domestic demand to contain broader financial risks.
item.content:encoded:
South Korea’s central bank has raised interest rates for a second straight month, with analysts saying its semiconductor boom has given policymakers room to confront inflation, a weak won and rising home prices, but at the cost of a deeper squeeze on indebted households and small businesses.

The Bank of Korea (BOK) lifted its benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage point to 3.0 per cent on Thursday, a month after an identical increase took it to 2.75 per cent in July.

The latest move brought the rate to its highest level since February 2025 and signalled a central bank willing to accept some damage to domestic demand to contain broader financial risks.

Households with housing-related loans, small businesses and other borrowers are expected to feel the pressure most acutely. But with semiconductor exports and investment driving stronger-than-expected growth, economists said the BOK had decided the greater danger lay in moving too slowly.

The Monetary Policy Board made that priority clear in its statement, saying: “It is important to prevent inflationary pressures from becoming widespread through pre-emptive action, and it is also necessary to continue paying attention to financial stability risks.

“The board will decide the timing and pace of further increases in the Base Rate while assessing trends in inflation and the domestic economy, as well as financial stability.”

BOK Governor Shin Hyun-song described the consecutive July and August rate increases as “a step outside convention” intended to send “a strong signal” about the central bank’s determination to stabilise financial markets.

The rate increase came as the BOK sharply upgraded its economic growth forecasts for both this year and next, citing robust semiconductor exports and investment.

It now expects the South Korean economy to grow 3.3 per cent in 2026 – up from its previous forecast of 2.6 per cent – and 2.9 per cent in 2027, up from 2.1 per cent.

The central bank said the domestic economy continued to grow strongly, led by exports and investment, while improving income conditions supported a gradual recovery in consumption.

It expects robust growth to continue as semiconductor exports and investment remain strong.

South Korea’s external accounts have also benefited from the semiconductor boom.

The country recorded a cumulative current-account surplus of US$191.01 billion in the first six months of 2026, the largest half-year surplus on record and roughly four times the US$47.87 billion surplus recorded during the same period in 2025.

“By controlling inflation expectations through pre-emptive measures and responding early before price increases spread, we can ultimately reduce the costs to the economy,” Shin said.

He also expressed concern about continued rapid increases in housing prices in the Seoul metropolitan area. Although price growth has slowed in some parts of Seoul, overall housing costs across the capital region have continued to rise at a high pace, and household loans have also increased.

Shin acknowledged that “it is unreasonable to control housing prices solely through interest rates”, but said the latest rate increase would help ease the upward trend.

The weak won against the US dollar is another factor behind the BOK’s move to raise rates.

The currency had fallen to around 1,550 won per dollar in late June, its weakest level in 17 years, but has since recovered to the upper 1,300-won range.

“The won-dollar rate has stabilised to a large extent, but historically, the won is still very weak,” Shin said, adding that a stronger won would help curb inflation by lowering import prices.

Economics Professor Song Heon-jae of the University of Seoul said he was surprised by the back-to-back rate increases.

“Through the rate increases, the central bank is seeking to stabilise the financial market, even if it may hurt households and small businesses saddled with debts and other borrowers,” Song told This Week in Asia.

South Korea’s household credit balance topped 2,000 trillion won (US$1.45 trillion) for the first time in the second quarter of 2026, driven by rising housing transactions and debt-financed investments.

Younger households are particularly exposed to the effects of higher borrowing costs because of their leveraged investments in equities and housing.

“Financial authorities are confident that robust exports led by semiconductors would be enough to make up for the increases’ negative impact on domestic demand,” Song said.

Inflation remains another major concern.

Consumer prices rose 3.1 per cent year on year in May and 3.2 per cent in June before easing to 2.8 per cent in July.

Although the July figure was the lowest in three months, it remained above the BOK’s 2 per cent target.

The BOK expects inflation to remain above its target for a considerable period as elevated cost pressures pass through to consumer prices and stronger incomes gradually boost demand.

It forecasts headline inflation at 2.7 per cent this year and 2.3 per cent next year.

High economic growth can add to inflationary pressure as rising incomes increase demand. The BOK has therefore emphasised the need to act before price increases become more broadly entrenched.

The rate increase could also support the won by narrowing the interest-rate gap between South Korea and the United States as a smaller differential can reduce incentives for investors to move funds into dollar-denominated assets.

Economics Professor Kim Sung-hyun of Sungkyunkwan University said the growth trend was likely to continue into next year, citing long-term semiconductor contracts and strong demand for products from Samsung and SK Hynix.

“The government and the central bank are giving priority to stabilising the financial market through the rate increases, even though it would slow economic growth somewhat and increase the burden on borrowers, including the government,” Kim said.

Hur Jung, an economics professor at Sogang University, said the won’s recent appreciation against the dollar could prove temporary, partly because of increased foreign-currency supplies from major semiconductor exporters such as Samsung and SK Hynix.

“However, there will soon be a great demand for dollars when South Korea starts implementing its promised US$350 billion investment in the US, driving the exchange rate higher again,” he said.

At the same time, the government was pursuing an expansionary fiscal policy to stimulate economic growth and address income disparities, despite inflation concerns, Hur said.

“Under these circumstances, the bank is likely to raise the rate again by another 0.25 percentage point sometime in the coming six months,” he said.

The BOK’s latest decision highlighted the “difficult balance” facing South Korean policymakers: keeping inflation and housing-market risks under control without undermining domestic demand, Hur added.

Economics Professor Kim Gwang-suk of Hanyang University said inflation was likely to ease towards 2 per cent, while the central bank could seek to maintain its benchmark rate between 3.25 per cent and 3.5 per cent in the foreseeable future.

“The rate increases will help curb rising housing prices. But they will put greater burdens on those relying on debt, while causing no major impact on large companies that are enjoying the export boom,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Xi’s crusade against corruption has gone well beyond economic crime
item.description:
The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the fourth part of an accompanying series, Yuanyue Dang and William Zheng delve into the broader reach of the campaign.

While economic crimes are often seen as the target of President Xi Jinping’s crusade against corruption, the campaign has become much wider.

Thirteen years since it began, it is now increasingly about how officials use their power, whether they toe the line, and what they do in their private lives.
item.content:encoded:
The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the fourth part of an accompanying series, Yuanyue Dang and William Zheng delve into the broader reach of the campaign.

While economic crimes are often seen as the target of President Xi Jinping’s crusade against corruption, the campaign has become much wider.

Thirteen years since it began, it is now increasingly about how officials use their power, whether they toe the line, and what they do in their private lives.

The South China Morning Post analysed the findings of hundreds of disciplinary investigations conducted by the anti-corruption watchdog from 2013 to 2025. The findings suggest that Xi’s campaign has expanded from economic corruption to a broader effort to reshape how the bureaucracy is run.

While bribery is still the legal foundation for cases to enter the court system, political loyalty, discipline, policy implementation and cadre management have become part of how corruption is defined and punished in China.

The SCMP analysis looked at the cases of 423 cadres who were “centrally managed” – meaning senior officials who reported directly to the Central Committee of the ruling Communist Party.

Cadres at this level are overseen by the party’s personnel agency – the Central Organisation Department – which is responsible for administration, assessment and recommendations on who is in and who is out.
