Most cadres in the analysis were ranked at deputy provincial or ministerial level or above. A small number were slightly lower in rank but headed financial institutions, state-owned enterprises or other key organisations.

The findings analysed were released by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection after an investigation and most cases were then passed to judicial authorities.

They are not court judgments and do not provide a complete account of the evidence held by investigators, but are more like a public explanation from the authorities as to why an official crossed a red line.

‘Political sin’

The anti-corruption campaign was launched after Xi became China’s top leader in 2013. Beijing has said there would be “no forbidden zones, full coverage and zero tolerance”.

As the campaign has rolled on, the CCDI has released longer statements on its investigations, mainly to include political-related accusations.

Economic crimes have remained part of nearly every case. But these cases now include allegations involving “improper” banquets, resisting investigation, and issues around policy implementation, use of power and political risk.

Of the 423 cases reviewed, 93.4 per cent of the officials were accused of using their positions to seek benefits for others. Some 88.7 per cent were accused of taking bribes, and 67.1 per cent were accused of accepting cash or gifts.

These were the three most common allegations.

Economic corruption and integrity violations accounted for 52.4 per cent of the allegations from 2013 to 2017 – about five years after the party congress when Xi became leader.

In the next five years to 2022, they made up 43.2 per cent of the allegations, and in the period from 2023 to 2025 it was 46.4 per cent.

This does not mean bribery has become less important in the campaign, rather that the party’s definition of corruption is now broader.

Qian Jingyuan, an assistant professor of political science at Boston College, said this reflected the dual nature of the campaign.

“From Beijing’s perspective, corruption has been viewed not just as an economic crime, but also as a political sin,” Qian said.

“Thus, public announcements must emphasise the political nature of an official’s wrongdoing before the economic aspects, while the latter often constitute the substantive basis for the criminal indictment.”

Power and conduct

To assess how the campaign has changed over time, the SCMP analysis divided the cases into three periods in line with the party congress cycles, according to the year the CCDI released its findings.

There were 159 cases from 2013 to 2017; 124 from 2018 to 2022; and 140 from 2023 to 2025.

From 2013 to 2017, 18.9 per cent of cases contained allegations involving political security or political risk.

The CCDI accusations included seeking political patronage, forming cliques and factions, damaging the political environment, saying one thing while doing another, associating with political swindlers and engaging in superstitious activities.

There was a jump in these cases – to 64.5 per cent – in the period from 2018 to 2022. They fell slightly to 59.3 per cent in the period from 2023 to 2025.

The language used in these allegations is in line with the Regulations on CPC Disciplinary Action – or rules of conduct within the party – which underwent a major revision in 2015.

Six forms of discipline are listed: political, organisational, integrity, “mass” discipline governing relations with the public, work and personal conduct.

As political allegations have increased, there have been fewer occurrences of specific claims like forming cliques or making improper comments about the central leadership.

Deng Yuwen, a former deputy editor of Study Times, the official newspaper of the Central Party School, said that reflected a move away from dealing with questions of political alignment and towards more detailed scrutiny of administrative conduct.

“After the major political cliques like [those of former public security vice-minister] Sun Lijun have been brought down, Beijing’s effort went into the details of how the senior cadres use their power, and their conduct,” Deng said.

“Systematic power abuse will lead to systematic economic and social risks. Abusive official conduct will accumulate social discontent. Both are dangerous for the legitimacy and the long-term rule of the Communist Party.”

When an official’s political loyalty is questioned, they are often also accused of concealing personal matters, lying during interviews, or resisting investigation, according to the SCMP analysis.

These allegations appeared in 48.4 per cent of cases in the 2013-17 period.

That jumped to 82.3 per cent from 2018 to 2022, and reached 88.6 per cent in the 2023-25 period.

This has coincided with an expansion of the supervisory system. China amended the constitution in 2018 to establish supervisory commissions at every level and enacted the Supervision Law.

The commissions – which work with discipline inspectors – extend oversight from party cadres to all officials who exercise public power.

An expanded detention system known as liuzhi replaced the party’s largely informal shuanggui disciplinary system.

The way anti-corruption bodies publish their investigation findings and their format has also become more standardised since the law took effect.

Qian from Boston College said the campaign had brought “both greater institutionalisation of cadre supervision and more personalised control”.

Toeing the line

As the campaign has progressed, the clearest shift in the CCDI’s investigation notices can be seen in their direct assessments of governance.

In the 2013-17 period, only 23.9 per cent of cases involved allegations of failure to implement central decisions, other governance problems, departures from the “new development philosophy”, abuse of power, and interference in market, judicial and law enforcement activities.

That proportion rose to 53.2 per cent in the period from 2018 to 2022, and hit 73.6 per cent from 2023 to 2025.

These governance issues are now in the disciplinary rules after they were again revised, in 2023. The latest version says officials can be punished for violating political discipline if they express support for central decisions but fail to implement them, carry them out half-heartedly, or dilute or circumvent them.

The rules now also include – under problems with governance performance – any departures from the “new development philosophy” and “high-quality development” as well as wasteful “vanity projects”.

Qian said the sectors targeted by anti-corruption investigators were increasingly connected to the party’s governance priorities. He cited the more intensive scrutiny of financial and banking officials as Beijing sought to guard against “systemic risk”.

“Apparently the central leadership has used anti-corruption as a means to enforce its policy agenda and incentivise the officials’ governance outcomes by targeting specific sectors,” he said.

That view was echoed by Jiangnan Zhu, an associate professor with the University of Hong Kong’s Department of Politics and Public Administration.

“The concept of corruption in the Chinese party-state is broad and dynamic,” Zhu said, adding that it could change with the leadership’s governing priorities.

But she said there had been a consistent theme in the anti-graft campaign from the start: improving governance while strengthening party control.

Path to jobs

Another new focus as the campaign has gathered pace is how cadres are selected for jobs.

Cases involving irregularities in personnel selection and appointments or post-retirement misconduct rose from 39 per cent in the first period (2013-17) to 60 per cent in the latest period (2023-25).

Inspectors are now looking at bribery that has already occurred but also the entry, promotion and exit of cadres. They aim to break corrupt chains formed through money and private networks and to continue supervision once officials have retired.

In Zhu’s book, Bribery as a Third Path to Power? Political Selection in China Beyond Performance and Patronage, she described the buying and selling of public sector jobs as “personnel corruption”.

She wrote that this type of corruption allowed money to replace competence and loyalty in determining who could enter or rise through public office, ultimately causing “the privatisation of public power and deinstitutionalisation of meritocracy”.

Zhu said Xi’s anti-corruption campaign had a focus on the networks formed through the buying and selling of posts because they could develop into power bases beyond the central leadership’s control.

Her research found that explicit cases of buying and selling official positions have fallen sharply since 2017, suggesting the campaign had reduced these activities and helped the party regain control over personnel selection.

Officials’ personal and family lives have also become part of cadre supervision. Across the entire sample analysed by the SCMP, 49.2 per cent of officials were accused of improper family conduct, failing to supervise or educate relatives, or involvement in family-based corruption.

This accountability framework extends a senior official’s responsibility to their family, subordinates and political networks.

Whether a cadre is loyal, reports personal matters truthfully, selects personnel appropriately, keeps family members and those around them under control, and implements central policy can now appear alongside bribery allegations.

But analysts cautioned that this does not point to comprehensive changes to the party-state system.

“I do not see clear evidence that the campaign itself is reshaping the general structure of the party-state bureaucracy,” according to Qian.

He said the campaign had brought large-scale personnel changes, altered promotion standards, performance evaluations and officials’ incentives, and established new institutions intended to tighten control over the bureaucracy.

But he said the broader centralisation of power and strengthening of party leadership could not be attributed entirely to the campaign.

The SCMP analysis also suggests that the party is changing the standards it uses to assess the performance of officials.

That was expressed more directly in a party-wide education campaign on “correct” governance launched by the Central Committee earlier this year.

It identified a number of problems that needed to be corrected, including short-sighted decision-making, falsification, blind expansion and “vanity projects” that waste labour and money.

Assessment of governance must also include the implementation of central decisions and “high-quality development”.

Economic growth and policy outcomes remain important in the evaluation of cadres’ performance. But there is now greater weight given to political loyalty, integrity, control over subordinates and family members, and the ability to carry out central directives.

“As the scope of ‘corruption’ has broadened, some officials would rather choose to ‘lie flat’ and may be reluctant to experiment with policies that could potentially cross the lines drawn by higher authorities,” Qian said.

For Beijing, this means the next phase of the anti-corruption campaign will involve not only continuing to identify problems, but also finding the line between control and encouraging initiative.

“Finding a balance between enforcing discipline and incentivising officials’ performance and innovation remains an important task for the central leadership,” Qian said.

item.title: [SCMP] The path to America is narrowing. Here’s what that means for legal immigrants
item.description:
US green card interviews are on hold worldwide, student and work visas are subject to new restrictions, and citizenship is under fresh scrutiny. Here’s what the latest US immigration crackdown means for people planning to study, work or settle in America.

Why did the US cancel immigrant visa interviews?

US embassies and consulates around the world have postponed immigrant visa interviews so that officers can train on a stricter “public charge” test: whether an applicant is likely to rely on public benefits.
item.content:encoded:
US green card interviews are on hold worldwide, student and work visas are subject to new restrictions, and citizenship is under fresh scrutiny. Here’s what the latest US immigration crackdown means for people planning to study, work or settle in America.

Why did the US cancel immigrant visa interviews?

US embassies and consulates around the world have postponed immigrant visa interviews so that officers can train on a stricter “public charge” test: whether an applicant is likely to rely on public benefits.

The freeze came days after a federal judge struck down a separate 75-country visa block built on the same idea.

The State Department emphasises that officers must apply the test “comprehensively and consistently”.

The factors themselves are not new: age, health, family size, money, education, skills and job prospects. What has been added is the instruction to apply them more aggressively, including by issuing public charge bonds in some cases.

Sarah Pierce, director of social policy at Washington-based think tank Third Way – who is also a former US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) analyst – said the Donald Trump administration “chose the most disruptive possible way to roll this out”.

Charles Kuck, an Atlanta immigration lawyer who last year represented more than 100 students against the administration, said officers were being trained “on how to deny cases under public charge rules”.

Family applicants would find it “much harder to immigrate”, he said, adding that the change would also hurt diversity lottery applicants.

Does this cancel my green card petition?

A cancelled interview does not usually erase an approved petition or a priority date.

“State is postponing the interview; it has not announced that these underlying approvals are being revoked,” Pierce said.

“The real harm is delay” for people who have already booked flights, sold homes or attended medical examinations. “State has not said when normal scheduling will resume,” she said.

Diversity visas generally must be issued by the end of the financial year, which for the US government is September 30. Make sure the National Visa Centre has a working email, phone number and mailing address for you.

Does the pause affect non-immigrant visas?

No. This freeze applies to green-card interviews abroad. H-1B, student and tourist windows are not part of it.

However, the public charge provision could legally apply to non-immigrants too, Kuck noted, while adding that “as of right now, it only appears to be applying to immigrant visa holders”.

That does not mean those visas are easy to obtain. Pierce said that much of the H-1B agenda was “forward-looking”: the proposed US$103,000 fee is not in force yet and a new lottery is not the problem for people already selected.

The people most exposed are those who still need a stamp outside the US, according to Pierce.

What is the public charge test?

Officers weigh age, health, family, money, education, skills and sometimes past benefits. A proper I-864 affidavit of support was normally enough in family cases, unless there were “unusually significant concerns”, she said.

While Pierce would not call the new push “a legal blanket ban”, she warned that the danger was that aggressive implementation “begins functioning like one for certain populations”.

Kuck’s worry is the vacuum. “There is no guidance in the statute,” he said, which “allows for a great deal of mischief”.

What should I do if my visa interview was cancelled?

If the appointment is gone, the petition usually is not. Kuck’s advice is to stay put unless you already hold a work visa that lets you return and keep the job.

Most people who received the cancellation email are not in this position. “They should remain in their home country until the interview is reset,” Kuck said.

Can the US revoke an petition after it is approved?

“A consular officer does not simply get to overrule USCIS,” Pierce said. If the interview turns up fraud, a big change in facts or a clear error, the officer can send the file back. USCIS then decides.

Her advice to applicants is to know what was filed in your name and “don’t guess when an officer asks about something you don’t know”.

Family cases are hard to unwind, because “somebody is either a spouse or not a spouse”, according to Kuck. Employment files get more second guessing. Many returned petitions were later reapproved, he said.

Should I leave the US to stamp my visa?

If you already have lawful status, do not travel unless you must.

“No one should leave the United States unless they have an emergency need to travel,” Kuck said.

Pierce’s test was the same. “Think harder before international travel if returning depends on a new visa,” she said. An approved O-1 petition was not a reason to fly out for a stamp.

What documents should visa holders carry in the US?

Carry proof of status: the green card, or an I-94 plus an I-797 or employer letter. Keep copies where family can reach them, Pierce said.

“This administration has dramatically increased the volume and aggressiveness of immigration enforcement, which makes the consequences of bureaucratic mistakes much higher.”

Workers flying in should carry pay stubs and a job letter, Kuck said. People with no lawful status, including those on a 240-day extension after an H-1B has ended, or those with only a pending green card or asylum case, should not travel.

What is changing for F-1 students?

New arrivals lose open-ended duration of status. They get a fixed date, generally up to four years, plus a 30-day grace period, down from 60.

Students already in the US on September 15 can usually keep the old terms until they leave and come back. Travel can switch the clock. “Work with your foreign student adviser,” Kuck said.

How can OPT students avoid unlawful presence?

Do not overstay. Put the end date on a calendar and “do not take any chances of leaving even one day late”, Kuck said.

A tidy record in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System will not save you if the I-94 has expired. The advice is to track the I-94, I-20, EAD and any pending filing, and act before the earliest date.

What if an H-1B worker is laid off?

The law still offers 60 days, but Kuck advised not to trust it. “Legally, they still have the 60 days. Yeah, but in reality, they have none.” File to change status before the job ends.

Pierce said that people who already held valid H-1B status inside the United States were less exposed than those who needed a stamp abroad.

Can the US take away citizenship?

Only through a narrow civil case, and it is still rare – the Justice Department says it has filed 123 such cases since 20 January 2025, which is a record.

“The government cannot simply strip citizenship from a naturalised American because it later decides that person is undesirable,” Pierce said. It must show citizenship was illegally procured or obtained by hiding a material fact.

What had changed was “the government’s appetite for reopening old files”, she added.

Many of Kuck’s clients used a second identity after an old deportation order. “If you were deported under a different name, you should be very worried.”

What about the citizenship of children born there?

The United States cannot take away citizenship of children born in the US because of their parents’ immigration status, the Supreme Court ruled in June. Denaturalising a parent is a separate process and does not, by itself, revoke the citizenship of a child who was a citizen at birth.

In Trump vs Barbara, the court held that children born in the United States to parents who were in the country unlawfully or only temporarily “are citizens at birth”.

“Birthright citizenship is fundamentally different from naturalisation,” Pierce said. A citizen at birth did not “procure” naturalisation, so the government “cannot simply use the denaturalisation process to retroactively turn that person into a non-citizen”.

Kuck pointed out that children and spouses were not automatically stripped of their citizenship when the government was targeting visa fraud.

Are green card holders safe to travel?

The ones at risk will be those on the way back to the US who are residents convicted of a crime after they received the card, according to Kuck. “No one else needs to worry about it.” Long trips can still raise old abandonment questions. Carry the card.

Who is safe, and who is at high risk?

“The vast majority of people who follow the rules, they’re fine. That’s 99 per cent,” Kuck said. The heat is on old fraud, a second name or no status.

Pierce offered a different caution: following the rules no longer means a calm process. “Build in more time. Expect more scrutiny.”

Highest risk: prior fraud, travel without status, diversity visa deadlines and family applicants who look poor under a tougher public-charge screen.

Is legal immigration to the US still possible?

Yes, but it will be slower, with more scrutiny. “There is no doubt that this administration is engaged in a systematic attack against legal immigration,” Pierce said.

Asked what she would tell people, Pierce said: “I would tell them to stop assuming that following the rules guarantees a smooth process.” The agenda “is not confined to illegal immigration. It has made a deliberate choice to make legal immigration harder as well.”

Kuck’s advice was to keep a backup plan for now. “This episode will rest in the ash heap of history soon enough.” Until interviews resume, treat a cancelled date as a delay, not a dead case.

This article is for general information only and is not legal advice. Readers should consult a qualified immigration lawyer about their own case.

item.title: [SCMP] Can Singapore’s new anti-scam rules help stop online fraud before it occurs?
item.description:
Singapore’s new rules for messaging platforms mark a significant shift in the country’s fight against scams, placing greater responsibility on digital services to help stop fraudsters before they reach potential victims, as the government seeks stronger penalties for non-compliance.

Analysts said the requirements could reduce the number of people exposed to scams and offer a potential model for other Southeast Asian countries, while cautioning that sophisticated fraudsters could adapt and seek ways around the new safeguards.

Singapore police announced earlier this month that online messaging platforms must implement measures to make it more difficult for unknown contacts to engage users and to alert people to potential scam risks.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s new rules for messaging platforms mark a significant shift in the country’s fight against scams, placing greater responsibility on digital services to help stop fraudsters before they reach potential victims, as the government seeks stronger penalties for non-compliance.

Analysts said the requirements could reduce the number of people exposed to scams and offer a potential model for other Southeast Asian countries, while cautioning that sophisticated fraudsters could adapt and seek ways around the new safeguards.

Singapore police announced earlier this month that online messaging platforms must implement measures to make it more difficult for unknown contacts to engage users and to alert people to potential scam risks.

The rules build on the Online Criminal Harms Act (Ocha), which gives authorities powers to issue directions, codes of practice and implementation directives aimed at disrupting online criminal activity, including scams.

Singapore authorities have framed the measures as part of a wider effort to reduce scam exposure before victims are drawn into conversations with fraudsters.

The stakes are high: scam victims in Singapore lost about S$410.6 million (US$323 million) in the first half of this year, despite an overall fall in scam cases and losses from the same period previous year, according to the police’s midyear scam and cybercrime brief, issued on Wednesday. Authorities said messaging platforms were the top contact method used to reach victims in 27.6 per cent out of 16,821 scam cases.

The new requirements include displaying warnings or signs of risk – such as country of origin or date of creation of an unknown account – and requiring users to give consent before being added to chat groups or channels by unfamiliar contacts.

Platforms will also have to allow users to silence, filter or block messages or calls from numbers not saved in their contacts.

The requirements will apply to seven platforms and services – WhatsApp, Telegram, WeChat, Apple iMessage, Apple FaceTime, Google Message and Google Meet – which must comply with the broader code by January 31, 2027. Measures relating to spoofing the Singapore government must be in place by September 30.

The new requirements were a “wise” move likely to reduce scam cases, said David Lam, an associate fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

“Online scamming is a dynamic threat landscape with scammers constantly evolving their methods and tactics to exploit victims,” he said, adding that messaging platforms had a critical role in stemming communication between fraudsters and potential victims.

Failure to comply with Ocha directives without a reasonable excuse currently carries a fine of up to S$1 million, a figure the Ministry of Home Affairs has proposed raising to S$10 million as the city state battles a scam scourge.

Chew Han Ei, an adjunct senior research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies, said the new measures were a part of a significant shift to increase platform-level responsibility. “People text quickly, often under distraction or time pressure, and malicious actors deliberately exploit those opportunities. Good platform design should therefore help users make safer choices by default,” he said.

Limits of prevention

Analysts said the requirements could make it harder for scammers to reach potential victims, but warned against viewing them as a way to eradicate scams altogether.

“Scams are a multibillion-dollar industry. The actors are constantly innovating at the same time as the companies, and they would probably find ways to circumvent these technical features,” said Shahzeb Mahmood, head of research at Tech Global Institute.

Fraudsters could easily move to other platforms to conduct operations, he said. “A lot of people in Singapore, especially migrant workers, use platforms other than the seven mentioned and those are falling through the cracks.”

Nuurrianti Jalli, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, said scammers could take control of accounts in potential victims’ contact lists, or use a local number or established account to appear less suspicious.

She also warned of user fatigue, whereby people become accustomed to dismissing warnings that are too vague or frequent.

“Ultimately, these measures should reduce the number of people entering the scam funnel, but they will not eliminate scams,” Nuurrianti said. “I would describe them as friction rather than a firewall.”

Analysts said non-compliance by major technology companies was less likely to be the main obstacle.

Ocha took effect in February 2024, with its first directive issued last year to Meta Platforms – which owns Facebook and WhatsApp – to implement measures curbing Facebook impersonation scams. Similar directives were also issued to Apple and Google.

Singapore’s authorities had reported compliance in earlier cases involving online platforms, Nuurrianti said.

“Many of these capabilities are not being developed entirely from scratch,” she said. “Major platforms already have different forms of spam detection, unknown-sender filtering, blocking, group privacy controls and scam warnings.”

Mahmood said scams should also be understood within a wider transnational criminal ecosystem, which could include offences such as human and drug trafficking, increasing the incentive and urgency for companies to cooperate.

“Scams in isolation might not be a huge policy priority for companies, but when you look at it more holistically, it’s connected to illegal operations around the world and that’s something companies take very seriously,” he said.

A regional model?

Singapore’s expanded requirements may set a precedent for Southeast Asian countries to adopt a similar framework to tackle scams, given the scale and cross-border nature of online fraud, according to Ysa Marie Cayabyab, an associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore.

“Southeast Asia has a highly connected digital environment, but this leaves us exposed to a wider range of scams and vulnerabilities,” she said.

Neighbouring countries have also started placing more responsibility on platforms to stop online harm.

In June, Malaysia implemented rules requiring online service providers to include safeguards that limit account registration and ownership by users under the age of 16, and to implement stronger content governance.

Thailand in May introduced requirements for social media platforms to verify the identity of advertisers before publication, in a bid to prevent online crimes.

In March, Indonesia started enforcing a social media ban for under-16s to shield some 70 million children from the threats of online pornography, cyberbullying and internet addiction.

Cayabyab said, however, that effectiveness would vary considerably across the region.

“Differences in digital literacy, regulatory capacity, platform penetration, languages, and patterns of online behaviour mean that a measure that works well in Singapore may not translate directly elsewhere,” she said.

But a regional approach would still be useful, she said, urging greater information sharing among governments and platforms, such as common standards for identifying suspicious behaviour and faster mechanisms to act on red flags.

Lam urged coordination and cooperation between Southeast Asian nations, citing a precedent case which resulted in positive action.

In January, Indonesia and Malaysia temporarily blocked or restricted access to the Grok AI chatbot operated by Elon Musk’s xAI amid growing concern internationally over sexualised images, while officials in the Philippines also signalled action. Within the month, xAI imposed new restrictions limiting image editing.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korean ex-spy reveals toll of secret missions to North: ‘treated as expendable’
item.description:
In 1984, Ha Tae-jun, then 24, spotted a notice recruiting for a special unit at the Military Manpower Administration office in central Seoul’s Yongsan district. The notice was scrawled on the wall in marker, with little explanation.

Ha applied, and his life was changed forever – training as a South Korean operative for covert missions into North Korea.

“About a month after submitting background check documents, they said I’d passed and told me to meet at a cafe near my house,” said Ha, now 66 and president of the Association of Bereaved Families of Special Mission Agents.
item.content:encoded:
In 1984, Ha Tae-jun, then 24, spotted a notice recruiting for a special unit at the Military Manpower Administration office in central Seoul’s Yongsan district. The notice was scrawled on the wall in marker, with little explanation.

Ha applied, and his life was changed forever – training as a South Korean operative for covert missions into North Korea.

“About a month after submitting background check documents, they said I’d passed and told me to meet at a cafe near my house,” said Ha, now 66 and president of the Association of Bereaved Families of Special Mission Agents.

At the time, he had no idea it would be three years before he saw home again.

Taken to a safe house on Mount Cheonggye in Seongnam, Gyeonggi province, he passed a fitness test and got into a car, believing it would take him home.

Instead, the car took him to another safe house in Sokcho, Gangwon province, operated by the Headquarters of Intelligence Detachment, a South Korean military unit that trained and dispatched agents on covert infiltration missions into North Korea.

The next morning, he woke up surrounded by North Korean military uniforms, with every weapon in sight made for use by hostile forces. From that day, his life took an unexpected path.

According to Ha, four people were assigned to each agent. He lived in a villa with an officer, a non-commissioned officer and two enlisted men, one handling daily chores, the other monitoring him as a training assistant.

Constant surveillance

One of the most important principles they operated under was, ironically, keeping him in the dark. That way, if he were captured in North Korea, he would have nothing to tell them.

“I didn’t even know the names of the people I lived with, only surnames like Kim, Lee or Park, or nicknames like ‘big teacher’ and ‘little teacher’. I was trained only for the operation I’d carry out in the North, nothing else.”

Training began at 6am with a 4km (2.5-mile) run. Twice a week, he ran 12km of mountain terrain in an hour, carrying 25kg of sand, 1kg weights on each leg, and his rifle. Because operations took place at night, infiltration drills were concentrated after dark. He was also drilled in Morse code, used to stay in contact with headquarters after crossing into North Korea.

Agents trained in isolation, being kept apart so they never met. Trainees learned North Korean dialect and trained in skydiving and scuba diving, since a single agent had to operate on land, sea and air alike. Every piece of equipment at the safe house, down to the firearms, was not South Korean.

Unlike the way South Korean films often portray the training of agents who infiltrate North Korea, there was no beating or verbal abuse, Ha said. “The instructors spoke politely, because with weapons right there, pointing a gun the wrong way during training could turn deadly.”

But the hardest part mentally was the surveillance. “Once you go in, you can’t come out. They tell you it’s for two or three years, but that’s just talk. The state controlled us with no rule of law, and everyone knew the contract meant nothing.”

Once you go in, you can’t come out

Ha Tae-jun, former agent

The surveillance did not end with his discharge. Every time he moved and had a home phone installed, he would get a call asking if the move went well. To him, it meant he was still being watched, and knowing that made him instinctively withdraw.

That caution carried over to the operations themselves. Asked whether he had ever gone into North Korea, Ha said: “No comment.”

He added that no one who crossed over after the South-North joint statement on July 4, 1972, would ever tell. In that statement, the two Koreas agreed on principles for unification and pledged to stop sending armed agents into each other’s territory.

Licence to kill

The training reshaped more than what he could say. Learning to kill without hesitation, steal and blow things up turned Ha’s personality cruel. Three years of isolation ended with his discharge. To his family, he had simply vanished and reappeared.

“I went to my sister’s house. She and her husband asked where I’d been all this time without a word,” he said. “Just as I was trained to say, I told them I’d been out on a deep-sea fishing boat.”

Not long after, more trouble surfaced. One day, police showed up and tried to handcuff him. At the station, it turned out he had been considered a long-term missing person. During his years as an agent, he had also never once attended reserve forces training.

“If you skipped reserve forces training, you got hit with heavy fines. I later looked at my training record card, and for years there was a record of me being indicted.”

That indictment record made his return to society far harder. A month after he got a job at Samsung Electronics, the general affairs office showed him the record and asked for an explanation. He could not give one and was fired.

“The state abandoned the promise of a stable job to people who had their whole future ahead of them,” Ha said, adding that most former agents, like him, ended up with criminal records and could not find proper work.

In 2004, a law providing compensation and recognition for former infiltration agents was passed, but Ha said it was not enough.

“There should have been a fact-finding committee to determine how much we contributed and suffered, but none existed. Bereaved families don’t know whether their father, child or sibling went on an infiltration mission. The state didn’t notify them for decades whether the person was dead or alive. It treated us as expendable.”

For Ha, what the state owes its agents is more respect and sincerity.

“In the United States, people are given the highest respect the moment they put on the uniform. Is that really true in South Korea? The state needs to properly carry out the work of finding the bereaved families of North Korea infiltration agents.”

This article was first published by The Korea Times

item.title: [SCMP] Why US visa pause could have ‘real consequences’ for Asian applicants
item.description:
Asian workers and families already facing years-long waits for US visas could be pushed deeper into uncertainty by a global pause on immigrant visa appointments, as President Donald Trump’s administration tightens legal immigration through new screening and higher costs, experts warn.

The US State Department on Tuesday said it had launched a global training initiative for consular officers at all US embassies and consulates, and that immigrant visa appointments would be adjusted to accommodate it.

The department did not specify the scope or duration of the training, beyond saying it was intended to help officers screen out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on US public benefits and ensure they were evaluated “comprehensively and consistently”.
item.content:encoded:
Asian workers and families already facing years-long waits for US visas could be pushed deeper into uncertainty by a global pause on immigrant visa appointments, as President Donald Trump’s administration tightens legal immigration through new screening and higher costs, experts warn.

The US State Department on Tuesday said it had launched a global training initiative for consular officers at all US embassies and consulates, and that immigrant visa appointments would be adjusted to accommodate it.

The department did not specify the scope or duration of the training, beyond saying it was intended to help officers screen out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on US public benefits and ensure they were evaluated “comprehensively and consistently”.

Immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates have begun receiving notices that their appointments are being rescheduled, with new dates to follow, according to reports.

The disruption has left applicants uncertain not only about when they will be interviewed, but also whether documents tied to existing appointment dates – including police clearances, medical checks and financial records – will need updating.

For Asian applicants, experts say, the impact could be especially acute in countries with large visa pipelines and already crowded consular calendars.

“It’s not clear if this is being handled embassy by embassy or centrally. The Asian countries with the largest number of pending applications will likely be hit the hardest,” said Russell A. Stamets, a partner at the New Delhi-based law firm Circle of Counsels.

Srinivasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at the Indic Researchers Forum, said the immediate hit for Asian applicants was cancellation notices and open-ended waits, as no restart date was given.

“In high-volume places like India, the Philippines and Vietnam, where family queues already stretch years, this is unlikely to be a few days’ blip. It risks months of cascading delays as slots get rebooked amid heavier screening. India, with its massive skilled and family pipeline, stands especially exposed and will feel the backlog first,” he said.

The appointment pause announcement came a day after the Department of Homeland Security proposed a new US$103,265 fee for H-1B petitions subject to the annual cap – a move that could sharply increase the cost of hiring skilled foreign workers and is expected to hit Chinese and Indian professionals particularly hard.

Immigrant visas cover permanent migration, including family reunification and some employment-based categories, while H-1B visas are temporary skilled-worker visas.

Experts said the US moves suggested employment-based applicants could face particular scrutiny, even as family cases risked being swept into broader appointment delays.

“It’s possible that employment-based applicants will be treated differently than simple family reunification applicants. Taken together with the renewed push to add at least US$100,000 per visa for employment-based visas, there may be further implications for this type of applicant,” Stamets said.

Balakrishnan warned employment-based applicants would face “real consequences”, including postponed interviews, stalled careers, frozen job offers and prolonged uncertainty for highly skilled talent America still needs.

Washington’s move implied that family reunification cases from the Philippines, Vietnam, China and especially India would be among the hardest hit because those categories already dominated immigrant visa caseloads and waiting lists, Balakrishnan said.

Hoang Lan Anh, an Australia-based academic who has studied Vietnamese overseas migration, said US-bound Vietnamese applicants were concentrated mainly in student, skilled or employment-based visas and family sponsorship.

“Because these applicants – particularly student and skilled-visa applicants – tend to come from middle- and upper-class backgrounds, I wouldn’t expect this pause to trigger major economic shocks for the applicant pool itself, in the way a similar disruption might affect lower-income labour migrants elsewhere,” Anh said.

But the sudden halt could still significantly disrupt individual plans for study, work or family reunification, she said. “These are not abstract inconveniences, but plans people have built their lives around, sometimes over years.”

The consequences could be especially acute for family-sponsorship visas, which Anh said were often the outcome of years or even decades of planning, saving and coordination across generations.

“When processing queues are suddenly frozen, the immediate fallout is less about a single missed deadline than about the collapse of a whole scaffold of interdependent decisions built around an expected timeline,” Anh said.

“Families lose not just time, but also the ability to plan with any confidence at all.”

Those planning costs could quickly become financial ones if the pause lasts long enough for immigration documents to expire.

A Philippines-based immigration lawyer and lecturer, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, said the costs could be especially burdensome for family-based applicants because many documents required for US immigration cases were valid only for limited periods.

“Many US immigration requirements are supported by documents that are valid for only six months or other limited periods,” the lawyer said. “As a result, the reopening itself does not provide relief from document validity requirements, and affected applicants may be required to obtain and submit updated documentation at their own expense.”

Stamets agreed, saying: “Since the entire thrust of the administration’s immigration policy is to make immigration more difficult and expensive except for a favoured few classes and categories of people, I would anticipate that any time-sensitive documentation will need to be updated.”

The larger concern, Balakrishnan warned, was that the pause could be followed by a “permanently slower, more subjective process that could reshape legal immigration from Asia for years”.

Administration versus judiciary

The training is explicitly tied to public-charge screening, a US immigration law assessment of whether an applicant is likely to depend on certain government benefits.

That rationale has also placed the appointment pause in the middle of a wider legal and political fight over the Trump administration’s immigration agenda.

“A pause like this rarely translates into a short, contained disruption. Consular sections typically batch and schedule interviews weeks or months in advance, so even a brief suspension forces a backlog that takes far longer to clear than the pause,” said Amritraj Kaushal, an advocate in India’s Supreme Court.

Vivek Mishra, deputy director of strategic studies at the Observer Research Foundation, said the latest move appeared to be part of a showdown between the administration and the US judiciary.

A federal judge on Friday struck down a ban on visas for immigrants from 75 countries, finding it was contrary to law and outside the statutory authority of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The State Department had paused the issuance of immigrant visas from almost 40 per cent of the world’s nations in a move that it said would prevent the entry of people who would “take welfare and public benefits”.

The Philippines-based lawyer said the shift from a country-specific suspension to a worldwide training pause “appears to be an attempt to sidestep” the federal court ruling that barred nationality-based discrimination.

The State Department would still have to comply with the court’s ruling, but a legal block on the 75-country policy might not prevent consular officers from applying stricter scrutiny to otherwise eligible applicants, the lawyer said.

Mishra called the visa pause a “doubling down” by the US administration. “They are saying we are going ahead with a broader mandate this time. They are giving the alibi that consulates need training, which might be true.”

He predicted the US would issue new guidance and standard operating procedures to its embassies, resulting in more stringent visa checks.

“If they see what they consider as a red flag, it will reduce your chances of a visa,” he said.

Even if appointments resume, experts say the larger concern is that applicants could return to a system in which officers have wider discretion to reject cases under public charge and other screening rules.

Additional reporting by Vincent Tan and Sam Beltran

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore’s future island plan stirs concern over reefs and old fishing grounds
item.description:
Few have spent as much time in the waters surrounding Singapore’s southwestern islands as fisherman Hamzah Mohamad, 71.

The former resident of Pulau Sudong has been fishing, primarily by setting up bubu – wire fish traps in Malay – in the rocky coral reefs surrounding Sudong, Bukom and Semakau for more than half a century.

He knows the underwater reefs by heart, what the wind changes mean for visibility and which fish species are in season.
item.content:encoded:
Few have spent as much time in the waters surrounding Singapore’s southwestern islands as fisherman Hamzah Mohamad, 71.

The former resident of Pulau Sudong has been fishing, primarily by setting up bubu – wire fish traps in Malay – in the rocky coral reefs surrounding Sudong, Bukom and Semakau for more than half a century.

He knows the underwater reefs by heart, what the wind changes mean for visibility and which fish species are in season.

But the seascape he has long known may be set for another transformation.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced plans on Sunday to form a new island in the coming decades for industry, energy and defence needs by merging islands including Semakau, Bukom and Sudong, similar to how Singapore joined smaller islands through land reclamation to create the energy and chemicals hub Jurong Island.

Delivering his National Day Rally speech, Wong said: “Jurong Island shaped our economy for the last fifty years. This new western island can help shape Singapore for the next 50 years and beyond.”

Wong framed the proposal as part of Singapore’s long-term approach to land use, saying the city state had to plan over decades to create options for future generations while balancing development with green spaces, biodiversity and heritage.

The proposed western island, he said, could support advanced manufacturing, new power generation infrastructure and defence needs, while a new link would connect Jurong Island with the future island.

For former islanders, environmental groups and marine advocates, the long-term plan has raised questions over how Singapore can balance future land needs with coral reefs, access to fishing grounds and its remaining maritime traditions.

The islands were once home to hundreds of residents who made a living mainly as fishermen and had to relocate to mainland Singapore in the 1970s when their islands were earmarked for redevelopment.

Sudong has since become a military live-firing zone with an airstrip, while Semakau was joined with the smaller island of Pulau Seking to form a landfill and Bukom houses an oil refinery.

Since 1991, there have been proposals to increase the land mass surrounding the three islands under Singapore’s long-term plan from the Urban Redevelopment Authority. In the 2011 edition of the plan, the islands were earmarked for “possible future reclamation”. As of the latest plan dated 2022, the islands were not merged.

Former islanders, non-governmental organisations and environmentalists said they were concerned about what the project could mean for coral reefs and their former home, with some telling This Week in Asia they feared it could become another example of nature, memory and maritime heritage giving way to development.

The Straits Times quoted Huang Danwei, director of the National Institute for Marine and Ocean Sciences, as saying reefs in Pulau Hantu and Semakau dated back about 8,000 years and that there was “no mitigation” for reefs directly buried by land reclamation.

A Ministry of National Development spokesman told This Week in Asia that the government recognised the biodiversity value of the western islands and their surrounding waters, and was studying the plans carefully to prepare ahead and create options for the future.

He said “technical studies” would be conducted to guide the development plans, including the reclamation profile.

Feasibility studies, site investigations and surveys, as well as engineering and environmental studies, would also be undertaken to better understand possible development options and their preliminary impact on biodiversity and hydrodynamics.

The government would “engage stakeholders early” and consider their feedback before launching the studies and work. Their knowledge and expertise would be tapped to assess potential biodiversity impact and identify measures to avoid and mitigate effects where possible, he added.

Firdaus Sani, founder of non-governmental organisation Orang Laut SG, told This Week in Asia that the indigenous orang pulau, or island people, and orang laut, or people from the sea, communities felt overlooked and helpless about whether they could still have access to the southern waters.

“If you were to look at it from a different perspective of indigenous associations outside Singapore, indigenous spaces and viewpoints might be treated more seriously. Now it seems like the priority is more an economic one, as we’re not even consulted about the plans, which is a shame,” he added.

Han Jok Kwang, 72, a former resident of Bukom and a business development adviser, was concerned about the sea life surrounding the islands, having spent his first 16 years on the island.

“My level-headed brain is telling me that humans need to take care of humans, but I worry about the rich marine life there,” said Han, whose grandmother was a resident of neighbouring Semakau.

“It’s a very big project, and it’ll probably take so long to build that nobody will be upset any more by the time it opens,” he added.

End of bubu fishing?

Several former residents from Sudong, like Hamzah, regularly take boats out to fish in the area surrounding their former homes using the bubu traps, traditionally made using materials such as bamboo or rattan, to earn an income – a vanishing trade in modern Singapore.

Firdaus said: “What happens to the community’s livelihood? What happens to history, memory, waterways that we remember and that we know, and some of the places that we deem sacred? Some of the islands also have deep roots to these spaces, more than a physical sense. There are a lot of these things that have not been considered.”

If the islands and surrounding waterways were reclaimed, the fishing grounds would disappear as well, he said.

“It’s literally erasing an entire fishing and maritime culture that we still have a connection to. It’s the only thing that they had left.”

While their origins are unclear, bubu traps are an indigenous craft practised by the early Malay and local islander communities like the orang laut for generations, long before Singapore’s independence in 1965. Maritime communities throughout Southeast Asia also use the device for fishing.

At West Coast Park, Hamzah and other former islanders have built makeshift shelters over the years along a fenced-up beach area where they keep their bubu traps and moor their boats.

He and his brother, Ahmad Sah Mohamad, known in the community as the Sudong brothers, spend most days under their shelters weaving their bubu traps and make a weekly pilgrimage to the waters around Sudong to collect their catch and replace traps – a traditional way of life that has been passed down through generations. They are not allowed to go near the island or land as it is a restricted area.

“Once this place is gone, I’ll have to learn almost everything again because I know these places so well, and how the water is like here and what kind of fish are in season here. I don’t know if there will be other coral reefs we can go to,” Hamzah said.

The retired contractor hopes the waters remain open for fishing as he relies on it for income, and that there will still be rocky coral reefs in the area for him to place bubu traps.

“I don’t know what I’ll do if the area is closed off. If I have to go somewhere else, it has to be somewhere with coral reefs because that’s the only way you can really place a bubu,” Hamzah said.

Orang Laut SG’s Firdaus said he was not hopeful about prospects for the traditional fishing practice.

“The truth of the matter is I don’t know. We could continue to try, as a way of preserving cultural heritage, but it’s not going to be truly a living heritage. It’s really going to be how museums are – static and remaining in the past,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea hands police more power even as dead bodies expose the lies
item.description:
On a farm up in the hills of South Korea’s Jeju Island, investigators this week uncovered what a mother had spent three months fearing they would not find: the body of her daughter.

Jang Mi-ran, 37, vanished without a trace in May. Police records would later show her case had been quietly closed without anyone ever verifying if she was alive.

It was the second such discovery in a matter of days. The first was the skeletal remains of a man in his sixties, found on Saturday after his family warned officers he had spoken of suicide and left his children a farewell message.
item.content:encoded:
On a farm up in the hills of South Korea’s Jeju Island, investigators this week uncovered what a mother had spent three months fearing they would not find: the body of her daughter.

Jang Mi-ran, 37, vanished without a trace in May. Police records would later show her case had been quietly closed without anyone ever verifying if she was alive.

It was the second such discovery in a matter of days. The first was the skeletal remains of a man in his sixties, found on Saturday after his family warned officers he had spoken of suicide and left his children a farewell message.

Both cases had passed through the hands of the same officer, identified only by his surname Bu, who allegedly told worried relatives he had personally traced and spoken to the missing individuals – conversations investigators say never took place.

What began as a local scandal on the southern resort island has since turned into a far larger debate, on whether South Korea’s national police force is fit to inherit the sweeping investigative powers it is about to receive.

A president’s rebuke

“The recent breakdown in police discipline and irresponsibility in public safety matters have become serious problems,” President Lee Jae Myung told a cabinet meeting on Tuesday in response to the scandal, demanding the creation of a dedicated government body to police the police.

He spoke days after signing into law revisions to South Korea’s Criminal Procedure Act that will, from October, strip prosecutors of their remaining investigative powers and hand much greater authority to the police – the culmination of a decades-long campaign to cut the prosecution service down to size.

“Going forward, the police may exercise the greatest power among government agencies,” Lee said, noting that people were deeply concerned about the change.

“Power, when concentrated, always creates problems. The level of responsibility should be strengthened to match the extent of the authority.”

He acknowledged the public’s “scepticism” about whether the country’s police were equipped to wield such extensive authority responsibly – scepticism that has only grown as more details of the Jeju cases have come to light.

“Problems involving police discipline are not something that started yesterday or today,” Lee said. “Given the sheer size of the police force, problems can arise in many places, but we need both preventive measures and solutions.”

For the president, the failures were structural. “The police are a hierarchical organisation in which following orders is extremely important and command responsibility is therefore crucial,” he said.

“If a frontline officer is at fault, can the matter really end with disciplining that individual? If so, what is the command structure for? … Those who have the authority to command must also naturally bear responsibility commensurate with that authority.”

It’s high time for this country to overhaul the police

Choi Jin, Institute of Presidential Leadership

Compounding matters is a second scandal that unfolded in Gwangju, where a police inspector was arrested in July on suspicion of destroying evidence during the investigation of a high-profile murder whose suspect happens to be the son of a senior police official.

“These incidents reveal the shocking laxity in police discipline and accountability,” Choi Jin, head of the Institute of Presidential Leadership, told This Week in Asia.

“It’s high time for this country to overhaul the police, focusing on enhancing accountability and oversight, improving command and control, and strengthening investigative capabilities.”

Fabricated calls

Public anger has only grown since details of the Jeju disappearances began to emerge in mid-August.

Jang’s boyfriend reported her missing in May. Yet he says when he asked for updates, Bu told him she had been found and spoken to, but did not want her whereabouts shared

That was a fabrication, investigators allege: phone records show no such call was ever made. Bu is accused of instead deleting Jang’s file from the missing-persons system altogether, apparently to keep his unresolved-case count low.

An autopsy on the body recovered from the Jeju palm farm on Monday confirmed it was Jang. Police believe the circumstances suggest she may have taken her own life following a dispute with her boyfriend – the same dispute that had preceded her initial disappearance.

The man in his sixties suffered an almost identical fate. His family had explicitly warned police he was suicidal, but Bu allegedly closed that case too – again after supposedly claiming contact had been made.

The man’s remains were only located after the case was reopened.

Bu has since been placed under arrest and all four officer in his chain of command at Jeju Seobu Police Station have been suspended pending further investigations.

It has since emerged that Bu was previously investigated over an alleged bathroom intrusion and questioned in connected with suspected domestic violence, fuelling questions about how he remained on frontline duty.

‘Painful reform’

Analysts say the case reflects a structural blind spot rather than a single officer’s failures.

Lee Keon-su, a professor in Baekseok University’s Department of Police Science, pointed to a loophole: under current police rules, missing adults were typically treated as “runaways” – a category with non of the urgency reserved for cases involving people with intellectual disabilities or dementia.

“Sloppy initial responses, such as the false closure of Jang’s disappearance case, are entirely possible occurrences within the current system,” he said.

Bae Sang-hoon, a psychological analyst with more than 20 years’ experience in criminal profiling , argues that the fix must come from outside the chain of command itself.

“A system must be established to allow a third-party agency to look into and monitor police investigations into missing-person cases,” he said.

Political scientist Jhee Byong-kuen of Chosun University traced the deeper malaise to internal culture. He said promotion decision that hinged on the goodwill of superiors created fertile ground for exactly the kind of corner-cutting alleged in Jeju.

“Transparency and oversight are the two key words for police reform,” Jhee said.

The issue has since migrated to the National Assembly, South Korea’s parliament.

Han Byung-do, floor leader of the ruling Democratic Party, told a parliamentary meeting on Tuesday that “painful reform” was needed.

“The police are now at the final test of whether they can regain the public’s trust,” Han said.

For a force about to inherit more power than it has held in decades, the pressure is on to rebuild that relationship.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines eyes drones and ‘system of systems’ to boost asymmetric defence
item.description:
Facing a far larger Chinese military presence at sea, the Philippines is looking to drones not as a substitute for warships and aircraft but as a relatively low-cost way to make its forces harder to find, suppress and outmanoeuvre, analysts have said.

The administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr has focused on expanding the military’s drone fleet as part of its external defence strategy. Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr told lawmakers on Tuesday that Manila also needed to secure communications, artificial intelligence and operational networks to integrate unmanned systems into military operations.

During a House appropriations committee hearing on the Department of National Defence’s proposed budget, Teodoro said the initiative would be funded through a proposed 50 billion-peso (US$810 million) allocation for military modernisation in 2027, a 25 per cent increase from this year’s budget.
item.content:encoded:
Facing a far larger Chinese military presence at sea, the Philippines is looking to drones not as a substitute for warships and aircraft but as a relatively low-cost way to make its forces harder to find, suppress and outmanoeuvre, analysts have said.

The administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr has focused on expanding the military’s drone fleet as part of its external defence strategy. Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr told lawmakers on Tuesday that Manila also needed to secure communications, artificial intelligence and operational networks to integrate unmanned systems into military operations.

During a House appropriations committee hearing on the Department of National Defence’s proposed budget, Teodoro said the initiative would be funded through a proposed 50 billion-peso (US$810 million) allocation for military modernisation in 2027, a 25 per cent increase from this year’s budget.

“We have to integrate the capabilities and have proper working procedures in using them,” Teodoro said. “We currently have a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles, which provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance services for us. As we mature on the cycle, then we can acquire more.”

Acquiring drones was not the main challenge, he said, the more sensitive issue involved the systems they carried and the capabilities those systems could provide.

“Initially, we have to have the connectivity and the network capabilities to operate them as real time as possible … Connectivity and the security of connectivity is paramount for us,” he added, noting they were in “close contact” with several countries with drone expertise.

Analysts said Manila’s shift towards asymmetric external defence and integrated operations increased the strategic importance of acquiring low-cost, high-utility drones and strengthening its cyber capabilities.

“Drone development entails sustainable effort on subsidising local research and development, optimising technology transfers and building indigenous capability,” Chester Cabalza, president and chief executive of the Manila-based International Development and Security Cooperation think tank, told This Week in Asia.

“The Armed Forces of the Philippines is looking to Ukraine’s development of an indigenous drone capability as a model. Rather than relying solely on expensive conventional hardware, locally produced drones could support asymmetric maritime deterrence, with aerial and maritime drones serving as force multipliers.”

South China Sea concerns

Justin Kyle Malarayap, a visiting assistant professor at Arellano University in Manila, said the Philippines was building networks to support drone operations in preparation for a potential South China Sea contingency.

“As we’ve seen recently, the Philippines has been interacting with Ukraine, the US and Japan to build these networks and capabilities to improve Philippine joint military operations,” he said.

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and chief executive of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a Canadian foreign policy think tank, agreed that drones could serve as force multipliers.

She said the significance of Teodoro’s disclosure was that Manila was treating drones as part of a “system of systems” connecting unmanned platforms with sensors, secure communications, command-and-control networks, ships, aircraft and land-based missile systems.

“That is consistent with the Philippines’ broader Comprehensive Archipelagic Defence Concept. The lesson from Ukraine and other recent conflicts is that a drone is only as valuable as the network behind it,” Nadjibulla said.

The archipelagic concept is Manila’s framework for shifting its military focus towards external defence across the country’s territory, maritime zones and approaches.

Manila and Kyiv are reportedly in discussions to advance an October 2025 initiative to pursue drone co-production, a proposed partnership that could combine Ukraine’s battle-tested technology with the Philippines’ transition towards a more agile, technology-driven defence posture.

The Philippine military currently operates unmanned systems across all three service branches for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and emerging combat missions.

The army uses Elbit THOR and commercial DJI drones, while the air force operates Hermes 450 and 900 platforms. The navy and marine corps deploy ScanEagle drones for maritime surveillance and are developing unmanned surface and underwater systems.

In April, the air force and its government and industry partners also unveiled locally developed autonomous, loitering and armed drones for reconnaissance and precision-strike missions.

Discussing Manila’s drone expansion, Teodoro said the priority was integrating the systems into military operations, including the secure communications and network capabilities needed for effective use.

Multi-year investment

Building that integrated architecture, however, requires sustained funding.

Nadjibulla said the proposed allocation was insufficient to develop the full defence network Manila ultimately needed, adding that credible deterrence would require multi-year investment rather than the occasional acquisition of individual platforms.

“It can build a significantly better and operationally useful network in the near term. The priority has to be resilience and redundancy. Partners can substantially accelerate that process,” Nadjibulla said.

Philippine allies such as the US, Japan and Australia were coordinating investments in sensors, information-sharing systems and cybersecurity, while Canada was providing maritime domain awareness capabilities such as “dark vessel detection”, Nadjibulla said.

“The Philippines does not need technological parity with China. It needs sufficient awareness, resilience and distributed capability to complicate Chinese military planning and strengthen deterrence by denial,” she said.

However, achieving such capabilities will require Manila to make difficult spending decisions.

Malarayap said persistent financial constraints were forcing the government to prioritise military projects based on their demonstrated combat effectiveness and evolving threat assessments.

Yet he was optimistic that Manila could build the communications and operational networks needed to make unmanned systems effective in a near-term conflict.

The Philippine military was prioritising communications systems to improve its response to natural disasters and security contingencies, and thereby boost archipelagic logistics, Malarayap said.

Cabalza was more cautious, saying Manila’s AI-enabled surveillance and command-and-control capabilities were limited, but increased defence funding could help the armed forces address those gaps.

“This is a David vs Goliath scenario of UAVs. While military armaments are key to war success, strategy places the best part in its execution. The world has not yet seen a sea battle of swarming UAVs,” Cabalza said.

For Nadjibulla, unmanned systems could help offset the advantage of China’s much larger fleet but could not eliminate it, and that disparity was precisely why drones and other unmanned platforms made strategic sense for the Philippines.

“China will retain an overwhelming numerical advantage in ships and aircraft, so Manila cannot realistically compete platform for platform,” Nadjibulla said.

“Drones offer a relatively inexpensive way to generate persistent surveillance, distribute sensors across a very large maritime area and make Philippine forces harder to find and suppress.”

item.title: [SCMP] How China’s anti-corruption fight became Xi Jinping’s most important policy
item.description:
The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the first part of a series accompanying the data project, Phoebe Zhang looks at how the campaign became one of the Communist Party’s most important policies.

In the early years of President Xi Jinping’s first term, when graft fighters were taking down senior officials in ways that raised eyebrows, Chinese authorities constantly had to remind the public that the anti-corruption campaign was not “just a gust of wind”.

At that point, Beijing had already locked up dozens of senior officials, including Zhou Yongkang, a former member of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, the highest echelon in China’s political hierarchy. Before his downfall in 2013, Zhou had been one of China’s most influential politicians.
item.content:encoded:
The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the first part of a series accompanying the data project, Phoebe Zhang looks at how the campaign became one of the Communist Party’s most important policies.

In the early years of President Xi Jinping’s first term, when graft fighters were taking down senior officials in ways that raised eyebrows, Chinese authorities constantly had to remind the public that the anti-corruption campaign was not “just a gust of wind”.

At that point, Beijing had already locked up dozens of senior officials, including Zhou Yongkang, a former member of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, the highest echelon in China’s political hierarchy. Before his downfall in 2013, Zhou had been one of China’s most influential politicians.

Concerns were so widespread that the anti-corruption push would be a flash in the pan, especially at the local level, that Wang Qishan, then the party’s top anti-corruption chief, warned that local governments might fall back on temporary “movement-style” crackdowns.

A decade later, few need convincing as the anti-corruption fight expands, netting record numbers of senior officials and unearthing new types of graft involving cryptocurrency schemes and clandestine proxies.

A new analysis by the South China Morning Post found that the campaign has widened since its inception. Last year, anti-corruption agencies handed down punishments to 983,000 people, with the fallout ranging from mild warnings to investigations and criminal prosecution. The number of senior officials taken down last year was three times that of 2013.

The SCMP’s data bank project also found that from 2013 to 2025, 60 per cent of senior officials felled by China’s anti-corruption drive were serving in regional governments. The campaign has hit provincial administrations particularly hard, with resource-rich areas – notably Jiangxi, Liaoning, Shanxi and Hebei provinces, as well as Inner Mongolia, autonomous region – recording the highest number of dismissals.

What began as a crackdown on economic graft has evolved into a systemic overhaul of bureaucratic conduct. While bribery remains the main legal charge, the definition of corruption has expanded to include party discipline and adherence to policy directives.

By now, most experts agree that the anti-corruption campaign is among Xi’s most important policies, and one that is key to his vision of China’s future and the party’s ability to rule for generations to come.

And the party has shown no interest in pulling any punches.

During a January meeting of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, the party’s top anti-graft body, Xi declared that “the situation in the fight against corruption remains grave and complex”, urging officials to come up with new methods to discover, identify and tackle all types of wrongdoing.

Just last month, China’s top leadership announced that party governance would be the focus of the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee, expected to be held in October. This meeting is likely to be the party’s most important gathering ahead of its 21st national congress in autumn of next year. The five-yearly party congress is likely to feature a leadership reshuffle and the endorsement of a fourth term for Xi.

In a Xinhua report on the coming plenary session, the Politburo said party self-governance “faces new circumstances and challenges” and called for “consistently exercising full and rigorous governance over the party” – a phrase that typically means fighting corruption and tightening party discipline.

No end point

While generations of Communist Party leaders have pledged to uproot corruption, Xi has tried to convince the country from the outset that his fight is different.

In 2013, at the second plenary session of the party’s 18th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), Xi pledged to fight “tigers and flies at the same time” – targeting not only high-ranking officials but also misconduct at the grass-roots level – to underscore a policy of “no forbidden zones, full coverage and zero tolerance”.

Soon, Beijing introduced a set of “eight-point austerity rules” to restrict party cadre behaviour. These include banning the use of luxury cars and gifts, banning red carpets, floral arrangements and grand receptions during inspections, simplifying meetings, reducing unnecessary documents and limiting overseas visits.

The rules are still in effect today.

The anti-corruption campaign has deepened and broadened to cover all policy areas and sectors, including security, finance, education and the graft fighters themselves. In its first three years, it took down top leaders in all 31 provincial-level jurisdictions. The campaign has also hit the military’s top brass, especially in the past two years.

The push has become more institutionalised as well. In 2018, the National Supervisory Commission (NSC) was created and merged with the CCDI, giving the party’s anti-corruption campaign a legal basis.

Beijing has sought to supplement laws with party regulations. More than 70 per cent of the Communist Party’s regulations have been enacted since 2012.

China has also overhauled its corruption-fighting agencies to reflect a “vertical management” style, giving more oversight to higher authorities.

It has reinvented the inspection regime, inherited from Imperial China but largely inactive in the years before Xi, so inspectors dispatched from Beijing look for signs of corruption at the local level.

Over the past 14 years, Xi has repeatedly emphasised that his anti-corruption campaign has no end point, warning that no official should harbour any illusions of impunity.

At the 20th party congress in 2022, Xi said the anti-corruption fight should “never rest, not even for a minute”.

Staying disciplined

Corruption is the “greatest threat” facing the party, Xi said in a speech at the 19th party congress in 2017.

At times, he has argued that purging corruption is crucial for the Communist Party to escape China’s “historical cycles” of dynastic rise and collapse, and ensure its longevity.

Xi has said that corruption hinders governance and economic development. “If corruption is allowed to spread, it will eventually lead to the destruction of a party and the fall of a government,” he has warned.

Li Jian, a former researcher with the Publicity Department of the Central Committee, wrote in January that the reason that the party could not afford to lose the fight against corruption was because graft harmed the party’s vitality and ability to fight.

“[Corruption] seriously undermines fair and just market rules, distorts the efficiency of resource allocation, erodes the fruits of reform and development, and damages the business environment as well as social fairness and justice,” Li wrote. He concluded that there was a need to create a “sound political environment and a level playing field for high-quality development”.

“Combating corruption is like sailing against the current – if you do not advance, you will fall back,” said Zhiqun Zhu, a professor of political science and international relations at Bucknell University.

“Long-term goals such as rejuvenation of the Chinese nation or unification with Taiwan cannot be achieved any time soon, but the anti-corruption campaign has yielded concrete results, with a cleaner government, a more professional and efficient bureaucracy, and a more loyal and dedicated leadership team,” said Zhu, who is also director of Bucknell’s China Institute.
