Alfred Wu, associate professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy at the National University of Singapore, said Xi’s views on corruption were shared by his predecessors, though they never pushed the fight to the same level.

“Jiang Zemin had repeatedly said that ‘anti-corruption is a serious political struggle that matters to the life and death of the party and the nation’, while Hu Jintao said at the 18th party congress that failure to tackle the issue could prove fatal to the party,” he said, referring to China’s previous two presidents.

Beijing has also made the enforcement of its strategies part of the anti-corruption campaign.

The latest revision of party disciplinary regulations explicitly prohibits failing to implement the “new concept for development and high-quality development” – Beijing’s term for its new growth model, coined after Xi came to power.

This violation has been mentioned in the investigation findings of a handful of disgraced senior officials, including Lan Tianli, the former party secretary of Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, who was investigated last year.

Devendra Kumar, an associate fellow at the Centre of Excellence for Himalayan Studies at Shiv Nadar University, said the corruption-fighting efforts under Xi were ultimately about discipline.

“In this context, anti-corruption in China cannot be understood in the narrow sense of deviations from institutional rules and laws,” he said.

“Rather, it is fundamentally about ‘discipline’, which encompasses not only compliance with regulations but also officials’ political disposition and, increasingly, aspects of their family life, including whom they associate with, where family members work, and where they travel.”

Kumar added that the campaign was aimed at enforcing the party’s agenda and preferred modes of thinking through measures such as the campaign on the correct view of political performance, which began in March.

With local governments across China preparing for a leadership shuffle, Xi said a “correct view” of performance was particularly vital to ensure new appointments prioritised long-term public benefit over short-term vanity projects.

According to Xinhua, local party leaders were tasked with the “top priority” of implementing top leadership’s decisions with “unwavering focus”.

Party discipline also figures heavily in “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building”, a new branch of the Chinese leader’s political thought unveiled in June. Its key tenets include insistence on “a centralised, unified leadership of the party Central Committee” as well as “full and rigorous party self-governance” and ensuring that “officials do not have the audacity, opportunity or desire to commit corruption”.

Kumar added that there were similarities between Xi and his predecessors’ signature policies in that they all aimed to extend party rule and impose discipline.

For example, he said, Mao launched the “continuous revolution” – an ideological extension of the civil war the party won in 1949 – to prevent the party from becoming a stagnant bureaucracy. Xi, by contrast, sees bureaucratisation as a key remedy, with anti-corruption as a tool to fix the problems arising from the party’s organisational structure, according to Kumar.

Communist Party institutions lack mechanisms such as public oversight and transparency to foster bottom-up accountability. As a result, he said, top-down methods of enforcing discipline and accountability were necessary for maintaining order and preventing deviations from established regulations and norms, even during periods of weak leadership.

Xi laid bare some of those concerns in the report he delivered at the 20th party congress in 2022.

He said that China had made great achievements as a result of reform, opening up and socialist modernisation, but “a number of prominent issues and problems – some of which had been building for years and others which were just emerging – demanded urgent action”.

Among them, there were a “lack of clear understanding and effective action as well as a slide towards weak, hollow and watered-down party leadership in practice”, according to the Chinese leader. He added that despite repeated warnings, ills including pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance persisted.

Another problem Xi saw as serious was “privilege-seeking mindsets and practices”, with some “deeply shocking cases of corruption”.

“The intensity with which Xi has pursued disciplinary campaigns must be understood in context,” Kumar said.

“When Xi came to power, party institutions were not sufficiently effective in ‘caging’ cadres in their day-to-day functioning, and cadres’ ideological commitment was also considered weak.”

He noted there were structural reasons for the campaign to continue, as it had become part of Xi’s broader agenda of revitalising the party, both ideologically and institutionally, and the anti-corruption campaign and institutional changes of the past decade had embedded a “disciplinary regime” into the party’s day-to-day governance.

“Consequently, we should expect an intensification of anti-corruption efforts in the run-up to the 21st party congress,” Kumar said.

item.title: [SCMP] A rural city, once known for livestock, now provides China’s AI computing fuel
item.description:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.

As the global artificial intelligence boom fuels a scramble for more computing power and electricity, the same climate that has sustained Ulanqab’s pastoral economy is turning this Inner Mongolian city into one of China’s most coveted industrial assets.

Earlier this month, Chinese renewable energy company Envision Group brought its Galaxy Campus online in Ulanqab. The AI computing facility has, at its heart, a 120,000-square-metre AI data centre, roughly the area of 20 standard football pitches, according to a company statement.

Designed to accommodate up to one million AI accelerators, the campus has a planned power capacity of over two gigawatts, a scale that would make it one of the world’s largest AI computing facilities.

For comparison, Colossus 2, the massive US-based AI data centre run by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, has a projected 1.5-gigawatt IT power capacity, according to a ranking by consultancy Epoch AI.

Envision selected the Ulanqab location because it could pair computing infrastructure directly with renewable power, with the Galaxy Campus partly powered by Envision wind farms, according to the firm.

Ulanqab accounts for about one-tenth of China’s total wind resources and one-third of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region’s, according to China’s Xinhua news agency.

“Much of that wind once simply blew past, wasted,” said Yang Wenlong, a project director at Envision Group. “Now it can be turned into electricity for computing, and then into tokens.”

About 67 per cent of Ulanqab’s energy was powered by green electricity, including solar power, Yang noted.

A decade-long pivot

Ulanqab’s shift from raising cattle and potato harvesting to the AI frontier has followed a decade-long path.

In 2013, Huawei Technologies began working with the Ulanqab municipal government to expand its data centre presence there. Five years later, US tech giant Apple announced plans to host its iCloud service on data centres in the city, the same year Chinese cloud platform UCloud began building its own facility in Ulanqab.

Short video giant Kuaishou initiated construction of a data centre in 2020, and completed the first phase of a centre designed for 300,000 servers several years later.

Traditional data centre operators VNET, Centrin Data and Chindata have since added green, AI-focused computing projects in Ulanqab, and Hangzhou-based AI model start-up DeepSeek was reportedly set to add one gigawatt of computing capacity in the city earlier this year.

As of June, Ulanqab had signed 89 data centre deals, 86 of which were AI computing projects, according to local government figures.

The city has a combined 12.5 gigawatts of capacity under development or planned, three times the 4.2 gigawatts projected for Johor, the southern state of Malaysia that has emerged as one of the largest data centre sites in the Asia-Pacific region, according to recent research by investment bank Goldman Sachs.

“We are no longer selling computing power; we are selling tokens,” said Liu Huansuo, deputy director of Ulanqab’s big data management bureau, referring to the industry’s preferred measure for the units of text processed by AI models.

China’s appetite for those tokens has exploded in recent years. Daily consumption rose from about 100 billion at the beginning of 2024 to 100 trillion by the end of 2025, before exceeding 140 trillion in March 2026, according to government data.

This surge in token demand is driving a greater need for the electricity and computing infrastructure required to produce them. For Ulanqab, the wind blowing across the grasslands is no longer merely an energy resource – it helps to power an AI query.

And every AI token comes with a cost.

The power economy

“Every one million tokens generated requires two to three kilowatt-hours of electricity,” said Luo Xiyong of data centre operator Zhonglian Data.

In Ulanqab, data centre operators have access to some of China’s cheapest power.

Rates vary by supply arrangement, but some operators have secured electricity for about 0.35 yuan (US$0.05) per kilowatt-hour, less than half the roughly 0.70 yuan charged in eastern provinces. Electricity can account for 60 to 70 per cent of a data centre’s operating costs, making even modest savings significant.

At full utilisation, a one-gigawatt AI computing centre might consume as much as 8.76 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity a year. Cutting the electricity cost by just 0.1 yuan per kilowatt-hour might reduce a centre’s annual power bill by about 876 million yuan.

For China’s burgeoning AI industry, which is still searching for viable ways to monetise its models, cheap power is no marginal advantage – it is a central part of the business model.

But it is only half the equation. The electricity consumed by computing equipment ultimately becomes heat that has to be removed.

That is how Ulanqab’s cold, dry climate provides another advantage. With an annual average temperature of about 5 degrees Celsius, the city can use outside air as a natural cooling resource for much of the year, reducing reliance on energy-intensive mechanical systems and leaving more electricity available for computing.

Power usage effectiveness (PUE) measures the ratio between a data centre’s total electricity consumption and the electricity delivered to its servers. A PUE of 1.0 means every watt goes directly to computing, while a higher figure indicates more power is consumed by supporting systems such as cooling and power conversion.

Leading data-centre clusters in the region have a PUE below 1.15, against a national average of close to 1.5, meaning that more of each watt reaches its chips.

A difference of only a few cents can translate into hundreds of millions of yuan in savings at gigawatt scale. Those efficiencies matter because the amount of electricity consumed by computing has been rapidly rising.

China’s data centres consumed about 170 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 1.6 per cent of national power use, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA).

By 2030, annual consumption by the sector was expected to reach about 800 billion kilowatt-hours, nearly five times 2025 levels, and account for roughly 6 per cent of national electricity use, according to Wang Hongzhi, director of the NEA.

A coordinated system

The race to secure electricity for AI infrastructure is not unique to China. In the US, the rapid expansion of AI data centres has raised concerns about whether existing power grids can keep pace with demand, with some projects facing delays because of a bottleneck in securing enough electricity.

This is in contrast to Ulanqab, where AI giants and tech behemoths are betting that its wind and solar power, combined with a cooler climate, can provide a cheaper and more sustainable foundation for the next generation of AI infrastructure.

For China, the challenge is not only generating enough electricity, but also ensuring that electricity supply and computing capacity grow in tandem.

In 2026, China’s Government Work Report called for the coordinated development of computing capacity and electricity supply for the first time, reflecting Beijing’s push to better align its rapidly expanding AI infrastructure with the country’s power system.

The concept, known as “computing-power and electricity coordination”, aimed to bring together electricity generation, grid capacity, energy storage and computing resources so that renewable power could be used more efficiently to support growing AI demand.

Jiang Yi, spokesman for the National Development and Reform Commission, described the new power grid as providing stable, clean electricity, the computing network as the “brain” directing intelligent power-grid scheduling and renewable energy consumption, and the communications network as the “highway” supporting cross-regional computing.

That vision goes beyond simply building more data centres. It requires linking electricity, computing and communications infrastructure into a more coordinated, national system.

For Ulanqab, that could make its advantages more valuable. Its wind farms provide renewable electricity, data centres then convert that power into computing capacity, and a national network could help deliver that capacity to users far beyond Inner Mongolia.

But China’s computing boom has created another challenge: not all that capacity is being used.

While demand for AI computing is surging in some of the country’s biggest technology centres, large amounts of capacity elsewhere remain underused, leaving servers, power infrastructure and expensive data centre facilities running below their potential.

Data from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT) puts the gap in stark terms. In 2025, China’s intelligent-computing centres had about 3.8 billion card-hours of intelligent-computing capacity available, but only about 1.4 billion card-hours were actually used, putting utilisation at just 36.8 per cent.

CAICT has called for closer coordination between computing supply and demand, including better scheduling of computing resources and more precise matching between users and available capacity.

The mismatch reflects the geography of China’s computing buildout. Regions such as Ulanqab have attracted data centres because of cheap electricity, abundant land and favourable climates, while much of the demand for AI computing remains concentrated in China’s eastern cities and affluent regions, where technology companies and users are based.

Moving up the value chain

For Ulanqab, the next challenge is therefore not simply building more servers, but making sure those servers are connected to real demand.

The city is now seeking to move up the AI value chain. Under a three-year action plan for 2026-28, Ulanqab plans to expand computing capacity to more than 200,000 petaflops – a measurement of computing capacity – by 2026 and develop a platform for trading and settling AI tokens.

The plan calls for Ulanqab to evolve from a data centre hub into a broader computing and AI services centre, focusing on green computing for large AI model training and inference, while encouraging investment in liquid cooling, computing hardware, AI software and talent.

The aim is to capture more value from its renewable power: not simply selling electricity or computing capacity, but turning that power into AI computing and ultimately into the tokens generated by AI models.

For a user sitting thousands of kilometres away, an AI query may take only seconds to answer.

Behind that response, however, is a chain of infrastructure stretching back to places such as Ulanqab: servers drawing electricity, cooling systems removing heat and wind turbines turning the movement of air across the grasslands into power.

The next time someone asks a chatbot a question, part of the answer may begin with the wind passing through the grasslands of Inner Mongolia – transformed first into electricity, then computing power and finally into the words that appear on a screen.

item.title: [SCMP] Wall Street helped build modern China. But is it now being cast aside?
item.description:
For decades, Wall Street titans – from former Goldman Sachs chief Henry Paulson to Blackstone co-founder Stephen Schwarzman and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio – were hailed as “old friends of China”, feted by senior officials and granted rare access to the country’s top leadership.

Today, while American financiers continue to visit China and maintain commercial links, those private meetings with the top leadership have largely diminished, even as Beijing gradually opens its capital markets.

The shift has raised a crucial question for global investors: can Wall Street maintain its bridge to Beijing amid a changing US-China relationship?
item.content:encoded:
For decades, Wall Street titans – from former Goldman Sachs chief Henry Paulson to Blackstone co-founder Stephen Schwarzman and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio – were hailed as “old friends of China”, feted by senior officials and granted rare access to the country’s top leadership.

Today, while American financiers continue to visit China and maintain commercial links, those private meetings with the top leadership have largely diminished, even as Beijing gradually opens its capital markets.

The shift has raised a crucial question for global investors: can Wall Street maintain its bridge to Beijing amid a changing US-China relationship?

“The decline of such roles suggests they have stopped being useful,” said Christopher Marquis, Sinyi professor of Chinese management at Cambridge Judge Business School.

“China’s economy no longer needs foreign bankers’ capital and expertise the way it did 20-plus years ago.”

The “honeymoon period” for Wall Street and Beijing dates to China’s reform era in the late 1990s and 2000s, when Beijing relied heavily on foreign financial expertise to modernise its economy.

That era was epitomised by the 1995 establishment of China International Capital Corporation, the country’s first joint-venture investment bank, launched with Morgan Stanley to restructure state enterprises and build capital markets.

Goldman Sachs was another major beneficiary, paying US$2.58 billion for a stake in the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China in 2006 – then its largest-ever principal investment – and helping underwrite some of the country’s largest overseas listings. Others, including Morgan Stanley, built similarly close ties with Chinese banks and companies.

The partnership yielded massive returns. Alibaba Group Holding’s US$25 billion debut on the New York Stock Exchange in 2014 became the largest initial public offering in history at the time, paving the way for a wave of tech listings. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

At the same time, Chinese capital was flowing into global markets. The China Investment Corporation, Beijing’s sovereign wealth fund, ploughed a combined US$8 billion into Blackstone and Morgan Stanley in 2007 alone, opening another channel of engagement between Wall Street and Beijing.

“The relationship was two-way, mutually beneficial and trusting during those years,” said Kevin Chen Kaifeng, chief economist at Horizon Financial in New York.

“Almost all of those driving factors are now gone,” he added, citing the slowdown in Chinese listings in US markets, Wall Street’s exit from major stakes in Chinese state-owned banks, and declining Chinese investment in the US.

Regulators on both sides have added friction.

Nasdaq’s tighter rules have piled pressure on Chinese issuers already facing strict US audit scrutiny, while Beijing requires mainland firms to clear rigorous national security and data privacy reviews before listing abroad.

Only two mainland Chinese companies completed US debuts in the first half of the year, raising a combined US$59.5 million – the weakest half-year showing in five years in terms of both deal count and proceeds, according to a June report by accounting firm EY.

Chinese authorities have also tightened controls on cross-border capital flows by cracking down on unauthorised offshore brokerages, expanding outbound investment rules to individual residents, and applying a 20 per cent tax on offshore family trusts and insurance structures.

“The two-way streets of deals dried up on both ends,” Chen said.

Wall Street’s leverage has waned in another way.

Marquis said its traditional role as an advocate for market access had also lost much of its currency. Banks once lobbied heavily for policies that kept the pipeline of China deals open, but with Washington’s bipartisan hawkish turn on China, that advocacy carried far less weight than it once did, he said.

I don’t foresee future ‘old friend of China’ roles for Wall Street bankers

Christopher Marquis, Cambridge Judge Business School

During the 2018 US-China trade war, top Wall Street executives – traditionally Beijing’s strongest allies in Washington – attempted to leverage their political access to broker a truce, only to find their lobbying efforts powerless in the face of US President Donald Trump’s tariff and export ban agenda.

“No amount of Goldman or Blackstone advocacy can soften export controls or investment restrictions,” Marquis said. “Wall Street can no longer deliver its half of the bargain.”

The retreat also reflected a shift in Beijing’s own financial priorities, analysts said.

Today, Beijing is pursuing national self-sufficiency to insulate its economy from geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions and the risk of decoupling from the United States and its allies, with technology innovation as a central priority.

China’s top leadership has repeatedly stressed that finance should “serve the real economy”, part of a stated ambition – formalised in this year’s five-year plan – to build China into a “financial powerhouse” on its own terms. The policy is explicitly distanced from the profit-driven model long associated with Wall Street.

Finance had been defined “as an arm of state power rather than a sector to be developed with foreign help”, Marquis said.

Yet the market has not shut. At least seven foreign firms, including Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase, now wholly own mainland securities brokerages after Beijing removed foreign-ownership caps in 2020.

A high-profile business delegation – including Schwarzman, BlackRock’s Larry Fink, Goldman’s David Solomon, and Citi’s Jane Fraser – accompanied Trump on a state visit to Beijing in mid-May, where President Xi Jinping assured executives that China would expand access for foreign capital.

While some financiers continued to maintain strong links with China, analysts said those individual relationships were unlikely to restore Wall Street’s former role.

“I don’t foresee future ‘old friend of China’ roles for Wall Street bankers,” Marquis said. “There may still be a legitimate, narrower commercial role … but they should treat access for what it is: conditional and transactional.”

Chen struck a more hopeful note, arguing the bridge could be rebuilt if China reopens its financial markets further to foreign institutions and Chinese investment in the US recovers.

“The future depends on whether China can open up institutions, and revamp Chinese investments in the US,” he said. “If this happens, the future of the Wall Street bridge is bright.”

item.title: [SCMP] US economist Barry Eichengreen on reality of de-dollarisation and next currency reshuffle
item.description:
Barry Eichengreen is a leading American economist and one of the world’s foremost experts on international monetary systems. He is a professor of economics and political science at the University of California, Berkeley, where he has taught since 1987. He served as a senior policy adviser at the International Monetary Fund in 1997-98.

Here, he discusses why today’s “de-dollarisation” talk is different from past episodes, how close the world is to a reshuffling of the international monetary system, and what it will really take for the yuan to close the gap.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Barry Eichengreen is a leading American economist and one of the world’s foremost experts on international monetary systems. He is a professor of economics and political science at the University of California, Berkeley, where he has taught since 1987. He served as a senior policy adviser at the International Monetary Fund in 1997-98.

Here, he discusses why today’s “de-dollarisation” talk is different from past episodes, how close the world is to a reshuffling of the international monetary system, and what it will really take for the yuan to close the gap.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

Since last year, discussions about “de-dollarisation” have resurfaced with renewed intensity. In your view, how much of this reflects a genuine structural shift? And what, if anything, makes the current moment different from previous episodes of dollar scepticism?

My view is that a genuine structural shift is finally getting under way against the backdrop of some long-standing concerns about the US dollar – for example, concerns about the high level of public debt in the United States and whether the growth of the debt is sustainable or not.

If there are chronic debt problems, will they have negative implications for the stability of the dollar and the value of foreign central banks’ holdings of US Treasury securities? Those concerns are long-standing, and people have been pointing to them when asking whether the era of dollar dominance may be coming to a close – they have been pointing to them for a long time.

What is new and different, however, are two sets of questions that we did not use to ask about the United States and the dollar, but everyone is asking now.

First, the strength of US political institutions. The dollar’s stability and confidence in the greenback rest fundamentally on the rule of law, separation of powers, the independence of the central bank and the control of corruption.

People are beginning to ask whether those institutional arrangements are more fragile than previously assumed. This has begun to undermine the feeling of security among foreign central banks, governments and other investors holding financial portfolios heavy in dollars.

Second, new questions are being asked about US geopolitical alliances. We know from history that central banks, governments and others prefer to hold and use the currencies of their alliance partners, because those partners are viewed as reliable stewards of their reserve holdings. If one is in an alliance with the United States, moreover, holding and using US dollars is a show of good faith in the country.

However, US President Donald Trump has raised questions about the continued commitment of the United States to Nato and to its other security arrangements. That has led the Europeans and others to ask: Do we really want to be so reliant on the US and the dollar in this geopolitically uncertain world, or should we look to alternatives, including relying more on our own currency – the euro, in the European case?

So, I think questions about both US alliances and the strength of US institutions are new and different, and they imply that the prospects for the dollar may be different going forward as well.

It will take years, maybe even decades, for China to close that gap with the United States and the dollar – unless the US shoots itself in the foot

Some argue that the US dollar-centred monetary order that emerged after Bretton Woods may be nearing its end, giving way to a more multipolar system. Do you share that view? And what role do you expect the yuan to play in whatever comes next?

I have long shared that view. In 2011 – prematurely, perhaps – I published a book called Exorbitant Privilege about the rise and fall of the dollar.

My forecast then was that we would be moving gradually towards a more multipolar monetary and financial system, less centred on the dollar – a more multipolar monetary system that better matched our more multipolar global economy. We have moved in that direction as predicted, but more slowly than I expected.

The persistence of dollar dominance is very strong because so many banks, firms and governments use dollars, which creates network effects that lock in the use of the dollar.

So, I’ve been surprised in the last 15 years that we haven’t moved towards that multipolar system more rapidly. But that movement may now accelerate.

I think China’s currency will, over time, come to play a more consequential global role. But the important point to emphasise is that the yuan is starting out very, very far behind the dollar.

Hence it will take years, maybe even decades, for China to close that gap with the United States and the dollar – unless the US shoots itself in the foot and confidence in the dollar is abruptly lost.

We have seen progress in the yuan’s international use, from broader participation in China’s payment systems to growing panda bond issuance. Do you believe China is now in a particularly important window for advancing yuan internationalisation? How would you characterise the recent progress?

The US-Iran war is affording China additional opportunities to increase the use of its currency in global oil and gas trade, and to do more settlements with the energy exporters from the Middle East in its own currency.

And now, those energy exporters are likely happy to take yuan in payment. They can use those yuan to buy the services of Chinese construction companies and Chinese exports of solar panels, batteries, electronics and other advanced technologies.

The war in the [Persian] Gulf has, I think, accelerated the tendency for other central banks and governments to look for alternatives to the dollar, and in this way created a window for China.

Starting from ground zero 15 years ago, China has made impressive progress. But you have to put that in context, where the dollar still accounts for nearly 60 per cent of the foreign exchange reserves of central banks around the world, and the yuan accounts for 2 per cent.

And one sees the same thing along other dimensions, such as turnover in global foreign exchange markets, where the dollar is 10 times as important as the yuan.

I think China has been making rapid progress, for example, in transactions through China’s Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS). Those transactions had been growing at a 30 or 40 per cent annual rate – really fast, starting from basically nothing 10 years ago.

But that growth slowed sharply in 2025. This slowdown suggests that there still are important obstacles to the yuan’s internationalisation. So I would say: impressive progress, but still, the dollar remains in a different league than China’s currency.

China has developed the requisite financial and technological infrastructure. China is, in a way, ahead of the United States in terms of the digital financial revolution. But it has to create confidence among bankers that the markets and platforms on which the yuan can be traded constitute a safe, secure and reliable way to make payments. Creating confidence in a new, novel payments platform takes time. More time will be required.

The US correspondent banking system clears many more transactions per day than CIPS does. And it will take, as I said before, probably decades before that gap is closed.

Looking ahead, what do you see as the next steps for yuan internationalisation? Do you believe Beijing ultimately envisions the yuan on par with the US dollar, or as one of several major currencies in a more multipolar world?

China needs to continue to enhance the liquidity of its financial markets. If people are going to make payments using the yuan, they are going to have to hold balances in the currency, so they have the money ready to make those payments.

The kinds of securities that foreigners can hold in China are limited by regulation and capital controls. The availability of financial derivatives to hedge the risk of exchange rate changes – those markets are limited in China.

So China needs to move slowly but surely to liberalise access to those financial markets, increase the liquidity of its markets, and – where markets barely exist, as in the case of derivatives – to build them out.

I want to be clear here: China should move slowly but surely in this direction. It should not move quickly and abruptly, since doing the latter could create financial risks.

Back in 2015, China began to move rapidly to relax its capital controls. Money flowed out of the country, the stock market crashed and the authorities reversed course. This episode was a reminder that slow but steady wins the race, and that moving abruptly is not a good idea.

Regarding how Beijing envisions the path, the answer is not entirely under Beijing’s control. Whether the dollar remains the leading international currency – and for how long – depends first and foremost on Washington.

What Beijing can do is think about what the best Chinese policy is under different scenarios: under the scenario where the dollar remains sound and stable, and banks, governments, and others around the world feel comfortable in holding and using it; or, if there is a crisis of confidence in the dollar caused by the United States itself, how quickly China can ramp up its alternative, namely, own-currency settlement.

Beijing should be doing scenario planning, rather than having a blueprint for what they think will happen next.

In the event of a crisis of confidence in the US dollar, are widely discussed alternatives such as the euro and the yuan truly ready to step in as viable substitutes?

None of the alternatives, including the euro and the yuan, are ready to substitute for the dollar. What they can do is supplement the dollar on the margin. But they lack the scale as international currencies, and they have shortcomings.

In the case of China, it is the lack of access to domestic financial markets and the limited liquidity of those markets. In the case of Europe, it is the absence of a stock of safe and liquid assets for international investors to hold and use. Consequently, neither the euro nor the yuan can replace or substitute for the dollar any time soon.

While on some dimensions, like the use of currencies as reserves by central banks, the dollar has lost some of its global market share, the euro has gained none of that market share. The yuan has gained only about one-quarter of what the dollar has lost. The other three-quarters have been gained by non-traditional reserve currencies: the South Korean won, the Australian dollar, the Canadian dollar, the Danish krone, the Norwegian krone.

So far, you and I have been talking about the currencies of big economies. Traditionally, there has been an association between the widespread international use of a currency and the size of the issuing economy. Big economies engage in more foreign trade and foreign investment, so it makes sense that their currencies would be the dominant units in international transactions.

But we now live in a digital world where it is easier to buy, sell, hold and trade the Australian dollar, the Swedish krona, and so forth. These non-traditional reserve currencies are the currencies of small, open, well-managed, inflation-targeting countries. They are becoming more attractive in international use. They too lack the scale to replace the dollar, but they can help to supplement it on the margin.

What role do you see Hong Kong playing in the next phase of yuan internationalisation? As Beijing builds up Shanghai’s offshore financial capabilities, do you see the two cities as increasingly competitive?

Hong Kong in the next phase will play the same role that it has played in the previous phase – as a kind of sandbox, or pilot scheme, for yuan use, where Chinese authorities experiment with and observe the effects of different financial innovations.

This will continue to be the case. If you believe having markets and financial derivatives is important for the use of China’s currency, those markets will be developed, in part, in Hong Kong. And if they work smoothly there, they will be brought onshore.

Hong Kong now has a stablecoin ordinance and has issued two stablecoin licences to a couple of big banks. We don’t know whether stablecoins will become important going forward. I, for one, doubt that they will. But Hong Kong can be a place where banks and others can experiment with the payments technology provided by stablecoins.

And if that turns out to be important, it’ll be easier for China to catch up, because Hong Kong will already have provided evidence about how that new payments technology works, how it should be regulated, and so forth.

As for the competition between Hong Kong and Shanghai, economists generally think that competition is good. Competition forces banks, regulators and others to step up their game to avoid losing market share. So that is what Hong Kong will have to do.

Hong Kong has anchored its currency to the US dollar for more than four decades. If the world becomes more multipolar over time, do you believe the arrangement will still make sense? How do you see Hong Kong’s role evolving in a less US dollar-centric world?

The dollar peg has served Hong Kong well. It has had more advantages than disadvantages because the global economy has been dollar-dominated. Hong Kong links directly into that because markets for financial instruments denominated in US dollars are so big. This enables Hong Kong banks to act as global banks, because they have a big global market out there that they can service.

If people grow more sceptical about the US dollar and move away from it, the global system will become less dollar-centric. At that point, the advantages to Hong Kong of being linked to the US dollar obviously become less.

Hong Kong authorities ought to quietly engage in the same kind of scenario planning for different outcomes, depending on what kind of policies – stable or unstable – are followed in the US, so they can respond appropriately. But I would emphasise that they should do their scenario planning quietly.

As stablecoins and central bank digital currencies gain traction around the world, do you see them as game-changers that could disrupt the current monetary hierarchy, or will they simply reinforce the existing status quo?

If you look at the long sweep of history, you see that financial and payments technology is always changing. We moved from doing transactions using lumps of gold and silver, to tokens and coins, to bank money and bills of exchange, and so forth.

We are in another one of those periods where financial and payments technology is changing rapidly. An important new technology is blockchain, or distributed ledger technology. I am convinced that distributed ledger technology will be used to make cross-border payments going forward.

The question is: what kind of units run on those new payment rails? Will they be stablecoins on the one hand, or central bank digital currencies and tokenised commercial bank deposits on the other hand? And depending on the answer to that question, in what currency will they be denominated? In US dollars, or something else?

The US has taken a bet on stablecoins. If privately issued stablecoins become the dominant unit that runs on those payment rails, it is likely to cement the international role of the dollar, because 99 per cent of stablecoins are linked to the US dollar. And again, the US has a big head start in going down that road.

On the other hand, both the euro area and China are looking at central bank digital currencies and tokenised commercial bank deposits. If that turns out to be what runs on these new payment rails, it won’t be the dollar but the euro and the yuan that dominate in the future.

So you have to ask, will we be relying more on private digital money, which is what the US is aiming for, or publicly issued and regulated digital money, which is what China and Europe are developing?

The arrow of history points towards public provision of the public good of stable money. In the past, we tended to have lots of private issuers of banknotes and coins. Gradually, governments have taken over that function as a public utility. In effect, they have monopolised it. So if I have to bet on one outcome or another, I would bet on central bank digital currencies and tokenised bank deposits.

Just as a diverse ecosystem is good for planet Earth, a multipolar monetary system would be good for the global economy

Gold has outlasted every major currency in history. As central banks buy gold at the fastest pace in decades, are we witnessing a return of the world’s oldest monetary asset? What role do you see it playing in the future international monetary system?

I do not think gold will play a big role in the future. Central banks that inherited very dollar-heavy reserve portfolios in the past want to diversify. One direction they can diversify towards is by using some of their dollars to buy gold. We’ve seen a little bit of that on the margin.

If you are a country like Russia that is subject to sanctions, then buying gold is a way of protecting your reserves from being frozen by foreign authorities. You can buy gold, bring it home and vault it in St Petersburg or Moscow. We’ve seen examples of that kind of behaviour in the last decade and a half.

But it is important to note, number one: all the gold purchases that we’ve seen in the last 15 years have been by emerging markets that did not inherit a lot of gold from the past. Advanced countries that inherited gold from the Bretton Woods period and the earlier gold standard period have not added to their reserves.

And number two, it is important to note that most of the increase in the share of gold in central bank reserves has been due to the run-up in the price, and not active purchases.

We may see a little bit more of that behaviour, because every global investor wants a commodity play in their portfolio. Holding a little bit of gold is a way for central banks to acquire that exposure and a bit of additional diversification.

Many speak of a “multipolar” monetary system. In practice, how would such a system function? Would it inevitably require greater coordination among major economies, and is meaningful monetary cooperation still possible at a time of growing geopolitical fragmentation?

In practice, a multipolar system would be one in which several currencies play consequential international roles – in which several currencies are used in cross-border payments and are regarded as stable stores of value by international investors. Multiple central banks would act as international lenders and liquidity providers of last resort.

Just as a diverse ecosystem is good for planet Earth, a multipolar monetary system would be good for the global economy. If there were a shortage of liquidity, and one central bank fell down on the job – for instance, if the Federal Reserve were dominated by isolationist governors – then central banks in China and Europe could step up. When foreign central banks needed liquidity, they would turn to Beijing and Frankfurt, as well as New York and Washington.

However, we are in a world now where coordination is difficult to achieve, partly because the current US administration makes it difficult to coordinate – or to use another word, cooperate – smoothly with other governments.

The best we can do is hope that the central banks and governments responsible for these different currencies follow sound and stable policies, so that the exchange rates between their currencies remain relatively stable.

If they each understand that they have some responsibility for the stability and liquidity of the global system, they can act individually to help to stabilise the system.

If the issuers of the currencies that are internationally used all follow sound and stable policies, that would be better than our current dollar-dominated system.

Note, however, that my previous statement had a lot of sentences that began with the word “if”.

Consider, for example, the Federal Reserve and the dollar currency swap lines that it provides to other countries. By and large, it only provides them to friendly governments – countries that are geopolitically aligned with the United States – rather than providing them more widely.

On the other hand, the People’s Bank of China swap lines are very diverse. It provides them to politically aligned countries in Asia, but it also provides them to the Bank of England, the European Central Bank and others. I worry about whether the US model of only providing liquidity to the country’s friends is compatible with global stability.

Looking back through history, are there any precedents for a multipolar monetary system, or are we entering an entirely unprecedented paradigm?

One that is relevant to us today is the gold standard period before 1913, when currencies were linked to gold, but gold was not really used for international transactions. Gold is very heavy and risky to ship internationally, so currencies were used for payments.

The British pound sterling, the French franc, and the German mark – all three of them were widely used for cross-border transactions in that system before 1913. The system worked smoothly because the policies of the issuing central banks and governments were sound and stable.

A very different precedent would be the 1920s and 30s, when both the US dollar and the British pound sterling were used internationally. In the 1920s, the two currencies were equal in importance. But neither the issuing central bank nor government followed sound and stable policies. Both the US and the UK had crises of one sort or another in the early 1930s. There was flight from the two international reserve currencies. As a result, that system worked very poorly.

We have seen multipolar systems before. Whether they work well or poorly depends on the stability of the underlying policies.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘No bandwidth left for the family’: why many Singaporeans want to be child-free
item.description:
As Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong prepares to unveil plans to ease the strain on families during his National Day Rally speech on Sunday, a new survey points to a difficult question behind the city state’s record-low fertility rate: what if a substantial share of residents no longer want children at all?

Nearly one in four Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 surveyed by YouGov in July said they had no children and did not intend to have them in the future.

Zahir Latif and his fiancée are among them.
item.content:encoded:
As Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong prepares to unveil plans to ease the strain on families during his National Day Rally speech on Sunday, a new survey points to a difficult question behind the city state’s record-low fertility rate: what if a substantial share of residents no longer want children at all?

Nearly one in four Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 surveyed by YouGov in July said they had no children and did not intend to have them in the future.

Zahir Latif and his fiancée are among them.

For eight years, the couple have returned to the same question: should they have children? Each time, the conversation has ended in the same place.

They worry about money, time and the fear of losing themselves, Zahir, 42, said. The unstable income that comes with freelance work – he is a content creator and his fiancée is a writer – has also made parenthood feel incompatible with the life they have built.

Taking on a stable 9-to-5 job could mean giving up any semblance of work-life balance, he added.

“Besides money, time is something Singapore struggles to give back to its citizens,” he said. “If you want to get enough sleep, your day is pretty much over in a few hours after work.”

The couple’s decision reflects one of the most striking findings of the survey, based on responses from 496 Singaporean adults aged 18 to 44 collected in July: 23 per cent said they did not currently have children and did not plan to have them in the future. A 2023 YouGov poll found the proportion was 25 per cent among 1,023 respondents aged 18 to 55.

The limits of policy were also evident, with 30 per cent of Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 saying there was nothing the government could do to make them more willing to have children.

Lower-cost preschool and childcare was the policy most likely to encourage parenthood, cited by 35 per cent of respondents in that age group, while improved work-life balance through national initiatives and increased cash incentives were each mentioned by 31 per cent.

The findings showed that giving Singaporeans their time and lives back was as critical as providing financial support, said Vincent Chua, an associate professor of sociology and anthropology at the National University of Singapore.

Singapore’s economic system had made work and raising a family “mutually exclusive” activities, Chua said.

“Modern capitalism demands maximum extraction of labour – not just in terms of hours, but in cognitive focus and emotional energy, and raising a family is an intensive, non-market activity requiring immense emotional and physical bandwidth,” he said.

“In a highly competitive society, there is simply no bandwidth left for the family.”

Zahir said that any scenario they had considered involving children usually meant moving abroad, where cost and time pressures were less intense. “Unless Singapore changes its work culture, no amount of money can change our minds.”

Singapore’s resident total fertility rate fell to a record low of 0.87 in 2025, even after years of state support aimed at making parenthood more affordable and manageable.

Those measures include baby bonus cash gifts, grants and co-matching for children’s savings accounts, healthcare support for newborns, preschool subsidies and lower fee caps at government-supported childcare centres.

In April, Singapore also expanded its shared parental leave scheme from six to 10 weeks, increasing the total government-paid parental leave to 30 weeks for eligible parents.

Officials have repeatedly said the challenge goes beyond money.

In April, a work group chaired by Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office Indranee Rajah was formed to tackle the declining birth rate, with a mandate to review support across marriage and parenthood.

Last Saturday, Indranee told local media that the team had been receiving feedback from Singaporeans, with a full report expected early next year.

“What is clear is that many do aspire to get married and have children,” she said. “But at the same time, they do encounter challenges including the cost of raising children, the need for time with family, caregiving arrangements and housing.”

Prime Minister Wong earlier this month acknowledged the growing barriers faced by those navigating parenthood.

“Across the world, family life is coming under greater strain. Expectations have risen, and parents feel pressured to give their children the best possible start in life. At the same time, many are caring for ageing parents while balancing the demands of work,” he said during his National Day message on August 8.

The government was taking a fresh look at issues such as the cost of raising children, access to affordable childcare and other ways to lighten the load on families, he added.

Wong is expected to speak about the plans in more detail during his National Day Rally speech on Sunday.

Focus on family well-being

Even so, analysts say Singapore’s fertility challenge should not be read as beyond repair, but as one that may require a broader definition of success: making family life more sustainable for those who already have or still want children, rather than relying only on incentives to lift birth numbers.

“I would not call it hopeless,” said Tan Poh Lin, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies, of efforts to raise Singapore’s birth rate. “However, I do view that the demographic transition has now entered a new phase where more simply do not want children regardless of circumstances.”

Singapore was likely to shift its focus to improving family well-being throughout parenthood and expected measures would include enhancements to cash gifts and childcare leave to benefit families with older children, Tan added.

“Apart from more financial and workplace support, what is needed by families is a greater sense of economic security, including access to upskilling opportunities and employment support,” she said. “What is needed is the right environment, crucially a sense of stability and security.”

To have generous family-friendly policies like those in Nordic countries, Chua said society must accept a high-tax social model.

While the Nordic model was enticing, he added that it might not be replicated easily in Singapore due to its work culture.

“Workers who actually utilise such generous leave would likely face career discrimination and employers might simply self-censor and avoid hiring married couples with young children altogether,” he said.

Tax manager Debbie Lin has been wrestling with whether to have a second child. While her heart is set on giving her daughter a sibling, she vividly remembers the sacrifices she had to make for motherhood.

Lin rejoined the workforce in February after putting her decade-long career on pause for two years to focus on raising her daughter. “When I look at peers who are continuously employed, I estimate that I am now around 30 to 40 per cent behind some of them in terms of salary and career progression,” she said.

Companies needed to be encouraged to adopt family-friendly policies, Lin said, to dispel fears prospective parents might have about opportunity costs to their careers.

“A family-friendly policy that employees are afraid to use is not really a family-friendly policy,” she added.

item.title: [SCMP] Sado Island’s cultural renaissance: a Japanese journey from exile to artistic haven
item.description:
Dawn is still several hours away when we arrive at Ogi Port, on Sado Island’s southeast corner. The town is dark and silent as we cast our lines ashore and secure the boat.

As soon as the lines are made, we fall into our bunks, exhausted after a three-day voyage north through the Sea of Japan, or East Sea.

We plan to rest for 24 hours and then carry on towards Hokkaido, Japan’s main northern island, to escape the summer heat and typhoons of the country’s southern waters.
item.content:encoded:
Dawn is still several hours away when we arrive at Ogi Port, on Sado Island’s southeast corner. The town is dark and silent as we cast our lines ashore and secure the boat.

As soon as the lines are made, we fall into our bunks, exhausted after a three-day voyage north through the Sea of Japan, or East Sea.

We plan to rest for 24 hours and then carry on towards Hokkaido, Japan’s main northern island, to escape the summer heat and typhoons of the country’s southern waters.

After several hours of sleep, we walk into the town of Ogi in search of a late breakfast, stopping at Origine, a tiny six-seat restaurant where all is quiet, with no chef or customers in sight.

“These are the croissants I read about in the online reviews,” my partner says, pointing to a tray of flaky pastries. Fresh croissants after days of stodgy on-board meals are too much to pass up, so we sit down and wait, given hope by the fact that the kitchen counter shows signs of recent activity: used mixing bowls and cutting boards, ingredients chopped and ready for the stove.

Fifteen minutes later, just as we are about to leave, the chef steps inside from the street, surprised to see he has customers. Soon, we are drinking fresh coffee and enjoying a French-inspired brunch.

While we eat, we chat with Kaoru Ito, the chef, via translation apps. Sado, he tells us, is going through a renaissance, with tired professionals from Japan’s big cities coming to the island in search of a quieter life.

“It’s a beautiful island with a lot of nature,” he types, describing the mountains, ancient shrines and history of art and culture that drew him to Sado from a previous life in Tokyo and other mainland cities.

“I need to visit my baker to pay for those croissants. He speaks English. Do you want to come along and meet him,” he asks.

We have nowhere else to be, so we pile into Ito’s car and drive to the nearby village of Hamochihongo. There, we meet Marcus Soto, a baker from New York who moved to Japan decades ago. After chatting for a few minutes in his shop, T&M Bread Delivery, Soto asks us what our plans are for the coming days.

“Well, we were planning to leave tomorrow, but …”

“I’m hosting a dinner party in a few days,” says Soto. “You should join.”

And that is how our love affair with Sado begins.

The S-shaped, 855 sq km island (330 square miles), which also resembles the kanji character for “work” (工), if you look at it sideways, holds a complicated and dark place in Japanese history. Although it is only about 30km (19 miles) from the main island of Honshu, it long served as a place of exile for dissidents and political losers. Emperor Juntoku (1197-1242) and Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443), a master of Noh, the classic form of Japanese masked dance theatre, were both banished from Kyoto and sent into exile on Sado.

Another chapter in Sado’s life began in 1601, when gold was discovered in its mountains, which soon became home to Japan’s largest gold mine. The mine closed in 1989 – its tunnels and ivy-covered concrete structures have since become popular tourist sights – but was recently back in the news, when South Korea protested its designation as a Unesco World Heritage site because about 1,500 Koreans were conscripted and forced to work in the mine during World War II.

The story of forced labour has largely been brushed aside in Japan’s telling of the mine’s history, but the stain remains.

Sado has also suffered from the depopulation that has afflicted so much of rural Japan. The island’s population has fallen from 113,000 in 1960 to below 50,000, leaving it littered with abandoned farms and homes, known as akiya (“empty house”).

Despite those challenges, the intellectuals and artists who were exiled to Sado helped it develop a strong cultural identity, which endures. Sado has more Noh stages per capita than anywhere else in Japan, and it is home to a vibrant taiko drumming community, which includes Kodo, a group that tours the world.

Warm and cold ocean currents meet at the island, creating an ecosystem rich in plants from both Hokkaido, in the north, and Okinawa, far to the south. As well as seeds, those currents bring a bounty of marine life, from bonito and yellowtail tuna to squid, creating rich fishing grounds.

On Sado, mountain ridges hem in the Kuninaka Plain, which, during the summer months, is bright green with some of Japan’s highest-quality rice.

Ito and his wife, Sayuri, take a day off from their restaurant to lead us on a tour of the island. They show us the Seisui-ji temple, founded in AD808 and now gently rotting away in a forest of swaying cedar trees. We sip sake at Gakkogura, an unneeded school that has been refurbished into a brewery and cafe that hosts a sake-making course popular with participants from around the world.

That night, Ito invites us to join a summer solstice party at the shrine in Ogi, where we meet more of their friends: writers, actors and entrepreneurs who have brought an urban sense of style and ambition to the rural island.

After months of cruising Japan’s coastlines, from port to port, where we rarely meet the same people twice, we are glad of the social interaction. Few of our new friends speak enough English to carry a conversation, so we again rely on translation apps, our stilted conversations lubricated by sake and laughter.

Soto’s dinner party takes place in a grand old house in Aikawa, a seaside area that was once the administrative centre for the nearby gold and silver mines. Grand old homes here are interspersed with museums and relics of the mines: the decaying, ivy-clad processing plant, alongside a bell tower and a replica of the magistrate’s office, where gold was graded and stored.

Many guests at the party share a similar story – tired of high-stress, career-driven lifestyles in Japan’s big cities, they have come to Sado to become sommeliers, restaurateurs or farmers. Each one, in their own way, is contributing to the magic we feel on the island.

One morning, a week after arriving in Sado for our “24-hour rest stop”, we prepare to cast off our lines to return to sea. Just as we are pushing our boat off the dock, Ito and another friend appear with a giant drum and cymbals. They bang out a traditional taiko farewell and shout goodbyes as we steer our boat out past the sea wall.

“We’ll be back!” we shout across the water.

We spend the summer in Hokkaido, but everything we see and do is held up in comparison with the warmth we felt on the S-shaped island.

Four months later, with Japan’s summer heat having dissipated, we make the return voyage south, our boat seeming to steer itself towards Ogi Port.

This time, we stay with Tsuyoshi Ito (no relation to Kaoru), in an akiya that he bought, together with a large parcel of land, for the equivalent of about HK$300,000 (US$38,256).

Like many rice farmers on the island, Ito uses sustainable farming practices, with fewer pesticides and fertilisers, while relying on a labour-intensive method of hanging the rice on racks in the field to dry under the sun, which enhances its flavour. We pitch in, labouring in terraced fields surrounded by steep green hillsides and hanging the rice stalks up to dry.

We recognise familiar faces at the supermarket and see the same friends at social events. At a noodle-making party hosted by an enthusiastic collector of vintage Japanese noodle machines, we meet more people who are adding to Sado’s creative spirit, including a music composer and a kimchi maker.

Just down the coast from Ogi Port, on a tiny island in a protected bay and accessible only by walking bridge, stands Teijiro Yamamoto’s former villa. Built from driftwood and other timber scraps in 1911 by the first national-level government minister to come from Sado, it had been abandoned and fallen into disrepair until a few years ago. Refurbished by volunteers, it now hosts small cultural events and parties.

We visited the structure on our first visit, and met the people who were lovingly restoring it. On this trip, friends invite us to the villa for a moon-rising party, to celebrate October’s full harvest moon.

The simple house, with its twisted driftwood beams and raw-wood finish, has panels that open to sweeping views of the sea and surrounding forest. About a dozen of us sit on tatami mats, sipping tea, bathed in moonlight. Everyone speaks in whispers, an eye kept on the slow rise of the silvery orb.

The next morning, we once again untie our mooring lines and sail out of the harbour. This departure feels more final, as our travel plans will steadily take us further away from Sado in the coming months. We wonder if we’ll ever see our new friends again.

Ten months later, we are sailing through Setonaikai, the inland sea at the heart of Japan. We are far from Sado, but it is still on our minds. Our calendar reminds us that in a few weeks, the island will be flooded with visitors for the Earth Celebration, an annual three-day taiko drumming event.

We don’t have time to sail across for the festival so we moor our boat in a marina in Wakayama, rent a car, book ferry passage and go online to buy some of the last festival tickets available, then message our friends to tell them we are on our way.

It’s a 600km (373 miles) drive across Honshu and a three-hour ferry journey from Joetsu, but we make it back to Sado Island to find the normally quiet Ogi Port buzzing with festival energy and thudding to the beat of drums.

Sado’s guest houses are unable to cope with the influx, so visitors pitch tents in the lively festival camping area and we hop between friends’ homes, spending one night sleeping on the floor of a restaurant when a vacant room cannot be found.

A food and crafts market wraps around the harbour and small troupes of drummers and dancers, dressed in masks and colourful costumes, perform in the narrow streets during the day, cheered on by shoppers and fuelled by sake offered by business owners as they pass. Elsewhere, groups take to small stages erected around Ogi Port.

Each night, between 10 and 15 members of Kodo take to the main, harbourfront stage, accompanied by other percussionists from around the globe.

In between concerts, we see Sado from a different perspective, exploring the beaches and rocky shorelines by car, admiring weathered old farmhouses overlooking bright green rice fields.

Four days later, we awake to find the main stage being dismantled and a long queue of cars waiting to board the ferry back to the mainland. Despite the strong sense of island isolation, one could catch the first ferry of the day from Sado to Niigata city and then jump on the Shinkansen to be in Tokyo in time for an early lunch.

Once again, it is time for us to say goodbye to the island.

“You might as well just buy an akiya on Sado; you’re here often enough!” one of our friends jokes as they hug us another farewell.

It is just the kind of idea that will keep Sado alive in our dreams.

This year’s Earth Celebration takes place from August 21 to 23. Tickets cost between 17,000 yen (HK$850/US$108) and 21,000 yen, and are available here

item.title: [SCMP] US critical minerals proposals to Brazil go unanswered as China looms
item.description:
Brazil has not answered two American proposals to formalise cooperation on critical minerals, a senior US diplomat said at Latin America’s largest mining fair, leaving Washington without a bilateral deal as it races to build rare earth supply chains outside China.

Matthew Lowe, economic counsellor at the US embassy in Brasilia, said Washington invited Brazil years ago to join the Minerals Security Partnership, a US-led grouping that coordinates investment in mineral supply chains, but never received a response.

A draft framework agreement sent in February also went unanswered.
item.content:encoded:
Brazil has not answered two American proposals to formalise cooperation on critical minerals, a senior US diplomat said at Latin America’s largest mining fair, leaving Washington without a bilateral deal as it races to build rare earth supply chains outside China.

Matthew Lowe, economic counsellor at the US embassy in Brasilia, said Washington invited Brazil years ago to join the Minerals Security Partnership, a US-led grouping that coordinates investment in mineral supply chains, but never received a response.

A draft framework agreement sent in February also went unanswered.

“We’ll probably have to wait till the election, no matter what happens,” Lowe told the audience in Belo Horizonte on Tuesday, referring to Brazil’s presidential vote in October.

Lowe was speaking at Exposibram, the conference run by the Brazilian Mining Institute, alongside officials from France, Canada, Australia and Britain, most of whose governments have signed the kind of agreement Washington cannot get from Brasilia.

The five spent the session describing how they intend to loosen China’s grip on mineral processing without once naming China.

Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earths after China, a resource base that brought the five to a fair in the Brazilian interior.

Rare earths are a group of 17 metals that are common in the ground and difficult to separate from one another, and they sit inside the wider category of critical minerals that also covers lithium, nickel and cobalt.

Lowe came closest to naming China when he turned to separation, the chemical step that splits mined ore into the individual metals used to make magnets, and where China does close to 90 per cent of the world’s work.

“A lot of us are developing the technology from scratch because it’s controlled by the one country that has really been doing rare earths, and that’s a joint problem that we all share,” he said.

Benjamin Gallezot, France’s interministerial delegate for strategic minerals, said the choke point lies in refining rather than in mining, and described a market shaped by “some dominance of some country or some restriction”.

Asked whether building that capacity outside China is realistic, he said Brazil had the energy, the workforce and the permitting to do it. “There is nothing magic about processing,” Gallezot said.

USA Rare Earth expects to complete a US$2.8 billion takeover of the Brazilian miner Serra Verde within days, once its own shareholders vote on Friday.

On Monday it finished raising US$1.55 billion for a company set up by US government agencies and private investors, which will buy the whole of the mine’s output for 15 years at guaranteed minimum prices.

Serra Verde runs the Pela Ema mine in the central state of Goias, which entered production in 2024, and is the only operation outside Asia producing all four of the rare earths that go into permanent magnets.

Those magnets sit inside electric car motors, wind turbines, drones and guided weapons, and no substitute performs as well.

Pela Ema also yields dysprosium and terbium, the two heavier elements that stop a magnet losing its strength when it gets hot and which most Western projects cannot produce at all.

The geology explains the difference, because the metals there sit loosely in soft clay near the surface rather than locked inside hard rock, the same formation that underpins southern China’s dominance in the heavier elements.

Beijing put USA Rare Earth on its export control list on June 22, alongside MP Materials and eight other American firms, barring Chinese companies from selling them equipment with both civilian and military uses. China called the move retaliation for Washington’s expansion of its own list of Chinese firms it accuses of military links.

For all that, the mine at the centre of the deal still depends on China, because Serra Verde had committed Pela Ema’s output to Chinese processors under 10-year contracts.

It renegotiated last December and cut almost eight years off the term, but the half-finished product is still shipped to China to be separated into individual metals.

Left-wing deputies have asked the Brazilian courts to annul the sale, which the country’s antitrust authority cleared this month.

The US embassy has meanwhile pursued agreements at state level, signing a memorandum with Goias in March that Lowe said “became a bit of an issue” because critics questioned whether a governor may strike mineral deals with a foreign power. It hopes to try again elsewhere once the election is over, he said.

Lowe also criticised the bill now before the Brazilian Senate, which would let a new presidential council and the mining regulator approve or block changes in the control of companies holding mineral rights.

“That’s fine as long as it’s apolitical and predictable, but it cannot be done in a way that is susceptible to a change every four years with every new government,” he said. The bill passed the lower house in May and is on the agenda for the last sitting week before voting begins in October.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth term, said last week that the Senate would advance the law to defend the national interest.

“We will not allow anyone from outside to come here and exploit our mineral resources, because we want their processing and transformation to happen here,” Lula said.

Carlos Eduardo Braga Filho, who runs Brazilian operations for the cobalt and nickel processor Jervois, made the case for keeping processing in the country at a panel across the hall the same afternoon.

“You can’t take a mine to another country, but processing you can. So why do it here? You have to create value, you have to be competitive,” Braga Filho said, speaking in Portuguese.

He then named China directly, something none of the five diplomats across the hall had done.

“I want to have rare earths here, but I want to have rare earths to sell to China. We may end up deciding yes, but that is not the path we have understood to be the best,” he said.

His own plant shows how far that ambition sits from the ore, because the refinery Jervois is restarting in Sao Paulo will run on imported raw material when it opens next year with a capacity of about 12,000 tonnes of nickel a year. Almost all the nickel Brazil digs up is the grade that goes into stainless steel rather than the grade batteries and specialist alloys need.

Flavio Moraes da Mota of the state development bank BNDES said it is backing 12 critical minerals projects worth 35 billion reais (US$6.8 billion) in rare earths, nickel and lithium.

Chinese companies had filed no rare earth exploration applications of their own in Brazil as of June, according to an analysis of regulator records by the Associated Press and Reporter Brasil. China Nonferrous Metal Mining bought the tin producer Mineracao Taboca in 2024 and has said it will study the rare earth potential of its Amazon operation.

item.title: [SCMP] In a small Virginia town, distrust of Big Tech hampers Trump’s AI push
item.description:
The front page of the Danville Register & Bee, a local newspaper in southern Virginia with a circulation of fewer than 4,000, carried an unusual headline.

“LEADER: CHINA BEHIND THE MISCONCEPTIONS”, it read, above a photograph of two homes dwarfed by a data centre behind.

The leader in question was Vic Ingram, chair of the Danville-Pittsylvania Regional Industrial Facility Authority (RIFA), a local body jointly established by the city of Danville and neighbouring Pittsylvania County to promote economic development in one of the poorest parts of the state.
item.content:encoded:
The front page of the Danville Register & Bee, a local newspaper in southern Virginia with a circulation of fewer than 4,000, carried an unusual headline.

“LEADER: CHINA BEHIND THE MISCONCEPTIONS”, it read, above a photograph of two homes dwarfed by a data centre behind.

The leader in question was Vic Ingram, chair of the Danville-Pittsylvania Regional Industrial Facility Authority (RIFA), a local body jointly established by the city of Danville and neighbouring Pittsylvania County to promote economic development in one of the poorest parts of the state.

Ingram had just helped secure what officials described as the biggest economic development project in southern Virginia’s history: a proposed data-centre campus at Berry Hill, a 3,500-acre (1,400-hectare) industrial site about 16 kilometres (10 miles) outside Danville.

But some residents were questioning the project at public meetings and on social media over its environmental impact, power requirements, and the secrecy surrounding its approval.

As the chorus of discontent grew louder, Ingram told the local newspaper in June that much of the “propaganda” online against the area’s first-ever data centres was driven by the “Communist Chinese”.

Other supporters of the project have also invoked China in response to local resistance, portraying the data centres as essential to America’s ability to compete with Beijing in artificial intelligence – an increasingly common refrain of US President Donald Trump as data centres become increasingly unpopular nationwide.

Three-quarters of Americans now oppose having a data centre built near them, up from 42 per cent just a year ago, according to Heatmap.

Danville residents, however, say they do not need China to tell them what to think. Their concerns are rooted in distrust of local officials, a history of broken investment promises and an opaque decision-making process, they say.

The dispute is the latest chapter in Danville’s complicated relationship with China. After the collapse of its textile industry, the city turned to Chinese manufacturers to help revitalise its economy, but that turned into disappointment when those investments failed to materialise.

Now China is being used to justify Danville’s latest economic gamble and discredit those who question it.

A failed China strategy

To understand why the Berry Hill project has generated such intense debate, residents say it is necessary to understand what Danville has lost and its relationship with northern Virginia.

The city used to boast one of the biggest textile plants in the southeastern US, Dan River Mills, which employed over 18,000 people at its peak.

In the 2000s, manufacturing in the industrial town all but disappeared as textile jobs went overseas, mainly to China. When the mill closed in 2006, thousands lost their jobs, throwing the city into a tailspin that has lasted almost two decades.

“We’ve gone through some hard times socially, but when that mill closed, that was the hardest time economically,” said Frank Leist, a local entrepreneur.

Desperate to secure Danville’s next big economic driver, local officials turned to the big economic opportunity at the time: China.

In 2013, officials devised “The China Strategy” – an initiative to recruit Chinese companies to set up manufacturing plants in the area. They paid a Pittsburgh consulting firm US$150,000 as part of the strategy, according to official records.

The initiative seemed to bear fruit at first. City council announcements at the time hailed the arrival of Chinese companies like furniture company GOK International, which pledged to invest US$12.5 million and employ 300 locals.

None of those deals materialised, says Jonathan Travis Hackworth, a local historian. GOK failed to honour a US$1 million grant from a state economic development body. Danville was left to foot the bill.

Further disappointment followed in 2023 when officials sought to make Berry Hill the home of Ford Motor’s new US$3.5 billion battery plant, which licensed its technology from Chinese battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL).

The plant eventually went to Michigan after then-Virginia governor Glenn Youngkin removed Berry Hill from consideration, citing concerns about CATL’s involvement.
